script.text: Part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a presentation by an urban planning student about the role of rivers in cities around the world.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: It's quite hard to think of a city that doesn't have a big river running through it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you think about the major cities in the world, Shanghai, New York, Mumbai, London, they're nearly all built on rivers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When these cities were established hundreds or even thousands of years ago, the rivers were a big part of people's lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 16th century London, the quickest way to get from one part of the city to another was by river.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But people also used the river for fishing, as the water then was relatively clean.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they would also go on boat trips up and down the river just for pleasure, as a relaxing escape from the noise and bustle of the city streets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But as industries developed and populations increased city rivers suffered.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The rising number of people meant there was a huge increase in the amount of sewage discharged into the rivers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rivers had always been used for this purpose.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But when the number of inhabitants was so small, that wasn't such a problem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, as cities grew to over a million inhabitants, the impact on the rivers became more serious.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, other types of pollution increased as factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This got worse over time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As recently as 1957, scientists at London's Natural History Museum declared that the River Thames was dead, in biological terms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As the water was too filthy to support any kind of life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But in recent years, as rivers lost their industrial function, cities have begun to recognize their true value, and to take steps to clean them up.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, the River Thames is now cleaner than it's been for 150 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These days you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale, which had got lost and swam up the river from the sea by mistake.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Unfortunately they didn't succeed, but the problem was disorientation rather than the quality of the water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, all around the world Riverside areas are now seen as prime sites for development.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Warehouses that were once used for storing goods are now being converted into expensive restaurants, and also into apartments with river views, which are in great demand and sell for astronomical prices.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Los Angeles on the west coast of the USA, an architect has plans to revitalize the banks of the river.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And to make a park there, which can provide facilities for sports, as well as a natural environment for relaxing in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's also hoped that the Riverside can be used for other purposes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's been proposed that facilities could be provided for displaying projects related to various kinds of art that have been produced by local people, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the city of Paris, during the summer months of July and August, all the traffic is banned from the roads by the sides of the river, and the banks are transformed into beaches where people can relax in deck chairs under potted palm trees, sunbathe, or buy a drink or a snack while enjoying the view.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But to make the most of our rivers in our increasingly crowded cities, we need to allow them to regain their original purpose, and be used as a means of transport.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Reclaiming our streets from cars and lorries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To do this, we'll have to shift more traffic back to the river, but this time cleanly and silently.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Making the most of modern technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Already, more than 2 billion passengers use the ferry to travel in cities around the world, like Istanbul, San Francisco, and New York.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these numbers are set to rise further, admittedly it's not a fast way of traveling, but neither is a car when it's stuck in traffic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, passenger traffic on roads might decrease as more people start working from home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But another recent development, the huge rise in online shopping, has meant that another form of urban traffic just keeps on growing, and that's deliveries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Trucks and vans in the city pollute and double park while dropping off parcels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Imagine using the immense capacity of shipping to take these trucks off the road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One freight barge can replace 44 large trucks, uses far less energy, and causes less pollution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When the barge docks at the Riverside the parcels could be taken the last few kilometers to their final destination on cargo bikes, electric ones of course.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is already happening in the Dutch city of Amsterdam.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in future, the final stage could even be carried out by drone, although at present this isn't allowed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Wouldn't it be great to unblock our city centers in this way?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Looking further ahead...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1.

script.text: You will hear a woman who is caring for her elderly mother talking to a friend.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: It's really good to see you, Tom.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Since I had to give up work, I feel I'm losing touch with my friends and colleagues.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: We really miss you in the office.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: We were all so sorry you had to leave.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: But you must be relieved to have more time to look after your mother.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: How is she?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Well, she's very cheerful, but she needs a lot of help.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Have you tried to get any support from the local council?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: No, I didn't know I could.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Yes, they offer different kinds of practical support.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: They realize that carers sometimes need time for all the other responsibilities they have apart from the person they're caring for, and also that they sometimes need a break.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: uh Absolutely.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Ok, so tell me more.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: How do I go about getting this support?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Well, you'd have to have an assessment of your mother's needs.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That means someone would come round and talk to you about the situation and what you need.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: So for a start, they'd want to know the amount of time you spend looking after your mother every day.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Then they'll probably ask you what sorts of tasks you do for your mother during the day.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Things like if she needs help with getting dressed, for example.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Right, I help her with that, and also I help her get into the shower in the morning.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Yes, that sort of thing.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: They'll probably ask you if you do the shopping for her, and help her at meal times, and whether she can cope using money.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, that's becoming a bit of a problem.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: She used to be very good at it, but uh not anymore.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And be ready to tell them about anything you find particularly difficult about caring for your mother.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: So recently, I've noticed she started to have quite bad problems with her memory.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: If I wasn't there, I think she'd forget to eat for example, and often she doesn't seem quite sure what day it is.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Yes, tell them about that.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And are there any physical difficulties you have caring for her?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Lifting her for example?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, she's quite heavy, and I'm afraid of hurting my back.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: I'd be in real trouble if that happened.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: They can give you advice about that, and also about how to avoid the possibility of your mom having a fall.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: So once they've done this assessment, if I'm eligible, uh what happens next?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Well, they might support you financially, so they might help you with transport costs, like if you have to get a taxi to take your mother for an appointment for example.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I usually drive her myself, actually.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: So could I claim for the petrol?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: You could, and you can claim for the insurance too.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Oh, right.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: And if you need help with the housework, they can arrange for someone to come along once or twice a week.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And one other thing, I hope you don't mind me saying this, but it's important you look after yourself, and it seems to me you're under quite a bit of stress.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I am, yes.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Well tell the council, because they may be able to give you some advice on how to minimize it.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Though, actually, I feel so much better having talked to you.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: I'll get in touch with the council straight away.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Now, shall we go for coffee or some?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: That is the end of part 1.

script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a man who works for Elmleigh Town Council talking to some people who want to join the small town's volunteer scheme.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: I'm Steve Wainwright from Elmleigh Town Council, and I organize the town's volunteer scheme.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: I'm delighted you're all interested in joining the scheme.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Our volunteers help to create a sense of community among the many people who live in our historic town of Elmleigh, and make residents and visitors feel welcome at local events.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: At first, I'll mention just a few of the activities that volunteers carry out.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: One is to walk around the town center streets wearing our volunteer T-shirt.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Tourists often ask how to get to a particular shop, and they might also be grateful for recommendations about what to visit.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The town holds a large number of concerts each year, and part of the volunteers' role is to get everyone in the audience to the right place as smoothly as possible.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: You'd be surprised how many people buy tickets then don't check them, and head for the wrong section of the hall.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Volunteers may get involved with community groups.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Such as sports clubs or gardeners' associations, here the volunteers talk about how groups can help each other.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: For instance, a writing group might want to travel to another town to hear a talk by a well known author, but may not know that another club has a coach they could travel in.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The town produces a monthly magazine, and anyone who lives in the town can send in articles.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: It's free to residents, and is paid for by local businesses.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: That's the responsibility of the council's advertising department.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: We depend on volunteers though, to find out what people think of events they've attended, and any suggestions they have for the future.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The volunteers then send a summary to the editors.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: There are a number of clubs for retired people, and every year, the council arranges lunch for all the members.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The volunteers welcome the guests.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: And when everyone's sitting down and relaxing after the meal, some volunteers put on a show, usually around half an hour of songs and short plays.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The club members really welcome the chance to chat to the volunteers at these events.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The town council has a website of course, and volunteers are asked to help by making sure residents know about it.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: It's updated every day with information about future activities.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: And we want as many people as possible to use it.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Ok, now you know some of the things our volunteers do.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: I'll go on to some practical matters.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: As you probably know, the town arranges three major festivals every year, and they all depend on a large number of volunteers.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: The Book Festival lasts three days.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: And uses several venues, which all need volunteers.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: More are needed for the music festival, because that lasts a whole week, and even more help is required for the science festival.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Even though it's only two days long, it involves quite a lot of venues though.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: It's a good idea to help at the festival you're most interested in, because you can attend most of the events for free.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: We try to use volunteers who are flexible though, because some festival events are held outdoors, and the weather may affect the size of the audience, and even whether the event can take place.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: So there can be changes at short notice.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: What's essential though, is being able to get on well with other people, and also to deal with someone who's behaving badly.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: As occasionally happens.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Our plan is to get you all working in September, after a week's training starting on the 2nd.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: So we'll be timetabling you for duties the following week from the 9th onward.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Later, in the week beginning September 23rd, uh we have a chat with each of you to find out how you feel about being a volunteer, and what extra support you need.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: As a thank you to the volunteers, we arrange an annual event.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: In recent years, we've had a party in the town hall, and last year, a barbecue in Chamber Park.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Our forthcoming event is a trip along the canal from here to Dewhurst and back.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: It's on Saturday, September the 28th, and if you'd like to attend, you can sign up once you start work.
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: Now, this is the volunteers' T-shirt...
script.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Colin, I'm really struggling to think of a topic for our human geography assignment.

script.text: Suppose so, how about health?

script.text: I didn't get much out of that.

script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah, I hardly took any notes.

script.text: It didn't seem worth it.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Me neither.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: We could focus on poverty, that's something that's a global problem.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: The trouble is, Doctor Lee was saying, that you have to be careful with some of the figures relating to poverty - they're sometimes deliberately manipulated.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: You mean the information gets changed for political reasons?
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: That sort of thing, yes.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So what are we gonna do our assignment on?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I'll tell you what, one of the possibilities we haven't discussed is urbanization, and now over half the world's population lives in cities.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: That's really important.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Ok, good idea, rosie.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Let's do that.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I love living in a big city, but of course there are problems.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Things like theft and robbery.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yes, but where I come from that's linked to another more serious issue, which is that a lot of people don't have jobs.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: That's getting worse and worse, and we also still have quite a lot of people who are homeless, though that's not quite so bad as it was.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: It'd be nice to talk about some positive developments, uh like some of the new developments on the outskirts of cities.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yeah, they've opened some massive new shopping centers outside my city.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah, the same with mine.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: But it's meant a lot of the shops in the city center are closing down, but the outskirts are ideal for buildings that need a lot of space, like for conferences.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: They've opened a couple of big ones.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yes, we've got some too.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: It'd be nicer to have more facilities for things like football too, but that's not happening where I live.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Same in my area.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: We could include something about developing disused industrial sites.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: It seems like a good idea, because you're not doing any harm to the natural environment.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah, but aren't the buildings architecturally significant?
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Not really.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: And what people forget is that they often used quite dangerous materials, chemicals and things, which haven't been properly cleared away, so the whole site has to be made safe.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Hmm, that can't be cheap.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: And I bet it's often not budgeted for.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: You're right.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Have you read about Masdar City?
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: In Abu Dhabi?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yes, it was designed to be a green city, wasn't it?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: That might be a good example of a city which set out to depend entirely on renewable energy.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yes, we should say something about that.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: It was designed to be totally pedestrianized too, wasn't it?
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: With the transport underground.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yes, and they had big plans for recycling to reduce waste to the lowest possible level.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: But let's stick to talking about power sources.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Then there's that ecotown in England, Greenhill Abbots.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: It set out to conform to the usual principles, sustainability and so on.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: A lot of people were against it at first.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: They said the plans were unrealistic.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I'm not sure how far they've got with it.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: um I'll check.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Right, so it looks as if we have a sort of plan, and we can work from that.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: That is the end of part 3.

script.text: You will hear part of a food science lecture on fashions in food.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: There are trends in food, much as there are trends in clothing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Interest in food fashions has risen rapidly since the birth of the smartphone when people first began taking photos of their food and instantly sharing them with their friends.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The food industry in the UK in particular is obsessed with finding and exploiting the next big food trend.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Marketers aim to create a huge demand for a food item which was previously unknown or not needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the most effective ways of promoting a new food product is by using social media influencers as brand ambassadors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In return for free samples, many influencers will post content about a product.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although there are influencers with hundreds of thousands of followers who can command large fees for their services.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Companies which sell vegan produce were pioneers in being able to increase sales really quickly in this way.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For a food item to become really popular, it has to be readily available.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So supermarkets have a role to play in creating a new food trend.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They have dedicated teams closely following which new products or ingredients are trending on social media, and are particularly interested in what well known chefs are putting on their menus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd like to look at a few examples of marketing campaigns which were really successful in launching a new fashion trend.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Starting in the 1990s with the avocado.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A British PR company was hired to raise its profile and stimulate demand.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They paid for a group of journalists to travel out to South Africa to meet avocado farmers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Articles written following this visit helped to educate the British public about the avocado.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which at this time was certainly not the daily staple it's since become.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Advertisements were designed to promote the avocado as a superfood, rich in nutrients, and therefore beneficial for health.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Avocados became hugely fashionable, and within a few years, UK avocado sales had grown from 13 million pounds annually.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To around 150 million, making it one of the most successful fresh produce campaigns in UK history.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Oat milk is a recent example of a new product which became fashionable very quickly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, there are many brands available.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But one company which had early success was the Swedish brand Oatly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They attracted a lot of attention with a media campaign which used provocation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As a way of getting their message across effectively.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The fact that this campaign aggravated competitors producing milk from dairy cows was seen as a plus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it helped to make oat milk seem cool.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the USA, the brand decided against a big retail launch, in favor of getting the product into coffee chains, which removed the need for a big advertising budget.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This proved far more effective than offering samples in supermarkets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Oat milk had an advantage over other alternative milk products such as almond milk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many consumers prefer it, because it has less of an impact on the environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It requires significantly less water to produce than other alternative milk products, and it also has a relatively low carbon footprint.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Norwegian skrei, a rarely available seasonal fish delicacy, otherwise known as Arctic cod, is now found on the menus of Michelin starred restaurants throughout Europe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The demand for skrei has been used by a food marketing agency to build the reputation of Norway's fisheries in general.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Marketing surveys have shown that a significant number of shoppers now associate Norway with excellent seafood.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Food trends can be considered a good thing in some ways, as they can benefit farmers and food producers enormously.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The public can also be encouraged to buy things which are more sustainably produced, but ethical concerns have been raised about the effects a surge in demand can cause.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Quinoa is a classic example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This plant is native to Peru, and when demand peaked some years ago, the price soared.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Making it unaffordable for local people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While the popularity of quinoa has benefited farmers financially, there have been other negative consequences.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As demand grew, farmers began working the land all year round, in order to produce more quinoa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One issue has been that the fertility of the soil decreased dramatically, which could potentially lead to desertification in some areas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another example would be the case of...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning.

script.text: Hi, this is Shelley Mayer.
script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: I'm renting your house on Archwood Avenue.
script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: I'm due to move in next week.
script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: Oh yes, hello, Ms Mayer.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: What can I do for you?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: When I viewed the house, I told you I'll most probably need to rent some furniture - at least until I know whether my temporary work contract is going to be made permanent.
script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: Yes, of course.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I remember.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: And I said I could give you some information about furniture rental companies in the city.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: Well, the biggest company is called Peak Rentals.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I've recommended them to other people, and I've always heard positive reports about them.

script.text: Could you give me an idea of their costs?

script.text: Sure, I actually have one of their brochures here.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It says the monthly price per room starts at $105 and goes up to $239.

script.text: And you said you had some positive feedback about this company.

script.text: Yes. People have mentioned that the furniture from Peak Rentals is more modern than any of the other companies.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: And also, once you place an order, the furniture will be delivered to you in just 1 or 2 days.
script.speaker: MAN

script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

script.text: Right.

script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Oh, I see.

script.text: I probably won't need that.

script.text: There's another company called Larch Furniture.

script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear an archaeologist who is part of a community project to excavate an ancient village, talking to members of the public who are visiting the site.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, I'm Hayden.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: I'm one of the archaeologists investigating the site here at Bidcaster.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: This is the third summer for this community project.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: And most of the people digging here are volunteers.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: I'm a full-time archaeologist for the town council, but I was asked to join the project by NHA,
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: a charity which sets up projects like this up and down the country.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: As you can see, we're next to Bidcaster Castle, which is great, because the owners let us use their facilities.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: So, how did we get to where we are today?
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Many archaeology projects happen when an ancient object is found, and in our case that object was a gold coin.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Coins are often found by people using metal detectors to look for things buried in the ground, or coins are uncovered when wild animals like rabbits have been digging tunnels.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Here, a walker found it on the ground after a rainstorm washed away some of the earth and sand.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: When the story of the gold coin hit the news, Peter Swift, an amateur historian, contacted me to say he believed there had been a village on this site.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Centuries before the castle was built.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Just by chance, the team found some old maps and documents in our library, which showed 500-year-old drawings of ruined buildings on the grassy area between the outer stone walls of the castle and the river.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: We knew then we were onto something.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Over the three summers the team has been here, we found the remains of several buildings, and more broken pots than you can count.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Normally you'd expect to find brooches and other jewelry.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: But we're still waiting to uncover any such items.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: The people who once lived here were skilled at making tools from animal bones, as you'll see when you visit the exhibition.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Besides the discovery of the village, we've also found evidence of human activity on the other side of the river.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: No other houses or huts so far.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: But we can see the borders of an ancient field system.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: At one point we found a long wall and thought it was an ancient palace, but it turned out to be a modern wall.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: This summer's work will end soon, but we'll be back next summer.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: In the meantime, we're putting on a series of guided tours for school groups this autumn.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Oh, and um maybe you saw the TV documentary about our project.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: That suggested the objects we found are going to the town's museum, but we don't know that for sure yet.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: When you enter the site, please make sure you keep to the paths at all times.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: There are a few other things, um the highlights of the site if you like that I want to mention.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Take a look at the map.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Our present location is marked at the bottom.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: This year, we've identified the foundations of an ancient bridge, and it's really exciting today because a team of divers are in the river searching for lost objects.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: To reach the bridge, take the main path ahead of you, go straight on, and keep going till the path bends to the left.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: You'll see a smaller track leading off to the right.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Follow that to take you to the river where the divers are.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: You might be interested to see the rubbish pit.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: This is very near the castle walls in the northwest corner of the site.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: It actually dates to the time of the castle and not the ancient village.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: We found oyster shells and fish bones, and we assumed they were thrown from the castle kitchen above.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: One area we excavated in the first summer uncovered the site of a meeting hall.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: We knew it was an important building, because it had two rows of post holes.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Deep enough to support a large roof.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: It's the largest structure in the central area of the site, next to the current excavation area.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Last year we discovered a fish pond in the ancient village.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Normally these were beside a river.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: The pond here is further away, but it's possible the river has moved slightly.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Anyway, to get there from here, you turn right at the first information board you come to, and follow the path into the trees.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: Before you come out of the trees, you'll see it on your right.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: If you reach the river, you've gone too far.
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: So does anyone have an...
script.speaker: HAYDEN

script.text: That is the end of part 2.

script.text: You will hear two theater studies students, Maya and Finn, discussing their project on theater programs.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So Finn, I've done as much as I can for our project on theater programs.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: How's your research coming along?
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Ok, Maya.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: I didn't know theater programs are called playbills in the USA, till I started looking into the topic.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Even though I struggled to find many useful websites, I'm glad we picked this subject.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: No one else on the course is doing the same as us, although it is one of the research areas of the module convenor.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: That might actually put some people off.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Huh, I suppose so.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Anyway, I hadn't realized there are actually companies specializing in creating theater programs.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Yes, they're quite common nowadays.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Contrary to what many people think, theatres don't hire people to do the programs.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: In fact companies buy the rights to publish programs on the theatre's behalf.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: And then make their money selling advertising space within the program booklet.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: It must be easier for theaters to do it that way.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: I remember reading something about programs in early British theater.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: It said that the cast was always very important.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Yeah, audiences were very familiar with leading actors, and big names would draw huge crowds.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: But I hadn't realized that if the program named a famous actor, that's who the public expected to perform, and if that didn't happen, people accused the theater of breaking their agreement with the audience.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: They would demand refunds, and if they didn't get them, there were riots.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Outrageous. That'd never happen now.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: No, people are too polite, even when they're disappointed if the star of the show misses a performance.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: We should definitely include that information about early audiences in our project.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: I also think it's important to mention that lots of ordinary people at that time were illiterate, so theater programs were of limited value in advertising plays.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: When a company of actors arrived in a town, they'd parade around the streets in their costumes, beating drums and announcing their upcoming performances.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Interesting.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: I couldn't imagine that happening now either.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: There's also an interesting comparison to make between 18th and 19th century programs.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Wasn't it in the 19th century that theater programs started to resemble programs today?
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: And unlike programs from the 18th century, they always used color.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: And there was a greater variety of designs. But personally, I think 18th-century programs were superior, because they told the theater goers so many things, including about the actors.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: And about the writer, the plot, and sometimes the history of the play.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: What should we say about theater programs in the 20th century?
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: I reckon the most important thing is the dramatic change they underwent during World War 2.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: When the government imposed restrictions on the use of paper.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Yeah, but that was only in the UK, in the USA, programs or rather playbills continued to be published in the same format.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Well, here in the UK, programs became merely a single sheet of paper folded to create 4 pages for text.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: What I don't really get is that after the war, they didn't go back to being more than one sheet, or change in any way for over 25 years.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: I know there were paper shortages after the war, but only for 5 or 10 years.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Hmm, strange.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I found a couple too, Maya.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Let's go through and see what we think.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: um Oh, this is an old one, for a play called Ruy Blas.

script.text: Hmm, never heard of that, but the program looks very decorative.
script.speaker: FINN

script.speaker: MAYA

script.speaker: MAYA

script.speaker: MAYA

script.speaker: FINN

script.text: I thought this was a good program to show, not because of the pictures.
script.speaker: FINN

script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Good.

script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: It's for The Tragedy of Jane Shore, and it's said to be the earliest surviving document to have been printed on Australia's first printing press.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Fantastic.
script.speaker: FINN

script.text: Another program to talk about is for the Sailors Festival.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: It comes from the British Library's digitized collection of programs that was started a few years ago.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: It already comprises over 200,000 programs, which is amazing.
script.speaker: MAYA

script.text: Huh, wish I'd known about it while I was doing my research.

script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a design and technology lecturer talking about inclusive design.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: It's only relatively recently that designers have become aware of the need to be inclusive when designing products, but what does that mean exactly?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, it simply means designing products that span economic, social and cultural barriers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It means making sure products are accessible.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So that as many different types of people as possible can use them without any type of adaptation having to be made to the original design.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Inclusive design is often linked with universal design, although they are not quite the same thing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Universal design aims to make products that work for everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that includes considering the needs of people who have cognitive difficulties, which can present quite a challenge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, examples of successful inclusive design can be seen all around us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In workplaces, it is common to see desks which can be adjusted to suit people of different heights, or for wheelchair users.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This still isn't always the case, however, and is one reason why office workers often suffer from back or neck problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll find another example in the public toilets of countless hotels, airports and offices.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Taps that you activate by sensor require no pressing or twisting movements.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are not only more hygienic, they're also easier for people with dexterity or mobility issues.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The tech industry has been criticized in the past for focusing too much on young consumers, but this is changing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many products are now designed with the elderly in mind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, it's well known that vision declines with age, and that we also become worse at distinguishing between similar colors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In particular shades of blue, which is why software designers rarely create interfaces with this color.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Motor skills also decline with age.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And some people have difficulty doing everyday things, like picking up a cup or opening a door.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This can also affect their ability to use a mouse or keyboard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So voice access is now a routine way of making commands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's worth looking at the problems non-inclusive designs cause when not enough consideration is given to a range of users, as it can have a serious impact on people's lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Access is one obvious example, because it has such a huge impact on disabled people's independence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Not being able to access public transport because buses or trains are not wheelchair-friendly means many disabled people can't go out, unless someone goes with them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Safety is another issue, inexplicably, most cars are still crash tested using a dummy based on an average sized male.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This has safety implications for all women, particularly those who are pregnant, as the seat belts worn by the dummy are not adapted to accommodate them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Over the past 100 years, workplaces in the UK have on the whole become considerably safer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Employers are legally required to provide well maintained personal protective equipment or PPE.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Anything from goggles to full body suits, to workers who need it free of charge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But most PPE is designed to fit men.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A recent report found that employers often think that when it comes to female workers, all they need to do to comply with this legal requirement is to buy jackets for example designed for a small man.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The problem with this is that women can be tall and still have much smaller shoulders than the average man.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ill-fitting PPE such as hi-vis jackets vests and body armor can put women at risk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The report found that 95% of women said that their PPE often hampered their work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that this problem was worst in the emergency services, particularly the police.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another problem is related to comfort at work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A very common scenario in offices in summertime is to see women wrapped in blankets or wearing sweaters while the air conditioning is on high.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Meanwhile the men are in shorts and t-shirts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is due to differences in metabolic rates for men and women.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There is a standard setting for air conditioning to be at a temperature of 21 degrees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Designed to suit men, and in most modern offices, it's not possible to turn the air conditioning up or down.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means that many offices which mainly employ women are wasting energy by having the air conditioning set too high.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you can see from the examples I've just mentioned, there are serious consequences for designs which don't consider the needs of all users.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is that is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning and welcome to City Football Club.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd like to give you some useful information about your visit to the stadium today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then we'll start the tour of the areas of the stadium that are open to visitors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I can see lots of children here today, so just to let mums and dads know a few things before we start.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The stadium has lots of stairs, and the players' tunnel is very dark.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Please don't let your children wander off on their own, even for a minute.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't want any accidents or anyone getting frightened.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Cameras are permitted everywhere, and you can take pictures of your child shooting a penalty.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Assistants are helping to organize this, and hopefully the queue won't be too long.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's very hot and sunny out on the pitch today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can get food and drink at the cafe, and I really recommend the healthy lunch boxes for children.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Also in the cafe, children are invited to do a football themed drawing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll pick the best one at the end of the afternoon, so don't forget to put your name and contact details on the back.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That way, if you've left the stadium before then, we'll send your prize, but sadly we can't return drawings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd like to mention some features of the tour.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll start with the three-sixty cinema experience, which has been very popular over the years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then I'll take you to the players' dressing rooms, before going outside to the seating area and the pitch.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I should say if you'd prefer your visit to be self-guided, please collect headphones from the reception, and then you can listen to the pre-recorded information at your own speed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've only just introduced this feature.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And would appreciate your feedback.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're thinking of offering tours in other languages in future, so if you have any thoughts on that, we'd welcome those too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you plan to return another time, you might like to book one of our VIP tours.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've only just started offering these.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they can be booked online.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.text: Now, the stadium you see today was built in 1989, as part of a three-year redevelopment project.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While that project was going on the team had to play its matches at the ground of another club.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Apart from that, the club has been here on this site since 1870.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As some of you may know, that was the start of a really important decade in the history of football in this country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, 1870 was also the year that football teams started to include a player whose role it was to guard the goal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's hard to imagine what the game must have been like without someone in that position, isn't it?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1872 and 73, many other clubs were established, both here and abroad, and the following year, in 1874, referees were allowed to send players off if they committed certain offenses, and also in that year, teams started having to swap ends at half-time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One fact I was interested to discover was that in early football games, the aim was for the scorer to get the ball between two flag posts, and later between sticks joined at the top with a piece of tape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1875, that tape was replaced with the solid crossbar that we're familiar with today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: 1877 saw the founding of further new clubs, and the history books tell us that in the same year, all the clubs decided to set a limit of 90 minutes for each match.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before that, it was a more casual arrangement, and this sometimes caused huge arguments.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And sometimes fights during matches, when one team called the end of the game, and the other team wanted to play on to try and score a winning goal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By 1878 the number of teams in the Football League increased again.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, referees started using whistles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And electric lamps were installed on certain pitches.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was a significant change, as games could then be played in the evenings all year round.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1880, clubs began to charge fans for admission to games, even though players were still amateurs, and had other proper jobs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's hard to imagine in the modern professional game, where top players earn significant sums of money from both playing and commercial activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two education students discussing an assignment on teaching handwriting to children.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: How are you getting on with the assignment on handwriting?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Not too bad.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: You know, I hadn't realized that children benefit in so many ways from learning to write.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It's such an important skill, and yet most people think handwriting is less important than in the past, because people hardly ever write by hand these days.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: And all the evidence suggests children should learn to write by hand before they learn to type, not least because it helps their memory.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That's right, the physical act of writing helps children to remember letters.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That seems pretty obvious when you think about it.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Ha, what's less obvious is how it helps develop their concentration.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: They have to sit still and focus on one thing.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That aspect of handwriting had never occurred to me before.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Hmm, same here.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I'm not sure I understand how it improves children's imagination though.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Well, there was that study which showed that primary age children generated more ideas when they were writing by hand than using a keyboard.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I would have guessed that would be the case.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Hmm, yeah.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I've never associated spatial awareness with handwriting either.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I thought spatial awareness was more to do with knowing where you are in relation to objects or other people.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Hmm, I thought that too.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: But good spatial awareness is essential for writing, because you have to space words correctly.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It's not just fine motor skills that improve through writing, as I'd always assumed.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: hmm Handwriting is so much harder for children with dyspraxia, who have problems coordinating movement.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's good there are lots of things you can do in the classroom to help them.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: They need so much more support with letter formation.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: You need to play lots of games to help them distinguish letter shapes.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Huh, it takes a lot of patience.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I like the idea of using one of those pens that lights up if you press too hard.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That seems like a really simple solution.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, absolutely.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I'm not sure there's much you can do about children with dyspraxia writing very slowly.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's more important to focus on accuracy, and as they get more confident.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I think they eventually speed up.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: One quite simple thing you can do is to use grid paper.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: So they write each letter in a box, and that trains them to space the letters correctly.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Indeed.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That's more important for legibility than trying to get them to write in a straight line.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: For some children, it might be better to teach them to write on a laptop, rather than by hand.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Like children with dyslexia, they often really struggle with handwriting, and some just give up.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yeah, it's not as frustrating for them if they get things wrong on a keyboard, they can be more willing to have a go, but I read that developing fluency isn't any faster.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Did you read that article on the benefits of teaching print rather than cursive handwriting, where the letters are joined up?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, in the past cursive writing was certainly considered more stylish and educated.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: But not anymore.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Teachers' attitudes have changed because it's been proved that cursive is more difficult to learn, especially for children with learning difficulties who find joining up letters really challenging.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I agree.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I was always worried that my poor handwriting affected my exam results, and now research shows that I was right to worry.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I'm sure a lot of students think it's unfair that they're being judged on their handwriting.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Not just their knowledge, marks are definitely affected if examiners can't read the script.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That's why it's always been so important to teach children to write legibly.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Do you think the role of handwriting will change in the future?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: hmm I can't see that changing much.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Touch typing still isn't taught in most schools.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Which is a shame, but maybe that won't be necessary in the future, because people will also be able to write by hand on digital devices.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Anyway.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Teachers understand the value of handwriting.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's a basic life skill.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: True.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: However, the fact is that people are writing by hand less and less and relying on digital devices.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That does cause some problems.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: hmm You mean like notetaking?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: There are lots of apps for that, and for reading historical documents apparently.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: But my mom is shocked by my awful spelling and the fact that my punctuation is really inconsistent.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I think you can put that down to lack of practice.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Ha ha, I expect so.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Personally, I miss writing by hand.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I hardly ever write anything now.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I remember my grandparents had such beautiful handwriting, and it was so individual.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Nobody I know would be able to identify my handwriting now.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's a shame.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I know, I feel the same way.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I used to write a diary by hand.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And now I do that digitally.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It just seems less effort to do it that way.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: hmm So it's not just a problem.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part three.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about the impact of birds of prey on a farming community in Africa.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: We've been looking at different types of conflicts that may arise between wildlife and humans at the boundaries of protected areas, such as national parks and animal sanctuaries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd like to illustrate this by telling you about some research that I've been involved in recently, in the Central African country of Zambia, in the area around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which contains over 300 of the listed birds of Zambia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These include a number of birds of prey such as eagles, hawks and owls that live by hunting and killing other birds and animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, most of the people living in the local communities near to the bird sanctuary are small scale farmers, and these birds of prey provide important social and ecological benefits to them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, a lot of damage can be caused to farmers' crops by rodents such as rats, which would consume the crops as they grow in the fields, as well as after harvesting, if they weren't hunted and killed by the birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the predatory habits of these birds also protect farmers in other ways.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: uh For example, a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And birds of prey have a major role in keeping their populations under control.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Local people have always been aware of these benefits, and for years even before the sanctuary was opened in 1973, the birds played a key role in the culture of the region.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, more recently the sanctuary and its birds have also become increasingly important to the community in economic terms, because at present, after a relatively slow start.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Tourism has become an important source of revenue for them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, although these birds of prey are protected by the government, their numbers are falling.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of these deaths are accidental.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Fatalities occur when birds alight on roads to catch and eat their prey, and are hit by fast-moving traffic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Drivers in Zambia have to take special care at night, as birds may regard the quieter roads as safe places to sleep.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Accidental deaths may also occur if these birds fly close to high voltage power lines, as they may be electrocuted.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a particular danger in the heavy rain which can occur in the region in the months from December to April.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And local farmers also pose a threat to these birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as growing crops, small scale farmers in the area also rear chickens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These provide food for the farmer's families, as well as being an important source of income.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But they're also an easy target for birds of prey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And so farmers may shoot these birds, which is illegal but understandable, or they may poison the birds, which again is illegal and can have negative effects on the ecosystem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So how else can farmers protect their chickens from birds of prey?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some people believe that to prevent the predators from settling near the area where the chickens are kept.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's best to keep this area free from vegetation, but in fact this is counterproductive, as it means the chickens have no cover to hide in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they'll be easier for the birds to see.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another possibility would be to prevent the chickens from going outside at all, and to keep them safe from predators inside a building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But this would cost far too much to be a practical solution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Nearly all the farmers reported that they spent a lot of time and effort trying to frighten off the birds of prey without actually harming them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most of the farmers had at least one dog, and said this was a big help at scaring away the predators.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of the farmers also reported that during the breeding season.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When the chickens were particularly vulnerable, they encouraged their children to watch over the chickens, and to hit pans with a metal spoon, so that the resulting noise would succeed in driving away birds that were trying to seize the young chicks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: None of these methods was 100% effective, so as a result the village people told us that rather than just using one method.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They were forced to use a combination for them to have any effect. And even so, these birds of prey remain a major threat to the chickens' survival and cause considerable economic loss to farmers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So we looked at the possibility of a longer-term solution to...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1, you will hear a teaching assistant calling a country park about a school visit.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 1 to 6.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, Hinchingbrooke Country Park, Sally speaking.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: I'm one of the rangers.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Oh, hello, uh, my name is John Chapman, and I'm a teaching assistant at a local primary school.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I've been asked to arrange a visit to the park for two of our classes.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: OK, what would you like to know?
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Well, I'm new to this area.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: So perhaps you could tell me something about the park first, please.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Altogether the park covers 170 acres.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That's 69 hectares.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There are three main types of habitat, wetland, grassland, and woodland.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The woods are well established and varied.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: With an oak plantation and other areas of mixed species.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: The wetland is quite varied too.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The original farmland was dug up around 40 years ago to extract gravel.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Once this work was completed, the gravel pits filled with water, forming the two large lakes.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There are also several smaller ones.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Ponds and a stream that flows through the park.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: OK, so I suppose with these different habitats, there's quite a variety of wildlife.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: There certainly is.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: A lot of different species of birds and insects, and also animals like deer and rabbits.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And I understand you organize educational visits for school parties.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: We can organize a wide range of activities, and adapt them to suit all ages.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Can you give me some examples of the activities?
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Well, one focus is on science, where we help children to discover and study plants, trees and insects.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: They also collect and analyze data about the things they see.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Uh huh.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Another focus is on geography.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The park is a great environment to learn and practice reading a map.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And using a compass to navigate around the park.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Do you do anything connected with history?
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Yes, we do.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: For instance, the children can explore how the use of the land has changed over time.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Then there's leisure and tourism.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That focuses on your visitors, I would imagine.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Yes, mostly.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The children find out about them, their requirements, the problems they may cause, and how we manage these.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And another subject we cover is music.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Here the children experiment with natural materials to create sounds and explore rhythm and tempo.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That must be fun.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Most children really enjoy it.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And of course, all the activities are educational too.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Learning outside the classroom encourages children to be creative and to explore and discover for themselves.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: I would imagine they get a sense of freedom that might not be a normal part of their lives.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And very often the children discover that they can do things they didn't know they could do.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And they develop new skills.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: This gives them greater self-confidence.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: It sounds great.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: So what about the practical side of it?
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: How much does it cost for a full day visit?
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: We would expect to bring between 30 and 40 children
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: If there are over 30, it costs £4.95 for each child who attends on the day.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: We invoice you afterwards, so you don't pay for children who can't come because of sickness, for example.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There's no charge for leaders and other adults, as many as you want to bring.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That sounds very fair.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Well, thanks for all the information.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I'll need to discuss it with my colleagues, and I hope to get back to you soon to make a booking.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: We'll look forward to hearing from you.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Goodbye.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Goodbye, and thank you.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: That is the end of part 1.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear the chairman of Stanthorpe Twinning Association, which organizes the link between Stanthorpe in England and a town in France.

script.text: It's great to see so many members of the Twinning Association here tonight.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since the twinning link between our two towns, Stanthorpe here in England, and Malatte in France was established, the relationship between the towns has gone from strength to strength.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Last month, 25 members of the association from Stanthorpe spent a weekend in Malatte.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our hosts had arranged a great program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We learned how cheese is produced in the region, and had the chance to taste the products.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The theme park trip had to be cancelled, but we all had a great time on the final boat trip down the river.

script.text: That was the real highlight.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a special year for the association, because it's 25 years since we were founded.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Malatte, they're planning to mark this by building a footbridge in the municipal park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've been discussing what to do here, and we've decided to plant a Poplar tree in the museum gardens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We considered buying a garden seat to put there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the authorities weren't happy with that idea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In terms of fund raising to support our activities, we've done very well.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our pancake evening was well attended and made record profits, and everyone enjoyed the demonstration of French cookery, which was nearly as successful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Numbers for our film show were limited because of the venue, so we're looking for somewhere bigger next year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're looking forward to welcoming our French visitors here next week.

script.text: And I know that many of you here will be hosting individuals or families.

script.text: Don't try to do too much that first evening, as they'll be tired.

script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The weather looks as if it'll be OK, so you might like to plan a barbecue.
