script.text: Then the next morning's market day in town, and that's always a good place to stroll round.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Saturday evening, we'll all meet up at the football club.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Where once again we'll have Toby Sharp and his band performing English and Scottish country songs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Toby will already be well known to many of you, as last year he organized our special quiz night.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And presented the prizes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, on Sunday, we'll be taking our visitors to Farley House.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may not all be familiar with it, so here's a map to help you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can see the car park at the bottom of the map.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's an excellent farm shop in the grounds where our visitors can buy local produce.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's in the old stables, which is the first building you come to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I haven't seen you for a bit, Marie.

script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: It was.

script.speaker: MARIE

script.speaker: MARIE

script.speaker: MARIE

script.text: Right.

script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yes, there's all sorts of possibilities.

script.text: I was reading an article about food trends, predicting how eating habits might change in the next few years.

script.text: That seems so obvious, but the shops are still full of imported foods.

script.text: One thing everyone's aware of is the need for a reduction in unnecessary packaging, but just about everything you buy in supermarkets is still covered in plastic.

script.text: That's right.

script.text: Hmm.

script.text: But people aren't aware of that, it's all kept very quiet.

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: MARIE

script.text: Hmm.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear an archaeology student giving a presentation on an important site in Ireland called the Céide Fields.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about the Céide Fields in the northwest of Ireland, one of the largest Neolithic sites in the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I recently visited this site and observed the work that is currently being done by a team of archaeologists there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The site was first discovered in the 1930s by a local teacher, Patrick Caulfield.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He noticed that when local people were digging in the bog, they were constantly hitting against what seemed to be rows of stones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He realized that these must be walls, and that they must be thousands of years old for them to predate the bog which subsequently grew over them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He wrote to the National Museum in Dublin to ask them to investigate, but no one took him seriously.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It wasn't until 40 years later, when Patrick Caulfield's son Seamus, who had become an archaeologist by then, began to explore further.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He inserted iron probes into the bog, to map the formation of the stones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A traditional method which local people had always used for finding fuel buried in the bog for thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Carbon dating later proved that the site was over 5,000 years old, and was the largest Neolithic site in Ireland.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Thanks to the bog which covers the area, the remains of the settlement at Céide fields, which is over 5,000 years old, are extremely well preserved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A bog is 90% water, its soil so saturated that when the grasses and heathers that grow on its surface die, they don't fully decay, but accumulate in layers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Objects remain so well preserved in these conditions because of the acidity of the peat, and the deficiency of oxygen.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At least 175 days of rain a year are required for this to happen.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This part of Ireland gets an average of 225 days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Neolithic farmers at Céide would have enjoyed several centuries of relative peace and stability.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Neolithic farmers generally lived in larger communities than their predecessors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With a number of houses built around a community building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As they lived in permanent settlements, Neolithic farmers were able to build bigger houses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These weren't round as people often assume, but rectangular, with a small hole in the roof that allowed smoke to escape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is one of many innovations, and indicates that the Neolithic farmers were the first people to cook indoors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another new technology that Neolithic settlers brought to Ireland was pottery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Fragments of Neolithic pots have been found in Céide and elsewhere in Ireland.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The pots were used for many things, as well as for storing food.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Pots were filled with a small amount of fat, and when this was set alight, they served as lamps.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's thought that the Céide fields were mainly used as paddocks for animals to graze in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Evidence from the Céide fields suggests that each plot of land was of a suitable size, to sustain an extended family.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. They may have used a system of rotational grazing in order to prevent overgrazing and to allow for plant recovery and regrowth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This must have been a year-round activity, as no structures have been found which would have been used to shelter animals in the winter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, archaeologists believe that this way of life at Céide ceased abruptly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why was this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, several factors may have contributed to the changing circumstances.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The soil would have become less productive, and led to the abandonment of farming.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The crop rotation system was partly responsible for this, as it would have been very intensive and was not sustainable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there were also climatic pressures too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The farmers at Céide would have enjoyed a relatively dry period, but this began to change, and the conditions became wetter as there was a lot more rain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was these conditions that encouraged the bog to form over the area, which survives today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So now I'd like to show you some...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1, you will hear two friends talking about a guitar group.

script.text: Hi, Coleman.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: How are you?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Good, thanks.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: I wanted to have a chat with you, because our friend Josh told me that you've joined a guitar group.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And it sounds interesting.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I'd really like to learn myself.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Why don't you come along?
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: I'm sure there's room for another person.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: So, who runs the classes?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: He's called a coordinator.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: His name's Gary Mathieson.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Let me note that down.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Gary, how do you spell his surname?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It's MATHIESON.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Right, thanks.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: He's retired actually, but he's a really nice guy.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: And he used to play in a lot of bands.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Thanks.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: So, how long have you been going?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: About a month now.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: And could you play anything before you started?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I knew a few chords, but that's all.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: I'm sure everyone will be better than me.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That's what I thought too.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: When I first spoke to Gary on the phone, he said it was a class for beginners, but I was still worried that everyone would be better than me.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: But we were all equally hopeless.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Oh, that's reassuring.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: So, where do you meet?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, when I joined the group, they were meeting in Gary's home.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: But as the group got bigger, he decided to book a room at the college in town.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: I prefer going there.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: I know that place.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I used to go to tap dancing classes there when I was at secondary school.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I haven't been since though, and I can't remember what road it's in.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Is it Lock Street?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It's just beyond there, at the bottom of New Street, near the city roundabout.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Yes, of course.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: The guitar club is on the first floor, in room T347.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And when do you meet?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Is it at the weekend?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: We meet on Thursdays.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: It used to be 10:30 and that suited me well, but now we meet at 11.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: The class that's in there before us asked if they could have the room for another 30 minutes.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Oh, I see.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, I'd love to come.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That sells all kinds of guitars, violins, and so on.

script.text: I'm sure you'll find something there.

script.text: So, what's a typical lesson like with Gary?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, he always starts by getting us to tune our guitars.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: That takes about 5 minutes.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Uh huh.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Some people have an app they use, but others do it by ear.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Gary goes round and helps them.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: And while he's doing that, he tells us what he's going to do during the lesson.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: First, we usually spend about 10 minutes doing some strumming.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: So, is that using oh, what are they called plectrums?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Ha, no, we just use our thumbs.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Ha, much easier.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Gary reminds us where to put our fingers for each chord, and then we play them together.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Sometimes we all just start laughing.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Because we're so bad at keeping time.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: So Gary starts clapping to help us.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Do you learn to play any songs?

script.text: Yes.

script.text: We do at least one song with words and chords.

script.text: I mean, that's harder than you think.

script.text: Ha, oh, I'm sure it is.

script.text: That part of the lesson takes about 15 minutes.

script.text: He often brings a recording of the song, and plays it to us first.
script.speaker: COLEMAN

script.text: Do you do any finger picking?

script.text: That's the last 10 minutes of the lesson, when we pick out the individual notes from a tune he's made up.

script.text: It's always quite simple.

script.text: That must be hard though.

script.text: It is.

script.text: But people like it because they can really concentrate.

script.text: I'll go and have a look at that website I think.

script.text: I never really planned to be a lifeboat volunteer when I came to live in Northsea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd been working in London as a website designer, but although that was interesting,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I didn't like city life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd been really keen on boats as a teenager, and I thought if I went to live by the sea, I might be able to pursue that interest a bit more in my free time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, I found that the Lifeboat Institution was looking for volunteers, so I decided to apply.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Lifeboat Institution building here in Northsea's hard to miss.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's one of the largest in the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was built 15 years ago, with funds provided by a generous member of the public who'd lived here all her life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As the Lifeboat Institution is a charity that relies on that kind of donation, rather than funding provided by the government, that was a huge help to us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When I applied, I had to have a health assessment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The doctors were particularly interested in my vision.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I used to be short sighted, so I'd had to wear glasses, but I'd had laser eye surgery two years earlier, so that was OK.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They gave me tests for colour blindness, and they thought I might have a problem there, but it turned out I was OK.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When the coastguard gets an alert, all the volunteers are contacted and rush to the lifeboat station.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our target's to get there in five minutes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then we try to get the boat off the dock and out to sea in another six to eight minutes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our team's proud that we usually achieve that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The average time across the country's eight and a half minutes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I've recently qualified as what's called a helmsman, which means I have the ultimate responsibility for the lifeboat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I have to check that the equipment we use is in working order.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The crew have special life jackets that can support up to four people in the water, and it's ultimately my decision whether it's safe to launch the boat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it's very rare not to launch it, even in the worst weather.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as going out on the lifeboat, my work involves other things too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A lot of people underestimate how quickly conditions can change at sea, so I speak to youth groups and sailing clubs in the area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: About the sorts of problems that sailors and swimmers can have, if the weather suddenly gets bad.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We also have a lot of volunteers who organize activities to raise money for us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And we couldn't manage without them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The training we get is a continuous process, focusing on technical competence and safe handling techniques, and it's given me the confidence to deal with extreme situations without panicking.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I was glad I'd done a first aid course before I started, as that's a big help with the casualty care activities we do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've done a lot on how to deal with ropes and tie knots - that's an essential skill.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After a year, I did a one-week residential course.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Led by specialists, they had a wave-tank where they could create extreme weather conditions - so we could get experience at what to do if the boat turned over in a storm at night, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since I started, I've had to deal with a range of emergency situations, but the work's hugely motivating.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's not just about saving lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I've learned a lot about the technology involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: My background in IT's been useful here, and I can use my expertise to help other volunteers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They're a great group.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're like a family really, which helps when you're dragging yourself out of bed on a cold stormy night.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But actually, it's the colder months that can be the most rewarding time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's when the incidents tend to be more serious, and you realize that you can make a huge difference to the outcome.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, if any of you listeners are interested.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why don't you give us a call...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two students called Bella and Don, discussing a presentation they plan to do on recycling footwear.

script.text: Hi, Don.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Did you get the copy of the article on recycling footwear that I emailed you?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Yeah, it's here.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I've had a look at it.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: So, do you think it's a good topic for our presentation?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Well, before I started reading it, I thought recycling footwear.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Well, although it's quite interesting, perhaps there isn't enough to say about it.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: 'Cause we put shoes in recycling bins, they go to charity shops, and that's about it.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: But there's much more to it than that.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: I realize that now.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: And I'm keen to research the topic more.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: That's great.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: One of the things I didn't realize until I read the article was just how many pairs of trainers get recycled.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Well, a lot of young people wear them all the time now.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: They've become more popular than ordinary shoes.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: I know, I guess they are very hard wearing.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: But don't they look a bit casual for school uniform?
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I don't think they're right for that.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Actually, I think some of them look quite smart on pupils, better than a scruffy old pair of shoes.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: So, do you keep shoes a long time?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Yes, though I do tend to wear my old pairs for doing dirty jobs like cleaning my bike.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I must admit, I've recycled some perfectly good shoes that haven't gone out of fashion and still fit, just because they don't look great on me anymore.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: That's awful, isn't it?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: I think it's common because there's so much choice.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: The article did say that recent sales of footwear have increased enormously.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: That didn't surprise me.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: No.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: But then it said that the amount of recycled footwear has fallen, it's 6% now, compared to a previous level of 11% that doesn't seem to make sense.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: That's because not everything goes through the recycling process.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Some footwear just isn't good enough to resell for one reason or another, and gets rejected.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

script.text: So, let's find some examples in the article of footwear that was rejected for recycling.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: OK, I think there are some in the interview with the recycling manager.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Yeah, here it is.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Let's start with the lady's high heeled shoes.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: What did he say about those?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: He said they were probably expensive.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: The material was suede, and they were beige in colour.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: It looked like someone had only worn them once, but in a very wet field.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: So the heels were too stained with MUD and grass to resell them.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: OK, and the leather ankle boots, what was wrong with them?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Apparently, the heels were worn, but that wasn't the problem.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: One of the shoes was a much lighter shade than the other one.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: It had obviously been left in the sun.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I suppose even second-hand shoes should look the same.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Then there were the red baby shoes.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Oh yes.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: We're told to tie shoes together when we put them in a recycling bin.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: People often don't bother, you'd think it would have been easy to find the other, but it wasn't.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: That was a shame because they were obviously new.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: The trainers were interesting.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: He said they looked like they'd been worn by a marathon runner.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Yeah, weren't they split?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Not exactly.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: One of the soles was so worn under the foot that you could put your finger through it.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Well, we could certainly use some of those examples in our presentation to explain why 90% of shoes that people take to recycling centers or bins,
script.speaker: DON

script.text: get thrown into landfill.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: What did you think about the project his team set up to avoid this by making new shoes out of the good parts of old shoes?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: It sounded like a good idea.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: They get so many shoes, they should be able to match parts.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I wasn't surprised that it failed though.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: I mean, who wants to buy second-hand shoes really?
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Think of all the germs you could catch.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Well, people didn't refuse them for that reason, did they?
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: It was because the pairs of shoes weren't identical.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: They still managed to ship them overseas though.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: That's another area we need to discuss.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: You know, I used to consider this topic just from my own perspective.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: By thinking about my own recycling behavior, without looking at the bigger picture.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: So much happens once shoes leave the recycling area.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: It's not as simple as you first think, and we can show that by taking a very different approach to it.
script.speaker: BELLA

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: DON

script.text: So let's discuss...
script.speaker: DON

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation about an animal called tardigrade.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: For my project on invertebrates, I chose to study tardigrades.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are microscopic, or to be more precise, near microscopic animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are well over 1,000 known species of these tiny animals, which belong to the phylum tardigrada.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most tardigrades range in length from naught point naught five (0.05) to 1 millimetre.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though the largest species can grow to be 1.2 millimeters in length, they are also sometimes called water bears, water because that's where they thrive best.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And bear because of the way they move.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Moss piglet is another name for tardigrades, because of the way they look when viewed from the front.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They were first discovered in Germany in 1773 by Johann Goeze, who coined the name "Tardigrada".
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As I say, there are many different species of tardigrade, too many to describe here, but generally speaking, the different species share similar physical traits.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They have a body which is short and also rounded, a bit like a barrel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the body comprises four segments, each segment has a pair of legs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the end of which are between four and 8 sharp claws.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I should also say that some species don't have any claws.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What they have are discs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these work by means of suction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They enable the tardigrade to cling on to surfaces or to grip its prey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Within the body,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: there are no lungs or any organs for breathing at all.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, oxygen and also blood are transported in a fluid that fills the cavity of the body.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as the tardigrade's head is concerned, the best way I can describe this is that it looks rather strange - a bit squashed even - though many of the websites I looked at described its appearance as cute.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which isn't exactly very scientific.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The tardigrade's mouth is a kind of tube that can open outwards to reveal teeth-like structures known as "stylets".
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are sharp enough to pierce plant or animal cells.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So where are tardigrades found?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, they live in every part of the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In a variety of habitats, most commonly on the bed of a lake, or on many kinds of plants, or in very wet environments.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's been some interesting research which has found that tardigrades are capable of surviving radiation and very high pressure, and they're also able to withstand temperatures as cold as minus 200 degrees centigrade.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or highs of more than 148 degrees centigrade, which is incredibly hot.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has been said that tardigrades could survive long after human beings have been wiped out, even in the event of an asteroid hitting the earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If conditions become too extreme and tardigrades are at risk of drying out, they enter a state called cryptobiosis.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They curl into a ball called a tun.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's t u n, by retracting their head and legs, and their metabolism drops to less than 1% of normal levels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can remain like this until they're reintroduced to water, when they will come back to life in a matter of a few hours, while in a state of cryptobiosis.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Tardigrades produce a protein that protects their DNA.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 2016, scientists revived two tardigrades that had been tuns for more than 30 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There was a report that, in 1948 a 120-year-old tun was revived, but this experiment has never been repeated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are currently several tests taking place in space to determine how long tardigrades might be able to survive there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I believe the record so far is 10 days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So moving on, in terms of their diet, tardigrades consume liquids in order to survive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although they have teeth, they don't use these for chewing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They suck the juices from moss or extract fluid from seaweed, but some species prey on other tardigrades, from other species or within their own.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I suppose this isn't surprising given that tardigrades are mainly comprised of liquid and are coated with a type of gel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finally, I'd like to mention the conservation status of tardigrades.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It is estimated that they have been in existence for approximately half a billion years, and in that time, they have survived five mass extinctions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it will probably come as no surprise to you that tardigrades have not been evaluated by the International Union for conservation of Nature, and are not on any endangered list.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some researchers have described them as thriving.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Does anyone have any questions they'd like to ask?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear the organizer of a children's book festival giving some information about it on a local radio program.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The Children's Book Festival is coming up again soon, and here to tell us all about it is the festival's organizer, Jenny Morgan.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: So, tell us what we can expect this year, Jenny.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Uh, Well, as usual, we've got 5 days of action-packed exciting events for children, with writers coming from all over the country getting involved.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Just to give you an idea of what's on offer in the workshops.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: First of all, there's a very special event called Superheroes.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: This is a chance for deaf children to share their reading experiences with author Madeleine Gordon, who is herself hearing impaired.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: "Just do it" is a practical workshop, led by the well-known illustrator Mark Keane.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: He'll take participants on a magical journey to far away lands.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: With an opportunity for aspiring actors to do some role play.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: 'Count on me' is an inspiring and entertaining look at the issues of friendship for 13-14-year-olds.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: It looks at some of the friendships described in popular books.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: And asks participants to compare these with their own experiences.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Speak up is part of a series of workshops on the subject of mental health.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: This is a creative writing workshop, encouraging children to describe situations where young people experience loneliness.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: A recent survey revealed that children can be lonely, even when they're at home with their families.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: "Jump for joy", as many of you will know, is the heart-warming, best-selling story by Nina Karan, about a young girl's trip to visit her relatives in India.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: It recently received the gold medal at the Waterford Awards.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Nina will get children to celebrate the word joy by writing a poem.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: 'Sticks and stones' is the beautifully illustrated picture book for young readers about a community who organize an African-Caribbean festival to help local children learn about their Jamaican roots.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: This will be a musical event where children will have the chance to play steel drums.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: This is bound to be very popular, so please book as soon as possible.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Thanks, Jenny.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: That all sounds really interesting.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: I'm just wondering if you have a favourite book you could recommend for our readers?
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: It's hard to choose, but "Alive and Kicking" is definitely worth mentioning.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: You won't have heard of the writer, as it's her first book - which is really impressive.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: It's basically the teenage diary of a boy from Somalia who comes to live in the UK.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: It deals with the serious issue of immigration, and all the challenges the boy has to face at school, and with the language barrier, etc.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Usually, books like this are quite sad.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: But this one actually made me cry with laughter.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: On each page there are simple but hilarious black and white stick drawings of the boy with his friends and teachers.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: At the end of each diary entry, there are new English words the boy learns each day, which may help develop some children's vocabulary.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: I think my kids would enjoy that.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: What about any advice for parents on how to encourage their children to read more?
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Well, this is something I get asked about a lot.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: There are so many distractions for kids these days that it can be hard to find time for reading.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: One thing I'd say is to make time to sit down with your child and share books with them.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: A lot of parents give up reading aloud to their children as soon as they learn to read independently.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: But this is a mistake.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: It's good to read more advanced books to them, as it helps to develop their vocabulary.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: If you don't have time for this, then let them listen to audiobooks.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Often they'll want to read books they've listened to for themselves.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: I think it's a good idea to make a mental note of the type of books your child is reading.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Often they just read the same genre all the time, which can get a bit boring.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: You can introduce new authors and genres to them.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Librarians should be able to help you with this.
script.speaker: JENNY

script.text: Well, Jenny, I think that's really useful...
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear a trainee science teacher called Clare talking about her practical teaching work to another trainee called Jake.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.text: Hi, Jake.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: How are you getting on with the practical teaching?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Oh, it's harder than I expected, but I've got some great classes.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: How about you?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Not brilliant.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I'm really struggling with my Year 12 science class.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Hmm. Are they hard to control?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Well, I don't have discipline problems as such.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: It's just that they don't seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: It's depressing.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week, and the results weren't too bad, but there's no real engagement.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I was wondering about something on the children's diets, you know, asking them to record what they eat, and maybe linking it to their state of health.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Hmm, let's think.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat, OK?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But you'd also need to have access to the children's medical records.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And I don't think people would be happy about that, confidentiality would be an issue.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it's not going to be easy.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Wouldn't that be upsetting for the children?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Well, the animals don't have to be harmed in any way.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It could just be an experiment where they're given a certain diet and the effects are observed.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Yes, you'd have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It's quite straightforward.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But if we found out that say a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn't necessarily be true for people, would it?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: No, that's true.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But the findings for any experiment are going to be limited, it's inevitable.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I suppose so.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: So what animals could I use to investigate the effect of diet?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Mice?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Yes, you'd need experimental mice, ones that have been specially bred for experiments.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Well, uh something to do with nutrition.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: So maybe we could look at food supplements, things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Hmm. That might be rather broad, maybe just look at the effects of one supplement like sugar on the health of the mice.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar that they don't really need?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Do they eat it, or do they decide to leave it?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Then later on, you could do a follow up experiment, adding another variable, like you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don't do much.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Or I could repeat the experiment, but change the type of food I provided.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Or use mice with a different genetic structure, but I think your idea would be more interesting.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I might think about that some more.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Sure, I did a similar experiment in college, actually.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: So, how many mice would I need?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I'd say about 12, and all young ones, not a mixture of old and young.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: OK, and I'd need two groups of equal sizes, so 6 in each group.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: And how would I tell them apart?
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group, or just mark them in some way.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: You could use food coloring, that wouldn't hurt them.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Perfect.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let's call them group a, would be the control group.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: So they just have ordinary mouse food.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Uh. I suppose you can buy that.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they'd also have the extra sugar.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Would you just give them straight sugar?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It might be better to give them something like cereal with it.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Hmm. Then you'd need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week, and you'd need an electronic balance.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But we can't hold them on the balance, or it'd affect the reading.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: OK, so once we've measured the weight gain of each mouse, we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: And then see where we go from there.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: That sounds cool.
script.speaker: CLARE

script.text: I think the students will enjoy it.

script.text: Yes. One thing...

script.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about microplastics.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to be talking about microplastics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters in size.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Recently, there's been a greater awareness that there are large quantities of plastic waste big and small.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The amount of plastic waste in the oceans has received widespread attention, but far less is known about the effects of microplastics in fresh water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And particularly in soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Microplastics can enter the environment via a number of different sources.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Threads and microfibers detached from synthetic clothing every time they're put in a washing machine, and these find their way into the water system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Other sources include big pieces of plastic waste that are already in the environment, and these break down into microscopic particles over a period of time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On a larger scale, factory waste is another route, as are tyres, which wear down as cars, lorries, and so on, travel along road surfaces.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We already understand some of the impacts of microplastics from studies involving fish and other animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There is evidence that microplastics harm small creatures in a variety of ways.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as by damaging their mouths or by impairing their ability to feed, for example, when microplastics get lodged in their digestive system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Surprisingly, perhaps, it is likely that humans consume microplastics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As these have been detected in a wide range of food and drink products, including bottled water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as in water that comes direct from the tap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, salt and many kinds of seafood have also been found to contain microplastics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, it's important to underline that there is not yet conclusive proof that microplastics cause significant harm to people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In many countries, including here in the UK, there is legislation which prevents manufacturers from adding plastic microbeads to shower gels, facial cleansers and toothpaste.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It is very difficult to accurately estimate the total amount of microplastic particles in the soil, as they can be hard to detect.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we do know they are carried in the air.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And deposited in the soil by rain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, many of the fertilizers used by both farmers and gardeners contain microplastics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A team from the Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge has carried out a study of the effects of microplastics on the digestive tracts of earthworms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These worms, which live in topsoil, are an essential component of our agricultural system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By feeding on soil, they mix nutrients into it, thereby making it more fertile.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The researchers set out to discover whether the introduction of microplastics into the soil and the subsequent ingestion of these by earthworms would impact soil quality.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And ultimately inhibit plant growth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The short answer was yes, it did.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After placing three different types of microplastic particles into the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They planted perennial ryegrass.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The particles of microplastic, which included biodegradable PLA, and conventional high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, were then ingested by the earthworms in the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The result was that the worms lost weight rapidly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, a lower percentage than normal of the ryegrass seeds germinated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the researchers concluded that this was a direct result of the earthworms being unable to fulfill their normal role in making soil more fertile.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The team also discovered that there was an increase in the amount of acid found in the soil, and this was attributed mainly to the microplastic particles from conventional HDPE plastic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The conclusions of the study make for very interesting reading.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I've included the reference in the notes to give you at the end of this session.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To summarize, the authors proposed the idea that we need to regard soil as we would regard any other process in nature.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means we should accept the implications of soil being dependent on decaying and dead matter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Constantly being passed through the bodies of earthworms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is when soil becomes impoverished by the presence of microplastics, not only ecosystems but also the whole of society are negatively impacted.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a podcast by a running coach giving advice about taking up running and giving information about her club.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: My name's Liz Fuller, and I'm a running coach with Compton Park Runners Club.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Welcome to my podcast.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: If you're thinking about taking up running, I'm here to help.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: There are many training programs available online, which aim to help people build up to running 5 kilometers.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Some of them are great, and thousands of people of all ages are taking part in 5 kilometer races across the country as a result.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: People like them because they're easy to follow, and don't push them too hard.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: However, they don't work for everyone, especially if you suffer from something like heart condition or asthma.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Because they're aimed at people with average fitness and running ability.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Another thing is that everyone is different, and if you have any specific questions related to your needs.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: There's no one to provide any answers.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I have a couple of simple tips I always give to new runners.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I expect you've been told to run very slowly until your fitness increases.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Well, I find that can prevent progress.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: You should run at a speed that feels comfortable, but time yourself, and try to run a bit faster each time.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Listening to music can be very helpful.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: It takes your mind off things and helps your body get into a rhythm.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I'd say that is better than running with a friend.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Especially as most people are competitive, and that's not what you want when you're just starting.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I don't think the time of day is especially important.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Some people are better in the evening, while others are morning people.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But you need to be consistent, so aim to train regularly.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Twice a week is enough to begin with.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: New members often say to me that they've been put off running, either because they lack confidence, or they don't have time, or they think they dislike running.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Ceri, for example, joined the club two years ago at the age of 40.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: She'd always enjoyed running at school, but wasn't sure if she'd be able to do it.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: She was worried about being left behind and being the slowest runner, but she says she was made to feel so welcome, she soon forgot all about that.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: James had always hated the idea of running, but a friend encouraged him to come along for a taster session, and he hasn't looked back.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: He never misses a training session,
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: despite having a really demanding job.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Leo was worried about having to commit himself to training sessions every week, and wasn't sure he'd be able to fit training into his busy schedule.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But after experiencing a lot of stress at work, he came along to us and gave it a go.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Now he says he feels much more relaxed.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: And he looks forward to his weekly run.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Mark is quite typical of our new members.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: He's never considered himself to be a sporty person.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: And it was only when he retired that he decided to take up the challenge of trying to run 5 km.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: It took him months to find the courage to contact us.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But he felt reassured immediately, as there were other people his age who were only just taking up running for the first time.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: My own journey hasn't been easy.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I did my first marathon when I was 37, after having had two kids.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: My husband had been running marathons for years.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But I never dreamed I'd be doing one with him.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I managed to complete it in four hours, but I felt like giving up halfway through.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: It was only the support of the spectators that kept me going.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I do think signing up for a race of whatever length is motivating, whether it's 5 k or 25 k, because it's good to have something to work towards.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: And it gives you a sense of achievement.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: I did my first 10K after only six months, which was certainly very challenging, and not something I'd necessarily recommend.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But after you've been training for a few weeks, it's worth putting your name down for a 5 k.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Some people find they only need a few practice runs before taking part in a race.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: But I'd give yourself a couple of months at least.
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: Well, I hope that's given you a really good idea of...
script.speaker: LIZ FULLER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, Jane, you'll be off to Denmark soon to do your work placement.

script.text: Well, I hope they don't get spoiled.

script.text: It's OK.

script.text: My grandfather works in a bookshop, and he told me how to pack them.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Oh, that's helpful.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: He says you have to support the spine, otherwise the paper can come away from the cover.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Yeah, that's obvious.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: He also told me to pack them flat in the box, not on their side.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Again because they can bend, and if you leave them like that for, say, a year.

script.text: It's quite hard to get them back to their normal shape.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Well, it's pretty clear that ruins them, but a lot of people just can't be bothered to protect their books.

script.text: It's the acid in the paper that causes the problem, isn't it?
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Yeah, that's why old books go yellow.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: You know, some of the books my grandfather's given me are like that already.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I should dump them really, if they're going to deteriorate further, but I'd feel bad.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: They'll always remind me of him, he's quite a collector you know.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Well, if they're important to you.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Yeah, I'd regret just throwing them away.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: You know, maybe it's because I was taught to treasure books, but I hate seeing students force open the pages of paperbacks.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: They press so hard they end up breaking the spine.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: I know, but unfortunately paperbacks aren't designed to last a long time, and people know that.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Hardbacks aren't quite as weak.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Yeah, they're different, I suppose.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: But I still don't think people value hardbacks like they used to.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Well, they aren't decorative, are they, like other objects?
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Plus nowadays people don't keep them out on shelves as much as they used to.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: That's such a pity.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: When I visit someone - if they have, say, a colorful book on a table,
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: it's the first thing I'm drawn to.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: I agree.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And book covers can be a work of art in themselves.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Some are really eye-catching.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I've always been taught to handle books carefully.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: If you watch someone take a book off a shelf, well, they usually do it wrong.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Ah,
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: my grandfather says, you should put your hand right over the top of the book...
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: or if you can't do that, pull the other books on the shelf aside, so that you can hold the whole cover.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: When did you learn all this?
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: He watched me pull a heavy book off the shelf when I was small.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And it fell on the floor and broke apart.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Oh, dear.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: I can still remember it.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: You know what I really like?
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: What?
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: The smell of new books.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Me too.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: My parents used to laugh at me when I was a kid, because I loved putting books up to my nose.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: Almost as much as reading them.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: New books aren't cheap though, are they?
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I guess we're lucky we can buy them.
script.speaker: KIERAN

script.text: My grandfather stocks second-hand books as well as new ones.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And they don't smell quite as good.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental studies lecture on tree planting.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Tree planting now dominates political and popular agendas, and is often presented as an easy answer to the climate crisis, as well as a way for business corporations to offset their carbon emissions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But unfortunately, tree planting isn't as straightforward as some people think.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When the wrong trees are planted in the wrong place, it can do considerably more damage than good.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Failing to help either people or the environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Reforestation projects are currently being undertaken on a huge scale in many countries, and it's crucial that the right trees are selected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A mix of species should always be planted, typical of the local natural forest ecosystem, and including rare and endangered species in order to create a rich ecosystem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's important to avoid non-native species that could become invasive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Invasive species are a significant contributor to the current global biodiversity crisis.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And are often in competition with native species, and may threaten their long-term survival.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Restoring biodiversity that will maximize carbon capture is key when reforesting an area, but ideally any reforestation project should have several goals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These could include selecting trees that can contribute to wildlife conservation, improve the availability of food for the local community, and maintain the stability of soil systems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Meeting as many of these goals as possible, whilst doing no harm to local communities, native ecosystems and vulnerable species, is the sign of a highly successful tree-planting scheme.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To ensure the survival and resilience of a planted forest, it's vital to use tree seeds with appropriate levels of genetic diversity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The amount of genetic variation found within a species is essential for their survival.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Using seeds with low genetic diversity generally lowers the resilience of restored forests, which can make them vulnerable to disease, and unable to adapt to climate change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Choosing the right location for reforestation projects is as important as choosing the right trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ultimately, the best area for planting trees would be formerly forested areas that are in poor condition.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's better to avoid non-forested landscapes, such as natural grasslands, savannas or wetlands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As these ecosystems already contribute greatly to capturing carbon, it would also be advantageous to choose an area where trees could provide other benefits.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as recreational spaces, reforesting areas which are currently exploited for agriculture should be avoided.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As this often leads to other areas being deforested.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Large scale reforestation projects require careful planning.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Making the right decisions about where to plant trees depends on having the right information.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Having detailed and up-to-date maps, identifying high-priority areas for intervention is essential.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Drone technology is a useful tool in helping to prioritize and monitor areas of degraded forest for restoration, in Brazil, it's being used to identify and quantify how parts of the Amazon are being devastated by human activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as rearing cattle and illegal logging.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A good example of where the right trees were picked to achieve a restored forest is in Lampang province in northern Thailand.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A previously forested site which had been degraded through mining was reforested by a cement company together with Chiang Mai University.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After spreading 60 cm of top soil, they planted 14 different native tree species, which included several species of fig.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Figs are a keystone species, because of the critical role they play in maintaining wildlife populations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They are central to tropical reforestation projects.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As they accelerate the speed of the recovery process by attracting animals and birds, which act as natural seed dispersers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This helps to promote diversity through the healthy regrowth of a wide range of plant species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Unlike the majority of fruit trees, figs bear fruit all year round, providing a reliable food source for many species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At this site for example, after only three rainy seasons, monkeys started visiting to eat the fig fruits, naturally dispersing seeds through defecation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Reforestation projects should always aim to make sure that local communities are consulted and involved in the decision making process.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The restoration of mangrove forests in Madagascar is an example of a project which has succeeded in creating real benefits for the community.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Destruction of the mangrove forests had a terrible impact on plant and animal life, and also badly affected the fishing industry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which was a major source of employment for local people living in coastal areas, the reforestation project involved hiring local people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To plant and care for the new mangrove trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Millions of mangrove trees have now been planted, which has resulted in the return of a healthy aquatic ecosystem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The mangroves also act as a defense against the increased threat of flooding caused by climate change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, the local economy is more stable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And thousands more Madagascans are now able to send their children to school.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One other important point to consider.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a woman speaking to a group of people who are interested in becoming volunteers for an organization called ACE.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good evening everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let me start by welcoming you all to this talk, and thanking you for taking the time to consider joining ACE voluntary organization.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: ACE offers support to people and services in the local area, and we're now looking for more volunteers to help us do this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By the way, I hope you're all comfortable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have brought in extra seats so that no one has to stand, but it does mean that the people at the back of the room may be a bit squashed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll only be here for about half an hour, so, hopefully, that's OK.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the first questions we're often asked is how old you need to be to volunteer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, you can be as young as 16, or you can be 60 or over.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It all depends on what type of voluntary work you want to do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Other considerations such as reliability are crucial in voluntary work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And age isn't related to these in our experience.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another question we get asked relates to training.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, there's plenty of that, and it's all face to face.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, training doesn't end when you start working for us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It takes place before, during, and after periods of work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Often it's run by other experienced volunteers, as managers tend to prefer to get on with other things.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, I would ask you to consider a couple of important issues before you decide to apply for voluntary work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't worry about why you want to be a volunteer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People have many different reasons that range from getting work experience to just doing something they've always wanted to do, but it is critical that you have enough hours in the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For whatever role we agree is suitable for you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If being a volunteer becomes stressful, then it's best not to do it at all.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may think that your income is important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we don't ask about that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's up to you to decide if you can work without earning money.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What we value is dedication.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of our most loyal volunteers earn very little themselves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But still give their full energy to the work they do with us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, so let's take a look at some of the work areas that we need volunteers for, and the sort of things that would help you in those.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may wish simply to help us raise money.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you have the creativity to come up with an imaginative or novel way of fundraising, we'd be delighted.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As standing in the local streets or shops with a collection box can be rather boring.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One outdoor activity that we need volunteers for is litter collection, and for this it's useful if you can walk for long periods, sometimes uphill.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of our regular collectors are quite elderly, but very active and keen to protect the environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you enjoy working with children, we have three vacancies for what are called playmates.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These volunteers help children learn about staying healthy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Through a range of out of school activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You don't need to have children yourself, but it's good if you know something about nutrition, and can give clear instructions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If that doesn't appeal to you, maybe you would be interested in helping out at our story club for disabled children, especially if you have done some acting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We put on three performances a year based on books they have read, and we're always looking for support with the theatrical side of this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The last area I'll mention today is first aid.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Volunteers who join this group can end up teaching others in vulnerable groups who may be at risk of injury.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Initially though, your priority will be to take in a lot of information, and not forget any important steps or details.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Right, so does anyone have any questions...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
