script.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation on the process of moving wild elephants to a new reserve known as translocation.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: For my presentation today, I want to tell you about how groups of elephants have been moved and settled in new reserves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is known as translocation, and has been carried out in Malawi in Africa in recent years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The reason this is being done is because of overpopulation of elephants in some areas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Overpopulation is a good problem to have, and not one we tend to hear about very often, in Malawi's Majete National Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The elephant population had been wiped out by poachers who killed the elephants for their ivory, but in 2003 the park was restocked.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And effective law enforcement was introduced.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since then, not a single elephant has been poached.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In this safe environment, the elephant population boomed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Breeding went so well that there were more elephants than the park could support.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This led to a number of problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Firstly, there was more competition for food, which meant that some elephants were suffering from hunger.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As there was a limit to the amount of food in the national park, some elephants began looking further afield.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Elephants were routinely knocking down fences around the park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which then had to be repaired at a significant cost.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To solve this problem, the decision was made to move dozens of elephants from Majete National Park to Nkhotakota Wildlife Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Where there were no elephants. But obviously, attempting to move significant numbers of elephants to a new home 300 kilometers away.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Is quite a challenge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, how did this translocation process work in practice?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Elephants were moved in groups of between eight and 20, all belonging to one family.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because relationships are very important to elephants, they all had to be moved at the same time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A team of vets and park rangers flew over the park in helicopters, and targeted a group, which were rounded up, and directed to a designated open plain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The vets then used darts to immobilize the elephants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was a tricky maneuver, as they not only had to select the right dose of tranquilizer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For different sized elephants, but they had to dart the elephants as they were running around.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This also had to be done as quickly as possible, so as to minimize the stress caused.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As soon as the elephants began to flop onto the ground, the team moved in to take care of them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To avoid the risk of suffocation, the team had to make sure none of the elephants were lying on their chests, because their lungs could be crushed in this position.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, all the elephants had to be placed on their sides.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One person stayed with each elephant, while they waited for the vets to do checks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was very important to keep an eye on their breathing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If there were fewer than 6 breaths per minute, the elephant would need urgent medical attention.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Collars were fitted to the matriarch in each group, so their movements could be tracked in their new home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Measurements were taken of each elephant's tusks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Elephants with large tusks would be at greater risk from poachers, and also of their feet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The elephants were then taken to a recovery area, before being loaded onto trucks and transported to their new home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The elephants translocated to Nkhotakota settled in very well, and the project has generally been accepted to have been a huge success.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And not just for the elephants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Employment prospects have improved enormously, contributing to rising living standards for the whole community.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Poaching is no longer an issue, as former poachers are able to find more reliable sources of income.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, many of them volunteered to give up their weapons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As they were no longer of any use to them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: More than two dozen elephants have been born at Nkhotakota since relocation. With an area of more than 1,800 square kilometers, there's plenty of space for the elephant population to continue to grow.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Their presence is also helping to rebalance Nkhotakota's damaged ecosystem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And providing a sustainable conservation model, which could be replicated in other parks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All this has been a big draw for tourism, which contributes five times more than the illegal wildlife trade to GDP.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this is mainly because of the elephants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's also been a dramatic rise in interest from...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a student on a fashion design course giving a talk about the history of pockets.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now we've been asked to choose an aspect of European clothing or fashion, and to talk about its development over time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I decided to focus on a rather small area of clothing, and that's pockets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I chose pockets for two reasons really.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We all have them in jeans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Jackets, coats for example, and even though we often carry bags or briefcases as well, nothing is quite as convenient as being able to pop your phone or credit card into your pocket.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Yet, I suspect that other than that, people don't really think about pockets too much, and they're rather overlooked as a fashion item.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's certainly very interesting to go back in time, and see how pockets developed for men and women.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 18th century, fashions were quite different from the way they are now.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Pockets were too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If we think about male fashion first, that was the time when suits became popular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Trousers were knee length only, and referred to as breeches.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The waistcoats were short, and the jackets were long, but all three garments were lined with material, and pockets were sewn into this cloth, by whichever tailor the customer used.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The wearer could then carry small objects such as pencils or coins on their person, and reach them through a gap in the lining.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Coat pockets became increasingly decorative on the outside for men who wanted to look stylish, but they were often larger, but plainer, if the wearer was someone with a profession who needed to carry medical instruments, a doctor or physician for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The development of women's pockets was a little different.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For one thing, they weren't nearly as visible or as easy to reach as men's.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 18th and 19th centuries, women carried numerous possessions on their person, and some of these could be worth a lot of money.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Women were more vulnerable to theft, and wealthy women in particular worried constantly about pickpockets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what they did was to have a pair of pockets made.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That were tied together with string.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The pockets were made of fabric, which might be recycled cloth if the wearer had little money, or something more expensive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as linen, sometimes featuring very delicate embroidery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Women tied the pockets around their waist, so that they hung beneath their clothes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Remember, skirts were long then, and there was plenty of room to hide a whole range of small possessions between the layers of petticoats that were commonly worn.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They would have an opening in the folds of their skirts, through which they could reach whatever they needed, like their perfume.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Working women of course, also needed to carry around items that they might use for whatever job or trade they were involved in, but their pairs of pockets still remained on the inside of their clothing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They just got bigger or longer, sometimes reaching down to their knees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, the tie-on pockets went well into the 19th century, and only changed when fashion altered towards the end of that period.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's when dresses became tighter and less bulky, and the pairs of pockets became very noticeable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They stood out too much, and detracted from the woman's image.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Women who had been used to carrying around a range of personal possessions, and still wanted to, needed somewhere to carry these items about their person.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That was when small bags or pouches as they were known came into fashion, and of course, they inevitably led on to the handbag of more modern times.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Particularly when fashion removed pockets altogether.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: This evening, we're delighted to welcome Dan Beagle, who's just written a book on looking for and finding food in the wild.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: He's going to tell us everything we need to know about picking wild mushrooms.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Thank you very much.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Well, I need to start by talking about safety.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: You really need to know what you're doing because some mushrooms are extremely poisonous.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Having said that, once you know what to look for it's really worth doing for the amazing variety of mushrooms available, which you can't get in the shops.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: But of course you have to be very careful.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: And that's why I always say you should never consume mushrooms picked by friends or neighbors.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Always remember that some poisonous mushrooms look very similar to edible ones.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: And it's easy for people to get confused.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: The other thing to avoid is mushrooms growing beside busy roads for obvious reasons, but nothing beats the taste of freshly picked mushrooms.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Don't forget that the ones in the shops are often several days old and past their best.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: There are certain ideas about wild mushrooms that it's important to be aware of.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Don't listen to people who tell you that it's only OK to eat mushrooms that are pale.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Or dull.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: This is completely untrue.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Some edible mushrooms are bright red for example.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Personally I prefer mushrooms cooked, but it won't do you any harm to eat them uncooked in salads.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: It's not necessary to peel them.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Another thing you should remember is that you can't tell if a mushroom is safe to eat by its smell.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Some of the most deadly mushrooms have no smell.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: And taste quite nice, apparently.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Finally, just because deer or squirrels eat a particular mushroom, doesn't mean that you can.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Of course, mushroom picking is associated with the countryside, but if you haven't got a car, your local park can be a great place to start.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: There are usually a range of habitats where mushrooms grow, such as playing fields and wooded areas, but you need to be there first thing in the morning.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: As there's likely to be a lot of competition, not just from people, but wildlife too.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: The deer often get the best mushrooms in my local park.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: If you're a complete beginner, I wouldn't recommend going alone or relying on photos in a book, even the one I've written.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: There are some really good phone apps for identifying mushrooms, but you can't always rely on getting a good signal in the middle of a wood.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: If possible, you should go with a group led by an expert.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: You'll stay safe, and learn a lot that way.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Conservation is a really important consideration, and you must follow a few basic rules.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: You should never pick all the mushrooms in one area.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Collect only enough for your own needs.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Be very careful that you don't trample on young mushrooms or other plants.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: And make sure you don't pick any mushrooms that are endangered and protected by law.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: There's been a decline in some varieties of wild mushrooms in this part of the country.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Restaurants are becoming more interested in locally sourced food like wild mushrooms.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: But the biggest problem is that so many new houses have been built in this area in the last 10 years, and more water is being taken from rivers and reservoirs.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Because of this, mushroom habitats have been destroyed.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Anyway, a word of advice on storing mushrooms.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Collect them in a brown paper bag, and as soon as you get home, put them in the fridge.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: They'll be fine for a couple of days, but it's best to cook them as soon as possible.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: After washing them really carefully first, of course.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: So, everybody knows what a mushroom tastes like, right?
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Well, you'll be surprised by the huge variety of wild mushrooms there are.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Be adventurous.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: They're great in so many dishes, stir fries, risottos, pasta.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Just be aware that some people can react badly to certain varieties, so it's a good idea not to eat huge quantities to begin with.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: OK, so now I'm going to show you a few examples of poisonous...
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: That is the end of part 2.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear part of a lecture for astronomy students about the need for a system to manage satellites and other objects orbiting the Earth.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In today's astronomy lecture, I'm going to talk about the need for a system to manage the movement of satellites and other objects in orbit around the Earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In other words, a Space Traffic Management system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We already have effective Air Traffic Control systems that are used internationally to ensure that planes navigate our skies safely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, Space Traffic Management is a similar concept, but focusing on the control of satellites.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The aim of such a system would be to prevent the danger of collisions in space, between the objects in orbit around the Earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In order to do this, we'd need to have a set of legal measures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And we'd also have to develop the technical systems to enable us to prevent such accidents, but unfortunately, at present, we don't actually have a Space Traffic Management system that works.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So why not?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What are the problems in developing such a system?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, for one thing, satellites are relatively cheap these days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Compared with how they were in the past, meaning that more people can afford to put them into space.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So there's a lot more of them out there, and people aren't just launching single satellites.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But whole constellations consisting of thousands of them designed to work together, so space is getting more crowded every day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But in spite of this, one thing you may be surprised to learn is that you can launch a satellite into space, and once it's out there, it doesn't have to send back any information to Earth to allow its identification.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So while we have international systems for ensuring we know where the planes in our skies are, and to prevent them from colliding with one another.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When it comes to the safety of satellites, at present we don't have anything like enough proper ways of tracking them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it isn't just entire satellites that we need to consider.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A greater threat is the huge amount of space debris in orbit around the Earth, broken bits of satellite and junk from space stations and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And some of these are so small that they can be very hard to identify, but they can still be very dangerous.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, some operators may be unwilling to share information about the satellites they've launched.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, a satellite may be designed for military purposes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or it may have been launched for commercial reasons, and the operators don't want competitors to have information about it, and even if the operators are willing to provide it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The information isn't easy to collect.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Details are needed about the object itself, as well as about its location at a particular time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And remember that a satellite isn't very big, and it's likely to be moving at thousands of kilometers an hour.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't have any sensors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That can constantly follow something moving so fast, so all that the scientists can do is to put forward a prediction concerning where the satellite is heading next.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So those are some of the problems that we're facing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's consider now some of the solutions that have been suggested.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One key issue is the way in which information is dealt with.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need more information, but it also needs to be accessible at a global level.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So we need to establish shared standards that we can all agree on for the way in which this information is presented.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We already do this in other areas of science.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So although this is a challenge, it's not an impossible task.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then as all this information's collected, it needs to be put together so it can be used.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that will involve creating a single database on which it can be entered, as we continue to push forward new developments, congestion of the space environment is only going to increase.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To cope with this, we need to develop a system like the one I've described to coordinate the work of the numerous spacecraft operators.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it's also essential that this system is one that establishes trust in the people that use it, both nationally and at a global level.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One interesting development that I'll mention...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a guide at a farming museum talking to a group of visitors.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to the Museum of Farming Life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I understand it's your first visit here, so I'd like to give you some background information about the museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then explain a little about what you can see during your visit.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, where we're standing at the moment is the entrance to a large building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That was constructed in 1880, as the home of a local businessman, Alfred Palmer, of the Palmer Biscuit Factory.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was later sold, and became a hall of residence for students in 1911, and a museum in 1951.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 2005, a modern extension was built to accommodate the museum's collections.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The museum's owned by the university, and apart from two rooms that are our offices, the university uses the main part of the building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may see students going into the building for lessons, but it's not open to museum visitors, I'm afraid.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a shame, because the interior architectural features are outstanding.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Especially the room that used to be the library.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Luckily, we've managed to keep entry to the museum free.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This includes access to all the galleries, outdoor areas, and the rooms for special exhibitions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We run activities for children and students, such as the Museum Club, for which there's no charge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We do have a donation box just over there, so feel free to give whatever amount you consider appropriate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We do have a cloakroom.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you'd like to leave your coats and bags somewhere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Unlike other museums, photography is allowed here, so you might like to keep your cameras with you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You might be more comfortable not carrying around heavy rucksacks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though keep your coats and jackets on, as it's quite cold in the museum garden today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I'd like to tell you about the different areas of the museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just inside and outside the main gallery, we have an area called Four Seasons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here, you can watch a four-minute animation of a woodland scene.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was designed especially for the museum by a group of young people on a film studies course, and it's beautiful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Children absolutely love it, but then so do adults.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main gallery's called Town and Country. It includes a photographic collection of prize-winning sheep and shepherds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Leaving Town and Country, you enter Farmhouse Kitchen, which is... well, self-explanatory.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here we have the oldest collection of equipment for making butter and cheese in the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this morning, a specialist cheesemaker will be giving demonstrations of how it's produced.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may even get to try some.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After that, you can go in two directions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To the right is a staircase that takes you up to a landing, from where you can look down on the galleries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To the left is a room called A Year on the Farm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There is lots of seating here, as sometimes we use the room for school visits, so it's a good place to stop for a rest.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you're feeling competitive, you can take our memory test, in which you answer questions about things you've seen in the museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The next area is called Wagon Walk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This contains farm carts from nearly every part of the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's surprising how much regional variation there was.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Beside the carts are display boards with information about each one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The carts are old and fragile, so we ask you to keep your children close to you, and ensure they don't climb on the carts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From Wagon Walk, you can either make your way back to reception, or go out into the garden, or even go back to take another look in the galleries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the far corner of the garden is Bees are Magic, but we're redeveloping this area, so you can't visit that at the moment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can still buy our honey in the shop though.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finally, there is the pond, which contains all kinds of interesting wildlife.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are baby ducks that are only a few days old, as well as tiny frogs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The pond isn't deep, and there is a fence around it, so it's perfectly safe for children.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: I think it would have taken me ages to prepare examples showing each of the steps involved in making the bird.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: But that was a really good idea.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: The children could see what they were aiming for, and much better for them to be able to hold something, rather than just looking at pictures.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: Hmm, those physical examples supported her verbal explanations really well.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: It's strange that origami isn't used more widely.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: Why do you think that is?
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: Well, teachers may just feel it's not that appealing to children who are used to doing everything on computers, especially boys.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: Even if they're aware of the benefits.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: Oh, I don't know.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: It's no different to any other craft activity.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: I bet it's because so many teachers are clumsy like me.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: That's true.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: Too much effort required if you're not good with your hands.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: Well, anyway, I think we should try it out in our maths teaching practice with Year 3.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: I can see using origami is a really engaging way of reinforcing children's knowledge of geometric shapes, like they were doing in the video.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: But I think it would also work really well for presenting fractions, which is coming up soon.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: Good idea.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: That's something most of the kids in that class might struggle with.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: Origami would also be good practice for using symmetry, but I think they did that last term.
script.speaker: LIA

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: Well, let's try and get some ideas together, and plan the lesson next week.
script.speaker: SEB

script.text: OK, if you could all stop...
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: That is the end of part 3.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a literature student giving a talk about Victor Hugo, a famous 19th century French writer.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The person I've chosen to talk about is the French writer Victor Hugo.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many people have heard of him because his novel, Les Miserables,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which he wrote in 1862, is famous around the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It became a stage musical in the 1980s, and a film version was also released in 2012.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So some of us, I'm sure, have a pretty general idea of the plot, but we know much less about the author.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, I'm going to provide a little more insight into this talented man.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I'm going to talk particularly about the home he had on the island of Guernsey in the British Channel Islands, but first, his early career.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As I've said, he was a writer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He was at the height of his career in Paris, and he was very highly regarded by his colleagues.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as literature was concerned, he was the leading figure of the Romantic movement.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, as well as being a literary genius, he also gave many speeches about issues like the level of poverty in his society.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He felt very strongly about this, and about other areas where change was needed, like education.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This kind of outspoken criticism was not well liked by the rulers of France.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And eventually the emperor - Napoleon III - told Victor Hugo to leave Paris and not return.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In other words, he sent him into exile.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So Victor Hugo was forced to reside in other parts of Europe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Guernsey was actually his third place of exile.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And he landed there in 1855.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He produced a lot while on Guernsey, including Les Miserables.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And to do this, he had to spend a great deal of time in the home that he had there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was a property that he bought using the money he'd made in France, from the publication of a collection of his poetry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was the only property he ever owned, and he was very proud of it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The property Victor Hugo bought on Guernsey was a large five-storey house in the capital town of St Peter Port, and he lived there for 15 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Returning to France in 1870 when Napoleon's empire collapsed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He decorated and furnished each level or floor of the house in unique and wonderful ways, and many people consider the inside of the house to be a work of art.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, it's a museum that attracts 200,000 visitors a year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He lived in the house with his family, and portraits of its members still hang in rooms on the ground floor, along with drawings that he did during his travels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That he felt were important to him.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In other ground floor rooms, there are huge tapestries that he would have designed and loved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The walls are covered in dark wood panelling that Victor Hugo created himself using wooden furniture that he bought in the market.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The items were relatively inexpensive, and he used them to create intricate carvings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They gave an atmosphere on the lower level that was shadowy,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and rather solemn.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On the next level of the house, there are two impressive lounges where he entertained his guests.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One lounge has entirely red furnishings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as sofas and wall coverings, and the other blue.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's a strong Chinese influence in these areas, in things like the wallpaper pattern.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the lamps, which he would have made himself by copying original versions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: His library, where he left many of his favorite books, forms the hallway to the third floor, and was a comfortable area where he could relax and enjoy his afternoons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then, at the very top of the house, there's a room called the Lookout,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: called that because it looks out over the harbor.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In contrast to the rather dark lower levels, it's full of light, and was like a glass office where he would write until lunchtime.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Often at his desk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So Victor Hugo was a man of many talents, but he was also true to his values.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While living in his house on Guernsey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He entertained many other famous writers, but he also invited a large group of local children from the deprived areas of the island to dinner once a week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, he served them their food, which was an extraordinary gesture for the time period.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1927, the house was owned by his relatives, and they decided to donate it to the city of Paris.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has since been restored using photographs from the period, and as I mentioned earlier, is now a museum that is open to the public.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1, you will hear a woman called Jan, phoning a man about their local conservation group.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Oh hello, my name is Jan.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Are you the right person to talk to about the Buckworth Conservation Group?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Yes, I'm Peter, I'm the secretary.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Good, I've just moved to this area, and I'm interested in getting involved.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I was in a similar group where I used to live.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Could you tell me something about your activities, please?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Well we have a mixture of regular activities and special events.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: One of the regular ones is trying to keep the beach free of litter.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: A few of us spend a couple of hours a month on it.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: And it's awful how much there is to clear.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I wish people would be more responsible and take it home with them.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I totally agree.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I'd be happy to help with that.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Is it OK to take dogs?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I'm afraid not, as they're banned from the beach itself.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: You can take them along the cliffs though, and children are welcome.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: We also manage a nature reserve, and there's a lot to do there all year round.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Uh. For example, because it's a popular place to visit, we spend a lot of time looking after the paths.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: And making sure they're in good condition for walking.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I could certainly help with that.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: And we have a program of creating new habitats there.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: We've just finished making and installing nesting boxes for birds to use, and next we're going to work on encouraging insects.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: They're important for the biodiversity of the reserve.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: They certainly are.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Oh, and we're also running a project to identify the different species of butterflies that visit the reserve.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: You might be interested in taking part in that.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Sure, I was involved in something similar where I used to live, counting all the species of moths.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I'd enjoy that.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Another job we're doing at the reserve is replacing the wall on the southern side.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Between the parking area and our woodshed, it was badly damaged in a storm last month.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Then, as I said, we have a program of events as well, both at the weekend and during the week.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I presume you have guided walks.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: I'd like to get to know the local countryside, as I'm new to the area.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Yes, we do.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: The next walk is to Ruston Island a week on Saturday.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: We'll be meeting in the car park at Dunsmore Beach at low tide.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: That's when the sands are dry enough for us to walk to the island without getting wet.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Sounds good.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: The island's a great place to explore. It's quite small, and it's got a range of habitats.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: It's also an ideal location for seeing seals just off the coast or even on the beach.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: OK. And is there anything we should bring?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Like a picnic for instance.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Yes, do bring one, as it's a full-day walk, and of course it'll be wet walking across and back, so make sure your boots are waterproof.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I must buy a new pair.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: There's a hole in one of my current ones.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Well, I'd definitely like to come on the walk.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Then later this month, we're having a one-day woodwork session in Hopton Wood.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I've never tried that before.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Is it OK for beginners to take part?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Definitely, there'll be a couple of experts leading the session, and we keep the number of participants down, so you'll get as much help as you need.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: Excellent! I'd love to be able to make chairs.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Ha. That's probably too ambitious for one day!
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: You'll be starting with wooden spoons, and of course learning how to use the tools, and anything you make is yours to take home with you.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: That sounds like fun.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: When is it?
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: It's on the 17th, from 10 a.m. until 3.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: There's a charge of £35 including lunch,
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: or £40, if you want to camp in the wood.
script.speaker: PETER

script.text: I should think I'll come home the same day.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: Well, I'd certainly like to join the group.
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: It sounds like you've...
script.speaker: JAN

script.text: That is the end of part 1.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a tour guide, Lou Miller, speaking to a group of people about a boat trip they are going to take around the Australian island of Tasmania.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, hello everyone, my name is Lou Miller, and I'm going to be your tour guide today, as we take this fantastic boat trip around the Tasmanian coast.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Before we set off, I just want to tell you a few things about our journey.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Our boats aren't huge, as you can see, we already have three staff members on board.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And on top of that, we can transport a further 15 people, that's you, around the coastline.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: But please note, if there are more than 9 people on either side of the boat, we'll move some of you over.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Ha, otherwise all 18 of us will end up in the sea.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: We've recently upgraded all our boats.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: They used to be jet black, but our new ones now have these comfortable dark red seats and a light green exterior.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: In order to stand out from others and help promote our company.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: This gives our boats a rather unique appearance, don't you think?
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: We offer you a free lunch box during the trip.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And we have three types.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Lunch Box 1 contains ham and tomato sandwiches.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Lunch Box 2 contains a cheddar cheese roll.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And lunch box 3 is salad based, and also contains eggs and tuna.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: All three lunch boxes also have a packet of crisps and chocolate bar inside.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Please let staff know which lunch box you prefer.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: I'm sure I don't have to ask you not to throw anything into the sea.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: We don't have any bins to put litter in, but Jess, myself or Ray, our other guide, will collect it from you after lunch.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And put it all in a large plastic sack.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The engine on the boat makes quite a lot of noise, so before we head off, let me tell you a few things about what you're going to see.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: This area is famous for its ancient lighthouse, which you'll see from the boat as we turn past the first little island.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: It was built in 1838 to protect sailors, as a number of shipwrecks had led to significant loss of life.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: The construction itself was complicated, as some of the original drawings kept by the local council show.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: It sits right on top of the cliffs in a very isolated spot.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: In the 19th century, there were many jobs there, such as polishing the brass lamps, chopping firewood, and cleaning windows that kept lighthouse keepers busy.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: These workers were mainly prison convicts until the middle of that century, when ordinary families willing to live in such circumstances took over.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Some of you have asked me what creatures we can expect to see.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: I know everyone loves the penguins, but they're very shy, and unfortunately tend to hide from passing boats.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: But you might see birds in the distance, such as sea eagles flying around the cliff edges where they nest.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: When we get to the rocky area inhabited by fur seals, we'll stop and watch them swimming around the coast.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: They're inquisitive creatures, so don't be surprised if one pops up right in front of you.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Their predators, orca whales, hunt along the coastline too.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: But spotting one of these is rare.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Dolphins on the other hand can sometimes approach on their own or in groups, as they ride the waves beside us.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Lastly, I want to mention the caves.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: Tasmania is famous for its caves, and the ones we'll pass by are so amazing that people are lost for words when they see them.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: They can only be approached by sea, but if you feel that you want to see more than we're able to show you, then you can take a kayak into the area on another day.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And one of our staff will give you more information on that.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: What we'll do is to go through a narrow channel, past some incredible rock formations.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: And from there, we'll be able to see the openings to the caves, and at that point, we'll talk to you about what lies beyond.
script.speaker: LOU MILLER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two veterinary science students called Diana and Tim discussing their work placements and their course modules.

script.text: So, Tim, we have to do a short summary of our work experience on a farm.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: My farm was great, but arranging the work experience was hard.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: One problem was it was miles away, and I don't drive.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: And also, I'd really wanted a placement for a month, but I could only get one for two weeks.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Hmm. I was lucky.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: The farmer let me stay on the farm, so I didn't have to travel.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: But finding the right sort of farm to apply to wasn't easy.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: No, they don't seem to have websites, do they?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I found mine through a friend of my mother's, but it wasn't easy.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: No.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: My farm was mostly livestock, especially sheep.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I really enjoyed helping out with them.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I was up most of one night helping a sheep deliver a lamb.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: On your own?
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: No, the farmer was there, and he told me what to do.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: It wasn't a straightforward birth.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: But I managed.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: It was a great feeling to see the lamb stagger to its feet and start feeding almost straight away, and to know that it was OK.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Hmm. Then another time a lamb had broken its leg, and they got the vet in to set it, and he talked me through what he was doing.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That was really useful.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yes, my farm had sheep too.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: The farm was in a valley, and they had a lowland breed called Suffolks, although the farmer said they'd had other breeds in the past.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: So were they bred for their meat?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Mostly, yes.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: They're quite big and solid.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: My farm was up in the hills, and they had a different breed of sheep.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: They were Cheviots.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Oh.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I heard their wool's really sought after.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Yes, it's very hard wearing, and they use it for carpets.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I was interested in the amount of supplements they add to animals' feed nowadays.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Like, even the chickens got extra vitamins and electrolytes in their feed.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yes, I found that too, and they're not cheap.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: But my farmer said some are overpriced for what they are.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: And he didn't give them as a matter of routine, just at times when the chickens seemed to particularly require them.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Yes, mine said the same.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: He said certain breeds of chickens might need more supplements than the others.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: But the cheap and expensive ones are all basically the same.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: So did your farm have any other livestock, Diana?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yes, dairy cows.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Uh. I made a really embarrassing mistake when I was working in the milk shed.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Some cows had been treated with antibiotics, so their milk wasn't suitable for human consumption.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: And it had to be put in a separate container, but I got mixed up, and I poured some milk from the wrong cow in with the milk for humans, so the whole lot had to be thrown away.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: The farmer wasn't too happy with me.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I asked my farmer how much he depended on the vet to deal with health problems.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I'd read reports that the livestock's health is being affected.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: As farmers are under pressure to increase production.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Well, he didn't agree with that, but he said that actually some of the stuff the vets do like minor operations.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: He'd be quite capable of doing himself.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yeah. My farmer said the same. But he reckons vets' skills are still needed.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now we've got to give a bit of feedback about last term's modules, just short comments, apparently.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Shall we do that now?
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: OK, so medical terminology.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Well, my heart sank when I saw that, especially right at the beginning of the course. And I did struggle with it.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I thought it would be hard, but actually I found it all quite straightforward.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: What did you think about diet and nutrition?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: OK, I suppose.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Do you remember what they told us about pet food, and the fact that there's such limited checking into whether or not it's contaminated?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I mean in comparison with the checks on food for humans, I thought that was terrible.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I think the module that really impressed me was the animal disease one.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: When we looked at domesticated animals in different parts of the world, like camels and water buffalo and alpaca, the economies of so many countries depend on these.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: But scientists don't know much about the diseases that affect them.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Yes, I thought they'd know a lot about ways of controlling and eradicating those diseases, but that's not the case at all.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I loved the wildlife medication unit.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Things like helping birds that have been caught in oil spills.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That's something I hadn't thought about before.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: I thought I might write my dissertation on something connected with that.
script.speaker: DIANA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: So...
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear an anthropology student giving a presentation on spiral path designs known as labyrinths.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Labyrinths have existed for well over 4,000 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Labyrinths and labyrinthine symbols have been found in regions as diverse as modern day Turkey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ireland, Greece and India.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are various designs of labyrinth, but what they all have in common is a winding spiral path, which leads to a central area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There is one starting point at the entrance, and the goal is to reach the central area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finding your way through a labyrinth involves many twists and turns.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it's not possible to get lost, as there is only one single path.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In modern times, the word labyrinth has taken on a different meaning, and is often used as a synonym for a maze.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A maze is quite different.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it is a kind of puzzle with an intricate network of paths.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Mazes became fashionable in the 15th and 16th centuries in Europe, and can still be found in the gardens of great houses and palaces.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The paths are usually surrounded by thick high hedges, so that it's not possible to see over them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Entering a maze usually involves getting lost a few times.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before using logic to work out the pattern and find your way to the center, and then out again.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are lots of dead ends and paths which lead you back to where you started.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The word maze is believed to come from a Scandinavian word for a state of confusion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is where the word amazing comes from.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Labyrinths on the other hand have a very different function, although people now often refer to things they find complicated as labyrinths.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is not how they were seen in the past.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The winding spiral of the labyrinth has been used for centuries as a metaphor for life's journey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It served as a spiritual reminder that there is purpose and meaning to our lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And helped to give people a sense of direction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Labyrinths are thought to encourage a feeling of calm, and have been used as a meditation and prayer tool in many cultures over many centuries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The earliest examples of the labyrinth spiral pattern have been found carved into stone from Sardinia to Scandinavia, from Arizona to India.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Europe, these spiral carvings date from the late Bronze Age.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Native American Pima tribe wove baskets with a circular labyrinth design.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That depicted their own cosmology, in ancient Greece, the labyrinth spiral was used on coins around 4,000 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Labyrinths made of mosaics were commonly found in bathhouses, villas, and tombs throughout the Roman Empire.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Northern Europe, there were actual physical labyrinths designed for walking on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These were cut into the turf or grass, usually in a circular pattern.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The origin of these walking labyrinths remains unclear, but they were probably used for fertility rites, which may date back thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: 11 examples of turf labyrinths survive today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Including the largest one at Saffron Walden in England, which used to have a large tree in the middle of it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: More recently, labyrinths have experienced something of a revival.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some believe that walking a labyrinth promotes healing and mindfulness, and there are those who believe in its emotional and physical benefits,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which include slower breathing and a restored sense of balance and perspective.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This idea has become so popular that labyrinths have been laid into the floors of spas, wellness centers, and even prisons in recent years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A pamphlet at Colorado Children's Hospital informs patients that 'walking a labyrinth can often calm people in the midst of a crisis'.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And apparently, it's not only patients who benefit.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many visitors find walking a labyrinth less stressful than sitting in a corridor or waiting room.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some doctors even walk the labyrinth during their breaks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In some hospitals, patients who can't walk can have a paper finger labyrinth brought to their bed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The science behind the theory is a little sketchy, but there are dozens of small-scale studies which support claims about the benefits of labyrinths.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, one study found that walking a labyrinth provided 'short-term calming, relaxation and relief from anxiety' for Alzheimer's patients.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what is it about labyrinths that makes their appeal so universal?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1, you will hear a man asking about voluntary work in the village that he has just moved to.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, Jane Fairbanks speaking.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Oh, good morning.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: My name is Frank Pritchard.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I've just retired and moved to Southoe.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I'd like to become a volunteer.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: And I gather you coordinate voluntary work in the village.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: What sort of thing could I do?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Well, we need help with the village library.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: We borrow books from the town library, and individuals also donate them.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: So one thing you could do is get involved in collecting them.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: If you've got a car, that is.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Yes, that's no problem.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: The times are pretty flexible, so we can arrange it to suit you.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Oh, another thing is the records that we keep of the books we're given.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And those we borrow and need to return to the town library, it would be very useful to have another person to help keep them up to date.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I'm used to working on a computer, I presume they're computerized?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Oh, yes.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Is the library purpose built?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I haven't noticed it when I've walked around the village.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: No, we simply have the use of a room in the village hall, the West Room.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: It's on the left as you go in.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I must go and have a look inside the hall.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Yes, it's a nice building.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Do you run a lunch club in the village for elderly people?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I know a lot of places do.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Yes, we have a very successful club.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I could help with transport, if that's of any use.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Oh, definitely.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: People come to the club from neighboring villages, and we're always in need of more drivers.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And does the club have groups that focus on a particular hobby too?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I could get involved in one or two, particularly if there are any art groups.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Excellent.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I'll find out where we need help and get back to you.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Fine.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: What about help for individual residents?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Do you arrange that at all?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Yes, we do it as a one-off.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Oh, in fact, there's Mrs Carroll.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: She needs a lift to the hospital next week, and we're struggling to find someone.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: When's her appointment?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: On Tuesday, it would take the whole morning.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I could do that.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Oh, that would be great.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And also next week, we're arranging to have some work done to Mr Selsbury's house before he moves, as he isn't healthy enough to do it himself.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: We've got some people to decorate his kitchen.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: But if you could do some weeding in his garden, that would be wonderful.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: OK, I'd enjoy that, and presumably the day and time are flexible.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Oh, yes.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Just say when would suit you best, and we'll let Mr Selsbury know.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The volunteers group also organizes monthly social events, which is a great way to meet other people, of course.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Uh huh.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: So, next month on the 19th of October, we're holding a quiz.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: A couple of residents are great at planning unusual ones, and we always fill the village hall.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: That sounds like fun.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Can I do anything to help?
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Well, because of the number of people, we need plenty of refreshments for halfway through.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: So, if you could provide any, we'd be grateful.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I'm sure I could.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: I'll think about what to make and let you know.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Then on November the 18th.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: We're holding a dance, also in the village hall.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: We've booked a band that specializes in music of the 1930s - they've been before.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And we've had a lot of requests to bring them back.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: I'm not really a dancer, but I'd like to do something to help.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Well, we sell tickets in advance.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: And having an extra person to check them at the door as people arrive would be good.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: It can be quite a bottleneck if everyone arrives at once.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: OK, I'm happy with that.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Oh. We're also arranging a New Year's Eve party.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: We're expecting that to be a really big event, so instead of the village hall, it'll be held in the Mountfort hotel.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: The mountfort, MOUNTFORT Hotel.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: It isn't in Southoe itself, but it's only a couple of miles away.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: The hotel will be providing dinner, and we've booked a band.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: The one thing we haven't got yet is a poster.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: That isn't something you could do by any chance, is it?
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Well, actually, yes.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Uh. Before I retired, I was a graphic designer, so that's right up my street.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: Perfect, I'll give you the details, and then perhaps you could send me a draft.
script.speaker: JANE

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: FRANK

script.text: That is the end of part 1.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a guide at a tourist attraction called Oniton Hall talking to a group of visitors.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, and welcome to Oniton Hall, one of the largest estates in the area.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: My name's Nick, and I'm one of the guides.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: I'll give you a brief introduction to the estate while you're sitting down, and then we'll walk round.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The estate consists of the house, gardens, park land and farm, and it dates back to the 14th century.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The original house was replaced in the late 17th century.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: And of course, it has had a large number of owners.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Almost all of them have left their mark, generally by adding new rooms.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Like the ballroom and conservatory, or by demolishing others.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The farm looks much as it's always done, although the current owner has done a great deal of work to the flower beds.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: In the 17th century, the estate was owned by a very wealthy man called Sir Edward Downes.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: His intention was to escape from the world of politics.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: After years as an active politician, and to build a new house worthy of his big collection of books, paintings and sculptures.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: He broke off contact with his former political allies and hosted meetings of creative and literary people, like painters and poets.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Unusually for his time, he didn't care whether his guests were rich or poor, as long as they had talent.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Big houses like Oniton had dozens of servants until the 1920s or 30s, and we've tried to show what their working lives were like.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Photographs of course don't give much of an idea, so instead, as you go round the house, you'll see volunteers dressed up as nineteenth-century servants, going about their work.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: They'll explain what they're doing, and tell you their recipes, or what tools they're using.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: We've just introduced this feature to replace the audio guide.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: We used to have available.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: I see there are a number of children here with you today.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Well, we have several activities specially for children, like dressing up in the sorts of clothes that children wore in the past.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: And as it's a fine day, some of you will probably want to play in the adventure playground.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Our latest addition is child-sized tractors, that you can drive around the grounds.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: We'll also be going into the farm, that's part of the estate, where there's plenty to do.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Most of the buildings date from the 18th century.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: So you can really step back into an agricultural past.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Until recently, the dairy was where milk from the cows was turned into cheese.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: It's now the place to go for lunch, or afternoon tea, or just a cup of coffee, and a slice of homemade cake.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The big stone building that dominates the farm is the large barn, and in here is our collection of agricultural tools.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: These were used in the past to plough the earth, sow seeds, make gates, and much more.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: There's a small barn, also made of stone, where you can groom the donkeys and horses to keep their coats clean.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: They really seem to enjoy having it done.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: And children love grooming them.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The horses no longer live in the stables, which instead is the place to go to buy gifts, books, our own jams and pickles.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: And clothes and blankets made of wool from our sheep.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: Outside the shed, which is the only brick building, you can climb into a horse-drawn carriage for a lovely relaxing tour of the park and farm.
script.speaker: NICK

script.text: The carriages are well over 100 years old.
