script.text: Part 3, you will hear two Theater Studies students discussing stage and screen performances of Shakespeare's play Romeo and Juliet.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 and 22.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 and 22.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Did you make notes while you were watching the performances of Romeo and Juliet,
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Gemma?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yes, I did.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I found it quite hard though.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I kept getting too involved in the play.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Me too.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I ended up not taking notes.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I wrote down my impressions when I got home.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Do you mind if I check a few things with you, in case I've missed anything, and I've also got some questions about our assignment.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: No, it's good to talk things through.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I may have missed things too.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: OK, great.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: So first of all I'm not sure how much information we should include in our reviews.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Well, I don't think we need to describe what happens, especially as Romeo and Juliet is one of Shakespeare's most well-known plays.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Yeah, everyone knows the story.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: In an essay, we'd focus on the poetry and Shakespeare's use of imagery, et cetera.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: But that isn't really relevant in a review.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: We're supposed to focus on how effective this particular production is.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Hmm, we should say what made it a success or a failure.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: And part of that means talking about the emotional impact the performance had on us.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I think that's important.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: And we should definitely mention how well the director handled important bits of the play, like when Romeo climbs onto Juliet's balcony.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: And the fight between Mercutio and Tybalt.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: It would also be interesting to mention the theater space, and how the director used it, but I don't think we'll have space in 800 words.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: No, OK.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: That all sounds quite straightforward.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 23 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 23 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, what about the Emporium Theater's production of the play?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I thought some things worked really well, but there were some problems too.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: What about the set for example?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I think it was visually really stunning.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I'd say that was probably the most memorable thing about this production.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: You're right.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: The set design was really amazing, but actually I have seen similar ideas used in other productions.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Hmm. What about the lighting?
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Some of the scenes were so dimly lit, it was quite hard to see.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I didn't dislike it.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: It helped to change the mood of the quieter scenes.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: That's a good point.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: What did you think of the costumes?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I was a bit surprised by the contemporary dress, I must say.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I think it worked well, but I had assumed it would be more conventional.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Me too.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I liked the music at the beginning, and I thought the musicians were brilliant.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: But I thought they were wasted, because the music didn't have much impact in Acts 2 and 3.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Yes, that was a shame.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: One problem with this production was that the actors didn't deliver the lines that well.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: They were speaking too fast.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: It was a problem I agree, but I thought it was because they weren't speaking loudly enough, especially at key points in the play.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I actually didn't have a problem with that.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: It's been an interesting experience watching different versions of Romeo and Juliet, hasn't it?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Definitely.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: It's made me realize how relevant the play still is.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I mean a lot's changed since Shakespeare's time, but in many ways nothing's changed.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: There are always disagreements and tension between teenagers and their parents.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: That's something all young people can relate to, more than the violence and the extreme emotions in the play.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: How did you find watching it in translation?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Really interesting.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I expected to find it more challenging, but I could follow the story pretty well.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I stopped worrying about not being able to understand all the words, and focused on the actors' expressions.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: The ending was pretty powerful.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yes, that somehow intensified the emotion for me.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Did you know Shakespeare's been translated into more languages than any other writer?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: What's the reason for his international appeal, do you think?
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: I was reading that it's because his plays are about basic themes that people everywhere are familiar with.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: And they can also be understood on different levels.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: The characters have such depth.
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Which allows directors to experiment and find new angles.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: That's really important, because...
script.speaker: GEMMA

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a lecturer on a languages course talking about the impact of digital technology on Icelandic, the native language of Iceland.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's make a start.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Over the past few sessions, we've been considering the reasons why some world languages are in decline.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And today, I'm going to introduce another factor that affects languages, and the speakers of those languages, and that's technology, and in particular digital technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In order to illustrate its effect, I'm going to focus on the Icelandic language, which is spoken by around 321,000 people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most of whom live in Iceland, an island in the North Atlantic Ocean.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The problem for this language is not the number of speakers, even though this number is small, nor is it about losing words to other languages such as English.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, the vocabulary of Icelandic is continually increasing, because when speakers need a new word for something, they tend to create one, rather than borrowing from another language.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All this makes Icelandic quite a special language.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's changed very little in the past millennium, yet it can handle 21st century concepts related to the use of computers and digital technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Take for example the word for web browser.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is vafri in Icelandic, which comes from the verb 'to wander'.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I can't think of a more appropriate term, because that's exactly what you do mentally when you browse the internet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then there's an Icelandic word for podcast, which is too hard to pronounce, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Icelandic then is alive and growing, but, and it's a big but, young Icelanders spend a great deal of time in the digital world, and this world is predominantly English.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Think about smartphones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They didn't even exist until comparatively recently, but today young people use them all the time to read books, watch TV or films.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Play games, listen to music, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Obviously, this is a good thing in many respects, because it promotes their bilingual skills.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the extent of the influence of English in the virtual world is staggering.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it's all happening really fast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For their parents and grandparents, the change is less concerning, because they already have their native-speaker skills in Icelandic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But for young speakers, well, the outcome is a little troubling.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, teachers have found that playground conversations in Icelandic secondary schools can be conducted entirely in English, while teachers of much younger children have reported situations where their classes find it easier to say what is in a picture using English, rather than Icelandic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The very real and worrying consequence of all this, is that the young generation in Iceland is at risk of losing its mother tongue.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, this is happening to other European languages too, but while internet companies might be willing to offer say French options in their systems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's much harder for them to justify the expense of doing the same for a language that has a population the size of a French town, such as Nice.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The other drawback of Icelandic is the grammar, which is significantly more complex than in most languages.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the moment, the tech giants are simply not interested in tackling this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what is the Icelandic government doing about this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, large sums of money are being allocated to a language technology fund that it is hoped will lead to the development of Icelandic sourced apps.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And other social media and digital systems, but clearly this is going to be an uphill struggle.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On the positive side, they know that Icelandic is still the official language of education and government.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has survived for well over 1,000 years, and the experts predict that its future in this nation state is sound, and will continue to be so.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, there's no doubt that it's becoming an inevitable second choice in young people's lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This raises important questions when you consider how much of the past is tied up in a language.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Will young Icelanders lose their sense of their own identity?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another issue that concerns the government of Iceland is this. If children are learning two languages through different routes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Neither of which they are fully fluent in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Will they be able to express themselves properly?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1, you will hear a man called Jack giving advice to a friend about surfing holidays.

script.text: Jack, I'm thinking of taking the kids to the seaside on a surfing holiday this summer, and I wanted to ask your advice, as I know you're such an expert.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, I don't know about that.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: But yes, I've done a bit of surfing over the years.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I'd thoroughly recommend it.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I think it's the kind of holiday all the family can enjoy together.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: The thing about surfing is that it's great for all ages and all abilities.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: My youngest started when he was only 3.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Wow!
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: But it's quite physically demanding, isn't it?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I've heard you need to be pretty fit.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, you'll certainly learn more quickly, and won't tire as easily.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Well, that should be OK for us.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: You've been surfing a few times in Ireland, haven't you?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, there's some great surfing there, which people don't always realize.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: And which locations would you recommend?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: There seem to be quite a few.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, there are loads.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Last year we went to County Donegal.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: There are several great places to surf there.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: What about in County Clare?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I read that's also really good for surfing.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, it is.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I've been there a few times.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Most people go to Lahinch.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: My kids love it there, the waves aren't too challenging, and the town is very lively.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Are there good hotels there?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, some very nice ones.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: And there are also a few basic hostels and camp sites.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: It's great if you need lessons, as the surf schools are excellent.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Sounds good.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, and there's lots to see in the area.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Like those well-known cliffs, I've forgotten the name of them.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Oh, don't worry, I can look them up.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I've also been surfing in County Mayo.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Which is less well known for surfing, but we had a really good time.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: That was a few years ago, when the kids were younger.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: There's a good surf school at Carrowniskey beach.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: How do you spell that?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: CARROWNISKEY.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I put the kids into the surf camp they run during the summer for 10 to 16 year olds.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Oh, right.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: How long was that for?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: 3 hours every day for a week.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: It was perfect.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: They were so tired out after that.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I can imagine.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: One thing we did while the kids were surfing was to rent some kayaks to have a look around the bay, which is nearby.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: It's really beautiful.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Oh, I'd love to do that.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear the manager of a childcare service at a primary school talking to parents at an open day about the school's childcare service offered before and after school.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good afternoon.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: My name's Mrs Carter, and I run the before and after school extended hours childcare service.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: I hope you've had a chance to have a good look around the school, and talk to staff and pupils.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: I know that many of you are interested in using our childcare service when your child joins the school, and perhaps you already know something about it, but for those that don't, I'll go through the main details now.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: We offer child care for children from the ages of 4 to 11, both before and after school.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: I know that many parents who work find this service invaluable.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: You can leave your child with us, safe in the knowledge that they will be extremely well cared for.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: We are insured to provide care for up to 70 children, although we rarely have this many attending at any one session.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: I think we generally expect around 50 to 60 children for the afternoon sessions.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: And about half that number for the breakfast sessions, although we currently do have 70 children registered with us, not all of these attend every day.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: It's 10 years since we began offering an extended hours service, and we've come a long way during that time.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: When we first opened, we only had about 20 children attending regularly.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: We try to keep our costs as low as we can, and we think we provide very good value for money. For the afternoon sessions, which run from 3.30 until 6 p.m., it's £7.20.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: But if you prefer, you can pay for one hour only, which costs £3.50, or two hours which costs £5.70.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: The cost of the child care includes food and snacks.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: They'll be given breakfast in the morning, and in the afternoon, a healthy snack as soon as they finish school.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: At 5 pm, children are given something more substantial, such as pasta or a casserole.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: Please inform us of any allergies that your child might have.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: And we'll make sure they're offered a suitable alternative.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: As you may know, the childcare service runs through the school holidays from 8:00 am to 6:00 pm.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: We offer a really varied and exciting program to keep the children entertained.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: We don't want them to feel as if they are still at school.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: It will also feel different because they'll get the chance to make new friends with children from other schools.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: Spaces are available for them, because a lot of our term time children don't always attend during the holiday.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: In the past, parents have asked if children over the age of 11 are allowed to come with their younger brothers and sisters, but I'm afraid we're unable to do this.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: Because of the type of insurance we have.
script.speaker: MRS CARTER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear Holly, a student on an events management course, talking to her tutor about her work placement.

script.text: Hello, Doctor Green.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: I'm here to talk to you about my work placement.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Oh, yes, it's Holly, isn't it?

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: So, which work placement have you chosen?

script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I know, but it's the fresh air that attracts me.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Organizing something indoors doesn't have the same appeal, even though it might be fun.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Yes, I've already thought about that.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.speaker: HOLLY

script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Oh, I see.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: That'll include keeping everyone within the boundary once they're in their kit and on the field.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You'll need to inspect areas like changing rooms as well, for anything someone can trip over.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: But your main priority will be not to lose anyone.

script.text: Uh. Right.

script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: And don't forget about the spectators.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Hmm. I was thinking that many of them will be parents who could help run the event.

script.text: I wouldn't rely on that.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: They'll be more interested in filming their children than volunteering.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I'll need to make sure they don't interfere with events doing that.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: And that's not always easy, especially when a proud parent's trying to get a snap of their child,
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: and you want them to move elsewhere.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, uh, what about the scheduling?

script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Like rain for instance, though so far we've always been lucky with that.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yeah, and I was thinking about what to do if someone got hurt as well.

script.text: I know that last year that caused a terrible delay.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: You have to be prepared for such things.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Oh, what if a match ends in a draw?
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: That'll be up to you, and again, you need to plan for it.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, the aim of your work placement is to give you the opportunity to develop the skills that an events manager needs.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So, let's talk about those a bit.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well, I think my communication skills are pretty good.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: I can talk on the phone to people, and book venues, and that kind of thing.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Just remember, it isn't only about what you say.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: If you meet someone face to face and want to persuade them to be a sponsor, for example.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Oh, I'll dress up for that, sure.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Good. Let's go on to think about your organizational skills.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You're working in a very people-based industry, and that means things won't always go to plan.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I guess it's being prepared to make changes that matters.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You may have to make an on-the-spot change to a timetable because of a problem you hadn't anticipated.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Just do it! OK.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: How's your time management these days?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I'm working on it.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: I'm certainly better when I have a deadline, which is why this work suits me.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Yes, but it's how you respond as that deadline approaches.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I know I've got to look calm, even if I'm in a panic.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Just think to yourself, no one must know I'm under pressure.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yeah, even though I'm multitasking like crazy.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Another skill that events managers need is creativity.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Often your client has what we call the big picture idea, but it's up to the events manager to think of all the fine points that go to making it work.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Right, so I need to listen carefully to that idea, and then fill in all the gaps.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: That's right, and you'll have a team working under you.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So another key skill is leadership.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Your team may have lots of ideas too, but you've got to make the ultimate choices.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Do we have refreshments inside or out for example?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Isn't it better to be democratic?
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: It's a nice idea, but you have the ultimate responsibility.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So believe in what you think best.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Be prepared to say yes, that's a good idea, but it won't work here.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I see what you mean.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: What about the networking side of things?
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: I know it's an area that a lot of students worry about, because we don't have much experience to offer others.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: But even without it, you can still be an interesting person with useful ideas.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And the more people you impress, the better.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I guess that will help me when I apply for a real job.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Think ahead, remember what your ambitions are.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And keep them in mind.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Uh. Definitely.
script.speaker: HOLLY

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation on bird migration.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Scientists believe that a majority of the Earth's bird population migrate in some fashion or other.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some travel seasonally for relatively short distances.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as birds that move from their winter habitats in lowlands to mountaintops for the summers. Others, like the Arctic Tern, travel more than 25,000 miles seasonally.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Between the northern and southern poles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Bird migration has been studied over many centuries through a variety of observations, but until relatively recently, where birds went to in the winter was considered something of a mystery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The lack of modern science and technology led to many theories that we now recognize as error filled, and even somewhat amusing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Take hibernation theory for example, 2000 years ago, it was commonly believed that when birds left an area, they went underwater to hibernate in the seas and oceans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another theory for the regular appearance and disappearance of birds was that they spent winter hidden in mud, till the weather changed and food became abundant again.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The theory that some birds hibernate persisted until experiments were done on caged birds in the 1940s which demonstrated that birds have no hibernation instinct.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the earliest naturalists and philosophers from ancient Greece was Aristotle, who was the first writer to discuss the disappearance and reappearance of some bird species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At certain times of year, he developed the theory of transmutation, the seasonal change of one species into another, by observing redstarts and robins.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He observed that in the autumn, small birds called redstarts began to lose their feathers, which convinced Aristotle that they changed into robins for the winter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And back into redstarts in the summer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These assumptions are understandable, given that this pair of species are similar in shape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But are a classic example of an incorrect interpretation based on correct observations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The most bizarre theory was put forward by an English amateur scientist, Charles Morton, in the 17th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He wrote a surprisingly well regarded paper.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Claiming that birds migrate to the moon and back every year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He came to this conclusion as the only logical explanation for the total disappearance of some species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the key moments in the development of migration theory came in 1822 when a white stork was shot in Germany.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This particular stork made history because of the long spear in its neck, which incredibly had not killed it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Everyone immediately realized this spear was definitely not European.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It turned out to be a spear from a tribe in central Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was a truly defining moment in the history of ornithology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because it was the first evidence that storks spend their winters in sub-Saharan Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can still see the arrow stork in the zoological collection of the university of Rostock in Germany.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People gradually became aware that European birds moved south in autumn and north in summer, but didn't know much about it until the practice of catching birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And putting rings on their legs became established.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before this, very little information was available about the actual destinations of particular species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And how they traveled there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People speculated that larger birds provided a kind of taxi service for smaller birds by carrying them on their backs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This idea came about, because it seemed impossible that small birds weighing only a few grams could fly over vast oceans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This idea was supported by observations of bird behavior, such as the harassment of larger birds by smaller birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The development of bird ringing, by a Danish school teacher, Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen, made many discoveries possible.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is still common practice today, and relies upon what is known as recovery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is when ringed birds are found dead in the place they have migrated to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And identified.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Huge amounts of data were gathered in the early part of the 20th century, and for the first time in history, people understood where birds actually went to in winter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1931, an atlas was published showing where the most common species of European birds migrated to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: More recent theories about bird migration...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, Easy Life Cleaning Services, Jacinta speaking.

script.text: Oh, hello.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a training manager giving a talk to a group of senior staff from a hotel chain about the problem of high staff turnover.

script.text: As many of you here today have worked in the hotel industry for some time, I'm sure you have experienced the problem of high staff turnover in your hotels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Every hotel relies on having loyal and experienced members of staff who make sure that everything runs smoothly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If staff are constantly changing it can make life difficult for everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But why do staff leave frequently in many hotels?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, many hotel jobs such as cleaning are low skilled and are not well paid.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A lot of managers think it's this, and the long hours that are the main causes of high staff turnover, but what they don't realize is that it's the lack of training in many hotel jobs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which is a huge factor.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what kind of problems does a high turnover of staff cause?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, having to recruit new staff all the time can be very time consuming.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And managers may have to cover some duties while waiting for new staff to arrive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means they don't have time to think about less immediate problems, such as how to improve their service.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When staff leave, it can also severely affect the colleagues they leave behind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has a negative effect on remaining staff, who may start to feel that they too should be thinking about leaving.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what can be done to change this situation?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Firstly, managers should stop making basic errors, which leave their staff feeling upset and resentful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When organizing shifts, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Make sure you never give certain staff preferential treatment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All staff should be given some choice about when they work, and everyone should have to work some evening and weekend shifts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you treat staff fairly, they'll be more likely to step in and help when extra staff are needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Keeping staff happy has other tangible benefits for the business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Take the Dunwich Hotel as an example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It had been experiencing a problem with staff complaints, and in order to deal with this, invested in staff training and improved staff conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Not only did the level of complaints fall, but they also noticed a significant increase in the amount each customer spent during their stay.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They have now introduced a customer loyalty scheme, which is going really well.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, I'd like to look at some ways you can reduce staff turnover in your hotels, and I'll do this by giving some examples of hotels where I've done some training recently.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Sun Club received feedback which showed that staff thought managers didn't value their opinions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They weren't made to feel they were partners who were contributing to the success of the business as a whole.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This situation has changed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Junior staff at all levels are regularly invited to meetings where their ideas are welcomed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A year ago, The Portland recognized the need to invest in staff retention.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Their first step was to introduce a scheme for recognizing talent amongst their employees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The hope is that organizing training for individuals with management potential will encourage them to stay with the business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At Bluewater, managers decided to recognize 50 high achievers from across the company's huge hotel chain as a reward.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They're sent on an all-expenses-paid trip abroad every year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Fun is an important element in the trips, but there's also the opportunity to learn something useful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This year's trip included a visit to a brewery, where staff learned about the new beer that would be served in the hotel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Pentlow Hotels identified that retention of junior reception staff was an issue in order to encourage them to see that working in a hotel could be worthwhile and rewarding, with good prospects, they introduced a management program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These staff were given additional responsibilities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the chance to work in various roles in the hotel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Green Planet wanted to be seen as a caring employer. To make life easier for staff, many of whom had childcare responsibilities,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: the hotel began issuing vouchers to help cover the cost of childcare.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Louise Marsh at the Amesbury has one of the best staff retention rates in the business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since she joined the company, she's made a huge effort to achieve this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By creating a co-operative and supportive environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For her, the staff are part of a large family where everyone is valued.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, now I'd like to...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a presentation by a food science student about the production of maple syrup.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: For first, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today we're going to look at another natural food product, and that's maple syrup.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What is this exactly?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, maple syrup looks rather like clear honey, but it's not made by bees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's produced from the plant fluid or sap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Inside the maple tree, and that makes maple syrup a very natural product.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Maple syrup is a thick, golden, sweet-tasting liquid.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That can be bought in bottles or jars, and poured onto foods such as waffles and ice cream, or used in the baking of cakes and pastries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It contains no preservatives or added ingredients, and it provides a healthy alternative to refined sugar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's just talk a bit about the maple tree itself, which is where maple syrup comes from.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, there are many species of maple tree.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they'll grow without fertilizer in areas where there's plenty of moisture in the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, they'll only do this if another important criterion is fulfilled.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which is that they must have full or partial sun exposure during the day and very cool nights, and I'll talk more about that in a minute.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are only certain parts of the world that provide all these conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One is Canada, and by that, I mean all parts of Canada.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the other is the northeastern states of North America.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In these areas, the climate suits the trees perfectly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, Canada produces over two thirds of the world's maple syrup.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which is why the five pointed maple leaf is a Canadian symbol, and has featured on the flag since 1964.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So how did maple syrup production begin?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, long before Europeans settled in these parts of the world, the indigenous communities had started producing maple sugar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They bored holes in the trunks of maple trees, and used containers made of tree bark to collect the liquid sap as it poured out.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As they were unable to keep the liquid for any length of time, they didn't have storage facilities in those days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They boiled the liquid by placing pieces of rock that had become scorching hot from the sun.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Into the sap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They did this until it turned into sugar, and they were then able to use this to sweeten their food and drinks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since that time,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: improvements have been made to the process, but it has changed very little overall.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, let's look at the production of maple syrup today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Clearly, the maple forests are a valuable resource in many Canadian and North American communities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trees have to be well looked after, and they cannot be used to make syrup until the trunks reach a diameter of around 25 cm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This can take anything up to 40 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As I've already mentioned, maple trees need the right conditions to grow, and also to produce sap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why is this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, what happens is that during a cold night, the tree absorbs water from the soil, and that rises through the tree's vascular system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But then in the warmer daytime, the change in temperature causes the water to be pushed back down to the bottom of the tree.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This continual movement up and down leads to the formation of the sap, needed for maple syrup production.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When the tree is ready, it can be tapped, and this involves drilling a small hole into the trunk, and inserting a tube into it that ends in a bucket.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trees can often take several taps, though the workers take care not to cause any damage to the healthy growth of the tree itself.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The sap that comes out of the trees consists of 98% water and 2% sugar and other nutrients.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has to be boiled, so that much of that water evaporates.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this process has to take place immediately, using what are called evaporators.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are basically extremely large pans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The sap is poured into these, a fire is built, and the pans are then heated until the sap boils.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it does this, the water evaporates.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the syrup begins to form.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The evaporation process creates large quantities of steam, and the sap becomes thicker and denser, and at just the right moment, when the sap is thick enough to be called maple syrup, the worker removes it from the heat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After this process, something called sugar sand has to be filtered out, as this builds up during the boiling and gives the syrup a cloudy appearance and a slightly gritty taste.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Once this has been done, the syrup is ready to be packaged, so that it can be used for a whole variety of products.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It takes 40 liters of sap to produce 1 liter of maple syrup.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So you can get an idea of how much is needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So that's the basic process.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In places like Quebec where...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear the Managing Director of a company called Stevenson's welcoming a group of work experience students.

script.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to Stevenson's, one of the country's major manufacturers of metal goods.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Thank you for choosing us for your two weeks of work experience.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: My name is Julia Simmons, and since the beginning of this year, I've been the managing director.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Stevenson's is quite an old company.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Like me, the founder Ronald Stevenson went into the steel industry when he left school.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: That was in 1923.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: He set up this company when he finished his apprenticeship, in 1926, although he actually started making plans two years earlier, in 1924. He was a very determined young man!
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Stevenson's long-term plan was to manufacture components for the machine tools industry, although in fact that never came about, and for the automotive industry, that is, cars and lorries.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: However, there was a delay of five years before that happened.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Because shortly before the company went into production, Stevenson was given the opportunity to make goods for hospitals.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: And other players in the health care industry, so that's what we did for the first five years.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Over the years, we've expanded the premises considerably.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: We were lucky that the site is big enough, so moving to a new location has never been necessary.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: However, the layout is far from ideal for modern machinery and production methods, so we intend to carry out major refurbishment of this site over the next five years.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: I'd better give you some idea of what you'll be doing during your two weeks with us, so you know what to expect.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Most mornings you'll have a presentation from one of the managers.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: To learn about their department, starting this morning with research and development.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: And you'll all spend some time in each department, observing what's going on and talking to people,
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: as long as you don't stop them from doing their work altogether! In the past, a teacher from your school has come in at the end of each week to find out how the group were getting on.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: But your school isn't able to arrange that this year.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, now I'll briefly help you to orientate yourselves around the site.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: As you can see, we're in the reception area, which we try to make attractive and welcoming to visitors.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: There's a corridor running left from here, and if you go along that, the door facing you at the end is the entrance to the coffee room.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: This looks out onto the main road on one side, and some trees on the other.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: And that'll be where you meet each morning.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: The factory is the very big room on the far side of the site.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Next to it is the warehouse, which can be accessed by lorries going up the road to the turning area at the end.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: You can get to the warehouse by crossing to the far side of the courtyard, and then the door is on your right.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Somewhere you'll be keen to find is the staff canteen.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: This is right next to reception.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: I can confidently say that the food's very good, but the view isn't.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: The windows on one side look onto a corridor and courtyard.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Which aren't very attractive at all, and on the other onto the access road, which isn't much better.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: You'll be using the meeting room quite often, and you'll find it by walking along the corridor to the left of the courtyard, and continuing along it to the end.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: The meeting room is the last one on the right, and I'm afraid there's no natural daylight in the room.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Then you'll need to know where some of the offices are.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: The human resources department is at the front of this building, so you head to the left along the corridor from reception.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: And it's the second room you come to, it looks out onto the main road.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: And finally the board room where you'll be meeting sometimes.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: That has quite a pleasant view, as it looks out onto the trees.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Go along the corridor past the courtyard, right to the end.

script.text: The boardroom is on the left.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: Next to the factory.
script.speaker: JULIA SIMMONS

script.text: How are you getting on with your art project, Tom?

script.text: OK, like they gave us the theme of birds to base our project on, and I'm not really all that interested in wildlife.

script.text: Hmm. Me too.

script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What a letdown.

script.text: Yeah.

script.text: Oh. I missed those because I was ill.

script.text: I wish we could have seen the projects last year's students did.

script.text: Hmm. I suppose they want us to do our own thing, not copy.

script.text: Have you drafted your proposal yet?

script.text: I haven't actually evaluated anything, so I'll have to fix that.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Oh, I didn't know we had to do that.

script.text: I'll have to look at that too.

script.text: Really?

script.text: OK, I'll change that too then.

script.text: Like, I chose a painting of a falcon by Landseer.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I like it because the bird's standing there with his head turned to one side, but he seems to be staring straight at you.

script.text: But I can't just say it's a bit scary, can I?

script.text: Oh, OK.

script.text: Well, actually, I think I'll concentrate on the impression of rapid motion it gives.

script.text: Right.

script.text: I was out walking with my grandfather, and I've never forgotten it.

script.text: Wow.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a professor of philosophy giving a talk on the ancient philosophy of Stoicism.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Ancient philosophy is not just about talking or lecturing, or even reading long dense books.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, it is something people have used throughout history.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To solve their problems and to achieve their greatest triumphs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Specifically, I am referring to Stoicism, which in my opinion is the most practical of all philosophies, and therefore the most appealing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Stoicism was founded in ancient Greece by Zeno of Citium in the early 3rd century BC, but was practiced by the likes of Epictetus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Cato, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Amazingly, we still have access to these ideas, despite the fact that the most famous Stoics never wrote anything down for publication.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Cato definitely didn't, Marcus Aurelius never intended his Meditations to be anything but personal, Seneca's letters were, well, letters.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And Epictetus' thoughts come to us by way of a note-taking student.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Stoic principles were based on the idea that its followers could have an unshakable happiness in this life, and the key to achieving this was virtue.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The road to virtue in turn lay in understanding that destructive emotions like anger and jealousy are under our conscious control.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They don't have to control us, because we can learn to control them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the words of Epictetus, external events I cannot control, but the choices I make with regard to them, I do control.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The modern day philosopher and writer, Nassim Nicholas Taleb, defines a Stoic as someone who has a different perspective on experiences,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which most of us would see as wholly negative.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A Stoic "transforms fear into caution, pain into transformation, mistakes into initiation, and desire into undertaking". Using this definition as a model, we can see that throughout the centuries Stoicism has been practiced in more recent history by kings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Presidents, artists, writers, and entrepreneurs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The founding fathers of the United States were inspired by the philosophy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: George Washington was introduced to Stoicism by his neighbors at age 17.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And later put on a play based on the life of Cato to inspire his men.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Thomas Jefferson kept a copy of Seneca beside his bed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Writers and artists have also been inspired by the Stoics, Eugène Delacroix, the renowned French Romantic artist, known best for his painting Liberty Leading the People, was an ardent Stoic, referring to it as his consoling religion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The economist Adam Smith's theories on capitalism were significantly influenced by the Stoicism that he studied as a schoolboy, under a teacher who had translated Marcus Aurelius' works.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today's political leaders are no different, with many finding their inspiration from the ancient texts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Former US President Bill Clinton rereads Marcus Aurelius every single year, and many have compared former President Obama's calm leadership style to that of Cato.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Wen Jiabao, the former prime minister of China, claims that Meditations is one of two books he travels with, and that he has read it more than 100 times over the course of his life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Stoicism had a profound influence on Albert Ellis, who invented cognitive behavior therapy, which is used to help people manage their problems,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: by changing the way that they think and behave.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's most commonly used to treat depression.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The idea is that we can take control of our lives by challenging the irrational beliefs
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: that create our faulty thinking symptoms and behaviors by using logic instead.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Stoicism has also become popular in the world of business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Stoic principles can build the resilience and state of mind required to overcome setbacks, because Stoics teach turning obstacles into opportunity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A lesson every business entrepreneur needs to learn.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I would argue that studying Stoicism is as relevant today as it was 2,000 years ago, thanks to its brilliant insights into how to lead a good life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the very root of the thinking, there is a very simple way of living.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Control what you can, and accept what you can't.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is not as easy as it sounds, and will require considerable practice.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It can take a lifetime to master.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Stoics also believed the most important foundation for a good and happy life is not money, fame, power or pleasure, but having a disciplined and principled character.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Something which seems to resonate with many people today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Is there anything else you'd like to ask about our services?
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: Yes, I've roughly sorted out the photos into groups according to what they're about.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: So, can you keep them in those groups when you copy them?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Sure, we'll save each group in a different folder on the disk, and if you like, you can suggest a name for each folder.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: So, I could have one called 'Grandparents' for instance?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: And do you do anything besides scan the photos?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Like, can you make any improvements?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, in the standard service, each photo is checked, and we can sometimes touch up the color a bit, or improve the contrast,
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: that can make a big difference.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: OK, and some of the photos are actually quite fragile.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: They won't get damaged in the process, will they?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: No, if any look particularly fragile, we'd do them by hand.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: We do realize how precious these old photos can be.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And another thing is we can make changes to a photo if you want,
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: so, if you want to remove an object from a photo, or maybe alter the background,
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: we can do that.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I might be interested in that.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I'll have a look through the photos and see.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Oh, and talking of fixing photos.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I've got a few that aren't properly in focus.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Can you do anything to make that better?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: No, I'm afraid that's one thing we can't do.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Any other information I can give you?
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: Er... oh, how long will it all take?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: We aim to get the copying done in 10 days.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: Fine.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Right, well, I'll get the photos packed up in a box and post them off to you.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Right, if you've got a strong cardboard box, that's best.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: We've found that plastic ones sometimes break in the post.
script.speaker: EMPLOYEE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Right, thanks for your help.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Bye.

script.text: Bye.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a head teacher talking to parents of pupils about changes at the school.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, and thank you for coming here today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd like to bring you up to date with changes in the school that will affect your children.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you know, the school buildings date from various times, some from the 1970s, some from the last five years, and of course, Dartfield House is over a century old.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was commissioned by a businessman, Neville Richards, and intended as his family home, but he died before it was completed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: His heir chose to sell it to the local council,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: who turned it into offices.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A later plan to convert it into a tourist information center didn't come about through lack of money, and instead it formed the nucleus of this school when it opened 40 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The school has grown as the local population has increased, and I can now give you some news about the lower school site, which is separated from the main site by a road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Planning permission has been granted for development of both sites.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The lower school will move to new buildings that will be constructed on the main site.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Developers will construct houses on the existing lower school site.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Work on the new school buildings should start within the next few months.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A more imminent change concerns the catering facilities and the canteen.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The canteen is always very busy throughout the lunch period.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, it's often full to capacity, because a lot of our pupils like the food that's on offer there, but there's only one serving point.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So most pupils have to wait a considerable time to be served.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is obviously unsatisfactory, as they may have hardly finished their lunch,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: before afternoon lessons start. So we've had a new Food Hall built, and this will come into use next week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It'll have several serving areas, and I'll give you more details about those in a minute.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But one thing we ask you to do to help in the smooth running of the Food Hall,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: is to discuss with your children each morning which type of food they want to eat that day, so they can go straight to the relevant serving point.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There won't be any junk food, everything on offer will be healthy, and there's no change to the current system of paying for lunches by topping up your child's electronic payment card online.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may be wondering what will happen to the old canteen.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll still have tables and chairs in there, and pupils can eat food from the Food Hall or lunch they've brought from home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Eventually, we may use part of the canteen for storage, but first, we'll see how many pupils go in there at lunchtime.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, back to the serving points in the Food Hall, which will all have side dishes, desserts, and drinks on sale, as well as main courses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One serving point we call World Adventures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This will serve a different country's cuisine each day, maybe Chinese one day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And Lebanese the next.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The menus will be planned for a week at a time, so pupils will know what's going to be available, the whole of that week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Street Life is also international, with food from three particular cultures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll ask pupils to make suggestions, so perhaps sometimes there'll be food from Thailand,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ethiopia and Mexico, and then one of them will be replaced by Jamaican food for a week or two.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The speedy Italian serving point will cater particularly for the many pupils who don't eat meat or fish.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can be sure that all the food served there is suitable for them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There'll be plenty of variety, so they shouldn't get bored with the food.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, that's all on the new Food Hall.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now after-school lessons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are very popular with pupils, particularly swimming.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, there's a waiting list for lessons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Cycling is another favorite.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I'm delighted that dozens of pupils make use of the chance to learn to ride in off-road conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It means that more and more cycle to and from school every day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you know, we have a well-equipped performance center, and we're going to start drama classes in there too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Pupils will be able to join in just for fun.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or work up to taking part in a play.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We hope to put on at least one a year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We already teach a number of pupils to use the sound and lighting systems in the center, and a former pupil has given a magnificent grand piano to the school.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So a few pupils will be able to learn at the school, instead of going to the local college, as many of them do at the moment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two psychology students called Luke and Susie discussing their assignment on sleep and dreams.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, Luke, for our next psychology assignment, we have to do something on sleep and dreams.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I've just read an article suggesting why we tend to forget most of our dreams soon after we wake up.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I mean most of my dreams aren't that interesting anyway, but what it said was that if we remembered everything, we might get mixed up about what actually happened.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: And what we dreamed, so it's a sort of protection.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I hadn't heard that idea before.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I'd always assumed that it was just that we didn't have room in our memories for all that stuff.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Me too.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: What do you think about the idea that our dreams may predict the future?
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: It's a belief that you get all over the world.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Yeah, lots of people have a story of it happening to them.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: But the explanation I've read is that for each dream that comes true, we have thousands that don't.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: But we don't notice those, we don't even remember them.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: We just remember the ones where something in the real world, like a view or an action happens to trigger a dream memory.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: So it's just a coincidence really.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Something else I read about is what they call segmented sleeping.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: That's a theory that hundreds of years ago, people used to get up in the middle of the night, and have a chat or something to eat.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Then go back to bed.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: So I tried it myself.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Why?
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Well, it's meant to make you more creative.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I don't know why, but I gave it up after a week,
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: it just didn't fit in with my lifestyle.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: But most preschool children have a short sleep in the day, don't they?
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: There was an experiment some students did here last term.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: To see at what age kids should stop having naps, but they didn't really find an answer.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: They spent a lot of time working out the most appropriate methodology, but the results didn't seem to show any obvious patterns.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Anyway, let's think about our assignment.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Last time, I had problems with the final stage.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Where we had to describe and justify how successful we thought we'd been.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I struggled a bit with the action plan too.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I was OK with the planning, but I got marked down for the self assessment as well.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: And I had big problems with the statistical stuff.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: That's where I really lost marks.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, shall we plan what we have to do for this assignment?
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: First we have to decide on our research question.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: So, how about 'Is there a relationship between hours of sleep and number of dreams?'
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: OK, then we need to think about who we'll do the study on.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: About 12 people.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: And shall we use other psychology students?
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Let's use people from a different department.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: What about history?
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Yes, they might have interesting dreams, or literature students.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: I don't really know any.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: OK, forget that idea.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Then we have to think about our methodology.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: So we could use observation, but that doesn't seem appropriate.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: No, it needs to be self reporting, I think.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: And we could ask them to answer questions online.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: But in this case, paper might be better, as they'll be doing it straight after they wake up,
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: in fact, while they're still half-asleep.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: And we'll have to check the ethical guidelines for this sort of research.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Mm, because our experiment involves humans, so there are special regulations.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: I had a look at those for another assignment I did.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: There's a whole section on risk assessment, and another section on making sure they aren't put under any unnecessary stress.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Let's hope they don't have any bad dreams.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Then when we've collected all our data, we have to analyze it and calculate the correlation between our two variables.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: That's time sleeping and number of dreams, and then present our results visually in a graph.
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: Right, and the final thing is to think about our research and evaluate it.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: So that seems quite straightforward.
script.speaker: LUKE

script.text: Yeah, so now let's get started...
script.speaker: SUSIE

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
