script.text: Part 4, you will hear a sport Science student giving a presentation on the health benefits of dance.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Dancing is something that humans do when they want to have a good time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a universal response to music found in all cultures. But what's only been discovered recently,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: is that dancing not only makes us feel good, it's also extremely good for our health.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Dancing, like other forms of exercise, releases hormones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Such as dopamine, which make us feel relaxed and happy, and it also reduces feelings of stress or anxiety.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Dancing is also a sociable activity, which is another reason it makes us feel good.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One study compared people's enjoyment of dancing at home, in front of a video.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With dancing in a group in a studio.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The people dancing in a group reported feeling happier, whereas those dancing alone did not.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In another experiment, university researchers at York and Sheffield took a group of students and sent each of them into a lab where music was played for five minutes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each had to choose from three options, to sit and listen quietly to the music, to cycle on an exercise bike while they listened.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or to get up and dance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All were given cognitive tasks to perform before and after.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The result showed that those who chose to dance showed much more creativity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When doing problem solving tasks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Doctor Lovatt, at the University of Hertfordshire, believes dance could be a very useful way to help people suffering from mental health problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He thinks dance should be prescribed as therapy to help people overcome issues such as depression.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's well established that dance is a good way of encouraging adolescent girls to take exercise, but what about older people?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Studies have shown that there are enormous benefits for people in their 60s and beyond.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the great things about dance is that there are no barriers to participation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Anyone can have a go, even those whose standard of fitness is quite low.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Dance can be especially beneficial for older adults who can't run or do more intense workouts, or for those who don't want to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One 2015 study found that even a gentle dance workout helps to promote a healthy heart.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And there's plenty of evidence which suggests that dancing lowers the risk of falls.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which could result in a broken hip for example, by helping people to improve their balance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are some less obvious benefits of dance for older people too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One thing I hadn't realized before researching this topic was that dance isn't just a physical challenge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It also requires a lot of concentration, because you need to remember different steps and routines.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For older people, this kind of activity is especially important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because it forces their brain to process things more quickly, and to retain more information.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Current research also shows that dance promotes a general sense of well-being in older participants, which can last up to a week after a class.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Participants report feeling less tired, and having greater motivation to be more active, and do daily activities such as gardening.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or walking to the shops or a park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ballroom or country dancing, both popular with older people, have to be done in groups.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They require collaboration, and often involve touching a dance partner.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All of which encourages interaction on the dance floor.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This helps to develop new relationships, and can reduce older people's sense of isolation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which is a huge problem in many countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I also looked at the benefits of Zumba.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: 15 million people in 180 countries now regularly take a Zumba class.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: An aerobic workout based on Latin American dance moves, John Porcari, a professor of exercise and sport science at the University of Wisconsin,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: analyzed a group of women who were Zumba regulars, and found that a class lasting 40 minutes burns about 370 calories.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is similar to moderately intense exercises like step aerobics or kickboxing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A study in the American Journal of Health Behavior showed that when women with obesity did Zumba three times a week for 16 weeks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They lost an average of 1.2 kilos, and lowered their percentage of body fat by 1%. More importantly, the women enjoyed the class so much.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That they made it a habit, and continued to attend classes at least once a week, very unusual for an aerobic exercise program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Dance is never going to compete with high intensity workouts when it comes to physical fitness gains, but its popularity is likely to keep on rising.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because it's such a fun way to keep fit.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, Junior Cycle Camp, Jake speaking.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Hi.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I'm calling for some information about the cycle camp.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I'm thinking of sending my son.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Well, it's held every weekday morning over the summer vacation.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And we focus on basic cycling skills and safety.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: We have eight levels for children from 3 years upwards.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: How old's your son?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Charlie, he's 7.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: He can ride a bike, but he needs a little more training before he's safe to go on the road.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: He'd probably be best in level 5.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: They start off practicing on the site here, and we aim to get them riding on the road.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But first, they're taken to ride in the park, away from the traffic.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And can you tell me a bit about the instructors?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, all our staff wear different colored shirts.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: So we have three supervisors, and they have red shirts.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: They support the instructors, and they also stand in for me if I'm not around.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Then the instructors themselves are in blue shirts.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And one of these is responsible for each class.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: In order to be accepted, all our instructors have to submit a reference from someone who's seen them work with children.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Like if they've worked as a babysitter for example.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Then they have to complete our training course, including how to do lesson plans, and generally care for the well-being of the kids in their class.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: They do a great job, I have to say.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right, and tell me a bit about the classes.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: What size will Charlie's class be?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: We have a limit of 8 children in each class, so their instructor really gets to know them well.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: They're out riding most of the time.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But they have quiet times too, where their instructor might tell them a story that's got something to do with cycling.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Or get them to play a game together.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It's a lot of fun.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It must be.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: What happens if there's rain?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Do the classes still run?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Oh yes, we don't let that put us off.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: We just put on our waterproofs.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And keep cycling.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And is there anything special Charlie should bring along with him?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Well, maybe some spare clothes, especially if the weather's not so good.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: A snack for break time.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: How about a drink?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: No, we'll provide that.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And make sure he has shoes, not sandals.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: And just at present, Charlie has to take medication every few hours, so I'll make sure he has that.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Just give us details of when he has to take it, and we'll make sure he does.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Thanks.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Now, there are a few things you should know about day one of the camp.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: The classes normally start at 9:30 every morning, but on day one, you should aim to get Charlie here by 9:20.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: The finishing time will be 12:30 as usual.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: We need the additional time because there are a few extra things to do.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: The most important is that we have a very careful check to make sure that every child's helmet fits properly.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: If it doesn't fit, we'll try to adjust it, or we'll find him another one.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But he must wear it all the time he's on the bike.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Then after that, all the instructors will be waiting to meet their classes, and they'll meet up in the tent.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: You can't miss it.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Each instructor will take their class away and get started.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: OK, well that all sounds good.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Now, can you tell me how much the camp costs a week?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: We've managed to keep the price more or less the same as last year.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It was 190 then.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But the places are filling up quite quickly.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: OK, well, I'd like to book for the...
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That is the end of part 1.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a recruitment officer called Megan Baker, giving a talk at a jobs fair about opportunities for those interested in the food and agriculture sectors.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, everyone.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: My name is Megan Baker, and I'm a recruitment consultant at AVT Recruitment Specialists.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Now, our company specializes in positions that involve working in the agriculture and horticulture sectors, so that's fresh food production.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Garden and park maintenance and so on, and these sectors do provide some very special career opportunities.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: For a start, they often offer opportunities for those who don't want to be stuck with a 40 hour week, but need to juggle work with other responsibilities, such as childcare.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: And this is very important for many of our recruits.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Some people like working in a rural setting, surrounded by plants and trees instead of buildings.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Although we can't guarantee that. But there are certainly health benefits.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Especially in jobs where you're not sitting all day looking at a screen, a big plus for many people.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Salaries can sometimes be good too, although there's a lot of variety here.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: And you may have the opportunity in some types of jobs for travel overseas, although that obviously depends on the job, and not everyone is keen to do it.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Of course, working outdoors does have its challenges.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: It's fine in summer, but can be extremely unpleasant when it's cold and windy.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: You may need to be pretty fit for some jobs, though with modern technology, that's not as important as it once was.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: And standards of health and safety are much higher now than they used to be.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: So there are fewer work related accidents, but if you like a lively city environment surrounded by lots of people, these jobs are probably not for you.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: They're often in pretty remote areas, and some people worry about finding a suitable place to live, but in our experience, this usually turns out fine.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, let me tell you about some of the exciting jobs that we have on our books right now.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: One is for a fresh Food Commercial Manager.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Our client here is a very large fresh food producer, supplying a range of top supermarkets.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: They operate in a very fast paced environment with low profit margins.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: The staff there work hard, but they play hard as well.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: So, if you have a sociable personality, this may be for you.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: We have an exciting post as an agronomist, advising farmers on issues such as crop nutrition, Protection against pests, and the latest legislation on farming and agricultural practices.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: There are good opportunities for the right person to quickly make their way up the career ladder, but a deep knowledge of the agricultural sector is expected of applicants.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: A leading supermarket is looking for a fresh produce buyer, who is available for a 12-month maternity cover contract.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: You need to have experience in administration.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Planning and buying in the fresh produce industry, and in return will receive a very competitive salary.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: We have also received a request for a Sales Manager for a chain of garden centers.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: You will be visiting centers in the region to ensure their high levels of customer service are maintained.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: This post is only suitable for someone who is prepared to live in the region.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: There is also a vacancy for a tree technician to carry out tree cutting, forestry and conservation work.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Candidates must have a clean driving license.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: And have training in safety procedures.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: A year's experience would be preferred, but the company might be prepared to consider someone who has just completed an appropriate training course.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Finally, we have a position for a farm worker.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: This will involve a wide range of farm duties, including crop sowing and harvesting.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Machine maintenance and animal care.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: Perks of the job include the possibility of renting a small cottage on the estate, and a chance to earn a competitive salary.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: A driving license and tractor driving experience are essential.
script.speaker: MEGAN BAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two food science students called Adam and Rosie, starting to plan their presentation on diet and obesity.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, Rosie.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Shall we try to get some ideas together for our presentation on diet and obesity?
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I can talk about the experiment I did.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: To see if people can tell the difference between real sugar and artificial sweeteners.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Where you gave people drinks with either sugar or artificial sweeteners, and they had to say which they thought it was.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: It took me ages to decide exactly how I'd organize it, especially how I could make sure that people didn't know which drink I was giving them.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: It was hard to keep track of it all.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Especially as I had so many people doing it, I had to make sure I kept a proper record of what each person had had.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: So, could most people tell the difference?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: I hadn't thought that they would be able to, but most people could.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Then there's that experiment I did, measuring the fat content of nuts to see if the nutritional information given on the packet was accurate.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: The one where you ground up the nuts and mixed them with a chemical to absorb the fat.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Yes, my results were a bit problematic.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: The fat content for that type of nut seemed much lower than it said on the package.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: But I reckon the package information was right.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I think I should probably have ground up the nuts more than I did.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: It's possible that the scales for weighing the fat weren't accurate enough too.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I'd really like to try the experiment again sometime.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So what can we say about helping people to lose weight?
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: There's a lot we could say about what restaurants could do to reduce obesity.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: I read that the items at the start of a menu and the items at the end of a menu are much more likely to be chosen than the items in the middle.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: So, if you put the low calorie items at the beginning and end of the menu, people will probably go for the food with fewer calories without even realizing what they're doing.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: I think food manufacturers could do more to encourage healthy eating.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: How?
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Well, when manufacturers put calorie counts of a food on the label,
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: they're sometimes really confusing, and I suspect they do it on purpose, because food that's high in calories tastes better, and so they'll sell more.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yeah, so if you look at the amount of calories in a pizza.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: They'll give you the calories per quarter pizza, and you think oh that's not too bad, but who's going to eat a quarter pizza?
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I suppose another approach to this problem is to get people to exercise more.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: In England, the current guidelines are for at least 30 minutes of brisk walking.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: 5 days a week.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Now when you ask them, about 40% of men and 30% of women say they do this, but when you objectively measure the amount of walking they do with motion sensors.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: You find that only 6% of men and 4% of women do the recommended amount of exercise.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Hmm, so you can see why obesity is growing.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: So, how can people be encouraged to take more exercise?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Well, for example, think of the location of stairs in a train station.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: If people reach the stairs before they reach the escalator when they're leaving the station, they're more likely to take the stairs, and if you increase the width of the stairs.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: You'll get more people using them at the same time.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: It's an unconscious process and influenced by minor modifications in their environment.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: And it might not be a big change, but if it happens every day, it all adds up.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yes, but actually I'm not sure if we should be talking about exercise in our presentation.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Well, we've done quite a bit of reading about it.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I know, but it's going to mean we have a very wide focus, and our tutor did say that we need to focus on causes and solutions in terms of nutrition.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Oh, I suppose so.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: And we've got plenty of information about that.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: OK, well, that will be simpler.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: So what shall we do now?
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: We've still got half an hour before our next lecture.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: Let's think about what we're going to include, and what will go where.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Then we can decide what slides we need.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: OK, fine.
script.speaker: ADAM

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4, you will hear a lecturer on a fashion design course introducing the subject of hand knitting, which involves making things like woolen jumpers and scarves.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone, so today we're going to look at an important creative activity, and that's hand knitting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ancient knitted garments have been found in many different countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Showing that knitting is a global activity with a long history.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When someone says the word knitting, we might well picture an elderly person.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A grandmother perhaps, sitting by the fire, knitting garments for herself or other members of the family.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a homely image.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But one that may lead you to feel that knitting is an activity of the past, and indeed during the previous decade, it was one of the skills that was predicted to vanish from everyday life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For although humans have sewn and knitted their own clothing for a very long time, many of these craft-based skills went into decline.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When industrial machines took over, mainly because they were no longer passed down from one generation to another.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, that's all changing, and interest in knitting classes in many countries is actually rising.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As more and more people are seeking formal instruction in the skill. With that trend, we're also seeing an increase in the sales figures,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: for knitting equipment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, why do people want to be taught to knit at a time when a machine can readily do the job for them?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The answer is that knitting as a handicraft has numerous benefits for those doing it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's consider what some of these might be.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While many people knitted garments in the past, because they couldn't afford to buy clothes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's still true today that knitting can be helpful, if you're experiencing economic hardship.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you have several children who all need warm winter clothes, knitting may save you a lot of money. And the results of knitting your own clothes, can be very rewarding,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: even though the skills you need to get going are really quite basic, and the financial outlay is minimal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the more significant benefits in today's world are to do with well-being.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In a world where it's estimated that we spend up to nine hours a day online.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Doing something with our hands that is craft based makes us feel good.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It releases us from the stress of a technological fast paced life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, let's look back a bit to early knitting activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, no one really knows when knitting first began.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But archaeological remains have disclosed plenty of information for us to think about.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the interesting things about knitting is that the earliest pieces of clothing that have been found suggest that most of the items produced were round rather than flat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Discoveries from the 3rd and 4th centuries in Egypt show that things like socks and gloves that were needed to keep hands and feet warm were knitted in one piece using four or five needles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's very different.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From most knitting patterns today, which only require two.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's more, the very first needles people used were hand carved out of wood.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And other natural materials like bone, whereas today's needles are largely made of steel or plastic, and make that characteristic clicking sound.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When someone's using them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ancient people knitted using yarns made from linen, hemp, cotton, and wool.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these were often very rough on the skin.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The spinning wheel, which allowed people to make finer yarns, and produce much greater quantities of them, led to the dominance of wool in the knitting industry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Wool was often favored for its warmth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another interesting fact about knitting is that because it was practiced in so many parts of the world, for so many purposes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Regional differences in style developed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This visual identity has allowed researchers to match bits of knitted clothing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That have been unearthed over time to the region from which the wearer came, or the job that he or she did.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As I've mentioned, knitting offered people from poor communities a way of making extra money while doing other tasks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For many centuries, it seems, men, women and children took every opportunity to knit, for example, while watching over sheep, walking to market.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or riding in boats.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So let's move on to take...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.

script.text: Part 1.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a man phoning the owner of a holiday cottage.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello?
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Oh hello.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I was hoping to speak to Jack Fitzgerald about renting a cottage.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I'm his wife Shirley, and we own the cottages together, so I'm sure I can help you.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Great, my name's Tom.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Some friends of ours rented Granary Cottage from you last year, and they thought it was great.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: So my wife and I are hoping to come in May for a week.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What date did you have in mind?
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: The week beginning the 14th, if possible.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I'll just check.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: I'm sorry, Tom.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It's already booked that week.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It's free the week beginning the 28th though, for seven nights.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: In fact, that's the only time you could have it in May.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Oh, well, we could manage that, I think.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: We'd just need to change a couple of things.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: How much would it cost?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That's the beginning of high season, so it'd be £550 for the week.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Ah, that's a bit more than we wanted to pay, I'm afraid.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: We've budgeted up to £500 for accommodation.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Well, we've just finished converting another building into a cottage,
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: which we're calling Chervil Cottage.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Sorry? what was that again?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Chervil. C H E R, V for Victor, I L.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Oh, that's a herb, isn't it?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It grows fairly wild around here.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: You could have that for the week you want for £480.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: OK, so could you tell me something about it, please?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: The building was built as a garage.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It's a little smaller than Granary Cottage.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: So that must sleep two people as well.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: There's a double bedroom.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Does it have a garden?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, you get to it from the living room through French doors.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: And we provide two deck chairs.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: We hope to build a patio in the near future, but I wouldn't like to guarantee it'll be finished by May.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: The front door opens onto the old farmyard, and parking isn't a problem.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: There's plenty of room at the front for that.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: There are some trees and potted plants there.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: What about facilities in the cottage?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: It has standard things like a cooker and fridge, I presume.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: In the kitchen area, there's a fridge freezer.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: And we've just put in an electric cooker.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Is there a washing machine?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, there's also a TV in the living room which plays DVDs too.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: The bathroom is too small for a bath, so there's a shower instead.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: I think a lot of people prefer that nowadays anyway.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It's more environmentally friendly, isn't it?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Unless you spend half the day in it.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: What about heating?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: It sometimes gets quite cool at that time of year.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: There's central heating, and if you want to light a fire, there's a stove.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: We can provide all the wood you need for it.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It smells so much nicer than coal, and it makes the room very cozy.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: We've got one in our own house.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: That sounds very pleasant.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Perhaps we should come in the winter to make the most of it.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, we find we don't want to go out when we've got the fire burning.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: There are some attractive views from the cottage which I haven't mentioned.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: There's a famous stone bridge, it's one of the oldest in the region, and you can see it from the living room.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: It isn't far away.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: The bedroom window looks in the opposite direction, and has a lovely view of the hills, and the Monument at the top.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Well, uh, that all sounds perfect.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: I'd like to book it, please.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Would you want a deposit?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Yes, we ask for 30% to secure your booking.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: So that'll be, um, £144.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: And when would you like the rest of the money?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: You're coming in May, so the last day of March, please.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Fine.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Excellent.
script.speaker: SHIRLEY

script.text: Could I just take your details so that I can...

script.text: That is the end of part 1.

script.text: Part 2, you will hear a town councilor reporting on the local transport network and a recreation facility.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, next on the agenda, we have traffic and highways.
script.speaker: CHAIRPERSON

script.text: Councilor Thornton.
script.speaker: CHAIRPERSON

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: Well, we now have the results of the survey carried out last month.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: About traffic and road transport in the town.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: People were generally satisfied with the state of the roads.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: There were one or two complaints about potholes which will be addressed.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But a significant number of people complained about the increasing number of heavy vehicles using our local roads to avoid traffic elsewhere.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We'd expected more complaints by commuters about the reduction in the train service.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But it doesn't seem to have affected people too much.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: The cycle path that runs alongside the river is very well used by both cyclists and pedestrians, since the surface was improved last year, but overtaking can be a problem.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: So we're going to add a bit on the side to make it wider.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: At some stage, we'd like to extend the path, so that it goes all the way through the town, but that won't be happening in the immediate future.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: The plans to have a pedestrian crossing next to the Post Office have unfortunately had to be put on hold for the time being.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We'd budgeted for this to be done this financial year.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But then there were rumors that the Post Office was going to move, which would have meant there wasn't really a need for a crossing.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: Now they've confirmed that they're staying where they are.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But the Highways Department have told us that it would be dangerous to have a pedestrian crossing where we'd originally planned it, as there's a bend in the road there, so that'll need some more thought.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: On Station Road near the station and level crossing, drivers can face quite long waits if the level crossing's closed, and we've now got signs up requesting them not to leave their engines running at that time.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: This means pedestrians waiting on the pavement to cross the railway line don't have to breathe in car fumes.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We've had some problems with cyclists leaving their bikes chained to the railings outside the ticket office.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But the station has agreed to provide bike racks there.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So next on the agenda is 'Proposals for improvements to the recreation ground'. Councilor Thornton again.
script.speaker: CHAIRPERSON

script.text: Well, since we managed to extend the recreation ground, we've spent some time talking to local people.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: About how it could be made a more attractive and useful space.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: If you have a look at the map up on the screen, you can see the river up in the north, and the Community Hall near the entrance from the road.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: At present, cars can park between the Community Hall and that line of trees to the east, but this is quite dangerous for pedestrians.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: So we're suggesting a new car park on the opposite side of the Community Hall right next to it.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We also have a new location for the cricket pitch, as we've now purchased additional space to the east of the recreation ground, beyond the trees.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We plan to move it away from its current location, which is rather near the road, into this new area beyond the line of trees.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: This means there's less danger of stray balls hitting cars or pedestrians.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We've got plans for a children's playground, which will be accessible by a footpath from the Community Hall, and will be alongside the river.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We'd originally thought of having it close to the road.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: But we think this will be a more attractive location.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: The skateboard ramp is very popular with both younger and older children.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: We had considered moving this up towards the river, but in the end we decided to have it in the southeast corner near the road.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: The pavilion is very well used at present by both football players and cricketers.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: It will stay where it is now, to the left of the line of trees and near to the river.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: Handy for both the football and cricket pitches, and finally, we'll be getting a new notice board for local information, and that will be directly on people's right as they go from the road into the recreation ground.
script.speaker: COUNCILLOR THORNTON

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3, you will hear two urban planning students discussing bike-sharing schemes in different cities.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now that we've done all the research into bike-sharing schemes in cities around the world, we need to think about how we're going to organize our report.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: I think we should start by talking about the benefits.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: I mean it's great that so many cities have introduced these schemes where anyone can pick up a bike from dozens of different locations and hire it for a few hours.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: It makes riding a bike very convenient for people.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Yes, but the costs can add up, and that puts people on low incomes off in some places.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Hmm, I suppose so.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: But if it means more people in general are cycling rather than driving, then because they're increasing the amount of physical activity they do, it's good for their health.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But isn't that of less importance?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I mean, doesn't the impact of reduced emissions on air pollution have a more significant effect on people's health?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Certainly in some cities, bike-sharing has made a big contribution to that, and also helped to cut the number of cars on the road significantly.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Which is the main point.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: But I'd say it's had less of an impact on noise pollution, because there are still loads of buses and lorries around.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Shall we quickly discuss the recommendations we're going to make?
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: In order to ensure bike-sharing schemes are successful?
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Well, while I think it's nice to have really state-of-the-art bikes with things like GPS,
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I wouldn't say they're absolutely necessary.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But some technical things are really important, like a fully functional app, so people can make payments and book bikes easily.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Places which haven't invested in that have really struggled.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Good point.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Some people say there shouldn't be competing companies offering separate bike-sharing schemes.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But in some really big cities, competition's beneficial.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: And anyway, one company might not be able to manage the whole thing.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Deciding how much to invest is a big question.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Cities which have opened loads of new bike lanes at the same time as introducing bike-sharing schemes have generally been more successful, but there are examples of successful schemes where this hasn't happened.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: What does matter though, is having a big publicity campaign.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Definitely.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: If people don't know how to use the scheme, or don't understand its benefits, they won't use it.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: People need a lot of persuasion to stop using their cars.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Shall we look at some examples now, and say what we think is good or bad about them?
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: I suppose we should start with Amsterdam, as this was one of the first cities to have a bike-sharing scheme.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: There was already a strong culture of cycling here.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: In a way, it's strange that there was such a demand for bike-sharing, because you'd have thought most people would have used their own bikes.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: And yet it's one of the best used schemes.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Dublin's an interesting example of a success story.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It must be because the public transport system's quite limited.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Hmm. Not really.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: There's no underground, but there are trams and a good bus network.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I'd say price has a lot to do with it.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It's one of the cheapest schemes in Europe to join.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: But the buses are really slow.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Anyway, the weather certainly can't be a factor.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: No, definitely not.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: The London scheme's been quite successful.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Yes, it's been a really good thing for the city.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: The bikes are popular, and the whole system is well maintained, but it isn't expanding quickly enough.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Basically not enough's been spent on increasing the number of cycle lanes, hopefully that'll change.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Yes, now what about outside Europe?
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Well, bike-sharing schemes have taken off in places like Buenos Aires.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Hmm, they built a huge network of cycle lanes to support the introduction of the scheme there, didn't they?
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: It attracted huge numbers of cyclists where previously there were hardly any.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: An example of good planning.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: New York is a good example of how not to introduce a scheme.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: When they launched it, it was more than 10 times the price of most other schemes.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: More than it costs to take a taxi, crazy.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I think the organizers lacked vision and ambition there.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I think so too.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Sydney would be a good example to use.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: I would have expected it to have grown pretty quickly here.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: Yes, I can't quite work out why it hasn't been an instant success like some of the others.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: It's a shame really.
script.speaker: JAKE

script.text: I know.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: OK, so now we've thought about all those.
script.speaker: AMY

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 3.

script.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about a large bird called the dodo, which is now extinct.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: One of the most famous cases of extinction is that of a bird known as the dodo.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, there's even a saying in English, as dead as the dodo.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Used to refer to something which no longer exists.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But for many centuries, the dodo was alive and well, although it could only be found in one place, the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was a very large bird, about 1 meter tall, and over the centuries it had lost the ability to fly, but it survived happily under the trees that covered the island.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, in the year 1507, the first Portuguese ships stopped at the island.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The sailors were carrying spices back to Europe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And found the island a convenient stopping place where they could stock up with food and water for the rest of the voyage, but they didn't settle on Mauritius.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, in 1638 the Dutch arrived and set up a colony there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These first human inhabitants of the island found the dodo birds a convenient source of meat, although not everyone liked the taste.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's hard to get an accurate description of what the dodo actually looked like.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We do have some written records from sailors, and a few pictures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we don't know how reliable these are.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The best known picture is a Dutch painting, in which the bird appears to be extremely fat, but this may not be accurate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: An Indian painting done at the same time shows a much thinner bird.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although attempts were made to preserve the bodies of some of the birds, no complete specimen survives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the early 17th century, four dried parts of a bird were known to exist.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of these, three have disappeared.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So only one example of soft tissue from the dodo survives, a dodo head.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Bones have also been found, but there's only one complete skeleton in existence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This single dodo skeleton has recently been the subject of scientific research, which suggests that many of the earlier beliefs about dodos may have been incorrect.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, early accounts of the birds mention how slow and clumsy it was, but scientists now believe the bird's strong knee joints would have made it capable of movement, which was not slow, but actually quite fast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, one 17th century sailor wrote that he found the birds hard to catch.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's true that the dodo's small wings wouldn't have allowed it to leave the ground, but the scientists suggest that these were probably employed for balance,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: while going over uneven ground. Another group of scientists carried out analysis of the dodo's skull.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They found that the reports of the lack of intelligence of the dodo were not borne out by their research, which suggested the bird's brain was not small.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But average in size.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, in relation to its body size, it was similar to that of the pigeon, which is known to be a highly intelligent bird.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The researchers also found that the structure of the bird's skull suggested that one sense which was particularly well developed was that of smell.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, the dodo may also have been particularly good at locating ripe fruit and other food in the island's thick vegetation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it looks as if the dodo was better able to survive and defend itself than was originally believed, yet less than 200 years after Europeans first arrived on the island, they had become extinct.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what was the reason for this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For a long time, it was believed that the dodos were hunted to extinction, but scientists now believe the situation was more complicated than this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another factor may have been the new species brought to the island by the sailors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These included dogs, which would have been a threat to the dodos, and also monkeys, which ate the fruit that was the main part of the dodo's diet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These were brought to the island deliberately.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The ships also brought another type of creature, rats, which came to land from the ships and rapidly overran the island.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These upset the ecology of the island, not just the dodos, but other species too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, they were a particular danger to the dodos, because they consumed their eggs, and since each dodo only laid one at a time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This probably had a devastating effect on populations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, we now think that probably the main cause of the bird's extinction was not the introduction of non-native species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the introduction of agriculture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This meant that the forest that had once covered all the island, and that had provided a perfect home for the dodo, was cut down.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So that crops such as sugar could be grown.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, although the dodo had survived for thousands of years, suddenly it was gone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Uh. Hi, Amber.

script.text: Yes, fine.

script.text: So the agency I was talking about is called Bankside.

script.text: OK, thanks.

script.speaker: WILLIAM

script.speaker: WILLIAM

script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a woman giving a presentation about a holiday on an island in Britain that her company organizes.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: My name's Erica Matthews, and I'm the owner of Matthews Island Holidays, a company set up by my parents.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Thank you for coming to this presentation, in which I hope to interest you in what we have to offer.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: We're a small family-run company, and we believe in the importance of the personal touch.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: So we don't aim to compete with other companies on the number of customers.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: What we do is build on our many years' experience, more than almost any other rail holiday company,
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: to ensure we provide perfect holidays in a small number of destinations, which we've got to know extremely well.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: I'll start with our six-day Isle of Man holiday.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: This is a fascinating island in the Irish Sea, with Wales to the south, England to the east, Scotland to the north, and Northern Ireland to the west.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Our holiday starts in Heysham, where your tour manager will meet you.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Then you'll travel by ferry to the Isle of Man.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Some people prefer to fly from Luton instead.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: And another popular option is to go by train to Liverpool and take a ferry from there.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: You have five nights in the hotel, and the price covers five breakfasts and dinners.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: And lunch on the three days when there are organized trips.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Day 4 is free, and most people have lunch in a cafe or restaurant in Douglas.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: The price of the holiday includes the ferry to the Isle of Man, all travel on the island, the hotel, and the meals I've mentioned.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Incidentally, we try to make booking our holidays as simple and fair as possible.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: So unlike with many companies, the price is the same, whether you book 6 months in advance or at the last minute, and there's no supplement for single rooms in hotels.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: If you make a booking, then need to change the start date, for example because of illness, you're welcome to change to an alternative date or a different tour for a small administrative fee.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, so what does the holiday consist of?
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Well, on day one, you'll arrive in time for a short introduction by your tour manager, followed by dinner in the hotel.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: The dining room looks out at the river, close to where it flows into the harbor, and there's usually plenty of activity going on.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: On day two, you'll take the coach to the small town of Peel,
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: on the way calling in at the Tynwald Exhibition.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: The Isle of Man isn't part of the United Kingdom, and it has its own parliament called Tynwald.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: It's claimed that this is the world's oldest parliament that's still functioning, and that it dates back to 979.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: However, the earliest surviving reference to it is from 1422, so, perhaps it isn't quite as old as it claims.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Day three, we have a trip to the mountain Snaefell.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: This begins with a leisurely ride along the promenade in Douglas in a horse-drawn tram.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Then you board an electric train, which takes you to the fishing village of Laxey.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: From there, it's an eight-kilometer ride in the Snaefell Mountain Railway to the top.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Lunch will be in the cafe, giving you spectacular views of the island.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Day 4 is free for you to explore, using the pass which we'll give you.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: So you won't have to pay for travel on local transport, or for entrance to the island's heritage sites.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Or you might just want to take it easy in Douglas, and perhaps do a little light shopping.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: The last full day, day 5, is for some people the highlight of the holiday, with a ride on the steam railway from Douglas to Port Erin.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: After some time to explore, a coach will take you to the Headland that overlooks the Calf of Man, a small island just off the coast.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: From there, you continue to Castletown,
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: which used to be the capital of the Isle of Man, and its mediaeval castle.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: And on day 6, it's back to the ferry, or the airport, if you flew to the island.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: And time to go home.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: Now, I'd like to tell you a bit more.
script.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 3.

script.text: You will hear two psychology students discussing the effects of the order in which the children in a family are born.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Ed, how are you getting on with the reading for our presentation next week?
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Well, OK, Ruth, but there's so much of it.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I know.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: I hadn't realized birth order was such a popular area of research.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: But the stuff on birth order and personality is mostly unreliable.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: From what I've been reading, a lot of the claims about how your position in the family determines certain personality traits,
script.speaker: ED

script.text: are just stereotypes with no robust evidence to support them.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: OK, but that's an interesting point.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: We could start by outlining what previous research has shown.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: There are studies going back over 100 years.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Yeah, so we could just run through some of the typical traits, like the consensus seems to be that oldest children are generally less well adjusted, because they never get over the arrival of a younger sibling.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Right, but on a positive note, some studies claim that they were thought to be good at nurturing.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Certainly in the past when people had large families, they would have been expected to look after the younger ones.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: There isn't such a clear picture for middle children, but one trait that a lot of the studies mention,
script.speaker: ED

script.text: is that they are easier to get on with than older or younger siblings.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Hmm, generally eager to please and helpful, although that's certainly not accurate as far as my family goes.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: My middle brother was a nightmare, always causing fights and envious of whatever I had.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: As I said, none of this seems to relate to my own experience.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I'm the youngest in my family, and I don't recognize myself in any of the studies I've read about.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I'm supposed to have been a sociable and confident child who made friends easily.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: But I was actually terribly shy.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: That's funny.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: There have been hundreds of studies on twins, but mostly about nurture versus nature.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: There was one on personality which said that a twin is likely to be quite shy in social situations, because they always have their twin around to depend on for support.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: My cousins were like that when they were small.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: They were only interested in each other, and found it hard to engage with other kids.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: They're fine now though.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Only children have had a really bad press.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: A lot of studies have branded them as loners, who think the world revolves around them, because they've never had to fight for their parents' attention.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: That does seem a bit harsh.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: One category I hadn't considered before was children with much older siblings.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: A couple of studies mentioned that these children grow up more quickly and are expected to do basic things for themselves,
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: like getting dressed.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: I can see how that might be true, although I expect there's sometimes the exact opposite, playing the baby role and clamoring for special treatment.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: What was the problem with most of these studies, do you think?
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: I think it was because in a lot of cases, data was collected from only one sibling per family.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Who rated him or herself, and his or her siblings at the same time.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: Hmm, some of the old research into the relationship between birth order and academic achievement,
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: has been proved to be accurate though performances in intelligence tests decline slightly from the eldest child to his or her younger siblings.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: This has been proved in lots of recent studies.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Yes, although what many of them didn't take into consideration was family size.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: The more siblings there are, the likelier the family is to have a low socioeconomic status, which can also account for differences between siblings in academic performance.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: The oldest boy might be given more opportunities than his younger sisters for example.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: But the main reason for the marginally higher academic performance of oldest children is quite surprising, I think.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: It's not only that they benefit intellectually from extra attention at a young age, which is what I would have expected.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: It's that they benefit from being teachers for their younger siblings by verbalizing processes.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: And this gives them status and confidence, which again contributes in a small way to better performance.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: So, would you say sibling rivalry has been a useful thing for you?
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I think so.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: My younger brother was incredibly annoying, and we fought a lot.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: But I think this has made me a stronger person.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: I know how to defend myself.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: We had some terrible arguments, and I would have died rather than apologize to him.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: But we had to put up with each other, and most of the time we coexisted amicably enough.
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: Yes, my situation was pretty similar, but I don't think having two older brothers made me any less selfish.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: I was never prepared to let my brothers use any of my stuff.
script.speaker: ED

script.text: That's perfectly normal, whereas sometimes...
script.speaker: RUTH

script.text: That is the end of part 3.

script.text: Today, I'm going to talk about the eucalyptus tree.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a very common tree here in Australia, where it's also sometimes called the gum tree.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First, I'm going to talk about why it's important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then I'm going to describe some problems it faces at present.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Right, well, the eucalyptus tree is an important tree for lots of reasons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, it gives shelter to creatures like birds and bats.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these and other species also depend on it for food, particularly the nectar from its flowers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it supports biodiversity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's useful to us humans too, because we can kill germs with a disinfectant made from oil extracted from eucalyptus leaves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The eucalyptus grows all over Australia, and the trees can live for up to 400 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it's alarming that all across the country, numbers of eucalyptus are falling.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because the trees are dying off prematurely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what are the reasons for this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One possible reason is disease.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far back as the 1970s the trees started getting a disease called Mundulla Yellows.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trees' leaves would gradually turn yellow then the tree would die.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It wasn't until 2004 that they found the cause of the problem was lime, or calcium hydroxide to give it its proper chemical name.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which was being used in the construction of roads.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The lime was being washed away into the ground and affecting the roots of the eucalyptus trees nearby.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What it was doing was preventing the trees from sucking up the iron they needed for healthy growth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When this was injected back into the affected trees, they immediately recovered.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But this problem only affected a relatively small number of trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By 2000, huge numbers of eucalyptus were dying along Australia's East Coast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of a disease known as Bell-miner Associated Die-back.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The bell-miner is a bird, and the disease seems to be common where there are high populations of bell-miners.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Again, it's the leaves of the trees that are affected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What happens is that insects settle on the leaves and eat their way round them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Destroying them as they go, and at the same time, they secrete a solution which has sugar in it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The bell-miner birds really like this solution, and in order to get as much as possible, they keep away other creatures that might try to get it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So these birds and insects flourish at the expense of other species, and eventually so much damage is done to the leaves that the tree dies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But experts say that trees can start looking sick before any sign of bell-miner associated dieback.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, it looks as if the problem might have another explanation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One possibility is that it's to do with the huge bushfires that we have in Australia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A theory proposed over 40 years ago by ecologist William Jackson is that the frequency of bushfires in a particular region affects the type of vegetation that grows there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If there are very frequent bushfires in a region, this encourages grass to grow afterwards, while if the bushfires are rather less frequent, this results in the growth of eucalyptus forests.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So why is this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why do fairly frequent bushfires actually support the growth of eucalyptus?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, one reason is that the fire stops the growth of other species which would consume water needed by eucalyptus trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And there's another reason.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If these other quick-growing species of bushes and plants are allowed to proliferate, they harm the eucalyptus in another way.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By affecting the composition of the soil and removing nutrients from it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So some bushfires are actually essential for the eucalyptus to survive, as long as they are not too frequent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, there's evidence that Australia's indigenous people practiced regular burning of bushland for thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before the arrival of the Europeans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But since Europeans arrived on the continent, the number of bushfires has been strictly controlled.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now scientists believe that this reduced frequency of bushfires to low levels has led to what's known as dry rainforest, which seems an odd name, as usually we associate tropical rainforest with wet conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And what's special about this type of rainforest?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, unlike tropical rainforest, which is a rich ecosystem, this type of ecosystem is usually a simple one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It has very thick dense vegetation, but not much variety of species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The vegetation provides lots of shade, so one species that does find it ideal is the bell-miner bird.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which builds its nests in the undergrowth there, but again, that's not helpful for the eucalyptus tree.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
