script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a talk to a gardening club about a local park.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I'm very pleased to welcome this evening's guest speaker, Mark Logan, who's going to tell us about the recent transformation of Minster Park.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Over to you, Mark.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: I'm sure you're all familiar with Minster Park.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: It's been a feature of the city for well over a century, and has been the responsibility of the city council for most of that time.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: What perhaps isn't so well known is the origin of the park.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Unlike many public parks that started in private ownership, as the garden of a large house for instance, Minster was some waste land, which people living nearby started planting with flowers in 1892.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: It was unclear who actually owned the land.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: And this wasn't settled until 20 years later, when the council took possession of it.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: You may have noticed the statue near one of the entrances.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: It's of Diane Gosforth, who played a key role in the history of the park.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Once the council had become the legal owner, it planned to sell the land for housing.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Many local people wanted it to remain a place that everyone could go to, to enjoy the fresh air and natural environment.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Remember, the park is in a densely populated residential area.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Diane Gosforth was one of those people, and she organized petitions and demonstrations, which eventually made the council change its mind about the future of the land.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Soon after this, the First World War broke out, in 1914,
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: and most of the park was dug up and planted with vegetables,
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: which were sold locally, at one stage, the army considered taking it over for troop exercises, and got as far as contacting the city council, then decided the park was too small to be of use.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: There were occasional public meetings during the war, in an area that had been retained as grass.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: After the war, the park was turned back more or less to how it had been before 1914 and continued almost unchanged until recently.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Plans for transforming it were drawn up at various times, most recently in 2013, though they were revised in 2015 before any work had started.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: The changes finally got going in 2016 and were finished on schedule last year.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, let me tell you about some of the changes that have been made, and some things that have been retained.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: If you look at this map.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: You'll see the familiar outline of the park, with the river forming the northern boundary, and a gate in each of the other three walls.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: The statue of Diane Gosforth has been moved.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: It used to be close to the south gate, but it's now immediately to the north of the lily pond, almost in the center of the park, which makes it much more visible.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: There's a new area of wooden sculptures, which are on the river bank, where the path from the east gate makes a sharp bend.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: There are two areas that are particularly intended for children.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: The playground has been enlarged and improved, and that's between the river and the path that leads from the pond to the river.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Then there's a new maze, a circular series of paths separated by low hedges.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: That's near the west gate.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: You go north from there towards the river.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: And then turn left to reach it.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: There have been tennis courts in the park for many years, and they've been doubled from four to eight.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: They're still in the south-west corner of the park.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Where there's a right-angle bend in the path.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Uh. Something else I'd like to mention is the new fitness area.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: This is right next to the lily pond, on the same side as the west gate.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: Now, as you're all gardeners, I'm sure you'll like to hear about the plants that have been chosen for the park.
script.speaker: MARK

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two students of English called Cathy and Graham planning a display on 19th century British life and literature for a university event.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.

script.text: OK, Graham, so let's check we both know what we're supposed to be doing.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: So for the university's open day, we have to plan a display on British life and literature in the mid 19th century.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: But we'll have some people to help us find the materials and set it up, remember?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: For the moment, we just need to plan it.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: So have you gathered who's expected to come and see the display?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Is it for the people studying English or students from other departments?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: I'm not clear about it.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Nor me.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: That was how it used to be, but it didn't attract many people so this year it's going to be part of an open day to raise the university's profile.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: It'll be publicized in the city to encourage people to come and find out something of what goes on here.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: And it's included in the information that's sent to people who are considering applying to study here next year.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Presumably some current students and lecturers will come.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: I would imagine so.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: But we've been told to concentrate on the other categories of people.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: We don't have to cover the whole range of 19th century literature, do we?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: No, it's entirely up to us.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: I suggest just using Charles Dickens.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: That's a good idea.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Most people have heard of him and have probably read some of his novels or seen films based on them.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: So that's a good lead-in to life in his time.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: And his novels show the awful conditions that most people had to live in, don't they?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: He wanted to shock people into doing something about it.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Did he do any campaigning other than writing?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Yes, he campaigned for education and other social reforms and gave talks, but I'm inclined to ignore that and focus on the novels.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Yes, I agree.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, so now should we think about a topic linked to each novel?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Yes, I've printed out a list of Dickens's novels in the order they were published.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: In the hope you'd agree to focus on him.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Ha ha ha, you're lucky.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: I did agree.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Ha ha.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Let's have a look.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Uh. OK, the first was the Pickwick Papers.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Published in 1836 it was very successful when it came out, wasn't it?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: And was adapted for the theatre straight away.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: There's an interesting point though.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: That there's a character who keeps falling asleep, and that medical condition was named after the book, Pickwickian syndrome.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Oh, so why don't we use that as the topic?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: And include some quotations from the novel.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Right, next is Oliver Twist.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: There's a lot in the novel about poverty, but maybe something less obvious.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Well, Oliver is taught how to steal, isn't he?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: We could use that to illustrate the fact that very few children went to school, particularly not poor children, so they learned in other ways.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Good idea.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: What's next?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Maybe Nicholas Nickleby.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Actually he taught in a really cruel school, didn't he?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: But there's also the company of touring actors that Nicholas joins.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: We could do something on theaters and other amusements of the time.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: We don't want only the bad things, do we?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: OK, what about Martin Chuzzlewit?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: He goes to the USA, doesn't he?
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Yes, and Dickens himself had been there a year before.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: And drew on his experience there in the novel.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: I wonder though, the main theme is selfishness, so we could do something on social justice.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Hmm. No, too general.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Let's keep to your idea.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: I think it would work well.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: He wrote Bleak House next, that's my favorite of his novels.

script.text: Yes, mine too.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Oh, his satire of the legal system is pretty powerful.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: That's true, but think about Esther the heroine.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: As a child, she lives with someone she doesn't know is her aunt, who treats her very badly.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Then she's very happy living with her guardian, and he puts her in charge of the household, and at the end she gets married, and her guardian gives her and her husband a house, where of course they're very happy.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Yes, I like that.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: What should we take next?
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: Uh. Little Dorrit, old Mr Dorrit has been in a debtor's prison for years.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: So was Dickens's father, wasn't he?

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: CATHY

script.text: What about focusing on the part when Mr Dorrit inherits a fortune?

script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a presentation about an agricultural program in the country of Mozambique.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I'm going to report on a case study of a program which has been set up to help rural populations in Mozambique, a largely agricultural country in Southeast Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The program worked with three communities in Chicualacuala district near the Limpopo River.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a dry and arid region with unpredictable rainfall.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because of this, people in the area were unable to support themselves through agriculture, and instead they used the forest,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: as a means of providing themselves with an income, mainly by selling charcoal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, this was not a sustainable way of living in the long term, as they were rapidly using up this resource.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To support agriculture in this dry region, the program focused primarily on making use of existing water resources from the Limpopo River,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: by setting up systems of irrigation, which would provide a dependable water supply for crops and animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The program worked closely with the district government in order to find the best way of implementing this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The region already had one farmers' association, and it was decided to set up two more of these.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These associations planned and carried out activities, including water management, livestock breeding and agriculture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it was notable that in general, women formed the majority of the workforce.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was decided that in order to keep the crops safe from animals, both wild and domestic, special areas should be fenced off.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Where the crops could be grown.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The community was responsible for creating these fences, but the program provided the necessary wire for making them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Once the area had been fenced off, it could be cultivated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The land was dug, so that vegetables and cereals appropriate to the climate could be grown, and the program provided the necessary seeds for this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The program also provided pumps, so that water could be brought from the river in pipes to the fields.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, the labor was all provided by local people, and they also provided and put up the posts that supported the fences around the fields.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Once the program had been set up, its development was monitored carefully.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The farmers were able to grow enough produce, not just for their own needs,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: but also to sell.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, getting the produce to places where it could be marketed was sometimes a problem, as the farmers did not have access to transport.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this resulted in large amounts of produce, especially vegetables, being spoiled.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This problem was discussed with the farmers' associations, and it was decided that in order to prevent food from being spoiled.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The farmers needed to learn techniques for its preservation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There was also an additional initiative that had not been originally planned, but which became a central feature of the program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was when farmers started to dig holes for tanks in the fenced-off areas, and to fill these with water, and use them for breeding fish, an important source of protein.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After a time, another suggestion was made by local people, which hadn't been part of the program's original proposal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But which was also adopted later on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They decided to try setting up colonies of bees, which would provide honey, both for their own consumption and to sell.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what lessons can be learned from this program?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First of all, it tells us that in dry, arid regions, if there is access to a reliable source of water,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: there is great potential for the development of agriculture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Chicualacuala, there was a marked improvement in agricultural production,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which improved food security and benefited local people by providing them with both food and income.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, it's important to set realistic timelines for each phase of the program, especially for its design.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As mistakes made at this stage may be hard to correct later on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The program demonstrates that sustainable development is possible in areas where there is...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a woman called Alice Riches talking on the radio about a scheme which involves closing streets to traffic to allow children to play.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: My guest on the show today is Alice Riches, who started the street play scheme where she lives in Beechwood Road.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: For those of you that don't already know, street play involves local residents closing off their street for a few hours so that children have a chance to play in the street safely.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: She started it in her own street, Beechwood Road, and the idea caught on, and there are now street play schemes all over the city.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: So when did you actually start the scheme, Alice?
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Well, I first had the idea when my oldest child was still a toddler.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So that's about oh, 6 years ago now, but it took at least 2 years of campaigning before we were actually able to make it happen.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So the scheme's been up and running for 3 years now.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We'd love to be able to close our road for longer, for the whole weekend from Saturday morning until Sunday evening for example.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: At the moment, it's just once a week, but when we started, it was only once a month, but we're working on it.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So what actually happens when Beechwood Road is closed?
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: We have volunteer wardens.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Mostly parents, but some elderly residents too, who block off our road at either end.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: The council have provided special signs, but there's always a volunteer there to explain what's happening to any motorists.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Generally they're fine about it.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We've only had to get the police involved once or twice.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Now, I should explain that the road isn't completely closed to cars.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: But only residents' cars are allowed.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: If people really need to get in or out of Beechwood Road, it's not a problem, as long as they drive at under 20 km per hour.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: But most people just decide not to use their cars during this time, or they park in another street.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: The wardens are only there to stop through traffic.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So, can anyone apply to get involved in street play?
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We want to include all kids in the city, especially those who live on busy roads.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It's here that demand is greatest, obviously, there isn't such demand in wealthier areas where the children have access to parks or large gardens.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Or in the suburbs where there are usually more places for children to play outside.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I'd recommend that anyone listening who likes the idea should just give it a go.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We've been surprised by the positive reaction of residents all over the city.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: And that's not just parents, there are always a few who complain, but they're a tiny minority.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: On the whole, everyone is very supportive, and says they're very happy to see children out on the street.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Even if it does get quite noisy.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: There have been so many benefits of street play for the kids.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Parents really like the fact that the kids are getting fresh air, instead of sitting staring at a computer screen.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Even if they're not doing anything particularly energetic, and of course it's great that kids can play with their friends outside without being supervised by their parents.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: But for me, the biggest advantage is that kids develop confidence in themselves to be outside without their parents.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: The other really fantastic thing is that children get to know the adults in the street.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It's like having a big extended family.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It certainly does have a lot of benefits.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: I want to move on now and ask you about a related project in King Street.
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Well, uh, this was an experiment I was involved in, where local residents decided to try and reduce the traffic along King Street, which is the busiest main road in our area.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: By persuading people not to use their cars for one day.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We thought about making people pay more for parking, but we decided that would be really unpopular.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So instead, we just stopped people from parking on King Street, but left the other car parks open.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It was surprising how much of a difference all this made.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: As we'd predicted, air quality was significantly better, but what I hadn't expected was how much quieter it would be, even with the buses still running.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Of course, everyone said they felt safer, but we were actually amazed that sales in the shops went up considerably that day.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We thought there'd be fewer people out shopping, not more.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: That's really interesting, so the fact that the street was...
script.speaker: PRESENTER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two students called Hazel and Tom talking about Hazel's media studies assignment.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Tom, could I ask you for some advice, please?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Yes, of course.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: If you think I can help.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What's it about?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: It's my first media studies assignment, and I'm not sure how to go about it.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: You must have done it last year.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Is that the one comparing the coverage of a particular story in a range of newspapers?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Oh yes, I really enjoyed writing it.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: So, what sort of things do I need to compare?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Well, there are several things.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: For example, there's the question of which page of the newspaper the item appears on.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: You mean because there's a big difference between having it on the front page and the bottom of page 10 for instance?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And that shows how important the editor thinks the story is.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Then there's the size, how many column inches the story is given, how many columns it spreads over.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And I suppose that includes the headline.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: It certainly does.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: It's all part of attracting the reader's attention.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What about graphics?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Whether there's anything visual in addition to the text?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Yes, you need to consider those too.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Because they can have a big effect on the reader's understanding of the story, sometimes a bigger effect than the text itself.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Then you'll need to look at how the item is put together.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What structure is it given?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Bear in mind that not many people read beyond the first paragraph, so what has the journalist put at the beginning?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And if say there are conflicting opinions about something, does one appear near the end, where people probably won't read it?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And newspapers sometimes give wrong or misleading information, don't they?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Either deliberately or by accident, should I be looking at that too?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Yes, if you can, compare what's in different versions, and as far as possible.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Try and work out what's true and what isn't, and that relates to a very important point.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: What's the writer's purpose?
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Or at least the most important one, if they have several.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: It may seem to be to inform the public, but often it's that they want to create fear.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Or controversy, or to make somebody look ridiculous.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Gosh, I see what you mean.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: And I suppose the writer may make assumptions about the reader.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: That's right, about their knowledge of the subject, their attitudes, and their level of education, which means writing so that the readers understand without feeling patronized.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: All of that will make a difference to how the story is presented.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Does it matter what type of story I write about?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: No, national or international politics, the arts, anything.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: As long as it's covered in two or three newspapers, though of course it'll be easier and more fun if it's something you're interested in, and know something about.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And on that basis, a national news item would be worth analyzing.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: I'm quite keen on politics, so I'll try and find a suitable topic.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: What did you choose for your analysis, Tom?
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: I was interested in how newspapers express their opinions explicitly.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: So, I wanted to compare editorials in different papers, but when I started looking, I couldn't find two on the same topic that I felt like analyzing.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: In that case, I wouldn't even bother to look.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: So in the end, I chose a human interest story, a terribly emotional story about a young girl who was very ill.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: And lots of other people, mostly strangers, raised money so she could go abroad for treatment.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Actually, I was surprised.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Some papers just wrote about how wonderful everyone was.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: But others considered the broader picture, like why treatment wasn't available here.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Hmm, I usually find stories like that raise quite strong feelings in me.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: I'll avoid that.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Perhaps I'll choose an arts topic, like different reviews of a film or something about funding for the arts.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: I'll think about that.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: Yes, that might be interesting.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: OK, well, thanks a lot for your help, Tom.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: It's been really useful.
script.speaker: HAZEL

script.text: You're welcome.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: Good luck with the assignment, Hazel.
script.speaker: TOM

script.text: That is the end of part 3.

script.text: Part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the early history of keeping clean.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Nowadays, we use different products for personal cleanliness, laundry, dishwashing, and household cleaning.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But this is very much a 20th-century development.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The origins of cleanliness date back to prehistoric times.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since water is essential for life, the earliest people lived near water and knew something about its cleansing properties.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At least that it rinsed MUD off their hands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: During the excavation of ancient Babylon, evidence was found that soap making was known.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As early as 2800 BC, archaeologists discovered cylinders made of clay with inscriptions on them saying that fats were boiled with ashes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a method of making soap, though there's no reference to the purpose of this material.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The early Greeks bathed for aesthetic reasons, and apparently didn't use soap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, they cleaned their bodies with blocks of sand, pumice, and ashes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then anointed themselves with oil, and scraped off the oil and dirt with a metal instrument known as a strigil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They also used oil mixed with ashes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Clothes were washed without soap in streams.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The ancient Germans and Gauls are also credited with discovering how to make a substance called soap, made of melted animal fat and ashes. They used this mixture to tint their hair red.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Soap got its name according to an ancient Roman legend from Mount Sapo, where animals were sacrificed, leaving deposits of animal fat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rain washed these deposits along with wood ashes down into the clay soil along the river Tiber.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Women found that this mixture greatly reduced the effort required to wash their clothes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As Roman civilization advanced, so did bathing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first of the famous Roman baths, supplied with water from their aqueducts, was built around 312 BC.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The baths were luxurious, and bathing became very popular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And by the second century AD,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: the Greek physician Galen recommended soap for both medicinal and cleansing purposes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After the fall of Rome in 467 AD, and the resulting decline in bathing habits, much of Europe felt the impact of filth on public health.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This lack of personal cleanliness and related unsanitary living conditions were major factors in the outbreaks of disease in the Middle Ages.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And especially the Black Death of the 14th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Nevertheless, soap making became an established craft in Europe, and associations of soap makers guarded their trade secrets closely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Vegetable and animal oils were used with ashes of plants, along with perfume, apparently for the first time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Gradually, more varieties of soap became available for shaving and shampooing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as bathing and laundering.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A major step toward large scale commercial soap making occurred in 1791 when a French chemist Nicholas LeBlanc patented a process for turning salt into soda ash, or sodium carbonate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Soda ash is the alkali obtained from ashes that combines with fat to form soap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The LeBlanc process yielded quantities of good quality inexpensive soda ash.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Modern soap making was born some 20 years later, in the early 19th century, with the discovery by Michel Eugène Chevreul, another French chemist, of the chemical nature and relationship of fats, glycerin, and fatty acids.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: His studies established the basis for both fat and soap chemistry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And soap making became a science.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Further developments during the 19th century made it easier and cheaper to manufacture soap.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Until the 19th century, soap was regarded as a luxury item, and was heavily taxed in several countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it became more readily available, it became an everyday necessity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A development that was reinforced when the high tax was removed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Soap was then something ordinary people could afford, and cleanliness standards improved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With this widespread use came the development of milder soaps for bathing, and soaps for use in the washing machines that were available to consumers by the turn of the 20th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 1.

script.text: You will hear a representative from a train company talking to a woman about her train journey.

script.text: Hello, do you mind if I ask you some questions about your journey today?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: We're doing a customer satisfaction survey.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes, OK.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I've got about 10 minutes before my train home leaves.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I'm on a day trip.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Great, thank you.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: So first of all, could you tell me your name?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's Sophie Bird.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: And would you mind telling me what you do?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I'm a journalist.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Oh, really?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That must be interesting.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes, it is.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: So, what's the reason for your visit here today?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Work?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Actually, it's my day off.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I came here to do some shopping.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: All right.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: But I do sometimes come here for work.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Now, I'd like to ask some questions about your journey today, if that's OK.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes, no problem.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Right, so can you tell me which station you're traveling back to?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Staunfirth, where I live.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Uh. Can I just check the spelling?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: STAUNFIRTH?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Hmm. And you traveled from there this morning?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: OK, good.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Next, can I ask what kind of ticket you bought?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I assume it wasn't a season ticket, as you don't travel every day.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: No, I just got a normal return ticket.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I don't have a rail card, so I didn't get any discount.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I keep meaning to get one, because it's a lot cheaper.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Yes, you'd have saved 20% on your ticket today.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Uh. So you paid the full price for your ticket.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: I paid £23.70.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: OK, do you think that's good value for money?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Not really, I think it's too much for a journey that only takes 45 minutes.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Yes, that's one of the main complaints we get.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: So you didn't buy your ticket in advance?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: No, I know it's cheaper if you buy a week in advance, but I didn't know I was coming then.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I know, you can't always plan ahead. So, did you buy it this morning?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: No, it was yesterday.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Right, and do you usually buy your tickets at the station?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Well, I do usually, but the ticket office closes early, and I hate using ticket machines.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: I think ticket offices should be open for longer hours.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: There's always a queue for the machines, and they're often out of order.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Hmm. A lot of customers are saying the same thing.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: So to answer your question, I got an e-ticket online.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, thank you.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Now I'd like to ask you about your satisfaction with your journey.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: So what would you say you were most satisfied with today?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Well, I like the Wi-Fi on the train.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: It's improved a lot.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: It makes it easier for me to work if I want to.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: That's the first time today anyone's mentioned that.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: It's good to get some positive feedback on that.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: And is there anything you weren't satisfied with?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Well, normally the trains run on time and are pretty reliable, but today there was a delay.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: The train was about 15 minutes behind schedule.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Hmm. OK, I'll put that down.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Now, uh, I'd also like to ask about the facilities at this station.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: You've probably noticed that the whole station's been upgraded.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: What are you most satisfied with?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Uh. I think the best thing is that they've improved the amount of information about train times et cetera that's given to passengers.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: It's much clearer, before there was only one board, and I couldn't always see it properly, which was frustrating.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: That's good, and is there anything you're not satisfied with?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Let's see, I think things have generally improved a lot.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: The trains are much more modern, and I like the new cafe, but one thing is that there aren't enough places to sit down.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Especially on the platforms.

script.text: OK, so I'll put seating down, shall I, as the thing you're least satisfied with?

script.text: Yes, OK.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: Can I ask your opinion about some of the other facilities?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Uh huh.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: We'd like feedback on whether people are satisfied.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Dissatisfied or neither satisfied nor dissatisfied.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: OK, uh, what about the parking at the station?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Well, to be honest, I don't really have an opinion, as I never use it.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: So neither satisfied nor dissatisfied for that then?
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Yes, I suppose so.
script.speaker: SOPHIE

script.text: OK, uh, and what about these?

script.text: Part 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear the chair of a committee on park facilities, addressing her local town council about changes that have been made to the park.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: As chair of the Town Council Subcommittee on Park Facilities, I'd like to bring you up to date on some of the changes that have been made recently to the Croft Valley Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So if you could just take a look at the map I handed out, let's begin with a general overview.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, the basic arrangement of the park hasn't changed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It still has two gates, north and south, and a lake in the middle.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The cafe continues to serve an assortment of drinks and snacks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And is still in the same place, looking out over the lake, and next to the old museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're hoping to change the location of the toilets and bring them nearer to the center of the park, as they're a bit out of the way at present, near the adventure playground.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the corner of your map.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The formal gardens have been replanted, and should be at their best in a month or two.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They used to be behind the old museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we've now used the space near the south gate, between the park boundary and the path that goes past the lake towards the old museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have a new outdoor gym for adults and children, which is already proving very popular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's by the glass houses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just to the right of the path from the south gate, you have to look for it, as it's a bit hidden in the trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One very successful introduction has been our skateboard ramp.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's in constant use during the evenings and holidays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Near the old museum, at the end of a little path that leads off from the main path between the lake and the museum.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've also introduced a new area for wild flowers to attract bees and butterflies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's on a bend in the path.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That goes round the east side of the lake, just south of the adventure playground.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the presentation, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, let me tell you a bit more about some of the changes to Croft Valley Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of our most exciting developments has been the adventure playground.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We were aware that we had nowhere for children to let off steam, and decided to use our available funds to set up a completely new facility in a large space.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To the north of the park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's open year round, though it closes early in the winter months, and entrance is completely free.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Children can choose whatever activities they want to do, irrespective of their age.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we do ask adults not to leave them on their own there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are plenty of seats where parents can relax and keep an eye on their children at the same time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Lastly, the glass houses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A huge amount of work has been done on them to repair the damage following the disastrous fire that recently destroyed their western side.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Over £80,000 was spent on replacing the glass walls and the metal supports, as well as the plants that had been destroyed, although unfortunately the collection of tropical palm trees has proved too expensive to replace up to now.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At present, the glass houses are open from 10 am to 3 pm, Mondays to Thursdays, and it's hoped to extend this to the weekend soon.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're grateful to all those who helped us by contributing their time and money to this achievement.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The gardens have really been...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 2.

script.text: Part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two students of social history called Annie and Jack discussing their presentation about refrigeration.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, Jack.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Before we plan our presentation about refrigeration, let's discuss what we've discovered so far.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Fine, Annie.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Though I have to admit I haven't done much research yet.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Nor me.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: But I found an interesting article about ice houses.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I'd seen some 18th- and 19th-century ones here in the UK, so I knew they were often built in a shady area.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Or underground, close to lakes that might freeze in the winter.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Then blocks of ice could be cut and stored in the icehouse.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: But I didn't realize that insulating the blocks with straw or sawdust meant they didn't melt for months.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: The ancient Romans had refrigeration too.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I didn't know that.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Yes, pits were dug in the ground, and snow was imported from the mountains.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Even though they were at quite a distance, the snow was stored in the pits.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Ice formed at the bottom of it, both the ice and the snow were then sold.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: The ice cost more than the snow, and my guess is that only the wealthy members of society could afford it.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I wouldn't be surprised.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I also came across an article about modern domestic fridges.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Several different technologies are used, but they were too complex for me to understand.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: You have to wonder what happens when people get rid of old ones.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: You mean because the gases in them are harmful for the environment?
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: At least there are now plenty of organizations that will recycle most of the components safely, but of course some people just dump old fridges in the countryside.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: It's hard to see how they can be stopped unfortunately.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: In the UK, we get rid of 3 million a year altogether.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: That sounds a lot, especially because fridges hardly ever break down.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: In this country, we keep domestic fridges for 11 years on average.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: And a lot last for 20 or more.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: So if you divide the cost by the number of years you can use a fridge, they're not expensive compared with some household appliances.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: True.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I suppose manufacturers encourage people to spend more by making them different colors and designs.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I'm sure when my parents bought their first fridge, they had hardly any choice.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Yes, there's been quite a change.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, let's make a list of topics to cover in our presentation, and decide who's going to do more research on them.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Then later we can get together and plan the next step.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: OK, how about starting with how useful refrigeration is, and the range of goods that are refrigerated nowadays?
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Because of course, it's not just food and drinks.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: No, I suppose flowers and medicines are refrigerated, too.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: And computers. I could do that.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Unless you particularly want to.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: No, that's fine by me.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: What about the effects of refrigeration on people's health?
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: After all, some of the chemicals used in the 19th century were pretty harmful.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: But there have been lots of benefits too, like always having access to fresh food.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Do you fancy dealing with that?
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I'm not terribly keen to be honest.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Hmm, nor me.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: My mind just goes blank when I read anything about chemicals.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Oh, all right then, I'll do you a favor, but you owe me, Jack.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: OK?
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: What about the effects on food producers, like farmers in poorer countries being able to export their produce to developed countries?
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Something for you maybe?
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I don't mind, it should be quite interesting.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I think we should also look at how refrigeration has helped whole cities, like Las Vegas, which couldn't exist without refrigeration, because it's in the middle of a desert.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I had a quick look at an economics book in the library that's got a chapter about this sort of thing.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I could give you the title if you want to do this section.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Not particularly to be honest.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I find economics books pretty heavy going as a rule.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: OK, leave it to me then.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: Thanks.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Then there's transport, and the difference that refrigerated trucks have made.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: I wouldn't mind having a go at that.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Don't forget trains too.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I read something about milk and butter being transported in refrigerated railroad cars in the USA, right back in the 1840s.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: I hadn't thought of trains. Thanks.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: Should we have a separate section on domestic fridges?
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: After all, they're something everyone's familiar with.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: What about splitting it into two?
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: You could investigate 19th and 20th century fridges, and I'll concentrate on what's available these days, and how manufacturers differentiate their products from those of their competitors.
script.speaker: ANNIE

script.text: OK, that suits me.
script.speaker: JACK

script.text: That is the end of part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a history student giving part of a presentation about changes in British society in the 19th century.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hi, everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In this session, I'll be presenting my research about the social history of Britain during the Industrial Revolution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I particularly looked at how ordinary lives were affected by changes that happened at that time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was a time that saw the beginning of a new phenomenon, consumerism, where buying and selling goods became a major part of ordinary people's lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, it was in the 19th century that the quantity and quality of people's possessions was used as an indication of the wealth of the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before this, the vast majority of people had very few possessions, but all that was changed by the Industrial Revolution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was the era from the mid 18th to the late 19th century, when improvements in how goods were made, as well as in technology, triggered massive social changes that transformed life for just about everybody in several key areas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First, let's look at manufacturing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When it comes to manufacturing, we tend to think of the Industrial Revolution in images of steam engines and coal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it's true that the Industrial Revolution couldn't have taken place at all, if it weren't for these new sources of power.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They marked an important shift away from the traditional watermills and windmills that had dominated before this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The most advanced industry for much of the 19th century was textiles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This meant that fashionable fabrics and lace and ribbons were made available to everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before the Industrial Revolution, most people made goods to sell in small workshops, often in their own homes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But enormous new machines were now being created.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That could produce the goods faster, and on a larger scale, and these required a lot more space, so large factories were built.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Replacing the workshops and forcing workers to travel to work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, large numbers of people migrated from villages into towns as a result.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as manufacturing, there were new technologies in transport contributing to the growth of consumerism.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The horse-drawn stagecoaches and carts of the 18th century which carried very few people and goods, and traveled slowly along poorly surfaced roads, were gradually replaced by the numerous canals that were constructed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These were particularly important for the transportation of goods.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The canals gradually fell out of use, though, as railways were developed,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: becoming the main way of moving goods and people from one end of the country to the other, and the goods they moved weren't just coal, iron, clothes, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Significantly, they included newspapers, which meant that thousands of people were not only more knowledgeable about what was going on in the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But could also read about what was available in the shops, and that encouraged them to buy more.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So faster forms of transport resulted in distribution becoming far more efficient.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Goods could now be sold all over the country, instead of just in the local market.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The third main area that saw changes that contributed to consumerism was retailing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The number and quality of shops grew rapidly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in particular, small shops suffered, as customers flocked to the growing number of department stores, a form of retailing that was new in the 19th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The entrepreneurs who opened these found new ways to stock them with goods, and to attract customers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For instance, improved lighting inside greatly increased the visibility of the goods for sale.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another development that made goods more visible from outside resulted from the use of plate glass, which made it possible for windows to be much larger than previously.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: New ways of promoting goods were introduced too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Previously, the focus had been on informing potential customers about the availability of goods.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, there was an explosion in advertising, trying to persuade people to go shopping.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Flanders claims that one of the great effects of the Industrial Revolution was that it created choice, all sorts of things that had previously been luxuries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From sugar to cutlery became conveniences, and before long, they turned into necessities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Life without sugar or cutlery was unimaginable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rather like mobile phones these days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a manager giving a welcome talk to a group of apprentices who are starting their training at the company.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: My name's Janet Parker, and I'm the Human Resources manager.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: We're very happy to welcome you to your new apprenticeship.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: I hope that the next 6 months will be a positive and enjoyable experience for you.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: I'd like to start with some general advice about being an apprentice.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Most of you have very little or no experience of working for a big organization, and the first week or so may be quite challenging.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: There will be a lot of new information to take in, but don't worry too much about trying to remember everything.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: The important thing is to check with someone if you're not sure what to do.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You'll find your supervisor is very approachable, and won't mind explaining things or helping you out.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You're here to learn, so make the most of that opportunity.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You'll be spending time in different departments during your first week, so make an effort to talk to as many people as possible about their work.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You'll make some new friends and find out lots of useful information.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: As well as having a supervisor, you'll each be assigned a mentor.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: This person will be someone who's recently completed an apprenticeship, and you'll meet with them on a weekly basis.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Their role is to provide help and support throughout your apprenticeship.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Of course, this doesn't mean they'll actually do any of your work for you.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Instead, they'll be asking you about what goals you've achieved so far, as well as helping you to identify any areas for improvement.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You can also discuss your more long-term ambitions with them as well.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, I just want to run through a few company policies for our apprenticeship scheme with you.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Most importantly, the internet.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: As part of your job, you'll be doing some research online, so obviously you'll have unlimited access for that, but please don't use it for personal use.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You'll have your own phones for that.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Some of you have already asked me about flexible working.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: After your probationary 3 month period, some of you will be eligible for this.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: But it will depend on which department you're in, and what your personal circumstances are.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: So please don't assume you'll automatically be permitted to do this.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: I want to make sure there's no confusion about our holiday policy.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Apart from any statutory public holidays, we ask that you don't book any holidays until after your 6 month apprenticeship has finished.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Time off should only be taken if you are unwell.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Please speak to your supervisor if this is going to be a problem.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You'll be expected to work a 40 hour week, but there may be opportunities to do overtime during busy periods.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Although you're not required to do this, it can be a valuable experience.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: So we advise you to take it up if possible.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Obviously, we understand that people do have commitments outside work, so don't worry if there are times when you are unavailable.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: As you know, we don't have a formal dress code here.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: You may wear casual clothes as long as they are practical, and the only restriction for shoes we have is on high heels for health and safety reasons.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Comfortable shoes like trainers are preferable.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: There's a heavily subsidized canteen on site, where you can get hot meals or salads cheaply.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: Snacks and drinks are also provided.
script.speaker: JANET PARKER

script.text: So we've decided to introduce a no packed lunch policy.

script.text: This is partly to encourage healthy eating at work, and partly to stop people from eating at their workstation, which is unhygienic.

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two urban planning students called Carla and Rob discussing their presentation on cities built by the Sea, following instructions from their tutor.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, so what I'd like you to do now is to talk to your partner about your presentations on urban planning.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You should have done most of the reading now, so I'd like you to share your ideas.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And talk about the structure of your presentation and what you need to do next.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, Rob, I'm glad we chose quite a specific topic, cities built next to the sea.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: It made it much easier to find relevant information.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Yeah, and cities are growing so quickly.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: I mean we know that more than half the world's population lives in cities now.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yeah, though that's all cities, not just ones on the coast, but most of the biggest cities are actually built by the sea.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: I'd not realized that before.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Nor me.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: And what's more, a lot of them are built at places where rivers come out into the sea, but apparently this can be a problem.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Why?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Well, as the city expands, agriculture and industry tend to spread further inland along the rivers.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: And so agriculture moves even further inland up the river.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: That's not necessarily a problem, except it means more and more pollutants are discharged into the rivers.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So these are brought downstream to the cities.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Did you read that article about Miami on the east coast of the USA?
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: No.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Well, apparently back in the 1950s, they built channels to drain away the water in case of flooding.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Sounds sensible.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Yeah, they spent quite a lot of money on them, but what they didn't take into account was global warming.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So they built the drainage channels too close to sea level, and now sea levels are rising, they're more or less useless.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: If there's a lot of rain, the water can't run away.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: There's nowhere for it to go.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: The whole design was faulty.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So, what are the authorities doing about it now?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: I don't know.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: I did read that they're aiming to stop disposing of waste water into the ocean over the next 10 years.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: But that won't help with flood prevention now, will it?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: No, really, they just need to find the money for something to replace the drainage channels, in order to protect against flooding now.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: But in the long term, they need to consider the whole ecosystem.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Really though, coastal cities can't deal with their problems on their own, can they?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: I mean, they've got to start acting together at an international level, instead of just doing their own thing.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: The thing is, everyone knows what the problems are, and environmentalists have a pretty good idea of what we should be doing about them.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So they should be able to work together to some extent.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: But it's going to be a long time before countries come to a decision on what principles they're prepared to abide by.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yeah, if they ever do.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, I think we've probably got enough for our presentation.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: It's only 15 minutes.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: OK, so I suppose we'll begin with some general historical background about why coastal cities were established.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: But we don't want to spend too long on that, the other students will already know a bit about it.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: It's all to do with communications and so on.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yes, we should mention some geographical factors, uh, things like wetlands and river estuaries and coastal erosion and so on.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: We could have some maps of different cities with these features marked, on a handout you mean?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Or some slides everyone can see.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yeah, that'd be better.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: It'd be good to go into past mistakes in a bit more detail.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Did you read that case study of the problems there were in New Orleans with flooding a few years ago?
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Uh. We could use that as the basis for that part of the talk.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: I don't think the other students will have read it, but they'll remember hearing about the flooding at the time.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Hmm, OK.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So that's probably enough background.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: So, then we'll go on to talk about what action's being taken to deal with the problems of coastal cities.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: What else do we need to talk about?
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Maybe something on future risks, looking more at the long term, if populations continue to grow.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yeah, we'll need to do a bit of work there.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: I haven't got much information, have you?
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: No, we'll need to look at some websites, shouldn't take too long.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: OK, and I think we should end by talking about international implications.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: Maybe we could ask people in the audience.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: We've got people from quite a lot of different places.
script.speaker: CARLA

script.text: That would be interesting if we have time.
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: Yes, so now should we go on?
script.speaker: ROB

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
