script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture on renewable energy that uses the power of the sea.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Producing enough energy to meet our needs has become a serious problem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Demand is rising rapidly, because of the world's increasing population.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And expanding industry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Burning fossil fuels like gas, coal and oil, seriously damages the environment, and they'll eventually run out.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For a number of years now, scientists have been working out how we can derive energy from renewable sources such as the sun and wind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Without causing pollution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, I'll outline marine renewable energy, also called ocean energy, which harnesses the movement of the oceans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Marine renewable energy can be divided into three main categories, wave energy, tidal energy, and ocean thermal energy conversion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I'll say a few words about each one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First, wave energy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Numerous devices have been invented to harvest wave energy with names such as Wave Dragon.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Penguin and Mighty Whale, and research is going on to try and come up with a really efficient method.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This form of energy has plenty of potential.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As the source is constant, and there's no danger of waves coming to a standstill.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Electricity can be generated using onshore systems, using a reservoir or offshore systems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the problem with ocean waves is that they're erratic, with the wind making them travel in every direction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This adds to the difficulty of creating efficient technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ideally, all the waves would travel smoothly and regularly along the same straight line.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another drawback is that sand and other sediment on the ocean floor might be stopped from flowing normally, which can lead to environmental problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The second category of marine energy that I'll mention is tidal energy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One major advantage of using the tide, rather than waves as a source of energy is that it's predictable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We know the exact times of high and low tides for years to come.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For tidal energy to be effective, the difference between high and low tides needs to be at least 5 meters, and this occurs naturally in only about 40 places on earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the right conditions can be created by constructing a tidal lagoon, an area of seawater, separated from the sea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One current plan is to create a tidal lagoon on the coast of Wales.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This will be an area of water within a bay at Swansea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Sheltered by a U-shaped breakwater or dam built out from the coast, the breakwater will contain 16 hydro turbines.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And as the tide rises, water rushes through the breakwater, activating the turbines, which turn a generator to produce electricity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, for three hours as the tide goes out, the water is held back within the breakwater, increasing the difference in water level until it's several meters higher within the lagoon, than in the open sea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, in order to release the stored water, gates in the breakwater are opened, it pours powerfully out of the lagoon,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: driving the turbines in the breakwater in the opposite direction, and again generating thousands of megawatts of electricity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As there are two high tides a day, this lagoon scheme would generate electricity four times a day, every day, for a total of around 14 hours in every 24.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And enough electricity for over 150,000 homes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This system has quite a lot in its favor, unlike solar and wind energy, it doesn't depend on the weather.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The turbines are operated without the need for fuel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it doesn't create any greenhouse gas emissions, and very little maintenance is needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's estimated that electricity generated in this way will be relatively cheap, and that manufacturing the components would create more than 2,000 jobs, a big boost to the local economy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On the other hand, there are fears that lagoons might harm both fish and birds, for example by disturbing migration patterns.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And causing a buildup of silt, affecting local ecosystems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are other forms of tidal energy, but I'll go on to the third category of marine energy: ocean thermal energy conversion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This depends on there being a big difference in temperature between surface water and the water a couple of kilometers below the surface, and this occurs in tropical coastal areas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The idea is to bring cold water up to the surface using a submerged pipe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The concept dates back to 1881, when...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a guide talking to a group of tourists who are about to visit an English castle.

script.text: We'll be arriving at Branley Castle in about five minutes, but before we get there, I'll give you a little information about the castle, and what our visit will include.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, in fact, there's been a castle on this site for over eleven hundred years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first building was a fort, constructed in 914 AD, for defense against Danish invaders.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By King Alfred the Great's daughter, who ruled England at the time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the following century, after the Normans conquered England, the land was given to a nobleman called Richard de Vere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And he built a castle there that stayed in the de Vere family for over 400 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, when Queen Elizabeth I (Queen Elizabeth the first) announced that she was going to visit the castle in 1576, it was beginning to look a bit run down, and it was decided that rather than repair the guest rooms,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: they'd make a new house for her, out of wood, next to the main hall.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She stayed there for four nights, and apparently it was very luxurious.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But unfortunately, it was destroyed a few years later by fire.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 17th century, the castle belonged to the wealthy Fenys family, who enlarged it and made it more comfortable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, by 1982, the Fenys family could no longer afford to maintain the castle.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Even though they received government support, and they put it on the market.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was eventually taken over by a company who owned a number of amusement parks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But when we get there, I think you'll see that they've managed to retain the original atmosphere of the castle.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When you go inside, you'll find that in the State Rooms, there are lifelike moving wax models dressed in costumes of different periods in the past.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which even carry on conversations together.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as that, in every room, there are booklets giving information about what the room was used for, and the history of the objects and furniture it contains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The castle park's quite extensive. At one time sheep were kept there, and in the 19th century the owners had a little zoo with animals like rabbits and even a baby elephant.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Nowadays the old zoo buildings are used for public displays of paintings and sculpture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The park also has some beautiful trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though the oldest of all, which dated back 800 years, was sadly blown down in 1987.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now you're free to wander around on your own until 4:30.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But then at the end of our visit, we'll all meet together at the bottom of the great staircase.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll then go on to the Long Gallery, where there's a wonderful collection of photographs showing the family who owned the castle 100 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Having tea and cakes in the conservatory, and we'll then take you to the same place where afternoon tea will be served to you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, if you can take a look at your plans, you'll see Branley Castle has 4 towers, joined together by a high wall, with the river on two sides.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Don't miss seeing the Great Hall, that's near the river in the main tower, the biggest one, which was extended and redesigned in the 18th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you want to get a good view of the whole castle, you can walk around the walls.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The starting point is quite near the main entrance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Walk straight down the path until you get to the south gate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it's just there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Don't go on to the north gate, there's no way up from there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There'll shortly be a show in which you can see archers displaying their skill with a bow and arrow.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The quickest way to get there is to take the first left.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After the main entrance, and follow the path past the bridge, then you'll see it in front of you at the end.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you like animals, there's also a display of hunting birds, falcons and eagles and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you go from the main entrance in the direction of the south gate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But turn right before you get there, instead of going through it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll see it on your right, past the first tower.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At 3 pm, there's a short performance of traditional dancing on the outdoor stage.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's right at the other side of the castle from the entrance and over the bridge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's about 10 minutes' walk or so. And finally the shop.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's actually inside one of the towers, but the way in is from the outside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just take the first left after the main entrance, go down the path, and take the first right.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's got some lovely gifts and souvenirs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Right, so we're just arriving.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two environmental science students called Rosie and Martin discussing their presentation on an extinct animal called the woolly Mammoth with their tutor.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, Rosie and Martin, let's look at what you've got for your presentation on woolly mammoths.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, we've got a short outline here.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Thanks, uh, so, it's about a research project in North America.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, but we thought we needed something general about woolly mammoths in our introduction.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: To establish that they were related to our modern elephant, and they lived thousands of years ago in the last ice age.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Maybe we could show a video clip of a cartoon about mammoths.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: But that would be a bit childish. Or we could have a diagram, it could be a timeline to show when they lived, with illustrations?
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Or we could just show a drawing of them walking in the ice?
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: No, let's go with your last suggestion.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Then you're describing the discovery of the mammoth tooth on St Paul's Island in Alaska.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And why it was significant?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, the tooth was found by a man called Russell Graham.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: He picked it up from under a rock in a cave.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: He knew it was special.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: For a start, it was in really good condition, as if it had been just extracted from the animal's jawbone.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Anyway, they found it was 6,500 years old.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: So why was that significant?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well, the Mammoth bones previously found on the North American mainland were much less recent than that.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: So this was really amazing.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Then we're making an animated diagram to show the geography of the area in prehistoric times.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: So originally, St Paul's Island wasn't an island.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: It was connected to the mainland, and mammoths and other animals like bears were able to roam around the whole area.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Then the climate warmed up, and the sea level began to rise, and the island got cut off from the mainland.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: So those mammoths on the island couldn't escape.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: They had to stay on the island.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: And in fact, the species survived there for thousands of years after they'd become extinct on the mainland.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: So, why do you think they died out on the mainland?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: No one's sure.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Anyway, next we'll explain how Graham and his team identified the date when the mammoths became extinct on the island.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: They concluded that the extinction happened 5,600 years ago, which is a very precise time for a prehistoric extinction.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: It's based on samples they took from MUD at the bottom of a lake on the island.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: They analyzed it to find out what had fallen in over time - bits of plants, volcanic ash,
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: and even DNA from the mammoths themselves.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: It's standard procedure, but it took nearly two years to do.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So why don't you quickly go through the main sections of your presentation and discuss what action's needed for each part?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, so for the introduction, we're using a visual.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: So once we've prepared that, we're done.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: I'm not sure.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I think we need to write down all the ideas we want to include here, not just rely on memory.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: How we begin the presentation is so important.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Hmm, you're right.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: The discovery of the Mammoth tooth is probably the most dramatic part, but we don't have that much information.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Only what we got from the online article.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I thought maybe we could get in touch with the researcher who led the team, and ask him to tell us a bit more.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Great idea.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: What about the section with the initial questions asked by the researchers?
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: We've got a lot on that, but we need to make it interesting.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: We could ask the audience to suggest some questions about it, and then see how many of them we can answer.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I don't think it would take too long.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yes, that would add a bit of variety.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Then the section on further research carried out on the island, analyzing the MUD in the lake.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: I wonder if we've actually got too much information here.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Should we cut some?
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: I don't think so, but it's all a bit muddled at present.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: Yes, maybe it would be better if it followed a chronological pattern.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: I think so.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: The findings and possible explanations section is just about ready, but we need to practice it, so we're sure it won't overrun.
script.speaker: ROSIE

script.text: I think it should be OK.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: But yes, ha, let's make sure.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Hmm. In the last section, relevance to the present day, you've got some good ideas, but this is where you need to move away from the ideas of others and give your own viewpoint.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, we'll think about that.
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: Now shall we...
script.speaker: MARTIN

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a lecture about the history of weather forecasting.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In this series of lectures about the history of weather forecasting, I'll start by examining its early history.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That'll be the subject of today's talk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, so we'll start by going back thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most ancient cultures had weather gods, and weather catastrophes such as floods, played an important role in many creation myths.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Generally, weather was attributed to the whims of the gods, as the wide range of weather gods in various cultures shows.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For instance, there's the Egyptian sun god Ra, and Thor, the Norse god of thunder and lightning.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many ancient civilizations developed rites such as dances,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: in order to make the weather gods look kindly on them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the weather was of daily importance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Observing the skies and drawing the correct conclusions from these observations was really important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, their survival depended on it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It isn't known when people first started to observe the skies, but at around 650 BC, the Babylonians produced the first short range weather forecasts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Based on their observations of clouds and other phenomena.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Chinese also recognized weather patterns, and by 300 BC, astronomers had developed a calendar, which divided the year into 24 festivals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each associated with a different weather phenomenon.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The ancient Greeks were the first to develop a more scientific approach to explaining the weather.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The work of the philosopher and scientist Aristotle in the fourth century BC is especially noteworthy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As his ideas held sway for nearly 2,000 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 340 BC, he wrote a book in which he attempted to account for the formation of rain, clouds, wind, and storms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He also described celestial phenomena such as haloes - that is, bright circles of light around the sun, the moon, and bright stars - and comets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many of his observations were surprisingly accurate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, he believed that heat could cause water to evaporate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But he also jumped to quite a few wrong conclusions, such as that winds are breathed out by the earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Errors like this were rectified from the Renaissance onwards.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For nearly 2,000 years, Aristotle's work was accepted as the chief authority on weather theory.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Alongside this, though, in the Middle Ages, weather observations were passed on in the form of proverbs, such as "Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning".
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many of these are based on very good observations, and are accurate, as contemporary meteorologists have discovered.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For centuries, any attempt to forecast the weather could only be based on personal observations, but in the 15th century, scientists began to see the need for instruments. Until then, the only ones available were weather vanes to determine the wind direction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And early versions of rain gauges.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the first invented in the 15th century was a hygrometer, which measured humidity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was one of many inventions that contributed to the development of weather forecasting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1592, the Italian scientist and inventor Galileo developed the world's first thermometer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: His student Torricelli later invented the barometer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which allowed people to measure atmospheric pressure.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1648, the French philosopher Pascal proved that pressure decreases with altitude.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This discovery was verified by English astronomer Halley in 1686.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And Halley was also the first person to map trade winds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This increasing ability to measure factors related to weather helped scientists to understand the atmosphere and its processes better, and they started collecting weather observation data systematically.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 18th century, the scientist and politician Benjamin Franklin carried out work on electricity and lightning in particular, but he was also very interested in weather.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And studied it throughout most of his life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was Franklin who discovered that storms generally travel from west to east.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition to new meteorological instruments, other developments contributed to our understanding of the atmosphere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People in different locations began to keep records.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in the mid 19th century, the invention of the telegraph made it possible for these records to be collated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This led by the end of the 19th century to the first weather services.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was not until the early 20th century that mathematics and physics became part of meteorology, and we'll continue from that point next week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a woman talking to a group of college students about volunteering to help other people.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, my name's Lucy Crittenden, and I'm the director of operations for an organization that arranges volunteering in this part of the country.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: I'm hoping I can persuade one or two of you to become volunteers yourselves.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Let me start by briefly explaining what we mean by volunteering.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Volunteers are teenagers and adults who choose to spend some time unpaid, helping other people in some way.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Most volunteers devote two or three hours to this every week.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: While a few do much more, the people they help may have physical or behavioral difficulties, for example. Volunteers can do all sorts of things, depending on their own abilities and interests.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: If they're supporting a family that's struggling for example, they may be able to give them tips on cooking.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Or recommend how to plan their budget, or how to shop sensibly on their income.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: They might even do some painting or wallpapering, perhaps alongside any members of the family.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Who are able to do it, or even do some babysitting, so that parents can go out for a while.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: The benefit from volunteering isn't only for the people being helped, volunteers also gain from it.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: They're using their skills to cope with somebody's mental or physical ill health.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: And volunteering may be a valuable element of their CV when they're applying for jobs.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Employers usually look favorably on someone who's given up time to help others.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Significantly, most volunteers feel that what they're doing gives them a purpose in their lives, and in my opinion, they're lucky in that respect.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: As many people don't have that feeling.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, I'd like to tell you what some of our volunteers have said about what they do, to give you an idea of the range of ways in which they can help people.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Habib supports an elderly lady who's beginning to show signs of dementia.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Once a week, they along with other elderly people, go to the local community center, where a group of people come in and sing.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: The songs take the listeners back to their youth.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: And for a little while, they can forget the difficulties that they face now.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Our volunteer Consuela is an amazing woman.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: She has difficulty walking herself.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: But she doesn't let that stop her.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: She helps a couple of people with similar difficulties, who had almost stopped walking altogether, by using herself as an example.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Consuela encourages them to walk more and more.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Minh visits a young man who lives alone, and can't leave his home on his own.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: So he hardly ever saw anyone, but together they go out to the cinema.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Or to see friends, the young man hadn't been able to visit for a long time.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Tanya visits an elderly woman once a week.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: When the woman found out that Tanya is a professional dressmaker.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: She got interested.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Tanya showed her some soft toys she'd made, and the woman decided to try it herself.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: And now she really enjoys it, and spends hours making toys.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: They're not perhaps up to Tanya's standard yet, but she gains a lot of pleasure from doing it.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Alexei is a volunteer with a family that faces a number of difficulties.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: By calmly talking over possible solutions with family members, he's helping them to realize that they aren't helpless, and that they can do something themselves to improve their situation.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: This has been great for their self-esteem, and the last volunteer I'll mention, though there are plenty more, is Juba.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: She volunteers with a teenage girl with learning difficulties.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Who wasn't very good at talking to other people.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Juba's worked very patiently with her, and now the girl is far better at expressing herself, and at understanding other people.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: OK, I hope that's given you an idea of what volunteering is all about.
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: Now I'd like to talk to you about...
script.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a trainee music teacher called Joe talking to his supervisor about the school marching band that he has been given responsibility for.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, how are you getting on with your teaching practice at the high school, Joe?
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Well, I've been put in charge of the school marching band, and it's quite a responsibility.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I'd like to talk it over with you.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Go ahead.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: You'd better start by giving me a bit of background.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Well, the band has students in it from all years.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: So they're aged 11 to 18, and there are about 50 of them altogether.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It's quite a popular activity within the school.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I've never worked with a band of more than 20 before, and this is very different.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I can imagine.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: They aren't really good enough to enter national band competitions, but they're in a regional one later in the term.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Even if they don't win, and I don't expect them to.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Hopefully it'll be an incentive for them to try and improve.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Yes, hopefully.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Well, now the town council's organizing a carnival in the summer.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: And the band has been asked to perform.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: If you ask me, they aren't really up to it yet, and I need to get them functioning better as a band, and in a very short time.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Have you been doing anything with them?
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Apart from practicing the music, I mean.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: I played a recording I came across of a drummer talking about how playing in a band had changed his life.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I think it was an after-dinner speech.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I thought it was pretty inspiring, because being in the band had stopped him from getting involved in crime.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: The students seemed to find it interesting too.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: That's good.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: I'm planning to show them that old film from the 1940s 'Strike Up the Band', and talk about it with the students.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: What do you think?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Good idea.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: As it's about a school band, it might make the students realize how much they can achieve if they work together.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: That's what I've got in mind.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I'm hoping I can take some of the band to a parade that's going to take place next month.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: A couple of marching bands will be performing, and the atmosphere should be quite exciting.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It depends on whether I can persuade the school to hire a coach or two to take us there.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Mmm. They sound like good ideas to me.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Thanks.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Can I tell you about a few people in the band who I'm finding it quite difficult to cope with?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I'm sure you'll have some ideas about what I can do.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Go ahead.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: There's a flautist who says she loves playing in the band.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: We rehearse twice a week after school, but she's hardly ever there.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Then she looks for me the next day, and gives me a very plausible reason.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: She says she had to help her mother, or she's been ill, but to be honest, I don't believe her.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Oh, dear.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Any more students with difficulties?
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Plenty.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Uh. There's a trumpeter who thinks she's the best musician in the band, though she certainly isn't.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: She's always saying what she thinks other people should do, which makes my job pretty difficult.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: She sounds a bit of a nightmare.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: You can say that again.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Uh. One of the trombonists has got an impressive sense of rhythm, and could be an excellent musician.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Except that he has breathing difficulties, and he doesn't really have enough breath for the trombone.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: He'd be much better off playing percussion for instance, but he refuses to give up, so he ends up only playing half the notes.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I suppose you have to admire his determination.
script.speaker: LIZZIE

script.text: Hmm. Maybe. One of the percussionists isn't too bad, but he never seems to interact with other people.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: And he always rushes off as soon as the rehearsal ends.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I don't know if there are family reasons or what, but it isn't good in a band where people really need to feel they're part of a group.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Hmm. There are others too, but at least that gives you an idea of what I'm up against.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Do you have any thoughts about what I can do, Lizzie?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a British university lecturer in music talking about concerts in an arts festival.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: As you all know, the university is planning an arts festival for later this year, and here in the music department, we've planned three concerts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These will be public performances, and the program has just been finalized.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The theme of the festival is links between the UK and Australia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this is reflected in the music.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each concert will feature both British and Australian composers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'll tell you briefly about the Australian music.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you probably won't be familiar with that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first concert will include music by Liza Lim, who was born in Perth, Western Australia in 1966.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As a child Lim originally learned to play the piano like so many children, and also the violin.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But when she was 11, her teachers encouraged her to start composing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She found this was her real strength, and she studied and later taught composition, both in Australia and in other countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As a composer, she has received commissions from numerous orchestras, other performers, and festivals in several countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Liza Lim's compositions are vibrant and full of energy, and she often explores Asian and Australian Aboriginal cultural sources.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Including the native instrument the didgeridoo.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is featured in a work called The Compass.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Her music is very expressive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So although it is complex, it has the power of connecting with audiences and performers alike.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the festival, we're going to give a semi-staged performance of The Oresteia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is an opera in seven parts, based on the trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By Aeschylus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Lim composed this when she was in her mid twenties, and she also wrote the text along with Barrie Kosky.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's performed by six singers, a dancer, and an orchestra that, as well as standard orchestral instruments, includes electric guitar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And a traditional Turkish stringed instrument.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Lim wrote that, because the stories in the tragedies are not easy to tell.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The sounds she creates are also disturbing, and they include breathing, sobbing, laughing, and whistling.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The work lasts around 75 minutes, and the rest of the concert will consist of orchestral works by the British composers Ralph Vaughan Williams.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And Frederick Delius.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Moving on now to our second concert, this will begin with instrumental music by British composers, Benjamin Britten and Judith Weir.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After the interval, we'll go to Australia for a piece by Ross Edwards, The Tower of Remoteness, according to Edwards.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The inspiration for this piece came from nature, when he was sitting alone in the dry bed of a creek, overshadowed by the leaves of palm trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Listening to the birds and insects.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Tower of Remoteness is scored for piano and clarinet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Edwards says he realized years after writing the piece.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That he had subconsciously modeled its opening phrase on a bird call.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ross Edwards was born in 1943 in Sydney, Australia, and studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music, and the universities of Adelaide and Sydney.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He's well known in Australia, and in fact, he's one of the country's most performed composers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He's written a wide range of music, from symphonies and concertos to some composed specifically for children.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Edward's music has been described as being 'deeply connected to Australia', and it can be regarded as a Celebration of the diversity of cultures that Australia can be proud of.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The last of the three Australian composers to be represented in our festival is Carl Vine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Born in 1954 Vine, like Liza Lim, comes from Perth, Western Australia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He took up the cornet at the age of five, switching to the piano five years later.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, he went to university to study physics before changing to composition.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After graduating, he moved to Sydney.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And worked as a freelance pianist and composer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before long, he had become prominent in Australia as a composer for dance, and in fact has written 25 scores of that type.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In our third concert, Vine will be represented by his music for the flag handover ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996. This seven-minute orchestral piece was of course heard by millions of people worldwide.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And we'll hear it alongside works written by British composers, Edward Elgar, and more recently, Thomas Adès.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.text: Good morning, Clare House Hotel, Andrew speaking, I'm the Events Manager.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Andrew is the Events Manager, so Events has been written in the space.

script.text: Now we shall begin.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, Clare House Hotel, Andrew speaking, I'm the Events Manager.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Good morning, Andrew.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: My name is Samantha.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: I'm arranging a party for my parents' 50th wedding anniversary.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: And I'm ringing to ask about hiring a room sometime next September, also my parents and several of the guests will need accommodation.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: OK, I'm sure we can help you with that.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Will you be having a sit down meal or a buffet?
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Probably a sit down.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: And do you know how many people there'll be?
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Around 80, I think.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Well we have two rooms that can hold that number.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: One is the Adelphi room, that can seat 85 or hold over 100 if people are standing for a buffet.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: If you have live music, there's room for four or five musicians in the gallery.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Overlooking the room, our guests usually appreciate the fact that the music can be loud enough for dancing, but not too loud for conversation.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Yes, I really don't like it when you can't talk.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Now the Adelphi Room is at the back of the hotel, and there are French windows.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Leading out onto the terrace.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: This has a beautiful display of pots of roses at that time of the year.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Which direction does it face?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Southwest, so that side of the hotel gets the sun in the afternoon and early evening.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Very nice.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: From the terrace, you can see the area of trees within the grounds of the hotel.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Or you can stroll through there to the river.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: That's on the far side, so it isn't visible from the hotel.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: OK, then another option is the Carlton room.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: This is a bit bigger.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: It can hold up to 110 people, and it has the advantage of a stage, which is useful if you have any entertainment.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Or indeed a small band can fit onto it.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Hmm. And can you go outside from the room?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: No, the Carlton room is on the first floor.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: But on one side, the windows look out onto the lake.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Lovely.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: I think either of those rooms would be suitable.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Can I tell you about some of the options we offer in addition?
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Please do.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: As well as a meal, you can have an mc, a master of ceremonies, who'll be with you throughout the party.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: What exactly is the MC's function?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: I suppose they make a speech during the meal, if we need one, do they?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: All our MCs are trained as public speakers, so they can easily get people's attention.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Many guests are glad to have someone who can make themselves heard above the chatter, and they're also your support.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: If anything goes wrong, the MC will deal with it, so you can relax.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Great, I'll need to ask you about food, but something else that's important is accommodation.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: You obviously have rooms in the hotel.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: But do you also have any other accommodation, like cabins, for example?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Yes, there are 5 in the grounds, all self contained.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: They each sleep 2 to 4 people, and have their own living room, bathroom, and small kitchen.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: That sounds perfect for what we'll need.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now you have various facilities, don't you?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Are they all included in the price of hiring the room?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: The pool for instance.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: Normally you'd be able to use it, but it'll be closed throughout September for refurbishment, I'm afraid.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: The gym will be available though, at no extra charge.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: That's open all day from 6 in the morning until midnight.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: And the tennis courts but there is a small additional payment for those.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: We have four courts, and it's worth booking in advance if you possibly can, as there can be quite a long waiting list for them.
script.speaker: ANDREW

script.text: Right, now could we discuss the food?
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: This would be dinner around 7 o'clock...
script.speaker: SAMANTHA

script.text: That is the end of section 1.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a holiday company representative talking to a group of tourists in a large hotel about things they can do during their holiday.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, everyone.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: I'm Jake Stevens, and I'm your rep here at the hotel.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: I'm sure you'll all have a great time here.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: So, let me tell you a bit about what's on offer.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: I'll start by telling you about some of the excursions that are available for guests.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: One thing you have to do while you're here is go dolphin watching.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: On our boat trips we pretty well guarantee you'll see dolphins.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: If you don't, you can repeat the trip free of charge.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: We organize daily trips for just 35 euros.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Unfortunately, there aren't any places left for this afternoon's trip, but come and see me to book for later in the week.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: If you're energetic, I'd recommend our forest walk.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's a guided walk of about 7 km.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: There'll be a stop halfway, and you'll be provided with a drink and sandwiches.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: There's some fairly steep climbs up the hills, so you need to be reasonably fit for this one.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: With good shoes, though, and bring a waterproof in case it rains.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's just 25 euros, all inclusive, and it's every Wednesday.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Then on Thursdays, we organize a cycle trip, which will give you all the fun of biking without the effort.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: We'll take you and your bike up to the top of Mount Larna.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And leave you to bike back.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's a 700 meter drop in just 20 kilometers, so this isn't really for inexperienced cyclists, as you'll be going pretty fast.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And if it's a clear day, you'll have fantastic views.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: On our local craft tour, you can find out about the traditional activities in the island.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And the best thing about this trip is that it's completely free.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: You'll be taken to a factory where jewelry is made, and also a ceramics center.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: If you want, you can buy some of the products, but that's entirely up to you.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: The trip starts after lunch on Thursday, and you'll return by 6:00 pm.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: If you're interested in astronomy, you may already know that the island's one of the best places in the world to observe the night sky.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: We can offer trips to the observatory on Friday for those who are interested.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: They cost €90 per person, and you'll be shown the huge telescopes, and have a talk from an expert who will explain all about how they work.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Afterwards, we'll head down to Sunset Beach, where you can have a dip in the ocean if you want, before we head off back to the hotel.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Finally, there's horse riding.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: This is organized by the Equestrian Center over near Playa Cortino, and it's a great experience if you're a keen horseback rider.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Or even if you've never been on a horse before, they take you down to the beach, and you can canter along the sand and through the waves.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It costs 35 euros.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And it's available every day.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, there's plenty to do in the daytime, but what about night life?
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Well, the No. 1 attraction's called 'Musical Favorites'.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Guests enjoy a three-course meal and unlimited free drinks, and watch a fantastic show, starting with a musical set in Paris, and then crossing the Atlantic to Las Vegas, and finally Copacabana.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: At the end, the cast members come down from the stage still in their stunning costumes.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And you'll have a chance to chat with them.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's hugely popular, so let me know now if you're interested, because it's no good leaving it until the last minute.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's on Friday night.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Tickets are just 50 euros each, but for an extra 10 euros, you can have a table right by the stage.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: If you'd like to go back in time, there's the Castle Feast on Saturday evening.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: It's held in a 12th century castle, and you eat in the great courtyard.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: With ladies in long gowns serving your food.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: You're given a whole chicken each, which you eat in the medieval way, using your hands instead of cutlery.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And you're entertained by competitions where the horseback riders attempt to knock one another off their horses.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: Then you can watch the dancers in the ballroom.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: And join in as well if you want.
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: OK, so now if anyone has...
script.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear Stephanie, who is thinking about taking a one year course in children's literature, talking to Trevor, who is currently taking the course.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25 now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, Trevor.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Hello, Stephanie.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: You said you wanted to talk about the course I'm taking on literature for children.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I'm thinking of doing it next year, but I'd like to find out more about it first.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: OK, well as you probably know, it's a one year course.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: It's divided into 6 modules, and you have to take all of them.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: One of the most interesting ones for me at least, was about the purpose of children's literature.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: You mean whether it should just entertain children, or should be educational as well?
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Right, and whether the teaching should be factual, giving them information about the world, or ethical, teaching them values.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: What's fascinating is that the writer isn't necessarily conscious of the message they're conveying. For instance, a story might show a child who has a problem as a result of not doing what an adult has told them to do, implying that children should always obey adults.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: I see what you mean.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: That module made me realize how important stories are.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: They can have a significant effect on children as they grow up.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Actually, it inspired me to have a go at it myself, just for my own interest.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: I know I can't compete with the really popular stories, like the Harry Potter books, they're very good.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: And even young kids like my 7 year old niece love reading them.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hmm, I'm very interested in illustrations in stories.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Is that covered in the course?
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Yes, there's a module on pictures.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: And how they're sometimes central to the story.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hmm, that's good.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I remember some frightening ones I saw as a child, and I can still see them vividly in my mind years later.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Pictures can be so powerful, just as powerful as words.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I've always enjoyed drawing, so that's the field I want to go into when I finish the course.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I bet that module will be really helpful.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I'm sure it will.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: We also studied comics in that module, but I'm not convinced of their value, not compared with books.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: One of the great things about words is that you use your imagination, but with a comic you don't have to.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: But children are so used to visual input on TV, video games, and so on.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: There are plenty of kids who wouldn't even try to read a book, so, I think comics can serve a really useful purpose.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: You mean it's better to read a comic than not to read at all?
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Yes, I suppose you're right.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: I just think it's sad when children don't read books.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: What about books for girls and books for boys?
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Does the course go into that?
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Yes, there's a module on it.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: For years, lots of stories in English at least, assumed that boys went out and did adventurous things, and girls stayed at home and played with dolls.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: I was amazed how many books were targeted at just one sex or the other.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Of course, this reflects society as it is when the books are written.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: That's true.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: So it sounds as though you think it's a good course.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Definitely.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Have you been reading lots of children's stories to help you decide whether to take the course?
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Yeah, I've gone as far back as the late 17th century, though I know there were earlier children's stories.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: So does that mean you've read Perrault's fairy tales, Cinderella, The Sleeping Beauty, and so on?
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Yes, they must be important, because no stories of that type had been written before.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: These were the first.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Then there's the Swiss family Robinson.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I haven't read that.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: The English name makes it sound as though Robinson is the family surname, but a more accurate translation would be the Swiss Robinsons, because it's about a Swiss family who are shipwrecked.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Like Robinson Crusoe in the novel of a century earlier.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Well, I never knew that.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Have you read Hoffmann's The Nutcracker and the Mouse King?
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Wasn't that the basis for Tchaikovsky's ballet The Nutcracker?
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: It has some quite bizarre elements.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I hope you've read Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: It's probably my favorite children's story of all time.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Ah. Mine too.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: And it's so surprising, because Wilde is best known for his plays, and most of them are very witty, but The Happy Prince is really moving.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I struggled with Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, they are long books, and I gave up after one.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: It's extremely popular though.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: But whereas something like The Happy Prince just carried me along with it, The Lord of the Rings took more effort than I was prepared to give it.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: I didn't find that, I love it.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Another one I've read is War Horse.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Oh yes, it's about the First World War, isn't it?
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Hardly what you'd expect for a children's story.
script.speaker: TREVOR

script.text: Exactly, but it's been very successful.
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: Have you read any...
script.speaker: STEPHANIE

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a branch of archaeology called Marine Archaeology.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In today's class, I'm going to talk about marine archaeology, the branch of archaeology focusing on human interaction with the sea, lakes and rivers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's the study of ships, cargoes, shipping facilities, and other physical remains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'll give you an example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then go on to show how this type of research is being transformed by the use of the latest technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Atlit-Yam was a village on the coast of the eastern Mediterranean.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which seems to have been thriving until around 7,000 BC, the residents kept cattle, caught fish, and stored grain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They had wells for fresh water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many of their houses were built around a courtyard, and were constructed of stone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The village contained an impressive monument, seven half-tonne stones standing in a semicircle around a spring, that might have been used for ceremonial purposes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Atlit-Yam may have been destroyed swiftly by a tsunami, or climate change may have caused glaciers to melt, and sea levels to rise.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Flooding the village gradually.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Whatever the cause, it now lies 10 meters below the surface of the Mediterranean, buried under sand at the bottom of the sea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's been described as the largest and best preserved prehistoric settlement ever found on the seabed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For marine archaeologists, Atlit-Yam is a treasure trove.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Research on the buildings, tools, and the human remains has revealed how the bustling village once functioned.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And even what diseases some of its residents suffered from.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But of course, this is only one small village, one window into a lost world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For a fuller picture, researchers need more sunken settlements.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the hard part is finding them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Underwater research used to require divers to find shipwrecks or artifacts, but in the second half of the 20th century, various types of underwater vehicles were developed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some controlled from a ship on the surface, and some of them autonomous, which means they don't need to be operated by a person.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Autonomous underwater vehicles, or AUVs, are used in the oil industry, for instance, to create maps of the seabed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before rigs and pipelines are installed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To navigate, they use sensors such as compasses and sonar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Until relatively recently, they were very expensive, and so heavy that they had to be launched from a large vessel with a winch.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the latest AUVs are much easier to maneuver.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can be launched from the shore or a small ship. And they're much cheaper, which makes them more accessible to research teams.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They are also very sophisticated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can communicate with each other.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And for example, work out the most efficient way to survey a site, or to find particular objects on the seabed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Field tests show the approach can work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, in a trial in 2015 three AUVs searched for wrecks at Marzamemi, off the coast of Sicily.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The site is the final resting place of an ancient Roman ship, which sank in the 6th century AD.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While ferrying prefabricated marble elements for the construction of an early church, the AUVs mapped the area in detail.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finding other ships carrying columns of the same material.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Creating an internet in the sea for AUVs to communicate is no easy matter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Wi-Fi networks on land use electromagnetic waves, but in water, these will only travel a few centimeters.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, a more complex mix of technologies is required.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For short distances, AUVs can share data using light, while acoustic waves are used to communicate over long distances.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But more creative solutions are also being developed, where an AUV working on the seabed offloads data to a second AUV, which then surfaces and beams the data home to the research team using a satellite.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's also a system that enables AUVs to share information from seabed scans and other data.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, if an AUV surveying the seabed finds an intriguing object, it can share the coordinates of the object, that is its position with a nearby AUV that carries superior cameras.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And arrange for that AUV to make a closer inspection of the object.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Marine archaeologists are excited about the huge potential of these AUVs for their discipline.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One site where they're going to be deployed is the Gulf of Baratti, off the Italian coast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In 1974, a 2,000-year-old Roman vessel was discovered here, in 18 meters of water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When it sank, it was carrying medical goods in wooden or tin receptacles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Its cargo gives us insight into the treatments available all those years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Including tablets that are thought to have been dissolved to form a cleansing liquid for the eyes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Other Roman ships went down nearby, taking their cargoes with them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some held huge pots made of terracotta.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some were used for transporting cargoes of olive oil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And others held wine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In many cases, it's only these containers that remain, while the wooden ships have been buried under silt on the seabed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another project that's about to be...
script.speaker: SPEAKER
