script.text: You will hear part of a presentation by a history student about the history of coffee.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In my presentation, I'm going to talk about coffee, and its importance both in economic and social terms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We think it was first drunk in the Arab world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there's hardly any documentary evidence of it before the 1500s, although of course that doesn't mean that people didn't know about it before then.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, there is evidence that coffee was originally gathered from bushes growing wild in Ethiopia, in the northeast of Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the early 16th century, it was being bought by traders, and gradually its use as a drink spread throughout the Middle East.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's also known that in 1522, in the Turkish city of Constantinople, which was the center of the Ottoman Empire, the court physician approved its use as a medicine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By the mid 1500s, coffee bushes were being cultivated in the Yemen, and for the next hundred years, this region produced most of the coffee drunk in Africa and the Arab world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's particularly interesting about coffee is its effect on social life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was rarely drunk at home, but instead, people went to coffee houses to drink it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These people, usually men, would meet to drink coffee and chat about issues of the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But at the time, this chance to share ideas and opinions was seen as something that was potentially dangerous, and in 1623, the ruler of Constantinople demanded the destruction of all the coffee houses in the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although after his death, many new ones opened, and coffee consumption continued.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 17th century, coffee drinking spread to Europe, and here too, coffee shops became places where ordinary people, nearly always men, could meet to exchange ideas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because of this, some people said that these places performed a similar function to universities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The opportunity they provided for people to meet together outside their own homes, and to discuss the topics of the day had an enormous impact on social life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And many social movements and political developments had their origins in coffee house discussions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the late 1600s, the Yemeni monopoly on coffee production broke down, and coffee production started to spread around the world, helped by European colonization.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Europeans set up coffee plantations in Indonesia and the Caribbean, and production of coffee in the colonies skyrocketed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Different types of coffee were produced in different areas, and it's interesting that the names given to these different types, like Mocha or Java coffee,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: were often taken from the port they were shipped to Europe from.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But if you look at the labor system in the different colonies, there were some significant differences.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Brazil and the various Caribbean colonies, coffee was grown in huge plantations, and the workers there were almost all slaves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But this wasn't the same in all colonies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, in Java, which had been colonized by the Dutch, the peasants grew coffee, and passed a proportion of this onto the Dutch.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it was used as a means of taxation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But whatever system was used, under the European powers of the 18th century, coffee production was very closely linked to colonization.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Coffee was grown in ever increasing quantities to satisfy the growing demand from Europe, and it became nearly as important as sugar production, which was grown under very similar conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, coffee prices were not yet low enough for people to drink it regularly at home,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: so most coffee consumption still took place in public coffee houses,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and it still remained something of a luxury item. In Britain, however, a new drink was introduced from China, and started to become popular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Gradually taking over from coffee, although at first it was so expensive that only the upper classes could afford it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was tea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And by the late 1700s it was being widely drunk.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, when the USA gained independence from Britain in 1776, they identified this drink with Britain, and coffee remained the preferred drink in the USA, as it still is today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, by the early 19th century, coffee was already being widely produced and consumed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But during this century, production boomed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And coffee prices started to fall.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was partly because new types of transportation had been developed, which were cheaper and more efficient.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So now, working people could afford to buy coffee.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It wasn't just a drink for the middle classes, and this was at a time when large parts of Europe were starting to work in industries, and sometimes this meant their work didn't stop when it got dark.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They might have to continue throughout the night.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So the use of coffee as a stimulant became important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It wasn't just a drink people drank in the morning for breakfast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There were also changes in cultivation...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a restaurant manager talking to a small group of new staff who are starting work as kitchen assistants in a restaurant.

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: My name's Joy Parkins, and I'm the restaurant manager.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And I understand that none of you've had any previous experience as kitchen assistants.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Well, you might be feeling a bit nervous now, but most of our kitchen assistants say they enjoy the work.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: OK, they might get shouted at sometimes, but it's nothing personal.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And they're pleased that they have so many different things to do, which means they never get bored.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And I'll tell you straight away that if you do well, we might think about moving you up and giving you some more responsibility.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Right, well, you've all shown up on time, which is an excellent start.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Now I'm glad to see none of you have unsuitable footwear, so that's good.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: You need to be careful as the floors can get very wet and slippery.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Those of you with long hair have got it well out of the way, but some of you'll need to remove your rings and bracelets, just put them somewhere safe for today.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And remember to leave them at home tomorrow, as they can be a safety hazard.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Now it's going to be a busy day for you all today.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: We don't have any tables free for this evening.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And only a few for lunch.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Fortunately, we've got our head chef back.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: He was away on holiday all last week, which meant the other chefs had extra work.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Now I'll tell you a bit more about the job in a minute, but first some general regulations for all of you, whatever your age.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: There's some equipment you mustn't use until you've been properly trained, like the waste disposal system for example, for health and safety reasons.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Then I think there are two of you here who are under 18.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: That's Emma and Jake, isn't it?
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Right, so for you two the meat slicer is out of bounds, and of course none of you are allowed to use the electric mixer until you've been shown how it works.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Now, you may have heard that this can be a stressful job, and I have to say that can be true.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: You'll be working an 8-hour day for the first week.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Though you'll have the chance to do overtime after that as well, if you want to.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: But however long the hours are, you'll get a break in the middle.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: What you will find is that you're on your feet all day long, lifting and carrying.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: So, if you're not fit now, you soon will be.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: You'll find you don't have much chance to take it easy, when someone tells you to do something, you need to do it straight away.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: But at least we do have a very efficient air conditioning system, compared with some kitchens.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

script.text: Now, let me tell you about some of the people you need to know.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: So, as I said, I'm Joy Parkins, and I decide who does what during the day and how long they work for.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: I'll be trying to get you to work with as many different people in the kitchen as possible, so that you learn while you're on the job.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: One person whose name you must remember is David Field.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: If you injure yourself at all, even if it's really minor, you must report to him, and he'll make sure the incident is recorded.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And you get the appropriate treatment.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: He's trained to give basic treatment to staff himself, or he'll send you off somewhere else if necessary.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Then there's Dexter Wills.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: He's the person you need to see, if you smash a plate or something like that.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Don't just leave it and hope no one will notice.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: It's really important to get things noted and replaced, or there could be problems later.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: And finally, there's Mike Smith.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: He's the member of staff who takes care of all the stores of perishables.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: So, if you notice we're getting low in flour or sugar or something, make sure you let him know, so he can put in an order.
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: OK, now the next thing...
script.speaker: JOY PARKINS

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two students called Trudie and Stewart, who are both studying to be librarians, discussing a paper that they are going to write together.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, Stewart, we need to start planning our paper on public libraries.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Have you thought of an angle yet?
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Well, there's so much we could look into, how libraries have changed over the centuries, for instance, or how different countries organize them, what do you think, Trudie?
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Maybe we should concentrate on this country and try to relate the changes in libraries to external developments, like the fact that far more people can read than a century ago, and that the local population may speak lots of different languages.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: We could include something about changes in the source of funding too.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Yes, but remember we're only supposed to write a short paper, so it's probably best if we don't go into funding in any detail.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Right, well, shall we just brainstorm a few ideas to get started?
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: OK, we obviously need to look at the impact of new technology, particularly the internet.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Now that lots of books have been digitalized, people can access them from their own computers at home.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: And if everyone did that, libraries would be obsolete.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: But the digitalized books that are available online for free are mostly out of copyright, aren't they?
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: And copyright in this country lasts for 70 years after the author dies.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: So you won't find the latest best-seller or up-to-date information.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: That's an important point.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Anyway, I find it hard to concentrate when I'm reading a long text on a screen.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: I'd much rather read a physical book, and it takes longer to read on a screen.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Oh, I prefer it.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: I suppose it's just a personal preference.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Hmm, I expect libraries will go on evolving in the next few years.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Some have already become centers where community activities take place.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Like local clubs meeting there, I think that'll become even more common.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: I'd like to think so, and that they'll still be serving their traditional function, but I'm not so sure.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: There are financial implications after all.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: What I'm afraid will happen is that books and magazines will all disappear, and there'll just be rows and rows of computers.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: They won't look anything like the libraries we're used to.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Well, we'll see.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 24 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I've just had an idea.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Why don't we make an in-depth study of our local public library as background to our paper?
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Yes, that'd be interesting, and raise all sorts of issues.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Let's make a list of possible things we could ask about, then work out some sort of structure.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: For instance, um, we could interview some of the staff, and find out whether the library has its own budget, or if that's controlled by the local council.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: And what their policies are.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: I know they don't allow food, but I'd love to find out what types of noise they ban.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: There always seems to be a lot of talking, but never music.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Hmm, I don't know if that's a policy or it just happens.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Ah. I've often wondered.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Then there are things like how the library is affected by employment laws.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: I suppose there are rules about working hours, facilities for staff and so on.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Then there are other issues relating to the design of the building and how customers use it, like what measures does the library take to ensure their safety?
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: They'd need floor coverings that aren't slippery,
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: and emergency exits for instance.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Oh, and another thing, there's the question of the kind of insurance the library needs to have, in case anyone gets injured.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Yes, that's something else to find out.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: You know something I've often wondered.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: What's that?
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Well, you know they've got an archive of local newspapers going back years.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Well, next to it, they've got the diary of a well known politician from the late 19th century.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: I wonder why it's there.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Do you know what his connection was with this area?
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: No idea.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Let's add it to our list of things to find out.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Oh, I've just thought - you know people might ask in the library about local organizations, like sports clubs?
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Hmm. Well, I wonder if they keep a database, or whether they just look online.
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: I quite fancy finding out what the differences are between a library that's open to the public and one that's part of a museum, for example.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: They must be very different.
script.speaker: STEWART

script.text: Hmm, then something else I'd like to know is...
script.speaker: TRUDIE

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture for business students about business values.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In public discussion of business, we take certain values for granted.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, I'm going to talk about four of them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Collaboration, hard work, creativity, and excellence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. Most people would say they're all good things.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm going to suggest that's an over-simple view.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trouble with these values is that they're theoretical concepts removed from the reality of day-to-day business, uh, pursue values by all means.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But be prepared for what may happen as a result.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can actually cause damage, which is not at all the intention.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Business leaders generally try to do the right thing, but all too often the right thing backfires.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If those leaders adopt values without understanding and managing the side effects that arise.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The values can easily get in the way of what's actually intended.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, so the first value I'm going to discuss is collaboration.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. Let me give you an example, on a management training course I once attended.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We were put into groups, and had to construct a bridge across a stream, using building blocks that we were given.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The rule was that everyone in the team had to move at least one building block during the construction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This was intended to encourage teamwork, but it was really a job best done by one person.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The other teams tried to collaborate on building the structure, and descended into confusion with everyone getting in each other's way.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our team leader solved the challenge brilliantly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She simply asked everyone in the team to move a piece a few centimeters to comply with the rule, and then let the person in the team with an aptitude for puzzles like this build it alone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We finished before any other team.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: My point is that the task wasn't really suited to team working, so why make it one?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Teamwork can also lead to inconsistency, a common cause of poor sales.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the case of a smartphone that a certain company launched.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One director wanted to target the business market, and another demanded it was aimed at consumers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The company wanted both directors to be involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So gave the product a consumer-friendly name, but marketed it to companies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The result was that it met the needs of neither group.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It would have been better to let one director or the other have his way, not both.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now industriousness or hard work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's easy to mock people who say they work hard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. After all, a hamster running around in a wheel is working hard, and getting nowhere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, hard work is valuable, but only when properly targeted, otherwise it wastes the resources that companies value most, time and energy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that's bad for the organization.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's a management model that groups people according to four criteria, clever, hard-working, stupid, and lazy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here, lazy means having a rational determination not to carry out unnecessary tasks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It doesn't mean trying to avoid work altogether.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most people display two of these characteristics, and the most valuable people are those who are both clever and lazy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They possess intellectual clarity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they don't rush into making decisions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They come up with solutions to save the time and energy spent by the stupid and hard-working group.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead of throwing more man hours at a problem, the clever and lazy group looks for a more effective solution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Next, we come to creativity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This often works well, creating an attention grabbing TV commercial for example, might lead to increased sales.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it isn't always a good thing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some advertising campaigns are remembered for their creativity without having any effect on sales.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This happened a few years ago with the launch of a chocolate bar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Subsequent research showed that plenty of consumers remembered the adverts, but had no idea what was being advertised.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trouble is that the creator derives pleasure from coming up with the idea.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And wrongly assumes the audience for the campaign will share that feeling.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A company that brings out thousands of new products may seem more creative than a company that only has a few, but it may be too creative.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And make smaller profits.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Creativity needs to be targeted to solve a problem that the company has identified.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just coming up with more and more novel products isn't necessarily a good thing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And finally, excellence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We all know companies that claim they strive for excellence, but it takes a long time to achieve excellence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In business, being first with a product is more profitable than having the best product.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A major study of company performance compared pioneers - that is, companies bringing out the first version of a particular product - with followers, the companies that copied and improved on that product.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The study found that the pioneers commanded an average market share of 29 percent, while the followers achieved less than half that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Only 13 percent, even though their product might have been better.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Insisting on excellence in everything we do is time consuming, wastes energy, and leads to losing out on opportunities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Sometimes, second-rate work is more worthwhile than excellence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: 'Make sure it's excellent' sounds like a good approach to business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the just get started approach is likely to be more successful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a man talking to a group of people about a tour of theatres in the city of Munich in Germany that he has arranged for them.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, I've now almost succeeded in finalizing plans for our tour, so I'll bring you up to date with what I know.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you know, we're flying first to Munich on Monday the 4th.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The flight is at 11:30 so it's too early to have lunch at the airport.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I suggest we meet there for coffee at 10, which should give us plenty of time for breakfast before we leave home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When we arrive in Munich, we'll be met at the airport by Claus Bauer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Claus works for a tour operator, and he'll look after us for the time we'll be in Germany.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He's already liaised with the managers of the theatres we're going to visit, and he's also arranged for an officer of the National Theatre in Munich to show us round the theater one afternoon during our stay.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now last time we discussed this trip, I didn't have the precise cost for hotel rooms, but now I have.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The normal rate at the hotel where we're staying is €150 a night for a double room.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'd hoped to get that down to 120 euros, but in fact I've been able to negotiate a rate of 110.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That'll be reflected in the final payment which you'll need to make by the end of this week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Tuesday, the day after our arrival, I had hoped we could sit in on a rehearsal at one of the theaters, but unfortunately that's proved very difficult to arrange.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So instead, we'll have a coach trip to one of the amazing castles in the mountains south of Munich.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Tuesday evening, we'll all have dinner together in a restaurant near our hotel, from talking to you all about your preferences.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was clear that a typical local restaurant would be too meat oriented for some of you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of you suggested an Italian restaurant.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But I must confess that I decided to book a Lebanese one, as we have plenty of opportunities to go to an Italian restaurant at home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Wednesday afternoon, the director of the play we're going to see that evening will talk to us at the theater.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She'll describe the whole process of producing a play.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Including how she chose the actors, and as the play we're going to see is a modern one, how she worked with the playwright.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, now I'd just like to make a few points about the plays we're going to see, partly because it might influence your choice of clothes to take with you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The play we're seeing on Wednesday evening is a modern one, and we're going to the premiere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So it'll be quite a dressy occasion, though of course you don't have to dress formally.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I gather it's rather a multimedia production with amazing lighting effects and a soundtrack of electronic music, though unfortunately the playwright is ill and is unlikely to be able to attend.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Thursday, we're seeing a play that was first performed last year, when it was commissioned to mark a hundred years since the birth in the town of a well-known scientist.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're going to see a revival of that production, which aroused a lot of interest.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Friday's play will really make you think hard about what clothes to pack, as it'll be in the garden of a palace.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a beautiful setting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But I'd better warn you, there won't be much protection from the wind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On Saturday, we're going by coach to a theater in another town, not far from Munich.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This will be the opening of a drama festival.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the mayor and all the other dignitaries of the town will be attending.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After the performance, the mayor is hosting a reception for all the audience.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And there'll be a band playing traditional music of the region.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After having a day off on Sunday, our final play is on Monday, and it's in the stunning setting of the Old Town Hall, which dates back to the 14th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The performance marks the fifty years that the lead actor has been on stage, and the play is the one where he made his first professional appearance, all those years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the day after that, we'll be flying back home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, have you got any questions before I...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear James, who is in the Scandinavian Studies department at his university, talking to his tutor Beth.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Oh, good morning.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Uh, You must be James.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I'm Beth Cartwright.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Please call me Beth.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Now as this is your first tutorial since you started on the Scandinavian Studies course.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I'd like to find out something about you.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Why did you decide to take this course?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Well, my mother is Danish, and although we always lived in England.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: She used to talk about her home a lot, and that made me want to visit Denmark.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: We hardly ever did though, my mother usually went on her own.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: But whenever her relations or friends were in England, they always came to see us.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: I see.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: So I assume you already speak Danish, one of the languages you'll be studying.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I can get by when I talk to people, though I'm not terribly accurate.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Now you probably know that you'll spend the third year of the course abroad.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Have you had any thoughts about that?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I'm really looking forward to it.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: And although Denmark seems the obvious place to go, because of my family connections, I'd love to spend the time in Iceland.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Oh, I'm sure it can be arranged.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Do you have any plans for when you graduate?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: A lot of students go on to take a master's degree.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I think the 4 years of the undergraduate course will be enough for me.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: I'm interested in journalism, and I quite like the idea of moving to Scandinavia and writing for magazines.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: I'd find that more creative than translating.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Which I suppose most graduates do.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: OK, now how are you finding the courses you're taking this term, James?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Well, I'm really enjoying the one on Swedish cinema.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: That'll continue next term, but the one on Scandinavian literature that's running at the moment will be replaced by more specialized courses.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Oh, and by the way.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: If you're interested in watching Danish television programs, there's going to be a course on that the term after next.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: That sounds good.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Have you started thinking about the literature paper that you have to write in the next few weeks?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Yes, my first choice would be to do something on the Icelandic sagas.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Hmm, the trouble with that is that a lot of people choose that topic, and it can be difficult to get hold of the books you'll need.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Why not leave that for another time?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: You might find modern novels or 19th century playwrights interesting.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I've read or seen several plays in translation, so that would be a good idea.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Fine, I'll put you down for that topic.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Right, so what would you advise me to aim at in the paper?
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: First, I suggest you avoid taking one writer and going into a great deal of detail.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: That approach certainly has its place, but I think you first need to get an understanding of the literature in the context of the society in which it was produced, who it was written for.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: How it was published and so on.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I also think that's more fruitful than placing it within the history of the genre.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: OK, that sounds reasonable.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Could I ask for some advice about writing the paper I'm working on about the Vikings?
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: I have to do that this week, and I'm a bit stuck.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Have you decided yet what to write about?
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: No, I haven't.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: There's so much that seems interesting, Viking settlement in other countries, trade, mythology.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Well, what I suggest is that you read an assignment a student wrote last year, which is kept in the library.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: It's short and well focused, and I'm sure you'll find it helpful.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I'll give you the details in a moment.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Textbooks usually cover so many topics, it can be very difficult to choose just one.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: I've got a DVD of the film about the Vikings that came out earlier this year.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Should I watch that again?
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: If it's the one I am thinking of... I'd ignore it.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: It's more fantasy than reality, but I've got a recording of a documentary that you should watch.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: It makes some interesting and provocative points, which I think will help you to focus your topic.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Right, so then should I work out an outline?
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Yes, just headings for different sections at this stage, and then you should start looking for suitable articles and books to draw on.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: And take notes which you organize according to those headings.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: I see.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: Then put short phrases and sentences as bullet points under each heading.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: Make sure that this skeleton makes sense and flows properly before writing up the paper in full.
script.speaker: BETH

script.text: OK, thanks.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: That's very helpful.
script.speaker: JAMES

script.text: That is the end of section 3.

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture about conflict at work, given by a business studies lecturer.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Over the years, attitudes towards workers have changed considerably.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After all, there was a time when workers had no rights at all.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And labored in appalling conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Conditions have improved a lot, but conflict in the workplace is still common.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And human resources managers nowadays need to be able to deal with it when necessary.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What is conflict in the workplace?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Definitions vary, but I'm taking it to refer to a whole range of behaviors that the victim finds unacceptable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From minor, harmless arguments to - at the opposite extreme - physical violence.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Much of this is covered by the term bullying.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By which I mean one or more people behaving abusively or aggressively against another who is in a weaker position.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although all behavior like this is a form of conflict, not all conflict can be described in these terms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As with all human behavior, there are numerous reasons for it, but often it's caused by someone who feels the need to show their superiority over someone else, in order to feel that they aren't at the lowest level in a hierarchy or a group of people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In some cases, one person simply dislikes the other, on the basis that the personality of one is in some way incompatible with that of the other person.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A general habit of optimism in one person could make them intolerant of a colleague who's constantly pessimistic - not that that justifies treating them badly, of course.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some conflicts arise when people are more interested in promoting themselves and their team than in the company as a whole.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These conflicts are called 'structural', and could come about, for example, when a sales team believe they are the only people in the business who do any useful work, and look down on behind-the-scenes administrators.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Conflict obviously affects the individuals concerned - the situation is likely to be very stressful for victims, resulting in their absence from work, possibly for months.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For the company, if no effort is made to deal with conflict, it can spiral out of control, and even lead to the breakdown of the business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some interesting work with chief executives - CEOs - has uncovered some of the reasons why they may treat colleagues badly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many CEOs combine two opposing characteristics: confidence - that is, the belief that they're capable of great achievements - with a high level of anxiety, a fear of missing targets, whether set by themselves or by the directors of the company.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This combination can make them respond badly to anyone who questions their decisions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In a high pressure work environment, such characteristics become problematic, and it's particularly difficult to tackle the situation where colleagues, managers, and board members are all trying to achieve their own visions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When they can't agree on strategic issues, and on where they see the business going, there are real problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For managers at lower levels within the organization, it might seem that an autocratic form of management - where the chief executive gives orders and everyone else has to obey - would see more conflict than others.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Interestingly though, a company with a more democratic business model can suffer more when uncertainty about who to report to leads to conflicting demands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now I'll say a little about dealing with the type of conflict that has harmful effects.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, the ideal is to prevent it arising in the first place.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A good manager at any level will make efforts to earn the respect of the people they work with, particularly those who report to them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That will involve politeness in all communications, and treating them as equals who happen to have a different role within the organization.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Sometimes, of course, conflict does occur, and can get out of hand.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In such cases, the human resources department often gets involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, if one of the parties in a conflict sees human resources as simply a mouthpiece for the chief executive, then an external mediator might be able to help. By talking to both sides and trying to find the truth of what's been happening.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can build a clear picture of the situation, and give feedback that both sides will accept, precisely because they're independent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a training session for new employees at a large travel company.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 17.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 17.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In this session in your training day, we're going to look at some of the more specialized holidays we offer at BC Travel.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, the travel business is very competitive and it's important to be aware of how the market's changing and developing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In terms of age groups, the over 65s are an important market, and one that's increasing steadily year on year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The fewest holidays are taken by the 31 to 42 year olds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that figure shows no sign of rising.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The biggest market at present is still the youngest group, the 16 to 30s, but this group's also seen the biggest drop over the last few years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Whereas there's a noticeable growth in the number of holidays taken by the 55 to 64 year olds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as the 43 to 54 year olds are concerned, bookings there are steady, but I have to say we haven't seen the increase we expected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One trend we're noticing with nearly all age groups is the growing popularity of holidays in which clients do some kind of specialized activity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm not talking here about adventure holidays where clients take part in high risk activities like white water rafting, just for the thrill of it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Activity holidays usually involve rather less high risk sports or things like art and music.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They're not necessarily cheaper than ordinary holidays, often the opposite in fact, but they do often take place outside the main tourist centers, which gives an opportunity for clients to find out more about the local people and customs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And many say this is one of the most positive features of these holidays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course, they offer the chance to develop a new skill or talent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But clients often say that more than this, it's the chance to create lasting relationships with other like minded people, that's the main draw.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let me give you some examples of BC Travel activity holidays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our painting holidays take place in four different centers in France and Italy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they're very popular with clients of all abilities from beginners onwards.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've got an excellent team of artists to lead the classes, some of them have been with us from the start, and five additional ones will be joining us this year, so that we can offer a greater number of classes in each center.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as cooking holidays are concerned, I know a lot of agents offer holidays where clients cook recipes related to one particular country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Usually the one they're staying in, but we focus on dishes from a great many different ones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Apart from that, you'll find the usual emphasis on good quality organic ingredients.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's more or less a given nowadays, and there are generally some meat free recipes included.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Photography holidays take place in a wide range of countries from Iceland to Vietnam, and clients have the opportunity to see some stunning scenery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Groups are small, no more than eight, so clients can have one on one tuition during the holiday, and excursions are arranged with fully trained guides.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the end of each holiday, an exhibition is held of the photographs taken, so that clients can see one another's work, and receive valuable feedback from the tutor.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the training session, you have some time to look at questions 18 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 18 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Finally, let me tell you about our fitness holidays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Ireland and Italy, we run one week general fitness classes for all ages and levels of fitness.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Clients start the course with a consultation with a trainer, and together they draw up an individual program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as improving general fitness, clients find that they end up losing much of the stress they've built up in their daily lives.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Greece, we have a two week holiday for clients who want to do something about their weight.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This has all the features you'd expect like a personalized diet program.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But one of its most popular features is that the exercise classes are all held on the beach.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People say it's far preferable to being in a gym.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finally, we offer several holidays in Morocco.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One very popular one is the mountain biking holiday.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Bikes are provided, and there are different routes according to people's ability.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We offer one which is tailored to the needs of families, which is particularly popular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, so that's about all the time I have today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, thank you very much.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two tourism students called Natalie and Dave talking about the tourism case study they are doing.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.

script.text: Dave, I'm worried about our case study.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I've done a bit of reading, but I'm not sure what's involved in actually writing a case study.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I missed the lecture where Dr Baker talked us through it.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: OK, well, it's quite straightforward.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: We've got our focus.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: That's tourism at the Horton Castle site.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: And you said you had done some reading about it?
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Yes, I found some articles and made notes of the main points.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Did you remember to keep a record of where you got the information from?
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Sure, I know what a pain it is when you forget that.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: OK, so we can compare what we've read.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Then we have to decide on a particular problem or need at our site, and then think about who we're going to interview to get more information.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: OK, so who'd that be?
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: The people who work there, and presumably some of the tourists too.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Yes, both those groups.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: So we'll have to go to the site to do that, I suppose.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: But we might also do some of our interviewing away from the site.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: We could even contact some people here in the city.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Like administrators involved in overseeing tourism.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: OK, so we'll need to think about our interview questions and fix times and places for the meetings.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: It's all going to take a lot of time.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Hmm. And if we can, we should ask our interviewees if they can bring along some numerical data that we can add to support our findings.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: And photographs?
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I think we have plenty of those already, but Dr Baker also said we have to establish with our interviewees whether we can identify them in our case study.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Or whether they want to be anonymous.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Oh, I wouldn't have thought of that.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: OK, once we've got all this information, I suppose we have to analyze it.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Yes, put it all together, and choose what's relevant to the problem we're focusing on.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: And analyze that carefully to find out if we can identify any trends or regularities there.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: That's the main thing at this stage, rather than concentrating on details or lots of facts.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: OK, and then once we've analyzed that, what next?
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Well, then we need to think about what we do with the data we've selected to make it as clear as possible to our readers.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Things like graphs or tables or charts.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Then the case study itself is mostly quite standard.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: We begin by presenting the problem, and giving some background, then go through the main sections.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: But the thing that surprised me is that in a normal report, we'd end with some suggestions to deal with the problem or need we identified.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: But in a case study, we end up with a question or a series of questions to our readers, and they decide what ought to be done.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Oh, I hadn't realized that.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So basically, the problem we're addressing in our case study of the Horton Castle site is why so few tourists are visiting it.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: And we'll find out more from our interviews, but I did find one report on the internet that suggested that one reason might be because as far as transport goes, access is difficult.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I read that too, but that report was actually written 10 years ago, when the road there was really bad.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: But that's been improved now, and I think there's plenty of fascinating stuff there for a really good day out, but you'd never realize it from the Castle website.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Maybe that's the problem.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Yes, it's really dry and boring.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I read somewhere a suggestion that what the castle needs is a visitor center.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: So we could have a look for some information about that on the internet.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: What would we need to know?
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Well, who'd use it for a start?
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: It'd be good to know what categories the visitors fall into too, like school parties or retired people.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: But I think we'd have to talk to staff to get that information.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: OK, and as we're thinking of suggesting a visitor center, we'd also have to look at potential problems.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: I mean obviously, it wouldn't be cheap to set up.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: No, but it could be a really good investment.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: And as it's on a historical site, it'd need to get special planning permission, I expect.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: That might be hard.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Especially as the only possible place for it would be at the entrance, and that's right in front of the castle.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: But it could be a good thing for the town of Horton, at present, it's a bit of a ghost town.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Once they've left school and got any skills or qualifications, the young people all get out as fast as they can to get jobs in the city, and the only people left are children and those who've retired.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Something else we could investigate would be the potential damage that tourists might cause to the castle site.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: I mean their environmental impact.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: At present the tourists can just wander around wherever they want.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: But if numbers increase, there might have to be some restrictions, like sticking to marked ways, and there'd need to be guides and wardens around to make sure these are enforced.
script.speaker: NATALIE

script.text: Yes, we could look at that too.
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: OK, well we certainly...
script.speaker: DAVE

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a lecturer on an environmental studies course discussing how birds are affected by environmental change.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, so we've been looking at how manmade changes in our environment can affect wildlife.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, I'll discuss a particular example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's take a look at mercury.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Mercury is one of the 120 or so elements.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That make up all matter, and it has the symbol Hg.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a shiny silvery substance, you may have seen it in old-fashioned thermometers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it's not used much for domestic purposes now, because it's highly toxic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the problem is that the amount of mercury in the environment is increasing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main reason for this is the power plants used to produce electricity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main source of energy that most of them use is still coal, and when it's burned, it releases mercury into the atmosphere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of this gets deposited into lakes and rivers, and if it's ingested by a fish, it's not excreted, it stays in the fish's body.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it enters the food chain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, it's been known for some time that birds which eat fish may be affected, but what wasn't known until quite recently is that those that eat insects can also be affected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, a woman called Claire Varian-Ramos is doing some research on how this is affecting birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And rather than looking at how many birds are actually killed by mercury poisoning, she's looking for more subtle sub-effects.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these may be to do with the behavior of the birds, or with the effect of mercury on the way their brain works, so whether it leads to problems with memory for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And she's particularly focusing on the effects of mercury on bird song.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, the process of song learning happens at a particular stage in the birds' development.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And what you may not know is that a young bird seems to acquire this skill by listening to the songs produced by its father, rather than by any other bird.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And Varian-Ramos has already found in her research that if young male birds are exposed to mercury, if they eat food contaminated with mercury,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: then the songs they produce aren't as complex as those produced by other birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So quite low-level exposure to mercury is likely to have an impact on male birds in a natural situation, because it can mean that they're less attractive to female birds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And so it can affect their chances of reproduction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, the way she's carrying out this research is worth thinking about.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She's using a mixture of studies, using birds kept in laboratories, and studies carried out outdoors in the wild.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The lab-based studies have the advantage that you don't get all the variables you would in a natural setting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So the experimenter has a much higher level of control, and that means they can be more confident about their results in some ways.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And of course, they don't have to worry about going out and finding the birds in order to observe them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what are the implications here for humans?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, because many birds are migratory, they may be transporting mercury far from contaminated sites, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's been found that ducks who'd been feeding at a contaminated site were later shot by hunters over 1,000 km away.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And presumably eaten, but these birds likely had mercury levels high enough to warrant concern for human consumption.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, going back to song learning by birds, we saw that this may be affected by mercury contamination.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, we also know that in humans, mercury causes developmental delays in the acquisition of language, and in fact this process is very similar in the brain regions it involves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And even the genes that are involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But mercury contamination has other important implications for humans as well.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's now known that an unborn child can be affected if the food eaten by its mother contains high levels of mercury, and these effects can be quite substantial.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the end, it comes down to whether more value is placed on human economic well-being or environmental well-being.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's true, there are new regulations for mercury emissions from power plants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But these will need billions of dollars to implement and increase costs for everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some argue that's too much to pay to protect wildlife.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But as we've seen, the issues go beyond that, and I think it's an issue we need to consider very carefully.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.text: Oh, hello.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I've seen your advert for people to lead cycle trips.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Are you the right person to speak to?
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Yes, I am.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Could I have your name please?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: It's Margaret Smith.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Are you looking for a permanent job, Margaret?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: No, temporary.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I've got a permanent job starting in a few months' time.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: And I want to do something else until then.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: What work do you do?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: This will probably sound crazy.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I used to be a lawyer, and then I made a complete career change, and I'm going to be a doctor.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I've just finished my training.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Right, and have you had any experience of leading cycle trips?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Yes, I've led several bike tours in Africa.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: The trip to India that I had arranged to lead next month has now been canceled.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: So when I saw you were advertising for tour leaders, I decided to apply.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Now we normally have 2 or 3 leaders on a trip, depending on the size of the group.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Some tours are for very experienced cyclists, but we've got a tour coming up soon in Spain.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Which is proving so popular, we need an additional leader.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: It's a cycling holiday for families, would that suit you?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: It certainly would.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I enjoy working with children.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: And I probably need some more experience before I go on a really challenging trip.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: That tour includes several teenagers.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Have you worked with that age group before?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Yes, I'm a volunteer worker in a youth club, where I help people to improve their cycling skills.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Before that, I helped out in a cycling club where I taught beginners.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Well, that's great.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Now the trip I mentioned is just for a fortnight, but there might be the possibility of leading other tours after that.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Would that fit in with your plans?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: That would be fine.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I'll be free for five months.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: My job is due to start on October the second, and I'm available from May the 1st until late September.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Good, now is there anything I need to know about the food you eat?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: We usually have one or two people in the group who don't eat meat, or have some sort of food allergy.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: So we're always very careful about that.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Yes, I'm allergic to cheese.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Would that be a problem?
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: No, as long as we have enough notice, we can deal with that.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: That's great.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: It sounds really interesting.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Would you like me to fill in an application form?
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Yes, please.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Where should I post it to?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Could you send it to 27 Arbuthnot Place - ARBUTHNOT - Place, Dumfries.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: And what's the postcode please?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: DG74PH.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Was that P papa or B bravo?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: P papa.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Got that, if you could return the application form by Friday this week, we can interview you on Tuesday next week, say 2:30 would that be possible for you?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Yes, it's fine.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: You're quite a long way from where I live, so I'll drive over on Monday.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Should I bring anything to the interview?
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: We'll have your application form of course.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: But we'll need to see any certificates you've got that are relevant in cycling, first aid or whatever.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: And at the interview, we'd like to find out about your experience of being a tour guide.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: So, could you prepare a 10 minute talk about that please?
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: You don't need slides or any complicated equipment, just some notes.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: I'll start thinking about that straight away.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Well, we'll look forward to receiving your application form, and we'll contact you to confirm the interview.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Thanks very much.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: Thank you, Margaret.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Goodbye.
script.speaker: BOB

script.text: Bye.
script.speaker: MARGARET

script.text: That is the end of section 1.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a podcast about an area called the Sheepmarket in a New Zealand city.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Welcome to this podcast about the Sheepmarket, which is one of the oldest parts of the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As its name suggests, there was originally a market here where farmers brought their sheep.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But now it's been redeveloped into a buzzing vibrant area of the city, which is also home to one of the city's fastest growing communities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The nearby university has always meant the area's popular with students who come in to enjoy the lively nightlife.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But now graduates embarking on careers in the world of fashion and design are buying up the new apartments recently built here to replace the small houses where the market workers used to live.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The narrow old side streets are great places for finding original pictures, jewelry, and ceramics which won't break the bank, as well as local produce like fruit and vegetables.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's also lots of pavement cafes where you can have a coffee and watch tourists from all over the world go by.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The oldest buildings in the area are on the main streets, including the city's first department store.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Built in the 1880s, which is still open today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Sheepmarket is a center for fashion, and there's a policy of encouraging new young designers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Young Fashion competition is open to local young people who are passionate about fashion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This year, they've been asked to design an outfit based on ideas from the music and technology that's part of their everyday life, using both natural and man-made fibers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The garments will be judged by a panel of experts and fashion designers, and the winning entries will be modeled at a special gala evening.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Parking at the Sheepmarket is easy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are plenty of pay and display car parking spaces on the roadsides, which are fine if you just want to stay for an hour or two.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But if you want to spend the day there, it's better to park in one of the four underground car parks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's not expensive, and if you can present a receipt from one of the local stores, you'll not be charged at all.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After 6 pm, many of the car parks have a flat rate which varies, but it is usually very reasonable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: The Sheepmarket is one of the main centers for art and history in the whole of the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you look at our map, you'll see some of the main attractions there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most visitors start from Crawley Road at the bottom of the map.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Reynolds House is one of the oldest houses in the city, and is open to the public.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's on the north side of Crawley Road, next to the footpath that leads to the public gardens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The area is particularly interesting for its unusual sculptures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Thumb's is just what its name suggests, but it's about 10 meters high.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll see it on Hill Road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Across the road from the bank.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The museum's got a particularly fine collection of New Zealand landscapes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's on the east side of the Sheepmarket on City Road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's on the other side of the road from the public gardens, immediately facing the junction with Hill Road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The contemporary art gallery is on a little road that leads off Station Square, not far from the public gardens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The road ends at the gallery, it doesn't go anywhere else.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's open every day except Mondays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Warner Gallery specializes in 19th century art.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's on City Road, near the junction with Crawley Road, on the same side of the road as the public gardens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's open on weekdays from 9 to 5, and entry is free.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Finally, if you're interested in purchasing high quality artwork, the place to go is Nucleus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You need to go from Crawley Road, up through Station Square, and east along Hill Road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Until you get to a small winding road turning off.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Go up there, and it's on your right.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you get to City Road, you've gone too far.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
