script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Will hear two students, Katie and Joe discussing a presentation in their Film Studies course.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Listen carefully, and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Joe, you know I'm giving a presentation in our film studies class next week.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Well, could we discuss it?
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I could do with getting someone else's opinion.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Of course, Katie.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: What are you going to talk about?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It's about film adaptations of Shakespeare's plays.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I've got very interested in all the different approaches that film directors take.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Uh huh.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: So I thought I'd start with Giannetti, who's a professor of film and literature, and in one of his books, he came up with a straightforward classification of film adaptations based on how faithful they are to the original plays and novels.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I've already made some notes on that, so I just need to sort those out before the presentation.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I thought that next, I'd ask the class to come up with the worst examples of Shakespeare adaptations that they've seen.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: And to say why, that should be more fun than having their favorite versions.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Yes, I can certainly think of a couple.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Right, next, I want to talk about Rachel Malchow.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I came across something on the internet about her work on film adaptations.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: And I was thinking of showing some film clips to illustrate her ideas.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Will you have enough time though, both to prepare and during the presentation?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: After all, I doubt if you'll be able to find all the clips you want.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Hmm. Perhaps you're right.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: OK, well, I'd better do some slides instead.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Saying how various films relate to what she says, that should encourage discussion.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Next, I want to say something about how plays may be chosen for adaptation.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Because they're concerned with issues of the time when the film is made.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: You mean things like patriotism, or the role of governments?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: It's quite tricky, but I've got a few ideas I'd like to discuss.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And finally, I want to talk about a few adaptations that I think illustrate a range of approaches, and make some comments on them.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Do you know the Japanese film Ran?
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I haven't seen it.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It was based on Shakespeare's King Lear, wasn't it?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: It was a very loose adaptation, using the same situation and story, but moving it to 16th century Japan.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Instead of 16th century Britain.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: So, for example, the king's daughters become sons, because in Japanese culture at that time women couldn't succeed to the throne.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: OK, I hope you're going to talk about the 1993 film of Much Ado About Nothing.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: I think that's one of the best Shakespeare films.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It really brings the play to life, doesn't it?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Yes, I agree.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: And I think filming it in Italy, where the play is set, makes you see what life was like at the time of the play.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Absolutely, right, what's next?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Uh. Next, I thought Romeo and Juliet, the 1996 film, which moves the action into the present day.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It worked really well, I thought, changing the two feuding families in the original to two competing business empires, even though they're speaking in the English of the original play.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: You'd expect it would sound really bizarre, but I found I soon got used to it.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Me too.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Then I thought I'd include a real Hollywood film.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: One that's intended to appeal to a mass commercial audience.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: There must be quite a number of those.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Yes, but I've picked the 1996 film of Hamlet.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: It included every line of the text, but it's more like a typical action hero movie.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: There are loads of special effects, but no unifying interpretation of the play.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: All show and no substance.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Then there's Prospero's Books, based on The Tempest. That was really innovative from a stylistic point of view.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Didn't it include dance and singing and animation as well as live actors?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: Yes, it did.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: I also want to mention Looking for Richard.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Did you ever see it?
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: No, but I've read about it.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: It was a blend of a documentary with a few scenes from Richard III, wasn't it?
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: It's more a way of looking into how people nowadays connect with the playwright.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: The play is really just the starting point, and that'll be where I finish.
script.speaker: KATIE

script.text: Well, it sounds as though it'll be very interesting.
script.speaker: JOE

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture about noise in cities.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: This lecture will be about the science of acoustics, the study of sound in relation to urban environments such as cities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As an acoustic engineer myself I think this is an area where we're likely to see great changes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the past, researching urban soundscapes was simple.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We measured levels of sound in decibels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So I used to take my sound meter, and I measured the noise somewhere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then I might ask a sample of people to say at what level the sound became annoying.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With data like this, acoustic engineers have been able to build up what we call noise maps, maps of the sound environment, but actually these aren't a lot of use.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What they do show is that the highest noise levels are generally on roads.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, that's not really very surprising.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there's quite a lot going on that these maps don't show, because they can't capture the complex way that sound varies over time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So they ignore important issues such as the noise someone might hear from the open windows or gardens of their neighbors, and this sort of noise can be quite significant in summer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't have any databases on this sort of information.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as that, these records of sound levels take no account of the fact that people vary in their perceptions of noise.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So someone like me with years of working in acoustics might be very different from you in that regard, but anyway, even though these noise maps are fairly crude, they've been useful in providing information and raising awareness that noise matters.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need to deal with it, and so it's a political matter.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that's important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need rules and regulations, because noise can cause all sorts of problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Those of you who are city dwellers know that things go on 24 hours a day, so city dwellers often suffer from interrupted sleep.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's also known that noise can lead to a rise in levels of stress.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Due to physical changes in the body, affecting the composition of the blood.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And there are other problems as well, for instance, if school children don't have a quiet place to study.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Their work will suffer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now one problem with decibel measurement is that it doesn't differentiate between different types of noise.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some types of sounds that most people would probably think of as nice and relaxing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Might well score quite highly in decibel levels.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Think of the sound made by a fountain in a town square, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's not necessarily something that we'd want to control or reduce.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So maybe researchers should consider these sorts of sounds in urban design.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is going to be tricky, because just measuring decibel levels isn't going to help us here.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, many researchers are using social science techniques, studying people's emotional response to sound by using questionnaires and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what exactly do people want to hear in an urban environment?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some recent interdisciplinary research has come out with results that at first sight seem contradictory.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A city needs to have a sense of activity, so it needs to be lively, with sounds like the clack of high heels on a pavement, or the hiss of a coffee machine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But these mustn't be too intrusive, because at the same time, we need to be able to relax.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the major problems in achieving this will be getting architects and town planners to use the research, apart from studying the basics of acoustics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These people receive very little training in this area, but in fact, they should be regarding sound as an opportunity to add to the experience of urban living.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Whereas at present, they tend to see it as something to be avoided or reduced as far as possible, or something that's just a job for engineers, like the street drainage system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What's needed is for noise in cities to be regarded as an aesthetic quality, as something that has the qualities of an art form.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If we acknowledge this, then we urgently need to know what governs it, and how designers can work with it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need to develop a complex understanding of many factors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What is the relationship between sound and culture?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What can we learn from disciplines such as psychology about the way that sound interacts with human development and social relationships?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the way that sound affects our thoughts and feelings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Can we learn anything from physics about the nature of sound itself?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today's powerful technologies can also help us. To show us their ideas, and help us to imagine the effect their buildings will have, architects and town planners already use virtual reality - but these programs are silent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So hopefully, using the best technology we can lay our hands on, the city of the future will be a pleasure to the ears as well as the eyes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.

script.text: Welcome to the Fiddy Working Heritage Farm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This open air museum gives you the experience of agriculture and rural life in the English countryside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the end of the 19th century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So you'll see a typical farm of that period, and like me, all the staff are dressed in clothes of that time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I must give you some advice and safety tips before we go any further.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it's a working farm, please don't frighten or injure the animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have a lot here, and many of them are breeds that are now quite rare.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And do stay at a safe distance from the tools.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of them have sharp points, which can be pretty dangerous, so please don't touch them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't want any accidents, do we?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The ground is very uneven, and you might slip if you're wearing sandals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So I'm glad to see you're all wearing shoes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We always advise people to do that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, children of all ages are very welcome here, and usually even very young children love the ducks and lambs, so do bring them along next time you come.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I don't think any of you have brought dogs with you, but in case you have, I'm afraid they'll have to stay in the car park, unless they're guide dogs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm sure you'll understand that they could cause a lot of problems on a farm.

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.text: Now let me give you some idea of the layout of the farm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The building where you bought your tickets is the New Barn, immediately to your right, and we're now at the beginning of the main path to the farmland.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And of course, the car park is on your left.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The scarecrow you can see in the car park in the corner beside the main path is a traditional figure for keeping the birds away from crops.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But our scarecrow is a permanent sculpture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's taller than a human being, so you can see it from quite a distance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you look ahead of you, you'll see a maze.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's opposite the New Barn, beside the side path that branches off to the right, just over there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The maze is made out of hedges, which are too tall for young children to see over them, but it's quite small, so you can't get lost in it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, can you see the bridge crossing the fish pool further up the main path?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you want to go to the cafe, go towards the bridge and turn right just before it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Walk along the side path, and the café's on the first bend you come to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The building was originally the schoolhouse, and it's well over 100 years old.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you may know, we run skills workshops here, where you can learn traditional crafts like woodwork and basket making.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can see examples of the work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And talk to someone about the courses in the Black Barn.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you take the side path to the right here, just by the New Barn, you'll come to the Black Barn, just where the path first bends.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now I mustn't forget to tell you about picnicking, as I can see some of you have brought your lunch with you.

script.text: You can picnic in the field.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though do clear up behind you, of course.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or if you'd prefer a covered picnic area, there's one near the farmyard, just after you cross the bridge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's a covered picnic spot on the right.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the last thing to mention is Fiddy House itself.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From here you can cross the bridge, then walk along the footpath through the field to the left of the farmyard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That goes to the house, and it'll give you a lovely view of it.

script.text: It's certainly worth a few photographs, but as it's a private home, I'm afraid you can't go inside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Right. Well, if you're all ready, we'll set off on our tour of the farm.

script.text: You will hear two psychology students called Lisa and Greg discussing a project they have to do.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 27.

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 21 to 27.

script.text: OK, Greg.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: So I finally managed to read the article you mentioned, the one about the study on gender in physics.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: About the study of college students done by Akira Miyake and his team?
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Yeah, I was interested that the researchers were actually a mix of psychologists and physicists.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That's an unusual combination.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: I got a little confused at first about which students the study was based on.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: They weren't actually majoring in physics, they were majoring in what's known as the STEM disciplines.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: That's science, technology, engineering, and...
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: ...and math.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Yes, but they were all doing physics courses as part of their studies.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That's correct.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: So, as I understood it, Miyake and co started from the fact that women are underrepresented in introductory physics courses at college.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: And also that on average, the women who do enroll on these courses perform more poorly than the men.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: No one really knows why this is the case.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Yeah, but what the researchers wanted to find out was basically what they could do about the relatively low level of the women's results, but in order to find a solution.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: They needed to find out more about the nature of the problem.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Now let's see if I can remember, it was that in the physics class, the female students thought the male students all assumed that women weren't any good at physics.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Was that it?
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: And they thought that the men expected them to get poor results in their tests.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: That's what the women thought, and that made them nervous, so they did get poor results.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: But actually they were wrong.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: No one was making any assumptions about the female students at all.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Anyway, what Miyake's team did was quite simple.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Getting the students to do some writing before they went into the physics class.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: What did they call it?
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Values-affirmation.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: They had to write an essay focusing on things that were significant to them.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Not particularly to do with the subject they were studying, but more general things like music or people who mattered to them.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: So the idea of doing the writing is that this gets the students thinking in a positive way.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: And putting these thoughts into words can relax them and help them overcome the psychological factors that lead to poor performance.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Yeah.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: But what the researchers in the study hadn't expected was that this one activity raised the women's physics grades from the C to the B range.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: A huge change.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Pity it wasn't to an A, but still!
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: No, but it does suggest that the women were seriously underperforming beforehand in comparison with the men.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Mind you, Miyake's article left out a lot of details, like did the students do the writing just once or several times, and had they been told why they were doing the writing?
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That might have affected the results.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: You mean if they know the researchers thought it might help them to improve, then they'd just try to fulfill that expectation?
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Exactly.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So anyway, I thought for our project we could do a similar study, but investigate whether it really was the writing activity that had that result.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: OK, so we could ask them to do a writing task about something completely different, something more factual, like a general knowledge topic.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Maybe, or we could have half the students doing a writing task, and half doing something else like an oral task.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Or even, half do the same writing task as in the original research, and half do a factual writing task.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Then we'd see if it really is the topic that made the difference, or something else.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: That's it.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: So, at our meeting with the supervisor on Monday, we can tell him we've decided on our project.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: We should have our aims ready by then.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: I suppose we need to read the original study.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: The article is just a summary.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: And there was another article I read by Smolinsky.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: It was about her research on how women and men perform in mixed teams in class,
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: compared with single-sex teams and on their own.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Let me guess... the women were better at teamwork.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That's what I expected, but actually the men and the women got the same results.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Whether they were working in teams or on their own.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Hmm. But I guess it's not that relevant to us.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: What worries me anyway is how we're going to get everything done in the time.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: We'll be OK, now we know what we're doing.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Though, I'm not clear how we assess whether the students in our experiment actually make any progress or not.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: No, we may need some advice on that.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: The main thing's to make sure we have the right size sample, uh, not too big or too small.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That shouldn't be difficult.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Right, what do we need to do next?
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: We could have a look at the timetable for the science classes, or perhaps we should just make an appointment to see one of the science professors.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: That'd be better.
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: And we could even get to observe one of the classes.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: What for?
script.speaker: LISA

script.text: Well, OK, maybe let's just go with your idea.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Right, well, I think that's everything for now.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.

script.text: I've been looking at ocean biodiversity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's the diversity of species that live in the world's oceans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: About 20 years ago, biologists developed the idea of what they called biodiversity hotspots.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are the areas which have the greatest mixture of species, so one example is Madagascar.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These hotspots are significant.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because they allow us to locate key areas for focusing efforts at conservation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Biologists can identify hotspots on land fairly easily.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But until recently, very little was known about species distribution and diversity in the oceans, and no one even knew if hotspots existed there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then a Canadian biologist called Boris Worm did some research in 2005 on data on ocean species that he got from the fishing industry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Worm located five hotspots for large ocean predators like sharks, and looked at what they had in common.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main thing he'd expected to find was that they had very high concentrations of food.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But to his surprise, that was only true for four of the hotspots.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The remaining hotspots were quite badly off in that regard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But what he did find was that in all cases, the water at the surface of the ocean had relatively high temperatures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Even when it was cool at greater depths, so, this seemed to be a factor in supporting a diverse range of these large predators.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, this wasn't enough on its own, because he also found that the water needed to have enough oxygen in it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So these two factors seem necessary to support the high metabolic rate of these large fish.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A couple of years later, in 2007, a researcher called Lisa Balance, who was working in California, also started looking for ocean hotspots.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But not for fish.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What she was interested in was marine mammals, things like seals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And she found three places in the oceans which were hotspots.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And what these had in common was that these hotspots were all located at boundaries between ocean currents, and this seems to be the sort of place that has lots of the plankton that some of these species feed on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So now people who want to protect the species that are endangered need to get as much information as possible.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, there's an international project called the Census of Marine Life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They've been surveying oceans all over the world, including the Arctic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One thing they found there, which stunned other researchers, was that there were large numbers of species which live below the ice.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Sometimes under a layer up to 20 meters thick.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some of these species had never been seen before.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They've even found species of octopus living in these conditions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And other scientists working on the same project, but researching very different habitats on the ocean floor have found large numbers of species congregating around volcanoes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Attracted to them by the warmth and nutrients there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, biologists still don't know how serious the threat to their survival is for each individual species.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So a body called the Global Marine Species Assessment is now creating a list of endangered species on land, so they consider things like the size of the population, how many members of one species there are in a particular place.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then they look at their distribution in geographical terms, although this is quite difficult when you're looking at fish, because they're so mobile, and then thirdly, they calculate the rate at which the decline of the species is happening.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So far, only 1,500 species have been assessed, but they want to increase this figure to 20,000 for each one they assess.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They use the data they collect on that species to produce a map showing its distribution.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ultimately, they will be able to use these to figure out not only where most species are located.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But also where they are most threatened.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So finally, what can be done to retain the diversity of species in the world's oceans?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Firstly, we need to set up more reserves in our oceans, places where marine species are protected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have some, but not enough.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, to preserve species such as leatherback turtles, which live out in the high seas, but have their nesting sites on the American coast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need to create corridors for migration, so they can get from one area to another safely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as this, action needs to be taken to lower the levels of fishing quotas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To prevent overfishing of endangered species. And finally, there's the problem of 'by-catch'.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This refers to the catching of unwanted fish by fishing boats.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They're returned to the sea, but they're often dead or dying.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If these commercial fishing boats used equipment which was more selective, so that only the fish wanted for consumption were caught.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This problem could be overcome.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So does anyone have any questions...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a woman who works in a theater talking to two new staff members on their first day of work.

script.text: Hi, great to see you.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: I'm Jody, and I'll be looking after both of you for the first month you're working here at the Amersham Theater.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: I'll tell you something about the theater now, then take you to meet two of the other staff.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: It's an old building, and it's been modernized several times.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: In fact, as you can see, we're carrying out a major refurbishment at the moment.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The interior has just been repainted, and we're about to start on the exterior of the building.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: That'll be a big job.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The work's running over budget.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: So we've had to postpone installing an elevator.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: I hope you're happy running up and down stairs.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: When the theater was built, people were generally slimmer and shorter than now.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: And the seats were very close together.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We've replaced them with larger seats with more legroom.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: This means fewer seats in total.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: But we've taken the opportunity to install seats that can easily be moved to create different acting spaces.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We've also turned a few storerooms over to other purposes like using them for meetings.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We try hard to involve members of the public in the theater.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: One way is by organizing backstage tours, so people can be shown round the building.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: And learn how a theater operates.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: These are proving very popular.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: What we're finding is that people want to have lunch or a cup of coffee while they're here.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: So we're looking into the possibility of opening a café in due course.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We have a bookshop, which specializes in books about drama, and that attracts plenty of customers.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Then there are two large rooms that will be decorated next month, and they'll be available for hire, for conferences and private functions such as parties.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We're also considering hiring out costumes to amateur drama clubs.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Now I want to tell you about our workshops.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We recently started a program of workshops that anyone can join.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Eventually, we intend to run courses in acting.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: But we're waiting until we've got the right people in place as trainers.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: That's proving more difficult than we'd expected.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: There's a big demand to learn about the technical side of putting on a production, and our lighting workshop has already started with great success.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We're going to start one on sound next month.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: A number of people have inquired about workshops on makeup, and that's something we're considering for the future.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: A surprise success is the workshop on making puppets.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: We happen to have someone working here, who does it as a hobby, and she offered to run a workshop.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: It was so popular, we're now running them every month.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.

script.text: Now, a word about the layout of the building.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The auditorium, stage and dressing rooms for the actors are all below ground level.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Here on the ground floor, we have most of the rooms that the public doesn't see.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The majority are internal, so they have windows in the roof to light them.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Standing here in the foyer, you're probably wondering why the box office isn't here, where the public would expect to find it.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Well, you might have noticed it on your way in.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Although it's part of this building, it's next door, with a separate entrance from the road.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: For the theater manager's office, you go across the foyer, and through the double doors, turn right, and it's the room at the end of the corridor.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: With the door on the left.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The lighting box is where the computerized stage lighting is operated, and it's at the back of the building.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: When you're through the double doors.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: Turn left, turn right at the water cooler, and right again at the end.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: It's the second room along that corridor.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The lighting box has a window into the auditorium, which of course is below us.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: The artistic director's office is through the double doors, turn right, and it's the first room you come to on the right-hand side.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: And finally, for the moment, the room where I'll take you next, the relaxation room.
script.speaker: JODY

script.text: So, if you'd like to come with me.

script.text: I've brought my notes on our biology field trip to Rocky Bay, Colin.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So we can work on our report on the research we did together.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: OK, I've got mine too.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Let's look at the aims of the trip first.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Right, what did you have?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I just put something about getting experience of the different sorts of procedures used on a field trip, but we need something about what causes different organisms to choose particular habitats.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I agree. And something about finding out how to protect organisms in danger of dying out?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: In our aims?
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: But we weren't really looking at that.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I suppose not.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: OK, now there's the list of equipment we all had to bring on the field trip.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: What did they tell us to bring a ruler for?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: It was something about measuring the slope of the shore.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: But of course we didn't need it, because we were measuring wind direction, and we'd brought the compass for that.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: But not the piece of string to hold up in the air.

script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Now, the next section's the procedure, I sent you the draft of that.

script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I'll look at that again.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Then we have to describe our method of investigation in detail.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: So let's begin with how we measured wave speed.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I was surprised how straightforward that was.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I'd expected us to have some sort of high-tech device, not just stand there and count the number of waves per minute.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Not very precise, but I suppose it was good enough. But the way we measured the amount of salt was interesting, in the water from the rock pools.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, oh, I wanted to check the chemicals we used in the lab when we analyze those samples.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Uh. Was it potassium chromate and silver nitrate?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: OK, and we need the map of the seashore.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: You just left that to me.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I had to do it while the tide was low.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Well, that was OK, but the place I started it from was down on the beach.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Then I realized I should have gone up higher to get better visibility.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So I had to start all over again, but at least I'd got the squared paper, or I'd have had problems drawing it all to scale.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, it looks good.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: We could get a map of the region off the internet and see if we need to make any changes.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Hmm, I had a look, but I couldn't find anything.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: But you took some pictures, didn't you?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, I'll email you them if you want.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: OK, I'll make my amendments using those, then I can scan it into our report.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Great.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, when we get to our findings, I thought we could divide them up into the different zones we identified on the shore, and the problems organisms face in each zone.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So for the highest area...
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: The splash zone.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yeah, we found mostly those tiny shellfish that have strong hard shells that act as protection.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: But not from other organisms that might eat them.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Predators.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: No, that's not the main danger for them, but the shells prevent them from drying out, because they're in the open air for most of the time.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: And since they're exposed they need to be able to find some sort of shelter or cover themselves up, so they don't get too hot.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Then in the middle and lower zones nearer the sea, we need to discuss the effects of wave action.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yes, and how organisms develop structures to prevent themselves from being swept away.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Or even destroyed by being smashed against the rocks.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Hmm. I haven't done anything on the geological changes.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I don't know what to put for that.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Hmm. No, we weren't concentrating on that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Maybe we need to find some websites.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Good idea.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I've got the lecture notes from Mr Blake's geology course, but they're too general.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: But we could ask him which books on our reading list might be most helpful.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: OK, now, I did a draft of the section of sources of possible error in our research.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: But I don't know if you agree, uh, for example, the size of the sample, and whether it's big enough to make any general conclusions from.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: But I thought actually we did have quite a big sample.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: We did.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: And our general method of observation seemed quite reliable, but we might not be all that accurate as far as the actual numbers go.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: Yeah, we might have missed some organisms, if they were hiding under a rock for example.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I wasn't sure about the way we described their habitats.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I decided it was probably OK.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, and the descriptions we gave of the smaller organisms, they weren't very detailed, but they were adequate in this context.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: I'm not sure we identified all the species correctly though.
script.speaker: COLIN

script.text: OK, we'd better mention that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Now, how are we going to...
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That is the end of section 3.

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture to students of architecture about the design of a public building.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: We've been discussing the factors the architect has to consider when designing domestic buildings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm going to move on now to consider the design of public buildings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I'll illustrate this by referring to the new Taylor Concert Hall that's recently been completed here in the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, as with a domestic building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When designing a public building, an architect needs to consider the function of the building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. For example, is it to be used primarily for entertainment?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or for education, or for administration.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The second thing the architect needs to think about is the context of the building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This includes its physical location obviously, but it also includes the social meaning of the building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: How it relates to the people it's built for.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And finally, for important public buildings, the architect may also be looking for a central symbolic idea on which to base the design.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A sort of metaphor for the building, and the way in which it is used.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's look at the new Taylor Concert Hall in relation to these ideas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The location chosen was a site in a rundown district that has been ignored in previous redevelopment plans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was occupied by a factory that had been empty for some years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The whole area was some distance from the high-rise office blocks of the central business district and shopping center.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it was only 1 km from the ring road.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The site itself was bordered to the north by a canal, which had once been used by boats bringing in raw materials when the area was used for manufacturing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The architect chosen for the project was Tom Harrison.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He found the main design challenge was the location of the site, in an area that had no neighboring buildings of any importance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To reflect the fact that the significance of the building in this quite run-down location was as yet unknown, he decided to create a building centered around the idea of a mystery.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Something whose meaning still has to be discovered.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, how was this reflected in the design of the building?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, Harrison decided to create pedestrian access to the building.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And to make use of the presence of water on the site.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As people approach the entrance, they therefore have to cross over a bridge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He wanted to give people a feeling of suspense.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As they see the building first from a distance, and then close up.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the initial impression he wanted to create from the shape of the building as a whole was that of a box.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first side that people see, the southern wall, is just a high flat wall, uninterrupted by any windows.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ha, this might sound off-putting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it supports Harrison's concept of the building, that the person approaching is intrigued, and wonders what will be inside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this flat wall also has another purpose.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At night time, projectors are switched on, and it functions as a huge screen onto which images are projected.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The auditorium itself seats 1500 people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The floor's supported by 10 massive pads.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are constructed from rubber, and so are able to absorb any vibrations from outside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And prevent them from affecting the auditorium.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The walls are made of several layers of honey colored wood, all sourced from local beech trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In order to improve the acoustic properties of the auditorium and to amplify the sound, they are not straight, they are curved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The acoustics are also adjustable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: According to the size of orchestra and the type of music being played, in order to achieve this, there are nine movable panels in the ceiling above the orchestra.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which are all individually motorized, and the walls also have curtains, which can be opened or closed to change the acoustics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The reaction of the public to the new building has generally been positive.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, the evaluation of some critics has been less enthusiastic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In spite of Harrison's efforts to use local materials, they criticize the style of the design as being international, rather than local, and say it doesn't reflect features of the landscape or society for which it is built.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a talk given by a woman called Shona Ferguson about changes in a town called Barford.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First of all, let me thank you all for coming to this public meeting to discuss the future of our town.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Our first speaker is Shona Ferguson from Barford Town Council.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Shona.
script.speaker: MAN

script.text: Thank you.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: First I'll briefly give you some background information, then I'll be asking you for your comments on developments in the town.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Well, as you don't need me to tell you, Barford has changed a great deal in the last 50 years.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: These are some of the main changes.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: 50 years ago, buses linked virtually every part of the town and the neighboring towns and villages.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Most people use them frequently, but not now, because the bus companies concentrate on just the routes that attract most passengers.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: So parts of the town are no longer served by buses.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Even replacing old uncomfortable buses with smart new ones has had little impact on passenger numbers.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: It's sometimes said that bus fares are too high.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: But in relation to average incomes, fares are not much higher than they were 50 years ago.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Changes in the road network are affecting the town.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The center was recently closed to traffic on a trial basis, making it much safer for pedestrians.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The impact of this is being measured.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The new cycle paths separating bikes from cars in most main roads are being used far more than was expected reducing traffic and improving air quality.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: And although the council's attempts to have a bypass constructed have failed, we haven't given up hope of persuading the government to change its mind.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Shopping in the town center has changed over the years.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Many of us can remember when the town was crowded with people going shopping.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Numbers have been falling for several years.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Despite efforts to attract shoppers, for instance by opening new car parks.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Some people combine shopping with visits to the town's restaurants and cafes.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Most shops are small independent stores, which is good, but many people prefer to use supermarkets and department stores in nearby large towns, as there are so few well-known chain stores here.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Turning now to medical facilities, the town is served by family doctors in several medical practices, fewer than 50 years ago, but each catering for far more patients.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Our hospital closed 15 years ago, which means journeys to other towns are unavoidable.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: On the other hand, there are more dentists than there used to be.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Employment patterns have changed along with almost everything else.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The number of schools and colleges has increased, making that the main employment sector.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Services such as website design and accountancy have grown in importance, and surprisingly perhaps, manufacturing hasn't seen the decline that has affected it in other parts of the country.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, I'll very quickly outline current plans for some of the town's facilities before asking for your comments.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: As you'll know, if you regularly use the car park at the railway station, it's usually full.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The railway company applied for permission to replace it with a multi-storey car park.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: But that was refused.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Instead, the company has bought some adjoining land, and this will be used to increase the number of parking spaces.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The grand, the old cinema in the High Street, will close at the end of the year.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: And reopen on a different site.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: You've probably seen the building under construction.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The plan is to have three screens with fewer seats, rather than just the one large auditorium in the old cinema.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: I expect many of you shop in the indoor market. It's become more and more shabby-looking, and because of fears about safety, it was threatened with demolition.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The good news is that it will close for 6 weeks to be made safe and redecorated, and the improved building will open in July.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Lots of people use the library,
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: including school and college students who go there to study.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: The council has managed to secure funding to keep the library open later into the evening, twice a week.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: We would like to enlarge the building in the not too distant future, but this is by no means definite.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: There's no limit on access to the nature reserve on the edge of town.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: And this will continue to be the case.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: What will change though, is that the council will no longer be in charge of the area.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: Instead, it will become the responsibility of a national body that administers most nature reserves in the country.
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: OK, now let me ask you, if you have...
script.speaker: SHONA

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear two students called Helen and Jeremy, who are studying creative writing, discussing a project for their course, which involves writing and illustrating stories for children.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Sorry I'm late.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Hi, Jeremy.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: No problem.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Well, we'd better work out where we are on our project, I suppose.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, I've looked at the drawings you've done for my story, 'The Forest'.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: And I think they're brilliant.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.speaker: JEREMY

script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Go ahead.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Now, I'm not sure about the drawing of the cave.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: It's got trees all around it, which is great, but the drawing's a bit too static, isn't it?
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: I think it needs some action.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Yes, there's nothing happening.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Perhaps I should add the boy Malcolm, isn't it?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yes, let's have Malcolm in the drawing.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: And what about putting in a tiger?
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: The one that he makes friends with a bit later.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Maybe it could be sitting under a tree washing itself.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: And the tiger stops in the middle of what it's doing when it sees Malcolm walking past.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That's a good idea.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: OK, I'll have a go at that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Then there's the drawing of the crowd of men and women dancing.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: You wanted them to be watching a carnival procession, but I thought it would be too crowded.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Do you think it works like this?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yes, I like what you've done.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: The only thing is, could you add Malcolm to it without changing what's already there?
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: What about having him sitting on the tree trunk on the right of the picture?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yes, that would be fine.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: And do you want him watching the other people?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: No, he's been left out of all the fun, so I'd like him to be crying.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: That'll contrast nicely with the next picture.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Where he's laughing at the clowns in the carnival.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Right, I'll do that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: And then the drawing of the people ice skating in the forest.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: I wasn't too happy with that one.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Because they're supposed to be skating on grass, aren't they?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That's right, and it's frozen over.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: At the moment, it doesn't look quite right.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: I see what you mean.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I'll have another go at that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: and I like the wool hats they're wearing.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Maybe you could give each of them a scarf as well.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Yeah, that's easy enough.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: They can be streaming out behind the people to suggest they're skating really fast.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: great.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Well, that's all on the drawings.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So you've finished writing your story, and I just need to finish illustrating it. And my story and your drawings are done.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, the next thing is to decide what exactly we need to write about in the report that goes with the stories, and how we're going to divide the work.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Right, Helen.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: What do you think about including a section on how we planned the project as a whole, Jeremy?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That's probably quite important.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Yeah, well you've had most of the good ideas so far.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: How do you feel about drafting something?
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Then we can go through it together and discuss it.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: OK, that seems reasonable.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: And I could include something on how we came up with the ideas for our two stories, couldn't I?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Well, I've started writing something about that, so why don't you do the same, and we can include the two things.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So what about our interpretation of the stories?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: Do we need to write about what we think they show, like the value of helping other people, all that sort of thing?
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: That's gonna come up later, isn't it?

script.text: I think everyone in the class is going to read each other's stories and come up with their own interpretations.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Which we're going to discuss.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Oh, I missed that.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: So it isn't going to be part of the report at all.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: No, but we need to write about the illustrations because they're an essential element of children's experience of reading the stories.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: It's probably easiest for you to write that section, as you know more about drawing than I do.
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: Maybe, but I find it quite hard to write about.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: I'd be happier if you did it.
script.speaker: HELEN

script.text: OK, so when do you think...
script.speaker: JEREMY

script.text: That is the end of section 3.

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture to business students about the use of one particular type of research known as ethnography.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So what I'm going to talk about to you today is something called ethnography.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is a type of research aimed at exploring the way human cultures work.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was first developed for use in anthropology, and it's also been used in sociology and communication studies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what's it got to do with business?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You may ask.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, businesses are finding that ethnography can offer them deeper insight into the possible needs of customers, either present or future, as well as providing valuable information about their attitudes towards existing products.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And ethnography can also help companies to design new products or services that customers really want.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's look at some examples of how ethnographic research works in business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One team of researchers did a project for a company manufacturing kitchen equipment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They watched how cooks used measuring cups to measure out things like sugar and flour.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They saw that the cooks had to check and recheck the contents.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because although the measuring cups had numbers inside them, the cooks couldn't see these easily.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, a new design of cup was developed to overcome this problem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it was a top seller.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another team of ethnographic researchers looked at how cell phones were used in Uganda in Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They found that people who didn't have their own phones could pay to use the phones of local entrepreneurs, because these customers paid in advance for their calls.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They were eager to know how much time they'd spent on the call so far.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So the phone company designed phones for use globally with this added feature.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ethnographic research has also been carried out in computer companies.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In one company, IT systems administrators were observed for several weeks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was found that a large amount of their work involved communicating with colleagues in order to solve problems, but that they didn't have a standard way of exchanging information from spreadsheets and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, the team came up with an idea for software that would help them to do this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In another piece of research, a team observed and talked to nurses working in hospitals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This led to the recognition that the nurses needed to access the computer records of their patients, no matter where they were.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This led to the development of a portable computer tablet that allowed the nurses to check records in locations throughout the hospital.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Occasionally, research can be done even in environments where the researchers can't be present.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, in one project done for an airline.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Respondents used their smartphones to record information during airline trips, in a study aiming at tracking the emotions of passengers during a flight.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what makes studies like these different from ordinary research?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's look at some of the general principles behind ethnographic research in business.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First of all, the researcher has to be completely open-minded.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He or she hasn't thought up a hypothesis to be tested, as is the case in other types of research.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, they wait for the participants in the research to inform them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as choosing the participants themselves is concerned, that's not really all that different from ordinary research.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The criteria according to which the participants are chosen may be something as simple as the age bracket they fall into, or the researchers may select them according to their income.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or they might try to find a set of people who all use a particular product for example, but it's absolutely crucial to recruit the right people as participants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As well as the criteria I've mentioned, they have to be comfortable talking about themselves, and being watched as they go about their activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Actually, most researchers say that people open up pretty easily.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Maybe because they're often in their own home or workplace.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what makes this type of research special is that it's not just a matter of sending a questionnaire to the participants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, the research is usually based on first-hand observation of what they are doing at the time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But that doesn't mean that the researcher never talks to the participants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, unlike in traditional research, in this case, it's the participant rather than the researchers who decides what direction the interview will follow.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means that there's less likelihood of the researcher imposing his or her own ideas on the participant.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But after they've said goodbye to their participants and got back to their office, the researcher's work isn't finished.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Most researchers estimate that 70 to 80% of their time is spent not on the collecting of data, but on its analysis, looking at photos, listening to recordings and transcribing them, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The researchers may end up with hundreds of pages of notes, and to determine what's significant, they don't focus on the sensational things or the unusual things.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, they try to identify a pattern of some sort in all this data, and to discern the meaning behind it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This can result in some compelling insights.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That can in turn feed back to the whole design process.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the museum - one with a remarkable range of exhibits, which I'm sure you'll enjoy.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: My name is Greg, and I'll tell you about the various collections as we go around.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: But before we go, let me just give you a taste of what we have here.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Well, for one thing, we have a fine collection of 20th and 21st century paintings, many by very well-known artists.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: I'm sure you'll recognize several of the paintings.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: This is the gallery that attracts the largest number of visitors, so it's best to go in early in the day before the crowds arrive.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Then there are the 19th century paintings.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: The museum was opened in the middle of that century, and several of the artists each donated one work to get the museum started, as it were.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: So they're of special interest to us.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: We feel closer to them than to other works.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: The Sculpture Gallery has a number of fine exhibits, but I'm afraid it's currently closed for refurbishment.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: You'll need to come back next year to see it properly, but a number of the sculptures have been moved to other parts of the museum.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Around the world is a temporary exhibition.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: You've probably seen something about it on TV or in the newspapers.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: It's created a great deal of interest because it presents objects from every continent and many countries.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: And provides information about their social context, why they were made, who for, and so on.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Then there's the collection of coins.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: This is what you might call a focused specialist collection.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Because all the coins come from this country and were produced between 2,000 and 1,000 years ago, and many of them were discovered by ordinary people digging their gardens and donated to the museum.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: All our porcelain and glass were left to the museum by its founder when he died in 1878, and in the terms of his will, we're not allowed to add anything to that collection.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: He believed it was perfect in itself, and we don't see any reason to disagree.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: OK, that was something about the collections, and now here's some more practical information, in case you need it.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Most of the museum facilities are downstairs in the basement.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: So you go down the stairs here.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: When you reach the bottom of the stairs, you'll find yourself in a sitting area, with comfortable chairs and sofas, where you can have a rest before continuing your exploration of the museum.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: We have a very good restaurant which serves excellent food all day, in a relaxing atmosphere.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: To reach it, when you get to the bottom of the stairs, go straight ahead.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: To the far side of the sitting area, then turn right into the corridor.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: You'll see the door of the restaurant facing you.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: If you just want a snack, or if you'd like to eat somewhere with facilities for children, we also have a cafe.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: When you reach the bottom of the stairs, you'll need to go straight ahead.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Turn right into the corridor, and the cafe is immediately on the right.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: And talking about children, there are baby changing facilities downstairs.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: Cross the sitting area, continue straight ahead along the corridor on the left.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: And you and your baby will find the facilities on the left-hand side.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: The cloakroom where you should leave coats, umbrellas and any large bags is on the left-hand side of the sitting area.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: It's through the last door before you come to the corridor.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: There are toilets on every floor, but in the basement, they're the first rooms on the left when you get down there.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: OK, now if you've got anything to leave in the cloakroom, please do that now, and then we'll start our tour.
script.speaker: GREG

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
