script.text: Section 3, you will hear a student called Joanna talking to her new supervisor about some research she has done on psychology and music.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hi, Joanna.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Good to meet you.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Now, before we discuss your new research project, I'd like to hear something about the psychology study you did last year for your master's degree.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: So, uh, how did you choose your subjects for that?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Well, I had six subjects, all professional musicians, and all female.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Three were violinists, and there was also a cello player, and a pianist, and a flute player.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: They were all very highly regarded in the music world, and they'd done quite extensive tours in different continents.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: And quite a few had won prizes and competitions as well.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: And they were quite young, weren't they?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Yes, between 25 and 29.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Um. The mean was 27.8.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I wasn't specifically looking for artists who'd produced recordings, but this is something that's just taken for granted these days, and they all had.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Now, you collected your data through telephone interviews, didn't you?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I realized if I was going to interview leading musicians, it would only be possible over the phone, because they're so busy.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I recorded them using a telephone recording adapter.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I'd been worried about the quality, but it worked out all right.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I managed at least a 30-minute interview with each subject, sometimes longer.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Did doing it on the phone make it more stressful?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: I'd thought it might...
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Um. It was all quite informal though, and in fact they seemed very keen to talk.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I don't think using the phone meant I got less rich data, rather the opposite in fact.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Interesting.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: And you were looking at how performers dress for concert performances.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Uh. My research investigated the way players see their role as a musician, and how this is linked to the type of clothing they decide to wear.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: But that focus didn't emerge immediately.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Uh. When I started, I was more interested in trying to investigate the impact of what was worn on those listening, and also whether someone like a violinist might adopt a different style of clothing from say someone playing the flute or the trumpet.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: It's interesting that the choice of dress is up to the individual, isn't it?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Yes, you'd expect there to be rules about it in orchestras, but that's quite rare.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You only had women performers in your study.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Was that because male musicians are less worried about fashion?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: I think a lot of the men are very much influenced by fashion.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: But in social terms, the choices they have are more limited.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: They'd really upset audiences if they strayed away from quite narrow boundaries.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Popular music has quite different expectations.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Uh. Did you read Mike Frost's article about the dress of women performers in popular music?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: No.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Well, he points out that a lot of female singers and musicians in popular music tend to dress down in performances.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: And wear less feminine clothes, um, like jeans instead of skirts.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Uh. And he suggests this is because otherwise they'd just be discounted as trivial.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: But you could argue they're just wearing what's practical.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: I mean a pop music concert is usually a pretty energetic affair.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Yes, uh, he doesn't make that point, but I think you're probably right.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: I was interested by the effect of the audience at a musical performance when it came to the choice of dress.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: The subjects I interviewed felt this was really important.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: It's all to do with what we understand by performance as a public event.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: They believed the audience had certain expectations.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: And it was up to them as performers to fulfill these expectations to show a kind of esteem.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: They weren't afraid of looking as if they'd made an effort to look good.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: I think in the past the audience would have had those expectations of one another too, but that's not really the case now, not in the UK anyway.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: No.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: And I also got interested in what sports scientists are doing too with regard to clothing.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Musicians are quite vulnerable physically, aren't they?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Because the movements they carry out are very intensive and repetitive.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: So, I'd imagine some features of sports clothing could safeguard the players from the potentially dangerous effects of this sort of thing.
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: Yes, but musicians don't really consider it.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: They avoid clothing that obviously restricts their movements, but that's as far as they go.
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: Anyway, coming back to your own research, do you have any idea where you're going from here?
script.speaker: SUPERVISOR

script.text: I was thinking of doing a study using an audience including...
script.speaker: JOANNA

script.text: That is the end of section 3.

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a way of reducing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: As we saw in the last lecture, a major cause of climate change is the rapid rise in the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over the last century.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If we could reduce the amount of CO₂, perhaps the rate of climate change could also be slowed down.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One potential method involves enhancing the role of the soil that plants grow in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With regard to absorbing CO₂.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rattan Lal, a soil scientist from Ohio State University in the USA, claims that the world's agricultural soils could potentially absorb 13% of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, the equivalent of the amount released in the last 30 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And research is going on into how this might be achieved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Lal first came to the idea that soil might be valuable in this way, not through an interest in climate change, but rather out of concern for the land itself, and the people dependent on it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Carbon rich soil is dark, crumbly and fertile, and retains some water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But erosion can occur if soil is dry, which is a likely effect.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If it contains inadequate amounts of carbon, erosion is of course bad for people trying to grow crops or breed animals on that terrain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the 1970s and '80s, Lal was studying soils in Africa, so devoid of organic matter that the ground had become extremely hard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Like cement, there he met a pioneer in the study of global warming, who suggested that carbon from the soil had moved into the atmosphere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is now looking increasingly likely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let me explain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For millions of years, carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere have been regulated in part by a natural partnership between plants and microbes, tiny organisms in the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Plants absorb CO₂ from the air, and transform it into sugars and other carbon-based substances.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While a proportion of these carbon products remain in the plant, some transfer from the roots to fungi and soil microbes, which store the carbon in the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The invention of agriculture some 10,000 years ago disrupted these ancient soil-building processes and led to the loss of carbon from the soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When humans started draining the natural topsoil and plowing it up for planting, they exposed the buried carbon to oxygen.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This created carbon dioxide and released it into the air, and in some places, grazing by domesticated animals has removed all vegetation, releasing carbon into the air.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Tons of carbon have been stripped from the world's soils where it's needed, and pumped into the atmosphere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, what can be done?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Researchers are now coming up with evidence that even modest changes to farming can significantly help to reduce the amount of carbon in the atmosphere.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some growers have already started using an approach known as regenerative agriculture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This aims to boost the fertility of soil and keep it moist through established practices.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These include keeping fields planted all year round, and increasing the variety of plants being grown.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Strategies like these can significantly increase the amount of carbon stored in the soil, so agricultural researchers are now building a case for their use in combating climate change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One American investigation into the potential for storing CO₂ on agricultural lands is taking place in California.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Soil scientist Whendee Silver of the University of California, Berkeley is conducting a first-of-its-kind study on a large cattle farm in the state.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: She and her students are testing the effects on carbon storage of the compost that is created from waste.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Both agricultural, including manure and cornstalks, and waste produced in gardens, such as leaves, branches, and lawn trimmings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Australia, soil ecologist Christine Jones is testing another promising soil enrichment strategy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Jones and 12 farmers are working to build up soil carbon by cultivating grasses that stay green all year round.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Like composting, the approach has already been proved experimentally.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Jones now hopes to show that it can be applied on working farms, and that the resulting carbon capture can be accurately measured.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's hoped in the future that projects such as these will demonstrate the role that farmers and other land managers can play in reducing the harmful effects of greenhouse gases.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, in countries like the United States, where most farming operations use large applications of fertilizer, changing such long standing habits will require a change of system.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rattan Lal argues that farmers should receive payment, not just for the corn or beef they produce, but also for the carbon they can store in their soil.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another study being carried out.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a fitness manager of a leisure club talking to some new members.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 and 12.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 11 and 12.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: On behalf of LP clubs, I'd like to welcome you all here today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: My name is Sandy Fisher, and I'm one of the fitness managers here.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before we start our tour of the club, I'll just run through some basic information about the facilities we have here, including recent improvements, and explain the types of membership available.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our greatest asset is probably our swimming pool, which at 25 meters isn't Olympic sized, but now we've expanded it to eight lanes, it's much wider.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means there are rarely more than a couple of people at a time in each lane.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Unfortunately, there isn't space for an outdoor pool here, but the glass roof on the swimming pool is partly retractable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which means you can enjoy something of the open air experience on warmer days.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our recently refurbished fitness suite has all the latest exercise equipment, including 10 new running machines.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And a wide range of weight training machines.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each member is given full training in how to operate the equipment, and there is always a trainer on duty to offer help and advice.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although we do have adult only times after 6, and at certain times at weekends.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Children are well catered for, older children continue to benefit from a wide range of tuition, anything from trampolining to yoga.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 13 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 13 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: One thing all our members appreciate about us is that we take very good care of them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This starts on day 1 with your personal assessment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You are asked to fill in a questionnaire giving details of any health problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of our personal trainers will then go through this with you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trainer will then take you through the safety rules for using the equipment in the fitness suite.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: During your next exercise session, a personal trainer will work with you to make sure you understand these.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's very important to do this, because we really do want to avoid having any sports injuries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's a lot more to looking after yourself than simply lifting weights.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the end of the personal assessment, the trainer will draw up a plan, outlining what you should try to achieve within a 6 week period.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This will then be reviewed at the end of the 6 weeks.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, I'll just quickly run through the types of membership we have available.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All members must pay a joining fee of £90, in addition to the rates for the monthly membership fees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Gold membership entitles you to free entry at all LP clubs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are now LP clubs in all major cities and towns, so if you travel a lot this will be a great advantage.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Individual gold membership costs £50 a month, and joint membership for you and your partner will cost £75.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Premier membership is for professional people whose work commitments make it difficult for them to use the club during the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And so LP gives booking preferences to premier members at peak times.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means you'll find it easier to book the sessions at times that suit you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Reciprocal arrangements with other LP clubs are available to Premier members.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Premier membership is for individuals only, but you'll be sent passes for guests every month.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The monthly fee is £65.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You don't have to have any special clothes or equipment when you visit the club.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We provide robes and hairdryers in the changing rooms, but it's very important to remember your photo card.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because you won't be able to get in without it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For people who aren't working during the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a student called John talking to a professor about a design competition he is entering.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Um, hello, professor.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I'm John Wishart.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I'm working on my entry for the global design competition.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: My tutor said you might be able to help me with it.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Oh, yes.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: I got a copy of your drawings.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Uh. Come in and tell me about it.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: What sort of competition is it?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, it's an international design competition, and we have to come up with a new design for a typical domestic kitchen appliance.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I see.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: And are there any special conditions? Does it have to save energy for example?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Actually that was the focus in last year's competition.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: This year is different, we have to adopt an innovative approach to existing technology, using it in a way that hasn't been thought of before.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I see, that sounds tricky.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: And what kitchen appliance have you chosen?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, I decided to choose the dishwasher.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Interesting.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: What made you choose that?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, they're an everyday kitchen appliance in most Australian houses, but they're all pretty boring, and almost identical to each other.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I think some people will be prepared to pay a little extra for something that looks different.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: It's a nice idea.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: I see you've called your design 'The Rockpool'.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Hmm. Why is that?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Basically because it looks like the rock pools you find on a beach.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: The top is made of glass, so that you can look down into it.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: And there's a stone at the bottom.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Is that just for decoration?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Actually it does have a function. Instead of pushing a button, you turn the stone.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: So it's really just a novel way of starting the dishwasher.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: It's a really nice design, but what makes it innovative?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, I decided to make a dishwasher that uses carbon dioxide.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: In place of water and detergent?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: How will you manage that?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: The idea is to pressurize the carbon dioxide so that it becomes a liquid.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: The fluid is then released into the dishwasher where it cleans the dishes all by itself.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Sounds like a brilliant idea.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Your system will totally do away with the need for strong detergents.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: So what happens once the dishes are clean?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, uh, to allow them to dry, the liquid carbon dioxide and the waste materials all go to an area called the holding chamber.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: That's where the liquid is depressurized, and so it reverts to a gas.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Then the oil and grease are separated out and sent to the waste system.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: It sounds like you've thought it all out very thoroughly.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: So what happens to the carbon dioxide once the process is complete?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Not wasted, I hope.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Actually, that's where the real savings are made.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: The carbon dioxide is sent back to the cylinder, and can be used again and again.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: What a terrific idea.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Do you think it will ever be built?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Hmm. Probably not, but that's OK.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Well, I'm sure a lot of positive things will come out of your design.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now you seem to have thought about everything, so what exactly did you need me to help you with?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, my design has made it to the final stage of the competition, and in a few months' time, I have to give a presentation.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: And that's the part I was hoping you could help me with.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Right, well that should be easy enough.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: What have you managed to do so far?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, I've got detailed drawings to show how it will work, and I've also written a 500-word paper on it.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: I see.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, if you want to stand a good chance of winning, you really need a model of the machine.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Yes, I thought I might, but I'm having a few problems.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: What's the main difficulty so far?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Let me guess, is it the materials?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Yes, I want it to look professional, but everything that's top quality is also very expensive.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Look, projects like this are very important to us.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: They really help lift our profile.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: So why don't you talk to the university about a grant?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Oh, I can help you fill out the application forms if you like.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Oh, that would be great.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: You'd better show me this paper you've written as well, for a global competition such as this.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: You need to make sure the technical details you've given are accurate and thorough.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Oh, that would be a great help.
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: Is there anything else I can do?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, I'm really...
script.speaker: JOHN

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a university lecture about an endangered bear in British Columbia, Canada, known as the spirit bear.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Today we continue our series on ecology and conservation with a look at a particularly endangered member of the black bear family.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One in 10 black bears is actually born with a white coat, which is the result of a special gene that surfaces in a few.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Local people have named it the spirit bear, and according to the legends of these communities, its snowy fur brings with it a special power.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because of this, it has always been highly regarded by them, so much that they do not speak of seeing it to anyone else.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It is their way of protecting it when strangers visit the area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The white bear's habitat is quite interesting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The bear's strong relationship with the old growth rainforest is a complex one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The white bear relies on the huge centuries old trees in the forest in many ways.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, the old growth trees have extremely long roots that help prevent erosion of the soil along the banks of the many fish streams.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Keeping these banks intact is important, because these streams are home to salmon, which are the bear's main food source.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In return, the bears' feeding habits nurture the forest.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As the bears eat the salmon, they discard the skin and bones in great amounts on the forest floor, which provide vital nutrients.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These produce lush vegetation that sustains thousands of other types of life forms.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From birds to insects and more.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, the Spirit bear lives off the coast of the province of British Columbia on a few islands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There is great concern for their survival.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Since it is estimated that less than 200 of these white bears remain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The best way to protect them is to make every effort to preserve the delicate balance of their forest environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In other words, their ecosystem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The greatest threat to the bear's existence is the loss of its habitat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Over many years, logging companies have stripped the land by cutting down a large number of trees.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In addition, they have built roads which have fractured the areas where the bear usually feeds, and many hibernation sites have also been lost.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The logging of the trees along the streams has damaged the places where the bears fish.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To make matters worse, the number of salmon in those streams is declining, because there is no legal limit on fishing at the moment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All these influences have a negative impact on the spirit bear's very existence, which is made all the more fragile by the fact that reproduction among these bears has always been disappointingly low.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And so, what's the situation going forward?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Community organizations, environmental groups, and the British Columbia government are now working together on the problem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The government is now requiring logging companies to adopt a better logging method, which is a positive step.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, these measures alone may not be sufficient to ensure a healthy population of the spirit bear in the future.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Other steps also need to be taken.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While it is important to maintain the spirit bear's habitat, there also needs to be more emphasis on its expansion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The move is justified.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it will also create space for other bears that are losing their homes...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2, you will hear a representative of a city council giving information about two new facilities which are opening soon in the city.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm very pleased to have this opportunity to say a little about two exciting new developments in the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Brackenside Open-air Swimming Pool, and the children's adventure playground in Central Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As many of you may know, the idea for these initiatives came from you, the public, in the extensive consultation exercise which the City Council conducted last year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And they have been realized using money from the SWRDC - the South West Regional Development Commission.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First of all, Brackenside Pool.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As many of the older members of the audience will remember, there used to be a wonderful open air pool on the seafront 30 years ago, but it had to close when it was judged to be unsafe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For the design of this new heated pool, we were very happy to secure the talents of internationally renowned architect, Ellen Wendon, who has managed to combine a charming 1930s design which fits so well with many of the other buildings in the area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: With up to the minute features such as a recycling system, the only one of its kind in the world, which enables seawater to be used in the pool.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's been quite a bit of discussion in the local press about whether there would be enough room for the number of visitors we're hoping to attract, but the design is deceptive, and there have been rigorous checks about capacity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. Also just in case you were wondering, we're on schedule for June 15th opening date, and well within budget, a testimony to the excellent work of local contractors Hickman's.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We hope that as many people as possible will be there on June 15th.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have engaged award winning actress Coral White to declare the pool open, and there'll be drinks and snacks available at the poolside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There'll also be a competition for the public to decide on the sculpture we plan to have at the entrance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You will decide which famous historical figure from the city we should have.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And now, moving on to the Central Park playground, which we're pleased to announce has just won the Douglas Award for safety.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The news came through only last week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The unique design is based on the concept of the Global Village, with the playground being divided into six areas showing different parts of the world, each with a representative feature.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, there is a section on Asia, and this is represented by rides and equipment in the shape of snakes, orangutans, tigers, and so on - fauna native to the forests of the region.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Moving south to the Antarctic, we couldn't run to an ice rink, I'm afraid, but opted instead for climbing blocks in the shape of mountains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I thought they could have had slides for the glaciers, but the designers did want to avoid being too literal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then onto South America, and here the theme is El Dorado, games replicating the search for mines full of precious stones, and then moving up to North America.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here there was considerable debate.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I know the contribution of cinema and jazz was considered, but the designers finally opted for rockets and the International Space Station.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Eastwards to Europe then, and perhaps the most traditional choice of all the areas, medieval castles and other fortifications, then last but not least, moving south to Africa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And a whole set of wonderful mosaics and trails to represent the great rivers of this fascinating and varied continent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, the opening date for our Global Playground is the 10th of July. And again, we'd love to see you there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, make a date and come and see this magnificent original new amenity right in the heart of the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3, you will hear two anthropology students called Victor and Olivia discussing their joint presentation about a Norwegian explorer called Thor Hyerdahl.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, well, for our presentation, shall I start with the early life of Thor Heyerdahl?
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Why don't you begin with describing the type of boy he was?
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Especially his passion for collecting things.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: That's right, he had his own little museum.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: And I think it's unusual for children to develop their own values, and not join in their parents' hobbies.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I'm thinking of how Heyerdahl wouldn't go hunting with his dad for example.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Yeah, he preferred to learn about nature by listening to his mother read to him, and quite early on, he knew he wanted to become an explorer when he grew up.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: That came from his camping trips he went on in Norway, I think.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: No, it was climbing that he spent his time on as a young man.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Oh, right.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: After university, he married a classmate, and together, they decided to experience living on a small island to find out how harsh weather conditions shaped people's lifestyles.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: As part of their preparation, before they left home, they learned basic survival skills like building a shelter.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I guess they needed that knowledge in order to live wild in a remote location.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: With few inhabitants cut off by the sea, which is what they were aiming to do.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: An important part of your talk should be the radical theory Heyerdahl formed from examining mysterious ancient carvings that he happened to find on the island.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: I think you should finish with that.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: All right, Victor.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: So after your part, I'll talk about Thor Heyerdahl's adult life, continuing from the theory he had about Polynesian migration.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Up until that time, of course, academics had believed that humans first migrated to the islands in Polynesia from Asia in the west.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Yes, they thought that travel from the east was impossible.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Because of the huge empty stretch of ocean that lies between the islands and the nearest inhabited land.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Yes, but Heyerdahl spent ages studying the cloud movements, ocean currents, and wind patterns to find if it was actually possible.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: And another argument was that there was no tradition of large ship building in the communities lying to the east of Polynesia, but Heyerdahl knew they made lots of coastal voyages in locally built canoes.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Yes, or sailing on rafts, as was shown by the long voyage that Heyerdahl did next.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: It was an incredibly risky journey to undertake.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Sometimes I wonder if he did that trip for private reasons, you know.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: To show others that he could have spectacular adventures.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: What do you think, Olivia?
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Well, I think it was more a matter of simply trying out his idea, to see if migration from the east was possible.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Yes, that's probably it.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: And the poor guy suffered a bit at that time, because the war forced him to stop his work for some years.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Yes, uh, when he got started again and planned his epic voyage, do you think it was important to him that he achieve it before anyone else did?
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Um. I haven't read anywhere that that was his motivation.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: The most important factor seems to have been that he use only ancient techniques and local materials to build his raft.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Yes, I wonder how fast it went.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Well, it took them 97 days from South America to the Pacific Islands.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Hmm.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: And after that, Heyerdahl went to Easter Island, didn't he?
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: We should mention the purpose of that trip.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: I think he sailed there in a boat made out of reeds.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: No, that was later on in Egypt, Olivia.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Oh, yes, that's right.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: But what he wanted to do was talk to the local people about their old stone carvings, and then make one himself.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: To learn more about the process.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I see.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Well what a great life, even though many of his theories have been disproven, he certainly left a lasting impression on many disciplines, didn't he?
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: To my mind, he was the first person to establish what modern academics call practical archaeology.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: I mean that they try to recreate something from the past today.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Like he did with his raft trip.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: It's unfortunate that his ideas about where Polynesians originated from have been completely discredited.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Right, well, I'll prepare a PowerPoint slide at the end that acknowledges our sources.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I mainly used The Life and Work of Thor Heyerdahl by William Oliver.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I thought the research methods he used were very sound, although I must say I found the overall tone somewhat old-fashioned.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I think they need to do a new revised edition.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: Yeah, I agree.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: What about the subject matter?
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: I found it really challenging.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: Well, it's a complex issue.
script.speaker: VICTOR

script.text: I thought the book had lots of good points.
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: What did you think of...
script.speaker: OLIVIA

script.text: That is the end of section 3.

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a business student predicting how management might change in the next few years.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Well, I've been talking to managers in a number of businesses, and reading surveys about the future of management.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And what I'm going to present in this seminar is a few ideas about how the activity is likely to change in the next 10 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It isn't a scientific statistical analysis, just some ideas for us to discuss.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One area I want to mention is business markets, and I'm sure a really significant development will be a major increase in competition with companies from all around the world trying to sell similar products.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Consumers will have much more choice, for instance, food products sold in Australia might be manufactured in the USA, China, Finland, and dozens of other countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At the same time, mergers and takeovers mean that governments are actually losing power to major global corporations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We can probably all think of companies that exert a great deal of influence, which may be good for consumers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A third point I want to make about markets is that in the rapidly expanding economies such as India, China, Brazil and Russia, demand is growing very fast.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is putting pressure on resources all over the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I think businesses are becoming more open to external influences, in particular, companies are consulting customers more and more before making their business decisions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Companies are finding out what they want and providing it, instead of making products and then trying to sell them, which is the model of years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another influence is that concerns about the environment will force manufacturers to extend product life cycles to reduce the amount of pollution and waste.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in some cases, regulation will need to be strengthened.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many societies are much more fluid and democratic, and the structure of companies is changing to reflect that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I think we're going to see a greater emphasis within companies on teams created with a specific project in mind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And when they're completed, the teams will be disbanded and new ones formed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: More and more people see work as simply one part of their lifestyle.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And not the most important one, and as the workforce is shrinking in some countries, businesses are having to compete for staff instead of being able to choose among a lot of applicants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Typical examples that will attract and retain staff are traditional ones like flexible hours, and something that has been made possible by advances in technology.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Remote working, with people based at their home, abroad, or almost anywhere they choose.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Management styles will almost certainly continue to change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Senior managers will require a lot more than the efficiency that they've always needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Above all, they'll need great skills in leadership, so that their organization can initiate and respond to change in a fast-moving world, where they face lots of competing requirements and potential conflicts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In most of the world, the senior managers of large businesses are mainly men in their 50s and 60s.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The predominant style of management will almost certainly become more consultative and collaborative.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Caused, above all, by more women moving into senior management positions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many of the changes are influenced by developments in the wider economy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The traditional emphasis of business was manufacturing, and of course the service sector is very important.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we shouldn't overlook the growing financial contribution of IP.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is intellectual property.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some books and films generate enormous sums from the sale of related DVDs, music, games, clothes, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another point I'd like to make is that although I've been talking about companies, one trend that they have to face is the move away from people working for the same employer for years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Instead, more and more people are becoming self-employed to gain the freedom and control over their lives that they're unlikely to get from being employed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, well, that's all I wanna say, so let's open it up for discussion.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2, you will hear a woman called Alice Bussell talking on the radio about the Dolphin Conservation Trust, an organization which tries to protect dolphins.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Today we're pleased to have on the show Alice Bussell from the Dolphin Conservation Trust.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Uh. Tell us about the trust, Alice.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, obviously, its purpose is to protect dolphins in seas all around the world.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It tries to raise people's awareness of the problems these marine creatures are suffering because of pollution and other threats.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It started 10 years ago, and it's one of the fastest growing animal charities in the country.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Although it's still fairly small compared with the big players in animal protection, we're particularly proud of the work we do in education.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Last year, we visited a huge number of schools in different parts of the country.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Going round to talk to children and young people, aged from 5 to 18.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: In fact, about 35% of our members are children.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: The charity uses its money to support campaigns, for example, for changes in fishing policy and so forth.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It hopes soon to be able to employ its first full-time biologist with dolphin expertise to monitor populations.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Of course, many people give their services on a voluntary basis, and we now have volunteers working in observation, office work, and other things.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I should also tell you about the award we won from the Charity Commission last year, for our work in education.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Although it's not meant an enormous amount of money for us, it has made our activities even more widely publicized and understood.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: In the long term, it may not bring in extra members, but we're hoping it'll have this effect.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Is it possible to see dolphins in UK waters?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes, in several locations, and we have a big project in the east part of Scotland.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: This has long been a haven for dolphins, because it has very little shipping.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: However, that may be about to change soon, because oil companies want to increase exploration there.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: We're campaigning against this, because although there'll be little pollution from oil,
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: exploration creates a lot of underwater noise.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: It means the dolphins can't rest and socialize.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: This is how I became interested in dolphin conservation in the first place.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I had never seen one, and I hadn't been particularly interested in them at school.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Then I came across this story about a family of dolphins who had to leave their home in the Moray Firth.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Because of the oil companies, and about a child who campaigned to save them.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I couldn't put the book down.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I was hooked.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I'm sure our listeners will want to find out what they can do to help.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: You mentioned the 'Adopt a Dolphin' scheme.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Can you tell us about that?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Of course, people can choose one of our dolphins to sponsor.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: They receive a picture of it, and news updates.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: I'd like to tell you about four, which are currently being adopted by our members.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Moondancer, Echo, Kiwi, and Samson.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Unfortunately, Echo is being rather elusive this year, and hasn't yet been sighted by our observers.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: But we remain optimistic that he'll be out there soon.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: All the others have been out in force.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Samson and Moondancer are often photographed together, but it's Kiwi who's our real character, as she seems to love coming up close for the cameras, and we've captured her on film hundreds of times.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: They all have their own personalities.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Moondancer is very elegant and curves out and into the water very smoothly, whereas Samson has a lot of energy.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: He's always leaping out of the water with great vigor.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: You'd probably expect him to be the youngest, he's not quite, that's Kiwi, but Samson's the latest of our dolphins to be chosen for the scheme.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Kiwi makes a lot of noise, so we can often pick her out straight away.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Echo and Moondancer are noisy too, but Moondancer is easy to find, because she has a particularly large fin on her back.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Which makes her easy to identify.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: So, yes, they're all very different.
script.speaker: ALICE

script.text: Well, they sound a fascinating group...
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.

script.text: Section 4, you will hear part of a lecture about leadership, introducing a theory called self-regulatory focus theory.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Today, I want to talk about self-regulatory focus theory, and how the actions of leaders can affect the way followers approach different situations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Self-regulatory focus theory is a theory developed by Tori Higgins.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He says that a person's focus at any given time is to either approach pleasure or avoid pain.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are two basic motivations that each and every one of us has, and they cause us to have different kinds of goals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Promotion goals in different life situations emphasize achievement.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Prevention goals are oriented towards the avoidance of punishment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In a specific situation, our thoughts might focus more on promotion goals, or more on prevention goals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The theory suggests that two factors affect which goals we are focusing on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First, there is a chronic factor.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This factor is connected to a person's personality, and says that each person has a basic tendency to either focus more on promotion goals or focus more on prevention goals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As part of his or her personality.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Second, there is a situational factor, which means that the context we are in can make us more likely to focus on one set of goals or the other.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, we are more likely to be thinking about pleasure and to have promotion goals when we are spending time with a friend.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In contrast, if we are working on an important project for our boss, we are more likely to try to avoid making mistakes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And therefore have more prevention goals in our mind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Research has shown that the goals we are focusing on at a given time affect the way we think, for example, when focusing on promotion goals, people consider their ideal self.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Their aspirations and gains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They don't think about what they can lose, so they think in a happier mode, they feel more inspired.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When people are focusing on prevention goals, they think about their ought self, what are they supposed to be?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What are people expecting from them?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They consider their obligations to others.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As a result, they experience more anxiety and try to avoid situations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Where they could lose.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now that I have talked about the two focuses, and how they affect people, I want to look at the idea that the way leaders behave.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or their style of leading can affect the focus that followers adopt in a specific situation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In talking about leadership, we often mention transformational leaders and transactional leaders.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Transformational leaders when interacting with their followers, focus on their development, in their words and actions, transformational leaders highlight change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Their speech is passionate and conveys a definitive vision.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All of these things can encourage followers to think about what could be.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In other words, they inspire a promotion focus in their followers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In contrast, transactional leaders focus on developing clear structures that tell their followers exactly what is expected of them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While they do explain the rewards people will get for following orders, they emphasize more how a follower will be punished.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or that a follower won't get rewarded, if his or her behavior doesn't change.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In short, they emphasize the consequences of making a mistake.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This emphasis will clearly lead followers to focus on avoiding punishment and problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is clearly a prevention focus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In conclusion, it is important to understand that one focus is not necessarily better than the other one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For a designer who works in a field where a lot of innovation is needed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A promotion focus is probably better.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In contrast, a prevention focus, which causes people to work more cautiously, and produce higher quality work,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: might be very appropriate for a job like a surgeon, for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main point of the research though, is that the actions of leaders can greatly influence whether people approach a situation with more of a promotion focus or more of a prevention focus.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: With all the weather damage, the glass in the door has cracked, and I'd need that fixing.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: I presume you mean replacing.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Oh yes, and as soon as possible.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: What I'll do is come round tomorrow morning and do that immediately.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Oh, thank you so much.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: The other things aren't so urgent, but..
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Now, I'll make a note of everything you want doing.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Well, in the kitchen, I'd like some painting doing.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: All the kitchen walls?
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Just the area over the cooker. It's very greasy...
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Right, it does tend to get that way.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Well, if you want a proper job done, what I'd need to do is strip the old paint and plaster it about a week before I paint it.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Of course.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Now, May tells me you also do work in the garden.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Well, I'd like you to replace a fence.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Just one.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: Yes, at the far end.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Fine, shouldn't be a problem.
script.speaker: MR THORNDYKE

script.text: And that's the lot.
script.speaker: EDITH

script.text: Fine, yeah, as I say, I can come round tomorrow morning to look over things with you.

script.text: Well, that's great.

script.text: Thank you.

script.text: Section 2, you will hear a recorded talk giving an introduction to the historical theme park of Manchester River Port in England.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Welcome to Manham Port, where 1,000 years of history are brought to life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All the family can enjoy a day out at Manham.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Visit our copper mine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: See models of the machinery it used, have your photo taken in 19th century costume, experience at first hand how people lived at different stages throughout history.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And especially how children studied, worked, and played.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The port of Manham is located in beautiful and peaceful countryside, on a bend in the great River Avon, and developed here because it's the highest navigable point of the Avon.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Boats can go no higher up this river, and proved a handy place to load and unload cargo to and from the sea, which is over 23 miles away.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A small port was already established here, when about 900 years ago, tin was discovered nearby.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though it wasn't until the Industrial Revolution,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: when a tremendous need for metals of all kinds developed, that Manham expanded to become one of the busiest ports in the country, and because it was already so busy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Prospectors began to look for other minerals, and by the end of the nineteenth century, lead, copper, manganese and arsenic were added to the cargoes leaving Manham.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the early days, the ores had been smelted or processed in the same area they were mined.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But as demand grew, the smelting process required huge factory furnaces or fires.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To melt the metal from the rock, and there was not enough coal in the local area, so the rocks containing minerals had to be shipped long distances.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Sadly, in the 20th century, the great port of Manham declined, and thousands of workers were forced to emigrate out of the area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The building at the port fell into disrepair.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the place became almost forgotten, but then the Manham Trust was formed to conserve the historical resources of the area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It organized scores of local volunteers to remove undergrowth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To find the original outlines of the installations, it then brought in paid professionals to match installations with maps of the original port complex.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And to set about reconstructing it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, you can see the results of this ambitious program of restoration.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The intention, and we believe this will be realized before the end of the year, is to return Manham Port.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To the condition it reached at its peak, as the greatest copper port in the country.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: But what can you do and see on your visit today?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here are just a few highlights.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We suggest you start with the visit to the copper mine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Travel on converted mining trains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And journey into the depths of the mountain, along seams once worked by hundreds of miners.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Watch out especially for the great pumping machines which rid the mine of water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But please be warned that like all mines, ours is very dark and closed in, and we do say that children under five, and also dogs should not be taken into the mine.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The next recommended visit is to the village school.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: While looking around the classrooms, take a special look at our display of games, which is one of the largest in the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it's recommended that you time your visit to coincide with a guided tour.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This will give you the opportunity to ask lots of questions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Near the school is the beautiful old sailing ketch called the George.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You're welcome to board the boat and look round the cabins.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Look out for the ship's wheel, which was missing until only five years ago, when it was dredged out of the silt by a local fisherman.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have no idea how it got there, but it's been polished and proudly restored to its original place on the boat.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Please take care going down the ladders, if you wish to visit the lower deck.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We don't recommend you allow young children to use them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So we hope you have a memorable visit to Manham Port, and will tell your friends all about us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3, you will hear two psychology students called Tim and Laura talking about Laura's work placement first.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hi, Laura, could you spare a few minutes to talk about the work placement you did last summer?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I'm thinking of doing one myself.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Hi, Tim.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Sure.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Didn't you do yours at an environmental services company?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It's only a very small company, and they needed someone to produce a company brochure.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: And I wanted to get some business experience, because I'm interested in a career in occupational psychology in a business environment.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It was good, because I had overall responsibility for the project.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: What kind of skills do you think you developed on the placement?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I mean apart from the ones you already had.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Did you have to do all the artwork for the brochure?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: The layout and everything.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: We hired the services of a professional photographer for that.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: I did have to use my IT skills to a certain extent, because I cut and pasted text from marketing leaflets.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: But that didn't involve anything I hadn't done before.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Do you think you got any better at managing your time and prioritizing things?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: You always used to say you had trouble with that.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Oh, definitely.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: There was so much pressure to meet the project deadline, and I also got better at explaining things, and asserting my opinions.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Because I had to have weekly consultations with the marketing manager, and give him a progress report.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It sounds as if you got a lot out of it then.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It was really worthwhile, but you know, the company benefited too.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Yes, they must have done.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: After all, if they'd used a professional advertising agency to produce their brochure, instead of doing it in-house.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Presumably they'd have paid a lot more.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Oh yes, I worked it out.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It would have been 250% more, and I thought the end result was good.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Even though we did everything on site, the company has quite a powerful computer, and I managed to borrow some scanning software from the university.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: The new brochure looks really professional.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: It enhances the image of the company straight away.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: So, in the long run, it should help them to attract clients and improve their sales figures.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That's the idea, yeah.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Well, all in all, it sounds very positive.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I think I'll go ahead and apply for a placement myself.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: How do I go about it?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: It's easy enough to do.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Because there's a government agency called STEP - S T E P - that organizes placements for students.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: You should start by getting their booklet with all the details.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: I expect you can download one from their website.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Actually, they've got copies in the psychology department.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I've seen them there.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I'll just go to the office and pick one up.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Right, and then, if I were you, after I'd looked at it, I'd go over all the options with someone.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: I suppose I should ask my tutor's advice.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: He knows more about me than anyone.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: One of the career officers would be better.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: They've got more knowledge about the jobs market than your personal tutor would have.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: And then, when you know what you want, you can register with STEP.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: You'll find their address in the booklet, and once you've registered, they assign you to a mentor who looks after your application.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: And then I suppose you just sit back and wait till you hear something.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: They told me at the careers office that it's best to be proactive and get updates yourself.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: By checking the website for new placement alerts.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Your mentor is supposed to keep you informed, but you can't rely on that.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: I don't suppose it's a good idea to get in touch with companies directly, is it?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Not really, but it is the company who notifies you if they want you to go for an interview.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: You get a letter of invitation or an email from the personnel department.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: And do I reply directly to them?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: Yes, you do.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: STEP only gets involved again once you've been made a job offer.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Right, so once you've had an interview, you should let your mentor know what the outcome is.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I mean, whether you're offered a job, and whether you've decided to accept it.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: They'll inform the careers office once a placement has been agreed, so you don't have to do that.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Is that all then?
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: More or less.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Only once you've accepted an offer, you'll probably have to supply a reference, because the placement will be conditional on that, and that's something you should ask your own tutor to provide.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: He knows about your academic ability, and also about your qualities like reliability.
script.speaker: LAURA

script.text: Well, thanks very much for the information.
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: I'm starting to look forward to...
script.speaker: TIM

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
