script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a conversation between an English teacher called Paul, and a former student of his called Kira.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, Kira.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: How are you?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Fine, thanks, Paul.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: How are you?
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Well, thanks.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: It's good to see you.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: It must be 12 months since you did our course.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: That's right.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: It's nice to come back and say hello.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: What course did you enroll in?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Actually, I went straight into 3rd year pharmacy.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: They credited me with 2 years which probably made it more difficult for me.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: On the other hand, you were lucky to be granted credits.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Is that why you chose the course?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Yes, and as I'd already finished a course in it in my country, I thought it would be easier if I studied something I already knew.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: I didn't realize you went into 3rd year.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: I thought you started in first year.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: No wonder it was so hard.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: And what do you think is one of the big differences between studying at a university here and studying in your country?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Well, I found it very difficult to write assignments.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Because I wasn't familiar with that aspect of the system here.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: The main problem is that the lecturers expect you to be critical.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: That made me feel really terrible.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: I thought "How can I possibly do it? How can I comment on someone else's research when they probably spent 5 years doing it?"
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: I think a lot of people who come from overseas countries have similar problems, but after a while, it became easier for me.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: People expect you to have problems with the process of reading and writing, but in fact, it is more a question of altering your viewpoint towards academic study.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Hmm, uh, how was the content of the lectures?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Was it easy for you?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: I didn't really have many problems understanding lectures.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: The content was very similar to what I'd studied before.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: And what about the lecturers themselves?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Are they essentially the same as lecturers in your country?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Uh. Well, actually no.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Here they're much easier to approach.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: After every lecture, you can go and ask them something you didn't understand, or you can make an appointment and talk to them about anything in the course.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Maybe you found them different because you're a more mature student now, whereas when you were studying in your country, you were younger and not so assertive.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: No, I don't think that's the difference.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Most of the students here do it.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: In my faculty, they all seem to make appointments, usually to talk about something in the course that's worrying them, but sometimes just about something that might really interest them.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Something they might want to specialize in.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Hmm. The lecturers must set aside certain times every week when they're available for students.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: That's good to hear.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: And how was your timetable?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Was it a very busy year?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Oh, very very busy.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: They make you work very hard.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Apart from lectures, we had practical sessions in a lot of subjects.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: We did these in small groups.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: I had to go and work 4 hours every week in a community pharmacy.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Hmm. Actually, I enjoyed this very much, meeting new people all the time.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Then in 2nd semester, we had to get experience in hospital dispensaries.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: So every second day we went to one of the big hospitals and worked there.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: And on top of all that we had our assignments, which took me a lot of time.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Oh, I nearly forgot, between 1st and 2nd semesters, we had to work full time for two weeks in a hospital.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: That does sound a very heavy year.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: So are you pleased now that you did it?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Do you feel some sense of achievement?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Yeah, I do feel much more confident, which I suppose is the most important thing.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: And have you got any recommendations for people who are studying from overseas?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Well, I suppose they need very good English.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: It would be much better if they spent more time learning English before they enter the university.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Because you can be in big trouble if you don't understand what people are saying, and you haven't got time to translate.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: Uh. Anything else?
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Well, as I said before.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: The biggest problem for me was lack of familiarity with the education system here.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: It sounds as if it was a real challenge.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Congratulations, Kira.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Hmm, thanks, Paul.
script.speaker: KIRA

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a talk about a project on the wildlife found in city gardens in Britain.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to present the findings of our Year 2 project on wildlife found in gardens throughout our city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'll start by saying something about the background to the project.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then talk a little bit about our research techniques, and then indicate some of our interim findings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First of all, how did we choose our topic?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, there are four of us in the group, and one day while we were discussing a possible focus,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: two of the group mentioned that they had seen yet more sparrow hawks - one of Britain's most interesting birds of prey - in their own city center gardens, and wondered why they were turning up in these gardens in great numbers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We were all very engaged by the idea of why wild animals would choose to inhabit a city garden.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why is it so popular with wildlife when the countryside itself is becoming less so?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first thing we did was to establish what proportion of the urban land is taken up by private gardens.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We estimated that it was about 1/5, and this was endorsed by looking at large scale usage maps in the town land survey office.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: 24% to be precise.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our own informal discussions with neighbors and friends led us to believe that many garden owners had interesting experiences to relate regarding wild animal sightings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So we decided to survey garden owners from different areas of the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just over 100 of them completed a survey once every two weeks for 12 months.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Ticking off species they had seen from a pro forma list, and adding the names of any rarer ones.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Meanwhile, we were doing our own observations in selected gardens throughout the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We deliberately chose smaller ones because they were by far the most typical in the city.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The whole point of the project was to look at the norm, not the exception.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Alongside this primary research on urban gardens we were studying a lot of books about the decline of wild animals in the countryside, and thinking of possible causes for this.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what did we find?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, so much that I just won't have time to tell you about here.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you're interested in reading our more comprehensive findings, we've produced detailed graphic representations on the college website, and of course any of the group would be happy to talk to you about them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just email us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What we've decided to present today is information about just three species, because we felt these gave a good indication of the processes at work in rural and urban settings as a whole.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The first species to generate a lot of interesting information was frogs, and there was a clear pattern here.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They proliferate where there is suitable water, garden ponds are on the increase.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rural ponds are disappearing, leading to massive migration to the towns.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Hedgehogs are also finding it easier to live in urban areas this time because their predators are not finding it quite so attractive to leave their rural environment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So hedgehogs have a better survival rate in cities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We had lots of sightings, so all in all we had no difficulties with our efforts to count their numbers precisely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our final species is the finest of bird singers, the song thrush.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: On the decline in the countryside, they are experiencing a resurgence in urban gardens, because these days gardeners are buying lots of different plants, which means there's an extensive range of seeds around, which is what they feed on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another factor is the provision of nesting places, which is actually better in gardens than the countryside.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Hard to believe it, but it's true.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Incidentally, we discovered that a massive new survey on song thrushes is about to be launched, so you should keep an eye open for that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, I'd be happy to answer any questions you may have.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear the education officer of a Dinosaur Museum giving information to some teachers who are planning a school visit.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 11 to 15.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Hello, and thank you for asking me to your teachers' meeting to talk about the Dinosaur Museum, and to tell you a bit about what you can do with your students there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, let me give you some of the basic information first.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In regard to opening hours, we're open every day of the week from 9 am to 8 pm, except on Mondays, when we close at 1:30 pm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in fact the only day in the year when we're closed is on the 25th of December.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can book a guided tour for your school group any time that we're open.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you bring a school group to the museum, when you arrive, we ask you to remain with your group in the car park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One or more of the tour guides will welcome you there,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and brief you about what the tour will be about.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We do this there because our entrance is quite small, and we really haven't got much room for briefing groups in the exhibition area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As far as the amount of time you'll need goes, if you bring a school group, you should plan on allowing a minimum of 90 minutes for the visit.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This allows 15 minutes to get on and off the coach, 45 minutes for the guided tour, and 30 minutes for after-tour activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you're going to have lunch at the museum, you will of course have to allow more time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are two cafes in the museum with seating for 80 people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you want to eat there, you'll need to reserve some seating, as they can get quite crowded at lunchtime.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then outside the museum at the back, there are tables, and students can bring their own lunch and eat it there in the open air.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: When the students come into the museum foyer, we ask them to check in their backpacks with their books, lunch boxes, et cetera, at the cloakroom before they enter the museum proper.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm afraid in the past we have had a few things gone missing after school visits, so this is a strict rule.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Also some of the exhibits are fragile,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and we don't want them to be accidentally knocked.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we do provide school students with handouts with questions and quizzes on them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's so much that students can learn in the museum,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and it's fun for them to have something to do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Of course they'll need to bring something to write with for these.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We do allow students to take photographs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For students who are doing projects, it's useful to make some kind of visual record of what they see, that they can add to their reports.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And finally, they should not bring anything to eat into the museum or drinks of any kind.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are also a few things that students can do after the tour.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the theatrette on the ground floor, there are continuous screenings of short documentaries about dinosaurs which they can see at any time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We used to have an activity room with more interactive things like making models of dinosaurs, and drawing and painting pictures, even hunting for dinosaur eggs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But unfortunately the room was damaged in a bad storm recently when water came in the roof, so that's closed at the moment.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we do have an IT center,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: where students have access to CD ROMs with a range of dinosaur games.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These games are a lot of fun, but they also teach the students about the lives of dinosaurs, how they found food,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: protected their habitat, survived threats, that kind of thing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I think that's all I have to tell you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Please feel free to ask any questions if you would like to know anything else about...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3, you will hear a student called Sandra talking to her tutor about a draft proposal she has written for a competition.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Right, Sandra.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You wanted to see me to get some feedback on your group's proposal, the one you're submitting for the Geography Society Field Trip competition.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I've had a look through your proposal, and I think it's a really good choice.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: In fact, I only have a few things to say about it, but even in an outline document like this.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You really have to be careful to avoid typos and problems with layout in the proposal, and even in the contents page.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So read it through carefully before submitting it, OK?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Will do.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: And I've made a few notes on the proposal about things which could have been better sequenced.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: As for the writing itself, I've annotated the proposal as and where I thought it could be improved.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Generally speaking, I feel you've often used complex structures and long sentences for the sake of it, and as a consequence, although your paragraphing and inclusion of subheadings help.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: It's quite hard to follow your train of thought at times.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Oh, so cut them down a bit, can you?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Yes, and don't forget simple formatting like numbering.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Didn't I use page numbers?
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: I didn't mean that.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Look, you've remembered to include headers and footers, which is good, but listing ideas clearly is important.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Number them or use bullet points, which is even clearer.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Then you'll focus the reader on your main points.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I thought your suggestion to go to the Navajo tribal park was a very good idea.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I've always wanted to go there.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: My father was a great fan of cowboy films and the Wild West, so I was subjected to seeing all the epics.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Many of which were shot there.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: As a consequence, it feels very familiar to me, and it's awesome both geographically and visually.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: So it's somewhere I've always wanted to visit.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: The subsequent research I did, and the online photographs made me even keener.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Interesting.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Right, let's look at the content of your proposal now.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Did you find it comprehensive enough?
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Well, yes and no.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You've listed several different topics on your contents page.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: But I'm not sure they're all relevant.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: No? well, I thought that from the perspective of a field trip, one thing I needed to focus on was the sandstone plateau and cliffs themselves.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Uh. The way they tower up from the flat landscape is just amazing.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: The fact that the surrounding softer rocks were eroded by wind and rain, leaving these huge outcrops high above the plain.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: It's hardly surprising that tourists flock to see the area.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Well, yes, I'd agree with including those points.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And then the fact that it's been home to Native American Navajos, and all the social history that goes with that.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: The hardships they endured trying to save their territory from the invading settlers, their culture is so rich, all those wonderful stories.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Well, I agree it's interesting, but it's not immediately relevant to your proposal, Sandra.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So, at this stage, I suggest you focus on other considerations.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: I think an indication of what the students on the trip could actually do when they get there should be far more central, so that certainly needs to be included, and to be expanded upon.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: And I'd like to see something about the local wildlife and vegetation too, not that I imagine there's much to see.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Presumably the tourist invasion hasn't helped.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, I'll do some work on those two areas as well, uh, but you're right, there's not much apart from some very shallow rooted species.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Although it's cold and snowy there in the winter, the earth is baked so hard in the summer sun that rainwater can't penetrate.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Hmm. So it's a case of flood or drought really.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: So I understand.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Now, before we look at everything in more detail, I've got a few factual questions for you.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: It would be a good idea to include the answers in your finished proposal.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Because they're missing from your draft.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Fine.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: So you mention the monoliths and the spires which was good, but what area does the tribal park cover?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Do you know?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: 12,000 hectares, and the plain is at about 5,850 meters above sea level.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Hmm, larger than I expected.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: OK, where's the nearest accommodation?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: That's a practical detail that you haven't included.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Have you done any research on that?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, there's nowhere to stay in the park itself.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: But there's an old trading post called Goulding quite near. All kinds of tours start from Goulding, too.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Hmm. What kind of tours?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well the most popular are in 4 wheel drive jeeps, but I wouldn't recommend hiring those.
script.speaker: SANDRA

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a lecturer's introduction to a geography module.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, welcome to your introductory geography lecture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll begin with some basics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Firstly, what do we learn by studying geography?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, we learn a great deal about all the processes that have affected and that continue to affect the Earth's surface, but we learn far more than that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Because studying geography also informs us about the different kinds of relationships that develop between a particular environment and the people that live there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, we like to think of geography as having two main branches.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's the study of the nature of our planet, its physical features, what it actually looks like.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then there's the study of the ways in which we choose to live, and of the impact of those on our planet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our current use of carbon fuels is a good example of that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there are more specific study areas to consider too, and we'll be looking at each of these in turn throughout the semester.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These include biophysical geography.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By which I mean the study of the natural environment and all its living things.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then there's topography, that looks at the shapes of the land and oceans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There's the study of political geography, and social geography too, of course, which is the study of communities of people.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have economic geography.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In which we examine all kinds of resources and their use, agriculture for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Next comes historical geography, the understanding of how people and their environments, and the ways they interact have changed over a period of time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And urban geography, an aspect I'm particularly interested in, which takes as its focus the location of cities, the services that those cities provide, and migration of people to and from such cities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And lastly, we have cartography.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's the art and science of map making, you'll be doing a lot of that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, to summarize before we continue, we now have our key answer.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Studying this subject is important, because without geographical knowledge, we would know very little about our surroundings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And we wouldn't be able to identify all the problems that relate to them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, by definition, we wouldn't be in an informed position to work out how to solve any of them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: OK, now for some practicalities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: What do geographers actually do?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, we collect data to begin with.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll be doing a lot of that on your first field trip.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: How do we do this?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are several means.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We might for example conduct a census, count a population in a given area, perhaps.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We also need images of the Earth's surface which we can produce by means of computer generation technology, or with the help of satellite relays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've come a very long way from the early exploration of the world by sailing ships.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: When geographers only had pens and paper at their disposal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After we've gathered our information, we must analyze it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We need to look for patterns, most commonly those of causes and consequences.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This kind of information helps us to predict and resolve problems that could affect the world we live in, but we don't keep all this information confidential.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We then need to publish our findings, so that other people can access it and be informed by it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And one way in which this information can be published is in the form of maps.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll all have used one at some stage of your life already.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's consider the benefits of maps from a geographer's perspective.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Maps can be folded and put in a pocket.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And can provide a great store of reference when they're collected into an atlas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They can depict the physical features of the entire planet if necessary, or just a small part of it in much greater detail.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there is a drawback.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can't exactly replicate something that is three dimensional like our planet on a flat piece of paper, because paper has only two dimensions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And that means there'll always be a certain degree of distortion on a map.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It can't be avoided.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We can also use aerial photographs, pictures taken by cameras at high altitude above the earth.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are great for showing all kinds of geographical features that are not easy to see from the ground.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can easily illustrate areas of diseased trees, or how much traffic is on the roads at a given time, or information about deep seabeds for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then, there are landsats.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are satellites that circle the earth and transmit visual information to computers at receiving stations.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They circle the earth several times a day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And can provide a mass of information.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll all be familiar with the information they give us about the weather for example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what we're going to do now is look at a short presentation in which you'll see all these tools.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2, you will hear an introductory talk about a new agricultural park.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Welcome to Green Vale Agricultural Park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you know, we've only been open a week, so you're amongst our first visitors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have lots of fascinating indoor and outdoor exhibits on our huge complex spreading hundreds of hectares.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Our remit is to give educational opportunities to the wider public, as well as to offer research sites for a wide variety of agriculturists and other scientists.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's start by seeing what there is to do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you can see, uh, here on our giant wall plan, we are now situated in the Reception block.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As you walk out of the main door into the park, there's a path you can follow.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you follow this route, you'll immediately come into the Rare Breeds section.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Where we keep a wide variety of animals, which I shall be telling you a little more about later.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Next to this, uh, moving east is the large grazing area for the rare breeds.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then further east in the largest section of our park is the Forest Area. South of the grazing area, and in fact just next to the Reception block is our experimental crop area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the middle of the park, uh, this circular area is our lake.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these two small rectangular shapes here are the fish farms where we rear fish for sale.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To the east of those is the marsh area, which attracts a great many migrant birds, and in the southeastern corner beyond the marsh is our market garden area.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Growing vegetables and flowers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: All these areas can be visited by the general public for almost all the year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Although please take note of the large signs at the entrance to each area, which tell which tell you when certain areas are being used for particular controlled experiments.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And are therefore temporarily out of bounds to the public.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You can see for yourself what a huge area the park covers, and a key question is always, how can we move around?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, you have a choice of means.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All environmentally friendly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Um. Cars are banned in the park.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We have bicycles, which you can hire behind the Reception block... here...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: the healthy ones of you can go on foot,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and finally there's our electric tram, powered from solar cells.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You find more information about this at the front entrance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A good place to start on your tour is the Rare Breeds section.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We keep goats, sheep, and hens, and other kinds of poultry.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. We're also thinking of bringing in cows and horses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But we do not as yet have facilities for these bigger animals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The animals are fed in public twice a day, and a short lecture given on their feeding habits and nutritional needs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are very popular with the public, but of course, we mustn't lose sight of the main purpose of having this section, not as such to preserve rare animals, but to maintain the diversity of breeds, to broaden the gene pool for agricultural development.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Green Vale changes with the seasons with different events happening at different times of the year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: May will be perhaps our most spectacular month with the arrival of the Canada geese.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And when our fruit trees will be in full blossom, but there are interesting events all year round... for example, John Havers, our expert fly fisherman, is currently giving displays on the lake.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each of the sections has its own seasonal calendar, and please consult the summary board at the main entrance. And the final section, as we return to the Reception block, is the orchard.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Do take time to browse round our shop, there's a wide selection of books on wildlife, some of them written by local authors, and the history of farming.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Including organic farming, something which the park will be diversifying into in the coming months.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.

script.text: Section 3, you will hear part of a seminar in which a researcher called Grant Freeman discusses his work on Australian honeybees.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: With a group of students.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Uh. In today's seminar, Grant Freeman, a biologist who specializes in identifying insects, and who works for the Australian Quarantine Service, has come to talk to us about his current research work.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, uh, over to you, Grant.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Good morning, everyone.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: I'm sure that you know that the quarantine service regulates all food brought into Australia.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Well, obviously they want to protect Australia from diseases that might come in with imported goods, but they also want to prevent insect pests from being introduced into the country.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: And that's where I have a part to play.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Anyway, my current research involves trying to find a particular type of bee, the Asian Honey Bee.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: And finding out whether there are any of them around in various states of Australia.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: We discovered a few of them in Queensland once and eradicated them.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Now we're pretty keen to make sure that there aren't any more getting in, particularly to New South Wales and other states.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: What's wrong with Asian Honey Bees?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Are they so different from Australian bees?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Well, in fact, they look almost the same, but they are infested with mites, microscopic creatures which live on them, and which can seriously damage our own homegrown bees, or could even wipe them out.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Well, what would happen if Australian bees died out?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Well, the honey from Australian bees is of excellent quality, much better than the stuff the Asian bees produce.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: In fact Australia exports native queen bees to a large number of countries because of this.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: When the European Honey Bee was first discovered out in the bush, we found they made really unpleasant honey, and they were also too big to pollinate many of our native flowers here in Australia.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: That must have had a devastating effect on the natural flora.
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Did you lose any species?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: No, we managed to get them under control before that happened, but if Asian bees got in, there could be other consequences.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: We could lose a lot of money, because you might not be aware, but it's estimated that native bees' pollination of flower and vegetable crops is worth $1.2 billion a year.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: So in a way, they're the farmers' friend.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Oh, and another thing is if you're stung by an Asian Honey Bee, it can produce an allergic reaction in some people, so they're much more dangerous than native bees.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the seminar, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: How will you know if Asian bees have entered Australia?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: We're looking at the diet of the bird called the Rainbow Bee Eater.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: The bee eater doesn't care what it eats, as long as they're insects.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: But the interesting thing about this bird is that we are able to analyze exactly what it eats, and that's really helpful if we're looking for introduced insects.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: How come?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Because insects have their skeletons outside their bodies, so the Bee Eaters digest the meat from the inside. Then they bring up all the indigestible bits of skeleton, and, of course, the wings in a pellet - a small ball of waste material which they cough up.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: That sounds a bit unpleasant, so how do you go about it?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: In the field, we track down the Bee Eaters and find their favorite feeding spots.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: You know the places where the birds usually feed.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: It's here that we can find the pellets.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: We collect them up and take them back to the laboratory to examine the contents.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: And how do you do that?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: The pellets are really hard, especially if they've been out in the sun for a few days.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: So, first of all, we treat them by adding water to moisten them.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: And make them softer.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Then we pull them apart under the microscope.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Everything's all scrunched up, but we're looking for wings, so we just pull them all out and straighten them.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Then we identify them to see if we can find any Asian bee wings.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: And how many have you found?
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: So far, our research shows that Asian bees have not entered Australia in any number.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: It's a good result, and much more reliable than trying to find live ones as evidence of introduced insects.
script.speaker: GRANT

script.text: Well, that's fascinating.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: Thank you Grant for those insights.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: I hope that you might inspire some of our students here to conduct some similar experiments.
script.speaker: PROFESSOR

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a student called Shona giving a presentation on her research report.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I've been doing some research into what people in Britain think of doctors, the ones who work in general practice - the first call for medical care - and comparing this with the situation in a couple of other countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I want to talk about the rationale behind what I decided to do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now I had to set up my program of research in three different countries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So I approached postgraduates in my field in overseas departments, contacting them by email to organize things for me at their end.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I thought I would have trouble recruiting help, but in fact everyone was very willing, and sometimes their tutors got involved too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I had to give my helpers clear instructions about what kind of sample population I wanted them to use.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I decided that people under 18 should be excluded, because most of them are students or looking for their first job.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And also I decided at this stage just to focus on men who were in employment, and set up something for people who didn't have jobs, and for employed women later on as a separate investigation.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I specifically wanted to do a questionnaire and interviews with a focus group, with the questionnaire rather than limiting it to one specific point.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I wanted to include as much variety as possible.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I know questionnaires are a very controlled way to do things, but I thought I could do taped interviews later on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: To counteract the effects of this, and the focus group may also prove useful in future, by targeting subjects I can easily return to.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As the participants tend to be more involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So I'm just collating the results now, at the moment it looks as if in the UK, despite the fact that newspapers continually report that people are unhappy with medical care.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, it is mainly the third level of care, which takes place in hospitals that they are worried about.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Government reforms have been proposed at all levels, and although their success is not guaranteed, long term hospital care is in fact probably less of an issue than the media would have us believe.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, I've still got quite a bit of data to look at.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Certainly, I will need to do more far-reaching research than I had anticipated, in order to establish if people want extra medical staff invested in the community.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Or if they want care to revert to fewer but larger key medical units.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The solution may well be something that can be easily implemented by those responsible in local government, with central government support of course.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This first stage has proved very valuable though.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I was surprised by how willing most of the subjects were to get involved in the project.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I had expected some unwillingness to answer questions honestly.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But I was taken aback and rather concerned that something I thought I'd set up very well didn't necessarily seem that way to everyone in my own department.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I thought you might also be interested in some of the problems I encountered in collecting my data.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There were odd cases that threw me.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the subjects who I had approached while he was out shopping in town decided to pull out when it came to the second round.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was a shame.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: As it was someone who I would like to have interviewed more closely.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And one of the first year students I interviewed wanted reassurance that no names would be traceable from the answers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I was so surprised, because they think nothing of telling you about themselves and their opinions in seminar groups.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then one of the people that I worked with got a bit funny.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The questions were quite personal, and one minute he said he'd do it, then the next day he wouldn't.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in the end, he did do it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's hard not to get angry in that situation, but I tried to keep focused on the overall picture in order to stay calm.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The most bizarre case was a telephone interview I did with a teacher at a university in France.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He answered all my questions in great detail.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But then when I asked how much access he had to dangerous substances, he wouldn't tell me exactly what his work involved.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a real eye-opener...
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2, you will hear a man talking on the radio about a national arts center.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.

script.text: Hello, and welcome to Focus on the Arts.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: I'm your host, Dave Green, and this is your very own local radio program.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Every Friday evening, we put the spotlight on different arts and culture facilities.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And look at the shows and events that are on offer in the coming week, and today the focus is on the National Arts Center.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Now, if you don't already know it yourself, I'm sure you've all heard of it.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: It's famous throughout the world as one of the major venues for classical music.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: But did you know that it's actually much more than just a place to hear concerts?
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: The center itself is a huge complex that caters for a great range of arts.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Under a single roof, it houses concert rooms, theaters, cinemas, art galleries, and a wonderful public library, as well as service facilities including 3 restaurants and a bookshop.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: So, at any one time, the choice of entertainment there is simply enormous.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: So, how did they manage to build such a big arts complex right in the heart of the city?
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Well, the area was completely destroyed by bombs during the war in 1940.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: So the opportunity was taken to create a cultural center that would be what they called: 'the City's Gift to the Nation'.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Of course, it took a while for such a big project to get started, but it was planned in the 60s, built in the 70s, and eventually opened to the public in 1983.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Ever since then, it has proved to be a great success.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: It's not privately owned, like many arts centers, but is still in public hands - it's run by the City Council.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Both our National Symphony Orchestra and National Theatre Company were involved in the planning of the project.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And they're now based there, giving regular performances every week.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And as the center is open 363 days of the year, there are plenty of performances to choose from.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the broadcast, you have some time to look at question 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer question 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: So, to give you some idea of what's on, and to help you choose from the many possibilities, we've made a selection of the star attractions.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: If you're interested in classical music, then we recommend you go along to the National on either Monday or Tuesday evening at 7:30 for a spectacular production of The Magic Flute, probably the most popular of all Mozart's operas.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: It's in the Garden Hall, and tickets start at only £8, but you'll have to be early if you want to get them that cheap.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And remember, it's only on for those two evenings.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: For those more interested in the cinema, you might like to see the new Canadian film, which is showing on Wednesday evening at 8 pm in Cinema 2.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And that's called Three Lives.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: It's had fantastic reviews, and tickets cost just £4.50, which is a reduction on the usual price of £5.50.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: So, it's really good value, especially for such a great movie.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: But you can see the center's main attraction at the weekend, because on Saturday and Sunday, 11:00 am to 10:00 pm, they're showing a wonderful new exhibition that hasn't been seen anywhere else in Europe yet.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: It's a collection of Chinese art called 'Faces of China'.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: That's in Gallery 1, and it has some really fascinating paintings and sculptures by leading artists from all over China.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And the good news is that it's completely free, so don't miss it.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: So why not go along to the National Arts Center next week for one or all of these great events?
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: And you can always pick up a program and check out all the other performances and exhibitions on offer or coming soon on almost every day of the year.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: Next week, we'll be looking at the new Museum of Science.
script.speaker: DAVE GREEN

script.text: That is the end of Section 2.

script.text: I get demotivated otherwise.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: What do you think you learned from your experience?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: It must have been a great opportunity to examine community life.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, but it was difficult at first to be accepted by the locals.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: It was a very remote village, and some of them were reluctant to speak to me.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Although they were always interested in my clothes, and how much I had to pay for them.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Well, that's understandable.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, but things soon improved.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: What struck me was that when people became more comfortable with me and less suspicious, we really connected with each other in a meaningful way.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: You made good friends?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, with two of the families in particular.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: What about management?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Did you have a project manager?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Yes, and he gave me lots of advice and guidance.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: And was he good at managing too?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: That wasn't his strong point.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: I think he was often more interested in the academic side of things than filing reports.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: He was a bit of a dreamer.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Uh. And did you have a contract?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: I had to stay for a minimum of 3 months.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: My parents were surprised when I asked to stay longer, 6 months in the end.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: I was so happy there.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: And did anything on the administration side of things surprise you?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: What was the food and lodging like?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Hmm. Simple.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: But there was plenty to eat, and I only paid $7 a day for that, which was amazing, really.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: And they gave me all the equipment I needed, even a laptop.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: You didn't expect that then?
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: No.
script.speaker: PAUL

script.text: Well, I'll look forward to hearing more.

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.speaker: WOMAN

script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Women are increasingly occupying positions in government, and in other elected leadership positions in Latin America.
script.speaker: WOMAN

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a lecture about success in business systems.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the last few lectures, I've been dealing with business finance, but now I'm going to move on to business systems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And in today's lecture, I'm going to talk about what can go wrong when businesses try to copy their own best practices.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Once a business has successfully introduced a new process, managing a branch bank say, or selling a new product, the parent organization naturally wants to repeat that success.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And capture it if possible on a bigger scale.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The goal then is to utilize existing knowledge, and not to generate new knowledge.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's a less glamorous activity than pure innovation, but it actually happens more often as a matter of fact.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However surprisingly getting things right the second time is not necessarily any simpler than it was the first time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, there's been a lot of research into how companies can repeat their previous successes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And it certainly hasn't been confined to the United States.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It seems that most large industries are trying to repeat their own successes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And manage the knowledge they've acquired.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But even so, it has been shown that the overwhelming majority of attempts fail.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: A host of studies confirm this, covering a wide range of business settings, branch banks, retail stores, real estate agencies, factories, call centers, to name but a few.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So why do so few managers get things right the second or third time?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's consider one reason for failure.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Placing too much trust in the people who are running the successful operation, the experts, shall we say?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Managers who want to apply existing knowledge typically start off by going to an expert, uh, such as the person who designed and is running a successful department store.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And picking their brains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now this approach can be used if you want to gain a rough understanding of a particular system, or understand smaller isolated problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The trouble is, even the expert doesn't fully grasp the whole thing, because when it comes to complex systems, the individual components of the process are interwoven with one another.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The expert never has complete access to the necessary information, and the situation's complicated even further by the fact that experts are usually not aware of their own ignorance.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The ignorance can take various forms, uh, for instance, a lot of details of the system are invisible to managers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some may be difficult to describe, learned on the job, and well known by workers perhaps, but impossible to describe in a way that's helpful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And there are some things that people know or do that they're not even aware of.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, let's consider two types of mistake that can occur when a manager actually starts to set up a duplicate system to replicate a successful process.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Firstly, perhaps he forgets that he was just trying to copy another process, and starts trying to improve on it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Another mistake is trying to use the best parts of various different systems in the hope of creating the perfect combination.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Unfortunately, attempts like these usually turn out to be misguided and lead to problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. Well for various reasons.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Perhaps there weren't really any advantages after all, because the information wasn't accurate, or perhaps the business settings weren't really comparable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: More typically, the advantages are real enough, but there are also disadvantages that have been overlooked.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. For example.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The modifications might compromise safety in some way.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what's the solution?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, I don't intend to suggest that it's easy to get things right the second time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's not, but the underlying problem has more to do with attitudes than the actual difficulty of the task, and there are ways of getting it right.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These involve adjusting attitudes first of all, being more realistic and cautious really.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Secondly, they involve exerting strict controls on the organizational and operational systems, and this in turn means copying the original as closely as possible, not merely duplicating the physical characteristics of the factory, but also duplicating the skills that the original employees had.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Reliance on a template like this offers the huge advantage of built-in consistency.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a man being interviewed on local radio about a plan to improve a suburb called Red Hill.

script.text: Good morning, and welcome again to Your City Today.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: With me today is Graham Campbell, a councillor from the city council.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: He'll be telling us about the plan to improve the fast growing suburb of Red Hill.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Good morning Graham and welcome to the show.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Good morning Carol.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Now Graham, I understand that there has been a lot of community consultation for the new plan.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Yes, we've tried to address some of the concerns that local groups told us about.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: People we've heard from are mainly worried about traffic in the area, and in particular the increasing speed of cars near schools.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: They feel that it's only a matter of time before there's an accident as a lot of children walk to the school.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: So, we're trying to do something about that.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Another area of concern is the overhead power lines.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: These are very old, and a lot of people we spoke to asked if something could be done about them.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Well, I'm happy to report that the power company have agreed to move the power lines underground at a cost of $800,000.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: I think that will really improve the look of the area, as well as being safer.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Hmm, that's good to know.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: But will that mean an increase in rates for the local businesses in that area?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Well, the power company have agreed to bear the cost of this themselves after a lot of discussion with the council.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: This is wonderful news, as the council now has some extra funds for us to put into other things like tree planting and artwork.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 14 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 14 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: We've also put together a map, which we sent out to all the residents in the area, and on the map we've marked the proposed changes.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Firstly, we'll plant mature pine trees to provide shelter and shade just to the right of the supermarket in Days Road.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: In order to address the traffic problems, the pavements on the corner of Carberry and Thomas Street will be widened.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: This will help to reduce the speed of vehicles entering Thomas Street.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: We think it's very important to separate the local residential streets from the main road, so the roadway at the entrance to Thomas Street from Days Road will be painted red.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: This should mark it more clearly, and act as a signal for traffic to slow down.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: One way of making sure that the pedestrians are safe is to increase signage at the intersections.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: A 'keep clear' sign will be erected at the junction of Evelyn Street and Hill Street, to enable traffic to exit at all times.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Something we're planning to do to help control the flow of traffic in the area is to install traffic lights halfway down Hill Street where it crosses Days Road.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Now, we haven't only thought about the cars and traffic of course, there's also something for the children.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: We're going to get school children in the area to research a local story, the life of a local sports hero perhaps, and an artist will incorporate that story into paintings on the wall of a building on the other side of Hill Street from the supermarket.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: And finally, we've agreed to build a new children's playground, which will be at the other end of Hill Street, close to the intersection with Carberry Street.
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: Wonderful.
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Now, uh, what's the next stage?
script.speaker: CAROL

script.text: Well, the final plan will...
script.speaker: GRAHAM

script.text: That is the end of section 2.

script.text: Hi, Jeannie, how's it going?

script.text: That's good.

script.text: It's our first performance next week, so we're rehearsing frantically.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: And I've got behind with my work.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I'm hoping to be in the spring production too.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: And I also joined the debating society.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I'm not very good, but I'd really miss it if I stopped.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I decided to try tennis when I came to college, and I'm finding it pretty tough going.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I'm simply not fit enough.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Nor me.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: I think I'll give that a miss.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: I'm hoping it'll help me to build up my stamina, but it'll probably be a long haul.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Good luck.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Thanks.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: What?

script.speaker: DAN

script.text: It's quite interesting, but I wonder if I'm clever enough to be doing this course.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: I find it helpful to listen to the other people.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I like the way we're exploring the subject, and working towards getting insight into it.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: How do you get on with your tutor?

script.speaker: DAN

script.text: It would be more productive to read a book instead.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Oh, mine's very demanding.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: She gives me lots of feedback and advice, so I've got much better at writing essays.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: And she's helping me plan my revision for the end-of-year exams.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Do tell me, I always struggle with revision.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Well, the first thing is to find out exactly what's required in the exams.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Would it help to get hold of some past papers?
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: They'll help to make it clear.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Right, I'll do that.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Then what?
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Then you can sort out your revision priorities based on what's most likely to come up.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I put these on a card and read them through regularly.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Uh-huh.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: But that isn't enough in itself.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: You also need a timetable to see how you can fit everything in the time available, then keep it in front of you while you're studying.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: I've done that before, but it hasn't helped me.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Maybe you need to do something different every day, so if you break down your revision into small tasks and allocate them to specific days, there's more incentive to tackle them.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: With big topics, you're more likely to put off starting.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Good idea.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: And as I revise each topic, I write a single paragraph about it.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Then later, I can read it through quickly.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: And it helps fix things in my mind.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Well, that's brilliant.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: I also write answers to questions for the exam practice.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: It's hard to make myself do it though.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: Well, I'll try.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Thanks a lot, Jeannie.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: That's a great help.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: No problem.
script.speaker: JEANNIE

script.text: See you around.
script.speaker: DAN

script.text: Bye.
script.speaker: JEANNIE
