script.text: Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about Australian rock art to a group of archaeology students.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I've been invited to talk about my research project into Australian Aboriginal rock paintings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Australian Aborigines have recorded both real and symbolic images of their time on rock walls for many thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Throughout the long history of this tradition, new images have appeared, and new painting styles have developed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And these characteristics can be used to categorize the different artistic styles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Among these are what we call the dynamic, yam, and modern styles of painting.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: One of the most significant characteristics of the different styles is the way that humans are depicted in the paintings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The more recent paintings show people in static poses.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the first human images to dominate rock art paintings over 8,000 years ago were full of movement.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These paintings showed people hunting and cooking food, and so they were given the name dynamic to reflect this energy.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's quite amazing considering they were painted in such a simple stick-like form. In the Yam period, there was a movement away from stick figures to a more naturalistic shape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, they didn't go as far as the modern style, which is known as x-ray, because it actually makes a feature of the internal skeleton, as well as the organs of animals and humans.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The yam style of painting got its name from the fact that it featured much curvier figures that actually resembled the vegetable called yam, which is similar to a sweet potato.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The modern paintings are interesting because they include paintings at the time of the first contact with European settlers.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Aborigines managed to convey the idea of the settlers' clothing by simply painting the Europeans without any hands,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: indicating the habit of standing with their hands in their pockets.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Size is another characteristic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The more recent images tend to be life size or even larger.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But the dynamic figures are painted in miniature.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Aboriginal rock art also records the environmental changes that occurred over thousands of years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, we know from the dynamic paintings that over 8,000 years ago Aborigines would have rarely eaten fish, and sea levels were much lower at this time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, fish didn't start to appear in paintings until the Yam period,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: along with shells and other marine images.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The paintings of the Yam tradition also suggest that during this time, the Aborigines moved away from animals as their main food source, and began including vegetables in their diet,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: as these feature prominently.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Fresh water creatures didn't appear in the paintings until the modern period from 4,000 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So these paintings have already taught us a lot, but one image that has always intrigued us is known as the Rainbow Serpent.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Rainbow Serpent which is the focus of my most recent project, gets its name from its snake or serpent like body, and it first appeared in the Yam period 4 to 6,000 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many believe it is a curious mixture of kangaroo, snake and crocodile, but we decided to study the rainbow serpent paintings to see if we could locate the animal that the very first painters based their image on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The Yam period coincided with the end of the last ice Age.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This brought about tremendous change in the environment, with the sea levels rising and creeping steadily inland.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This flooded many familiar land features, and also caused a great deal of disruption to traditional patterns of life, hunting in particular.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: New shores were formed, and totally different creatures would have washed up onto the shores.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We studied 107 paintings of the rainbow serpent, and found that the one creature that matches it most closely was the ribboned pipefish,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which is a type of seahorse.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This sea creature would have been a totally unfamiliar sight in the inland regions where the image is found, and it may have been the inspiration behind the early paintings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, at the end of the Ice Age, there would have been enormous changes in animal and plant life.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's not surprising then that the Aborigines linked this abundance to the new creatures they witnessed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Even today, Aborigines see the rainbow serpent as a symbol of creation, which is understandable given the increase in vegetation and the new life forms that featured when the image first appeared.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Thank you all for coming to my talk this evening.

script.text: It's nice to see so many people in the audience.

script.text: For those of you who don't know very much about PS Camping, let me start by giving you some background information about the company.

script.text: The company started 25 years ago.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It actually opened as a retail chain selling camping equipment, and then 20 years ago, it bought a small number of camp sites in the UK.

script.text: And began offering camping holidays.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The company grew rapidly, and has been providing holidays in continental Europe for the last 15 years.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If you book a camping holiday with us, you'll have a choice of over 300 sites.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Italy, we now have some 64 sites that we either own or have exclusive use of. France is where we have the majority of sites, and we currently have a project to expand into Switzerland.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We also have a number of sites in northern Spain, particularly in the mountainous region of Picos de Europa.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We've upgraded all these Spanish sites, and improved them considerably from their original 3 star rating.

script.text: We believe our holidays offer superb facilities for the whole family.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Parents who want their children to be fully occupied for all or part of the day can take advantage of our children's activities.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: These are organized by our well qualified and enthusiastic staff.

script.text: Each day kicks off with a sports match.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Perhaps football or volleyball, followed by an hour of drama for everyone.

script.text: This may include singing or dancing, MIME or other activities.

script.text: In the afternoon, there's a different art activity for each day of the week, including a poster competition or model making.

script.text: What's more, our sites are truly child friendly, and with this in mind, we operate a no noise rule in the evenings.

script.text: Children's evening activities usually finish at 9:30 or occasionally 10, and from 10:30 holiday makers are expected to be quiet.

script.text: Section 3, you will hear a tutor talking to two business students called Philip and Janice about their research on managing individuals.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 23.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Well, you've both been looking at different styles of managing individuals in companies and the workplace.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: How's the research going, Philip?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well I've been looking at why individualism, I mean individual differences are such an important area of management studies.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: When you think about any organization, be it a family business or a multinational company.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: They're all fundamentally a group of people working together, but it's what these individuals contribute to their places of work that makes you realize how important they are.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Of course, they bring different ideas.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: But it's also their attitudes and their experiences of learning.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Diversity is important in these areas too.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: So, why do people behave so differently from one another at work?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: There are lots of reasons, but research has shown that a lot of it comes down to personality, and the other factor is gender.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: It's a well-known fact that men and women do lots of things in different ways.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: And the workplace is no different.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Did you look at the effects of this variation on companies?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, I did.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: On the positive side, exposure to such diversity helps encourage creativity,
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: which is generally an asset to a company.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: But unfortunately, individual differences are also the root of conflict between staff, and they can lead to difficulties for management, which can sometimes be serious.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 24 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Thanks, Philip.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So now I guess the two main things to remember here are to identify individual talent, and then to utilize it.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So Janice, you were looking at identifying different talents in workers.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Do you think this is easy for managers to do?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well currently teamwork is in fashion in the workplace.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: And in my opinion, the importance of the individual is generally neglected.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: What managers should be targeting is those employees who can take the lead in a situation, and are not afraid to accept the idea of responsibility.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: Hmm, that's true, Janice, but unfortunately, many managers think the entire notion of encouraging individuality amongst their staff is far too hard.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, that may be true, but I think one of the most important tasks of managers is to consider the needs of the individual on one hand, and group cooperation and conformity on the other.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: It requires creative thinking on the part of management to avoid tension.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: So Janice, what kind of people do you think companies should be looking for?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well, uh, it has to start from the very beginning, when companies are looking for new employees.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: When the personnel department is choosing between applicants, they need to look for someone who's broken the mold, and can think for themselves.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: Instead, people making these decisions often use a range of psychological tests to see if a person is a problem solver, or will do as they're told.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: I'm not convinced these qualities are actually the most important.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: So do you think being a good team player is overrated?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: No, it's not overrated.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: You do need to learn the rules and learn them fast.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: No individual can get around this if they're working in an organization.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: So how should managers deal with this?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Rewards, when an individual demonstrates the behavior the organization expects, some kind of incentive can be given.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: What's important here is that this happens right at the beginning.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: So new recruits learn the rules of the system immediately.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: Also the incentive should be something the individual actually wants, and this isn't always just money.
script.speaker: JANICE

script.text: To come back to you, Philip.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: You were saying that recognition of good performers is essential.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: What else should managers be looking for?
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Well, managing people means you not only have an understanding of your employees.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: But you also recognize the culture of the organization.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: In fact, for some organizations creativity and individuality may be the last thing they want to see during working hours.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Very true.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes, but managing people isn't as easy as it looks.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: For example, change in the workplace can be quite tricky, especially if there's a need to increase profit.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: And at times like these, managers may have to give priority to profit rather than individual staff needs.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Hmm. Yes, and that creates difficult situations for people.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: But what's important is that managers are able to deal with quite high levels of personal stress. During times of change, they should be thinking not only about the strain on their staff, but take time out to think of themselves.
script.speaker: PHILIP

script.text: Absolutely.
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: So what are the implications of that for...
script.speaker: TUTOR

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear part of a lecture about cave paintings and other types of rock art.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good afternoon everyone.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is the first seminar in preparation for our archaeological fieldwork in Namibia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We are fantastically lucky to have received partial research funding for this trip from our institute.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So I shall expect 200% attention and participation from you all.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First in this seminar, I'm going to give a brief introduction to contemporary research on rock art, and in the second part, I'm going to give you some do's and don'ts for our field work trip in April.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So please listen very carefully.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm first going to focus on the interpretation of rock art in Namibia.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We are very fortunate to be going to an area where you can find some of the most important sites in the entire world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I hope to show you how easy it is for everyone to make mistakes in looking at cultures which are different from our own, the first and most important lesson we have to learn.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In Namibia, there are both paintings and engravings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That's where the surface of the rock is cut out.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many of the engravings show footprints of animals, and most scholars used to think that the purpose of these was simple and obvious.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This rock art was like a school book with pictures to teach children about tracks, which track belonged to which animal, giraffe, lion, and so on.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But there were some mysteries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: First, when you look at a typical Namibian painting or engraving, you see the tracks are repeated.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: There are dozens of tracks for the same animal.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, you'd expect just one clear illustration if the reason - the aim - was to teach tracking.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, there were two more problems.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Why are some of the engravings of animals very accurate as you'd expect?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: All clearly identifiable, and others quite unrealistic.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And another mystery, some of these unrealistic animals that's in the engravings seem to be half human.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Some for example have got human faces.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many researchers now think that these were pictures the wise men engraved of themselves.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: They believe they could use magic to control the animals they had drawn, so the hunters could then catch them for food.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This shows you some of the dangers of coming from one culture to another, as we'll be doing without understanding it fully.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Scholars imagined that children looked at rock art pictures to learn to track.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Just because they themselves had learned skills from pictures.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Many researchers now believe that rock art had a much more complex purpose, and we'll talk more about it next week.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, before I invite you to join in a discussion in this second part of the seminar, I'd like to make some very important points about our field work, and in fact any field trip to look at rock art.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We're going to a number of sites, and we won't always be together.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The single largest problem faced by people who manage the sites is, yes, I'm sure you've guessed, damage caused by visitors.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Even though it's usually unintentional.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Whenever you do go to a site, don't forget you can learn many things from observing at a distance, instead of walking all over it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This can really help to reduce visitor pressure.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: People often say, well there's only two of us, and just this one time, but maybe thousands of people are saying the same thing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And then some basic rules to guide you.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We'll have our own camp near a village, but remember never to camp on a site if you go on your own.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It may be disrespectful to the people of that culture.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And certainly don't make fires, however romantic it may seem.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's really dangerous in dry areas, and you can easily burn priceless undiscovered material by doing so.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, how are we going to enjoy the rock art on our field trip?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: By looking at it, drawing it, and photographing it, never by touching it or even tracing it.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Rock art is fragile and precious.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Remember that climbing on rocks and in caves can destroy in a moment what has lasted for centuries.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, no heroics in Namibia please.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Try to be extra careful and help others to be too.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Oh, and lastly, please don't even move rocks or branches to take photographs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You should leave the site intact.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm sure I can rely on you to do that.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, that's about all I want to say before today's first discussion, but if you have any questions, please ask them now.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Oh, and don't forget you'll find some fascinating information about worldwide sites on the Internet.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Right, first question then.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear a seminar with Dr Martin Merryweather of the Antarctic Center in Christchurch, New Zealand.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 21 to 26.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: We're pleased to welcome Dr Martin Merryweather of the Antarctic Center in Christchurch, New Zealand, who has come along to talk to us today about the role of the center and the Antarctic Treaty.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Now my first question is about the choice of location for the center.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Why Christchurch?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Was it because of the climate?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, actually New Zealand is the second closest country to Antarctica.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And Christchurch is often used on Antarctic expeditions.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Right.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: So it's because of where we are, coupled with our historical role.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: So tell us.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: What is the main purpose of the center?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Oh, well, we have two complementary roles.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: One is as a scientific base for expeditions and research, and the other is as an information center.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Tell us something about the role as a scientific base.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, we're able to provide information about what scientists should take with them to the South Pole.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: For example, the center contains a clothing warehouse where expeditions are supplied with suitable clothing for the extreme conditions.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: I suppose you need a bit more than your normal winter coat.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes, exactly.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And then there's also the specialist library and mapping services.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Right, and which countries are actually located at the center?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, the center houses research programs for New Zealand, for the United States as well as for Italy.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: There's even a US Post Office at the American Air Force Base here.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Really?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: And what does the visitor center offer?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, since very few people will ever experience the Antarctic firsthand, the visitor center aims to recreate the atmosphere of Antarctica.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: There's a mock campsite where you can see inside an Antarctic tent and imagine yourself sleeping there.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And the center also acts as a showcase for the unique international cooperation which exists in Antarctica today.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: What is it actually like at the South Pole?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: I know you've been there on a number of occasions.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes, I have, and each time I'm struck by the awesome beauty of the place.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: It's magnificent, but you can really only visit it in the summer months.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: October to March.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes, because it's completely dark for four months of the year.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And in addition, it has to be the coldest place on earth.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Uh. Colder than the North Pole.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Why is that?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Ah. Well, unlike the North Pole, which is actually a frozen sea, Antarctica is a land mass shaped like a dome, with the result that the winds blow down the slopes at speeds of up to 150 km an hour and that's what makes it so cold.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Oh.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: And one other interesting thing is that Antarctica is the driest continent on earth, surprisingly.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And so you have to drink large amounts of water when you're there.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: How old is Antarctica?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Oh, we're pretty sure it was part of a larger landmass, but it broke away from the rest of the continent 170 million years ago.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: How can you be certain of this?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Because fossils and rocks have been discovered in Antarctica, which are the same as those found in places such as Africa and Australia.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Amazing to think that it was once attached to Africa.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now, let's just have a look at the Antarctic Treaty.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: How far back does the idea of an international treaty go?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, as far back as the 19th century.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: When 11 nations organized an international event.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: When was that exactly?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: In 1870 and it was called the Polar Research Meeting.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And then, not long after that, they organized something called the First International Polar Year.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: And that took place when exactly?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Over two years from 1882 to 1883.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: But it wasn't until the 1950s that the idea of an international treaty was proposed, and in 1959 the treaty was actually signed.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: What do you see as the main achievements of the treaty?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, firstly, it means that the continent is reserved for peaceful use.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: That's Article 1, isn't it?
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: That's important since the territory belongs to everyone.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Yes, but not as important as Article 5, which prohibits any nuclear explosions or waste disposal.
script.speaker: DOCTOR

script.text: Which is marvelous.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Well, I'm afraid we're going to have to stop there, because I'm afraid we've run out of time.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: Thanks for coming along today and telling us all about the center and its work.
script.speaker: INTERVIEWER

script.text: That is the end of section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear a presentation given by a sport science student on her project on left and right handedness in sport.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: My topic is handedness, whether in different sports, it is better to be left or right sided, or whether a more balanced approach is more successful.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I'm left-handed myself, and I actually didn't see any relevance to my own life when I happened to start reading an article by a sports psychologist called Peter Matthews.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He spent the first part of the article talking about handedness in music instead of sport, which I have to say almost put me off from reading further.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But what I soon became struck by, was the sheer volume of both observation and investigation he had done in many different sports.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And I felt persuaded that what he had to say would be of real interest.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I think Matthews' findings will be beneficial, not so much in helping sports people to work on their weaker side.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But more that they can help them identify the most suitable strategies to use in a given game, although most trainers know how important handedness is.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: At present, they are rather reluctant to make use of the insights scientists like Matthews can give, which I think is rather shortsighted, because focusing on individual flexibility is only part of the story.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Anyway, back to the article.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Matthews found a German study, which looked at what he called 'mixed-handedness'.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. That is the capacity to use both left and right hands equally.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It looked at mixed-handedness in 40 musicians on a variety of instruments.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Researchers examined a number of variables, for example, type of instrument played, regularity of practice undertaken, and length of time playing instrument.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And found the following: keyboard players had high levels of mixed-handedness, whereas string players like cellists and violinists strongly favored one hand.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Also, those who started younger were more mixed-handed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Matthews also reports studies of handedness in apes.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Apes get a large proportion of their food by fishing ants from ant hills.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The studies show that apes like humans show handedness, though for them right and left-handedness is about equal, whereas about 85% of humans are right-handed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Studies showed that apes consistently using the same hand fished out 30% more ants than those varying between the two.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Matthews started researching several different sports, and found different types of handedness in each.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Uh. By the way, he uses handedness to refer to the dominant side for feet and eyes as well as hands.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Anyway, his team measured the hand, feet and eyes of 2,611 players,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: and found that there were really three main types of laterality: mixed - you work equally well on both sides - both hand and eye;
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: single - you tend to favor one side but both hand and eye favor the same side; and cross-laterality - a player's hands and eyes favor only one side but they are opposite sides.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's start with hockey.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Matthews found that it was best to be mixed-handed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is because a hockey stick must be deployed in two directions.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It would be a drawback to have hand or eye favoring one side.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: An interesting finding is that mixed-handed hockey players were significantly more confident than their single-handed counterparts.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Things are slightly different in racket sports like tennis.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Here, the important thing is to have the dominant hand and eye on the one side.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This means that there is a bigger area of vision on the side where most of the action occurs.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: If a player is cross lateral, the racket is invisible from the dominant eye for much of the swing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It means that they can only make corrections much later, and often the damage has been done by then.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And moving to a rather different type of sport, which involves large but precise movements, gymnastics.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It's been found that cross hand-eye favoring is best.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The predominant reason for this is because it aids balance, which is of course absolutely central to performance in this sport.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: This is where people promise to donate money to the charity if you achieve your goal, in this case to walk a certain number of miles.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Basically we are organizing a 10 day holiday, from the 6th to the 16th of November, with eight days actual walking, trekking in the Semira mountains.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's have a look at some of the details.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We require you to raise sponsorship money of at least $3,200 paying $250 of it upfront as a deposit.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And the rest in stages throughout the year.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Out of this about 35% will go on your expenses, and that leaves 65% guaranteed to go to the charity.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Which brings me to the most important part.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This trek is being specifically organized to help education in the Semira region.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Last year, we helped train teachers for the disabled.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And this year we're focusing on the pupils.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Each of the walkers' sponsorship money will go to help an individual special needs pupil in one of the mountain schools.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In the second part of the talk, I'll be giving you a lot more details.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But back to the basic information.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Age limits.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is the second time we've run this kind of holiday, and on the first we even had an 80 year old, but we found it was wise to establish limits this time.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You have to be at least 18, and the top limit is now 70.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Though you need to obtain a health certificate from your doctor if you are over 60 years old.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, the Semira Mountains are among the highest in the world, but you mustn't be too daunted.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We will mainly be trekking in the foothills only, although there will be spectacular views even in the foothills.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: However, you will need to be extremely fit, if you aren't now, and you're interested in coming with us.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You have plenty of time to get into shape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll be sleeping in tents, so you must have quite a bit of equipment with you, but you will be helped by local assistants.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Your bedding and so forth will be carried by them.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We ask that you only walk with a small rucksack with needs for the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I don't think I've really said enough about the marvelous area you'll be walking in.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Let's have a look at some of the sights you'll be seeing.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Apart from these spectacular snow covered peaks and valleys, there are marvelous historic villages.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The area has been famous for centuries for making beautiful carpets, although recently there has been a trend to move into weaving blankets and wood carving.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The people are extremely friendly and welcoming.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We deliberately keep the parties small in size to minimize disruption to people and landscape.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: I hope that there are still some people interested.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: I will be distributing leaflets at the end where you can find out more information, but just for the moment, I'll outline the itinerary,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: the main high points of the holiday.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Obviously you'll start by flying out to Kishba, the capital city on day one.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: After a couple of days to acclimatize yourself.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: You'll start the trek on day 3, walking through the enormous Katiba forest, which will take the whole of the day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Day 4 takes us higher up, going through the foothills, past a number of villages.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And visiting a school for the disabled in Sohan.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Then you have a rest day, that's day 5, before going to the spectacular Kumi temple, with twelfth-century carvings.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Set in a small forest by a lake, and that's day 6, the highlight for many.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: We stay near there for day 7, because then comes the hardest day, walking through very mountainous country, but culminating in a swim in the Parteh Falls.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: This is the highest waterfall in the region.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Day 9 is much easier with part of the day spent in a village where they make some of the gorgeous red blankets, then back down to Kishba, and the journey home.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So you can see it's a pretty packed timetable.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You will hear part of a seminar on ocean research given by a climate scientist.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 21 to 25.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Thanks to all of you for coming along today to hear about how the Robotic Float project is helping with ocean research.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Well, first of all, we'll look at what a robotic float does and its use.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: So let's start with the device itself.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: It looks a bit like a cigar, and it's about one and a half meters long.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: More importantly, it's full of equipment that's designed to collect data.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: So it can help us in building up a profile of different factors which work together within the world's oceans.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Sounds like a big project, isn't it too big for one country to undertake?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: That's quite true, but this project is a really good example of international cooperation.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Over the last five years, scientists from 13 countries have been taking part in the project, and launching floats in their area of ocean control.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: And next year, this number will rise to 14 when Indonesia joins the project.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That's impressive.
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: But let's move on to how floats work.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: The operational cycle goes like this, each of the floats is dropped in the ocean from a boat at a set point and activated from a satellite.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Then the float immediately sinks about 2,000 meters.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That's two whole kilometers down in the water.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: It stays at this depth for about 10 days, and is carried around by the currents which operate in the ocean at this level.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: During this time, it's possible for it to cover quite large distances, but the average is 50 km.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: So, what is it actually recording?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Well, at this stage nothing.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: But as it rises to the surface, it collects all sorts of data.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Most importantly variations in salinity, that's salt levels, and the changes in temperature, a bit like underwater weather balloons.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Then, when it gets back to the surface, all the data it's collected is beamed up to the satellite.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: After about 5 hours on the surface, the float automatically sinks, beginning the whole process again.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: What happens to the data?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Well, the information is transferred direct to onshore meteorological stations, like our one in Hobart, and within four hours the findings can be on computers.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: And they can be mapped and analyzed.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the seminar, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You say you're building models of the world's ocean systems, but how're they going to be used, and more importantly when?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Uh. Some of the data has already helped in completing projects.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: For example, our understanding of the underlying causes of El Nino events is being confirmed by float data.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Another way we are using float data is to help us to understand the mechanics of climate change.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Like global warming and ozone depletion.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That's part of an ongoing variability study, but the results are still a long way off.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: However, this is not the case with our ocean weather forecasting.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Because we know from the floats what the prevailing weather conditions will be in certain parts of the ocean, we can advise the navy on search and rescue missions.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That's happening right now.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: And many yachtsmen owe their lives to the success of this project.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: In addition, the float data can help us to look at the biological implications of ocean processes.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: Would that help with preserving fish stocks?
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Yes, and advising governments on fisheries legislation.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: We're well on the way to completing a project on this.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: We hope it will help to bring about more sustainable fishing practices.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: We'll be seeing the results of that quite soon.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: It sounds like the data from floats has lots of applications.
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Yes, it does.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: It's also a powerful agricultural tool.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: If we were aware of what the weather would be like, say next year, we could make sure that the farmers planted appropriate grain varieties to produce the best yield from the available rainfall.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That sounds a bit like science fiction.
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: Especially when now we can't even tell them when a drought will break.
script.speaker: STUDENT

script.text: I agree that this concept is still a long way in the future, but it will come eventually.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: And the float data will have made a contribution.
script.speaker: SIMON

script.text: That is the end of Section 3.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear part of a lecture about hotels and the tourist industry.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Good morning everyone.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Today's lecture forms part of the hospitality and tourism module.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Last week I looked at the economy end of the hotel business, this week I'm going to discuss the luxury end of the market.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Let's consider the following scenario.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: You wake up in the middle of the night.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: In a strange hotel, miles away from home, disoriented most probably from jet lag, when even the most expensive surroundings can seem empty and dispiriting.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: You have paid a great deal of money to stay in this first class hotel with its contemporary technology, but according to recent research carried out by an international travel and public relations company.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: All is not well.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: The research suggests that even the most opulent, luxurious hotels seem to have underestimated the most basic needs of their customers.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Be they traveling for work or pleasure, the need to feel at home in surroundings which are both familiar and inviting.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Do these findings, however, apply only to hotels situated in particular areas?
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Is it possible that the external environment can affect a guest's well-being?
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: The company's research covered a whole range of different hotel types, both independent hotels and those which are part of large chains.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: They investigated chic, so called boutique hotels in the heart of downtown business districts, stately mansions located in the depths of beautiful countryside.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And plush hotels built at the edge of tropical beaches surrounded by palm trees and idyllic blue ocean.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And the research concluded that what was outside the hotel building simply didn't matter.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: This is a fascinating revelation, and those of you hoping to move into careers in the travel and leisure industry would be well advised to look at the findings in more detail.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: But back to the main point of this lecture, the need to feel at home.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: What can the hotel industry do about it?
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And is the very idea so subjective that it's impossible to do anything about it on a global basis?
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: However, nothing stands still in this world.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: One company has come up with a slogan, 'Take Your Home With You', and aims to provide clients with luxury serviced apartments.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Those in the business travel industry maintain that these serviced apartments dispense with all the unwanted and expensive hotel services that business travelers don't want.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: While maximizing the facilities they do want.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: For example, not only sleeping and living accommodation, but also a sleek modern kitchen.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: That allows guests to cook and entertain if they wish at no additional cost.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: The attractions of such facilities are obvious, and it'll be interesting to see whether the company manages to establish a trend all over the world and make a lasting impact on the luxury accommodation market.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Now finally, I want to consider the psychology underpinning the traditional holiday hotel industry.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: As a hotelier, how do you go about attracting people to give up the security of their own home, and entrust themselves to staying in a completely strange place?
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And sleeping in an unfamiliar bed.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Firstly, hotels exploit people's need to escape the predictability of their everyday lives.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: For a few days, people can pretend they are free of responsibilities.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And can indulge themselves.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Secondly, there is something very powerful in our need to be pampered and looked after.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: It's almost as if we return to being a baby when everything was done for us, and we felt safe.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: And secure, and not far removed from this is the pleasure in being spoiled and given little treats, like the minuscule bottles of shampoo and tiny bars of soap.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: The chocolate on your pillow at night, and we actually forget that we are paying for it all.
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: Next week, I'm gonna look at eco-hotels, a fairly new phenomenon, but increasingly popular...
script.speaker: LECTURER

script.text: That is the end of section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 2, you will hear a guide giving a tour of a park.

script.text: Welcome to all of you.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Can everybody see and hear me?
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Good.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: I'm Sally, your guide for this tour of the Bicentennial Park.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: I hope that you're all wearing your most comfortable shoes, and that you can keep up the pace.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: So, let's get underway on our tour around this wonderful park.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: I'll start today with some general background information.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There used to be a lot of factories in this area until the 1960s.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Creating the park required the demolition of lots of derelict buildings on the site.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: So most of the exciting park space all around you was originally warehouses and storehouses.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The idea of building a public park here was first discussed when a property developer proposed a high-rise housing development, but the local community wasn't happy.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: If the land was to be cleaned up, they wanted to use the site for recreation.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Residents wanted open space for outdoor activities, rather than housing or even an indoor sports complex.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Now to the Bicentennial Park itself, it has two areas, a nature reserve, and a formal park with manmade features and gardens.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The tall blue-and-white building in front of us is called The Tower, and is the center point for the formal gardens.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: It stands 12 meters high.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: So follow me up the stairs to where we can take advantage of the fantastic views.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Before you hear the rest of the tour, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Well, here we are at the top of The Tower, and we're gonna look at the view from each direction.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Out to the east, the large buildings about a kilometer away are on the Olympic site.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There's an indoor arena for gymnastics, a stadium for track and field, and a swimming pool for races and synchronized swimming, and also diving.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: If you look carefully down there, you can see the train lines.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The Olympic site has its own station to encourage the use of public transport.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There is also a car park, but it only holds a limited number of cars.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The formal park has some specially created water features.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: If you look out here to the south, you can see a circular ornamental pond, and around to the west, you can relax and sit on a bench to smell the flowers in the rose garden.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And finally up to the north, if you look in front of you now.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: There's a lake with a small island in the center.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: You can hire rowing boats at the boat shed, which you can't see from here, but if you look through the trees, you can see the cafe, which has lovely views across the water.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: OK, let's climb down now.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: We will go now and have a look at the nature reserve section of the park, which has opened up natural wetland to the public.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: The mangroves have been made more accessible to visitors by the boardwalk built during the park's upgrade.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: You'd think that people would come here to look at the unusual plant life of the area, but in fact it's more often used for cycling, and is very popular with the local clubs.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: This is the far end of the park, and over there you can see the Frog Pond, a natural feature here long before the park was designed.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Just next to it, we have our outdoor classroom.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: A favorite spot for school parties, the area is now most often used by primary schools for biology lessons.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: And finally, let's pass by the waterbird refuge.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: This area is in a sheltered part of the estuary.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That's why the park's viewing shelter is a favorite spot for bird watchers who can use it to spy through binoculars.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: You can watch a variety of waterbirds, but most visitors expect to see black swans when they come to the shelter.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: You might spot one yourself right now.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: Well, here we are back at our starting point, the Visitor Center.
script.speaker: SALLY

script.text: That is the end of section 2.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Section 4, you will hear part of a lecture about a chemical substance called monosodium glutamate.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 31 to 40.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to talk about monosodium glutamate, or MSG as it's more commonly known.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Now, MSG as you probably know is a flavor enhancer,
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: which is used particularly in Chinese and Japanese cooking.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Today, I am going to explore why it is so popular in these cuisines.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: And more importantly, how does it enhance the flavor of food?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: The main reason why MSG is more commonly used in Japanese meals is tradition.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For many thousands of years, the Japanese have incorporated a type of seaweed.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Known as kombu in their cooking, as they discovered it had the ability to make food taste better.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But it wasn't until 1908 that the ingredient in kombu which was responsible for the improvement in flavor, was actually discovered to be glutamate by scientists working there.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: From 1908 until 1956 glutamate was produced commercially in Japan by a very slow and expensive means of extraction.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It was in 1956 that the speed of the process was improved, and industrial production increased dramatically, and still continues to increase to this day.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In fact, hundreds of thousands of tonnes of MSG are produced all over the world today.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what exactly is MSG?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well monosodium glutamate contains 78.2% glutamate, 12.2% sodium and 9.6% water.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Glutamate is an amino acid that can be found naturally in all protein containing foods.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So this includes food such as meat and cheese.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It is widely known that Chinese and Japanese food contains MSG.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: But many people don't seem to be aware that it is also used in foods in other parts of the world.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: For example, it is found in commercially made Italian pizzas.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: In American fast food, and in Britain, MSG is used in things like potato crisps.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So, how exactly does MSG work?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, in the western world, we commonly talk of four tastes, and I'm sure you're all familiar with the concepts of sweet, sour, bitter, and salt.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Well, in 1908, Kikunae Ikeda identified a fifth taste, and it is thought that MSG intensifies this naturally occurring 'taste' in some food.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: It does make perfect evolutionary sense that we should have the ability to detect or taste glutamate, because it is the amino acid which is most common in natural foods.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: John Prescott, an associate professor at the University of Chicago, suggests that this fifth taste serves a purpose just as the other tastes do.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: He suggests that it signals to us the presence of protein in food, in the same way that sweetness indicates that a food contains energy giving carbohydrates.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: Bitterness, he says, alerts us to toxins in the food, while sourness warns us of spoilage, and saltiness signals the presence of minerals.
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: So what else do we know about this fifth taste?
script.speaker: SPEAKER

script.text: That is the end of Section 4.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER

script.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
script.speaker: ANNOUNCER
